title: Historiography, 1920–2000
description: Teaching knowledge graph developed around Lynn Hunt’s Writing History in the Global Era, expanded with earlier traditions, enduring fields, and intellectual connections.

scope.geographic_emphasis: Primarily Western academic historiography, with selected independent and critical traditions.
notes: Dates describe approximate emergence or expansion, not termination.
Edges are selective teaching interpretations, not an exhaustive genealogy.
Connections may express influence, overlap, conceptual resources, or critique; read each relationship label.
A node’s source is a supporting reference and does not necessarily document every associated edge.
Nodes include traditions, fields, genres, methods, approaches, and individual thinkers.
New and revised relationships may include source_ids and evidence_note. A comparative teaching link does not assert influence merely because it has a source and target.
Sources published after 2000 can retrospectively support developments within the current 1920–2000 graph. The planned extension to 2026 is not yet represented as completed content.
Editorial revision 1.3 incorporates selected and rewritten Fable 5.1 proposals into the existing revision 1.2; the supplied feedback used an older base and its edge IDs were remapped.

Schema 1.2 adds optional edge directed and relationship_kind fields. Explicit comparisons have directed:false; missing direction metadata on inherited edges means not yet classified, not verified influence. Critique arrows point from critic to the position criticized.

Optional source citation and verification fields distinguish bibliographic identity or supporting-page checks from an unperformed passage-level audit. Missing verification metadata means unrecorded, never implicitly verified. Checked metadata does not certify all node or edge interpretations.

The map remains selective: a named work, school, or field does not imply that every associated thinker agrees. Paired nodes such as Progressive/consensus history are comparisons, not single paradigms.

Revision 1.4 distinguishes women as producers of historical knowledge from women’s history as a field. Women historians appear across economic, political, military, intellectual, and other inquiries; belonging to the profession does not imply a shared feminist method or a linear succession of feminist waves.

Schema 1.3 adds shared people records, explicit group/person entry kinds, and qualified representative_people rosters. Roster inclusion is not a new influence edge or a claim of formal school membership. Most rosters normalize existing curated prose; their inherited references are not new individual affiliation verification.

Directional neighborhood views place incoming directed relationships on the left and outgoing ones on the right. Comparisons and unclassified links sit separately. Thompson’s cultural contribution and feminist historians’ productive inheritance coexist with their criticisms; no uniform succession from class to culture is implied.

extension.note: Selected post-2000 interventions only. The 2026 cutoff is not a publication date or a claim of field completeness.

layers.label: Multiple intellectual traditions: earlier roots through c. 1920

nodes.label: Ludwig Wittgenstein
nodes.description: Language and meaning are situated in shared practices and forms of life. Geertz draws on this account of public meaning in interpreting culture. The Investigations examines varied uses of language, overlapping family resemblances and the practice of following rules. Skinner later explicitly credits its attention to use in developing his historical questions.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Philosophical Investigations (1953). This is the later Wittgenstein; it is not a claim that all interpretive anthropology derives from him.
nodes.scope_note: The later philosophy revises earlier assumptions without forming a general historical theory. The meaning/use formulation in §43 is explicitly qualified; agreement in forms of life is not a claim that majority opinion creates truth. The preface acknowledges Ramsey’s conversations and Sraffa’s criticism. Philosophical similarity to Ryle does not establish a single transmission direction.

nodes.label: Gilbert Ryle
nodes.description: Distinguishes a bodily movement from what someone is doing in a socially meaningful situation. Geertz explicitly borrows the term thick description. The Concept of Mind (1949) challenges category mistakes in accounts of mental life and distinguishes knowing how from prior theoretical instructions. The Thinking of Thoughts (1968) develops action descriptions and exploratory thinking; Geertz adapts a distinction from this philosophical project.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The twitch and the wink: similar movements can be different actions. Ryle is the immediate source of the term, alongside Geertz’s other influences.
nodes.scope_note: Rejecting a hidden parallel mechanism does not deny mental processes or reduce skilled action to automatic movements. Competence, purpose and circumstances distinguish what someone does. Ryle’s account of Cartesianism is a critical reconstruction; the atlas does not treat it as an independently established history of Descartes.

nodes.label: Clifford Geertz
nodes.description: Culture consists of publicly interpretable meanings. Thick description reconstructs the contexts that make actions intelligible; it is more than adding descriptive detail. “Deep Play” (1972) reads cockfighting through status and symbolic action; Negara (1980) examines ritual and political authority in nineteenth-century Bali. These are his interpretations, with their empirical reach open to debate.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Interpretation of Cultures (1973). Weber, Wittgenstein, and Ryle are explicit interlocutors; the approach becomes influential in cultural history.
nodes.scope_note: Thick description interprets public, situated meanings and constrains interpretations through evidence. Hunt’s adaptation is a specific historical reception; Asad’s religion-category criticism targets a particular argument. These readings do not summarize every Indonesian or Moroccan study or establish a uniform Geertzian cultural history.

nodes.label: Structural linguistics
nodes.date_label: Saussure’s Course, posthumous, 1916 · later linguistic programmes · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Relational signs, language states and historical change, phonological analysis, and social uses of language form distinct inquiries. Later semiology, anthropology, psychoanalysis and historical debates adapt and criticize particular concepts.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Saussure’s Course in General Linguistics (1916, posthumous); Roman Jakobson is an important intermediary for Lévi-Strauss.

representative_people.context: Relational value, social convention and distinct analyses of language states and change. The posthumous Course is an editorial reconstruction of teaching, not a finished authorial manuscript.
representative_people.works: Cours de linguistique générale (1916; consulted 1971 edition), Parts I–II

representative_people.context: A named resource in Lévi-Strauss’s phonological analogy; the chapter warns against literal transfer to kinship. His analysis of selection and combination also differentiates metaphoric and metonymic operations.
representative_people.works: “Principien der historischen Phonologie” (1931); “Observations sur le classement phonologique des consonnes” (1938); Kindersprache, Aphasie und allgemeine Lautgesetze (1941), cited in Structural Anthropology; “Two Aspects of Language and Two Types of Aphasic Disturbances” (selected reprint, pp. 95–114)

representative_people.context: Coeditor who helped reconstruct the Course from teaching materials and acknowledged editorial responsibility.
representative_people.works: Editorial preparation and first-edition preface of Cours de linguistique générale (1916)

representative_people.context: Coeditor credited in the preface with collating third-course notebooks; editorial arrangement mediates the published argument.
representative_people.works: Editorial preparation and first-edition preface of Cours de linguistique générale (1916)

representative_people.context: Student and collaborator whose notebooks and collation of the first two courses contributed to the posthumous book.
representative_people.works: Editorial preparation and first-edition preface of Cours de linguistique générale (1916)

representative_people.context: A distinct social and historical approach: changes in word meaning are related to group practices and circulation between vocabularies. This selection does not equate his programme with autonomous structural analysis.
representative_people.works: “Comment les mots changent de sens” (1906)

representative_people.context: Phonological relations provide a named resource in Lévi-Strauss’s methodological analogy, whose limits are explicit. Selection is supported by that reception, not a full review of Trubetzkoy’s corpus.
representative_people.works: “La phonologie actuelle” (1933), cited and discussed in Structural Anthropology

representative_people.context: Reworks langue/parole through schema, norm and usage; Barthes explicitly discusses this reformulation. His formal programme is distinct from Meillet’s social explanation.
representative_people.works: “Langue et parole,” Cahiers Ferdinand de Saussure 2 (issue dated 1942; bibliography lists 1943), 29–44

representative_people.context: A retrospective historical recipient who discusses relational signs, the linguistic turn and contested reference. Her later address is bibliography about the mapped period, not an extension of coverage.
representative_people.works: “The Task of the Historian” (2009, retrospective)

nodes.scope_note: A selective teaching umbrella, not one uniform school or a claim that all linguistics descends from Saussure. The Course is posthumously reconstructed; Meillet’s social explanation, phonological programmes and Hjelmslev’s formal distinctions differ. Later reception is separately evidenced. Benveniste and broader linguistic traditions remain review gaps.

strands.title: Teaching, notebooks and editorial reconstruction
strands.focus: The 1916 book joins material from three courses; its editors describe collation and reconstruction. Published order should not be confused with a single delivered course.

strands.title: Signs, convention and relational value
strands.focus: A sign joins signifier and signified; its value also depends on relations to other signs. Arbitrariness does not mean unrestricted individual choice.
strands.works: Course, Part I chapter I and Part II chapter IV

strands.title: Language states and historical change
strands.focus: Synchrony and diachrony distinguish analytical questions. Social inheritance and change remain part of the Course’s account; structural inquiry is not simply absence of history.

strands.title: Social groups and changing meanings
strands.focus: Meillet asks how vocabularies change within and between groups, explicitly drawing on Durkheim. This is a distinct causal inquiry rather than a synonym for relational value.

strands.title: Phonological relations and methodological transfer
strands.focus: Trubetzkoy and Jakobson are named resources in Lévi-Strauss’s analogy; transferring phonological models to kinship requires qualification.
strands.works: “La phonologie actuelle” (1933); Jakobson’s 1931/1938 works as cited in Structural Anthropology

strands.title: Schema, norm and usage
strands.focus: Hjelmslev’s reformulation distinguishes pure form from norms, habits and acts; the teaching account here follows Barthes’s explicit exposition.
strands.works: “Langue et parole” (1942/1943); Elements of Semiology, I.1.5

strands.title: Selection, combination and discourse
strands.focus: Jakobson differentiates similarity and contiguity, then metaphor and metonymy. These analytical distinctions are not a universal key to every historical text.
strands.works: “Two Aspects of Language,” sections II and V

strands.title: Adaptation, criticism and historical reception
strands.focus: Barthes proposes a revised semiology; Derrida questions speech/writing assumptions; Spiegel retrospectively discusses historical debates. These are distinct interventions.
strands.works: Elements of Semiology (1964); De la grammatologie (1967); “The Task of the Historian” (2009, retrospective)

nodes.label: Claude Lévi-Strauss
nodes.description: Analyzes kinship and myth through underlying relations, oppositions, and transformations. Structural explanation differs from Geertz’s interpretation of situated public meanings. The Savage Mind (1962; English 1966) uses bricolage to examine recombination of available signs and materials, while rejecting an evolutionary ranking of mythical and scientific thought.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Elementary Structures of Kinship (1949); Structural Anthropology (1958). Engagements with history vary; structuralism is not simply any interest in social structures.
nodes.scope_note: Relational models are distinct from simply studying social structure. The historical and linguistic chapters connect evidence and formal explanation without identifying anthropology with history. English 1963 passages are from the revised 1958 collection. Later adaptations by Hall and Hebdige, and Derrida’s criticism, are separately evidenced; the Braudel and Lacan exchanges still need stronger passage checks.

nodes.label: Roland Barthes
nodes.date_label: Semiology → textual plurality · Mythologies 1957 · author essay 1967
nodes.description: Analyzes myth as the naturalization of historically produced meanings and studies how historical narratives signify reality. His challenge to authorial closure shifts attention to textual plurality and the reader. Historians and cultural theorists adapt these arguments while disputing their scope.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Mythologies (1957); “The Death of the Author” (1967); S/Z (1970).
nodes.scope_note: Individual thinker with a changing trajectory, not one fixed structuralist method. Mythologies (1957), Elements of Semiology (1964), the history/authorship essays (1967), The Reality Effect (1968) and S/Z (1970) are distinct works. Saussure, Jakobson, Kristeva, Nietzsche, Marx and Vernant are named resources with different scopes. Bann questions the implied decline of historians’ concern with reality; Hebdige makes a particular style-analysis adaptation. Rhetorical effects do not alone establish that events are imaginary, and the theoretical reader is not a biography of actual readers. S/Z and later photographic inquiry await bounded primary reading; the clinical analogies and sweeping historical generalizations remain attributed.

nodes.label: Jacques Lacan
nodes.date_label: Freud reread through language · Rome report 1953 · Écrits 1966
nodes.description: Rereads Freud through identification, language and symbolic relations. The mirror-stage argument explains ego unity through an external image; later work recasts dream condensation and displacement through metaphor and metonymy. His divided subject becomes a resource and a problem for historical accounts of gender.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Freud is a fundamental antecedent; Saussure, Jakobson, and Lévi-Strauss inform Lacan’s approach. Écrits (1966).
nodes.scope_note: Individual thinker, not a uniform school. The 1949 mirror-stage paper, 1953 report first published in 1956, 1957 linguistic essay and 1966 Écrits collection are distinct witnesses. Saussure’s diagram is transformed, Jakobson explicitly credited, and Lévi-Strauss named as a resource. Althusser appropriates his reading of Freud; Scott finds constructed subjectivity instructive but questions universal sexual antagonism and limited historical variability. These are situated theoretical arguments, not independently established clinical or developmental facts. Later seminars and revisions remain outside this bounded primary reading.

nodes.label: Louis Althusser
nodes.description: Reinterprets Marx through problematics, an epistemological break and overdetermined contradictions. Political and ideological circumstances have explanatory force; material institutions and practices constitute subjects while remaining sites of class struggle. Collective reading, later qualifications and disputes over evidence and agency shape the program.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: For Marx and Reading Capital (1965). E. P. Thompson’s The Poverty of Theory (1978) directly attacks his approach.
nodes.scope_note: Individual thinker whose positions change; neither all Marxism nor a timeless structuralist system. For Marx and the five-author Reading Capital appeared in 1965; the consulted revised abridgment omits three contributors and acknowledges a unilateral theoreticism. Bachelard, Martin, Canguilhem, Cavaillès, Foucault, Lacan and Gramsci supply named resources with different evidential scopes. Thompson’s criticism and Hall’s productive disagreement are distinct interventions. Interpellation is a theoretical illustration, not a chronological experiment; apparatuses also involve resistance and struggle beyond institutions. Later political revisions and other collaborators’ original chapters remain bounded research limits.

nodes.label: Friedrich Nietzsche
nodes.description: Questions the historical formation and value of moral judgments. Genealogy distinguishes the emergence of a practice from its changing uses; perspectival knowledge requires active interpretation. His earlier essay examines the benefits and dangers of monumental, antiquarian and critical uses of the past.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: On the Genealogy of Morality (1887); Foucault’s “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History” (1971).
nodes.scope_note: Individual philosophical precursor, not simply an anticipation of Foucault. The 1874 history essay and 1887 Genealogy pose distinct questions. Rée and Schopenhauer are explicit interlocutors; Burckhardt supplies a named cultural-historical example. Documentary inquiry and disciplined plurality complicate a blanket relativist reading. Foucault and Barthes appropriate different aspects. Nietzsche’s hierarchical, gendered, religious and physiological generalizations remain situated arguments, not verified historical facts. Original German, cited interlocutors and the witness behind Barthes’s aphorism remain bounded limits.

nodes.label: Historical epistemology
nodes.description: Here the label denotes the French tradition associated with Bachelard and Canguilhem: histories of scientific concepts, norms, and discontinuities. It informs Foucault through a route distinct from structural linguistics. It is not an umbrella for every historical or sociological account of scientific knowledge. Bachelard’s own preliminary discourse distinguishes normative epistemology from a chronological history and calls its period labels approximate. Canguilhem’s norm/average discussion draws on Halbwachs and human geography; his later preface distinguishes newly encountered works from resources actually used in1943.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: French history and philosophy of science; this connection prevents treating Foucault as merely a descendant of structural linguistics. Bachelard, La formation de l’esprit scientifique (1938); Canguilhem, the normal/pathological essay (1943; expanded 1966) and La formation du concept de réflexe (1955).

representative_people.context: Examines obstacles to scientific reasoning and the correction of earlier knowledge.
representative_people.works: La formation de l’esprit scientifique (1938; English translation 2002)

representative_people.context: Studies medical norms and the history of concepts, allowing a wider historical narrative than Bachelard.
representative_people.works: Essai sur quelques problèmes concernant le normal et le pathologique (1943; expanded 1966); La formation du concept de réflexe (1955)

representative_people.context: Named with Bachelard, Canguilhem and Foucault among Althusser’s resources for reading scientific works; the particular original Cavaillès text is not identified by this acknowledgment.
representative_people.works: Althusser, Reading Capital, Part I, note 1 (1965; revised edition consulted)

representative_people.context: Reworks epistemological break and reading of scientific concepts in his disputed interpretation of Marx; explicitly credits Bachelard and Canguilhem among other resources.
representative_people.works: For Marx, introduction (1965); Reading Capital, Part I and notes 1, 20–21

representative_people.context: Reworks histories of concepts and knowledge, explicitly situating Canguilhem in a selective intellectual history. His map of traditions is a retrospective argument, not a fixed classification.
representative_people.works: The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969), selected chapters; “La vie: l’expérience et la science” (1985), opening excerpt

representative_people.context: Supplies a geographical comparison encountered after Canguilhem drafted his essay.
representative_people.works: Les fondements biologiques de la géographie humaine (1943)

representative_people.context: His statistical critique is an explicit resource in Canguilhem’s discussion.
representative_people.works: La théorie de l’homme moyen (1912)

nodes.scope_note: The French Bachelard–Canguilhem route differs from Kuhn, sociology of knowledge, and a generic philosophy of history.

strands.title: Obstacles and the correction of knowledge
strands.focus: Bachelard’s normative history evaluates earlier thought through scientific rationality.

strands.title: Medical norms and histories of concepts
strands.focus: Canguilhem’s conceptual histories preserve distinctions within the French tradition.
strands.works: The Normal and the Pathological (1943/1966); concept of reflex (1955)

strands.title: Scientific reading and the interpretation of Marx
strands.focus: Althusser explicitly credits several epistemological resources; acknowledgments document reception without establishing that these thinkers shared his entire Marx interpretation.
strands.works: Reading Capital, Part I, notes 1 and 20–21; For Marx introduction

strands.title: Conceptual histories and Foucault’s retrospective map
strands.focus: Foucault situates Canguilhem alongside Bachelard, Cavaillès and Koyré, comparing questions of rationality across distinct traditions without claiming a single doctrine.
strands.works: “La vie: l’expérience et la science” (1985), opening excerpt

strands.title: Norms, averages and social conditions
strands.focus: Canguilhem uses statistical and geographical inquiry when interpreting physiological norms.
strands.works: Le normal et le pathologique, Norme et moyenne

nodes.label: Michel Foucault
nodes.date_label: The Order of Things 1966 · Discipline and Punish 1975 · Sexuality I 1976
nodes.description: Studies how objects of knowledge and subjects take shape through historically specific practices. Archaeology examines discursive formations; genealogy traces contingent descent and emergence. Power works through actions upon possible actions, with institutions, resistance and changing forms of subjectivity entering the analysis.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Order of Things (1966); Discipline and Punish (1975); History of Sexuality I (1976). His association with structuralism is contested.
nodes.scope_note: Individual thinker with changing projects, not a uniform structuralist school. History of Madness (1961), archaeological inquiry, genealogy and the 1982 account of subjects are distinct contexts. Canguilhem and Nietzsche supply named resources. Derrida’s challenge and Foucault’s reply concern reason, madness, Descartes and discursive practice; neither settles their whole relationship. Historians including Scott, Chartier, Goldstein, Said and Stoler adapt and criticize different aspects, with separately scoped evidence. Comparative historical generalizations remain attributed. Later ethics and self-practice require further bounded primary reading.

nodes.label: Jacques Derrida
nodes.description: Works through conceptual hierarchies and the conditions of signification, writing and historical transmission. Critical engagements with Saussure, Husserl, Heidegger and Foucault distinguish deconstruction from a single structuralist method. His archive inquiry connects institutions, access, inscription and preservation with psychoanalytic questions.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “Structure, Sign, and Play” (1966); Of Grammatology (1967). Husserl and Heidegger are further important interlocutors beyond the links selected here.
nodes.scope_note: Individual thinker whose arguments change across works. Of Grammatology (French 1967; first American 1976; corrected English 1997) is distinct from the 1963 Cogito lecture, 1983 Japanese letter and 1994 archive lecture. Peirce, Freud and historian Sonia Combe are explicit resources in the selected passages. Scott and Spivak offer particular productive uses; Foucault supplies a specific objection. Deconstruction is not a license for arbitrary readings or a claim that institutions reduce to books. The original French witnesses, full archive argument and Austin/Searle exchange remain outside this bounded primary reading.

nodes.label: Critical historical scholarship
nodes.date_label: Earlier philological roots · Ranke’s preface 1824 · later archival scholarship · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Source criticism and historical particularity develop through many traditions: philology, antiquarian research, ecclesiastical scholarship, archives, and university seminars. Ranke is a major exemplar, not their sole origin. Its approaches distinguish documentary authenticity, language and meaning, historical questions, and interpretation of conditions; these operations can support political, social and cultural subjects.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Leopold von Ranke (1795–1886); archival practice spreads far beyond political and diplomatic subjects. This tradition is not simply synonymous with positivism.

representative_people.context: Combines close documentary work with relations among events, peoples and epochs. Historical individuality and religious commitments coexist; his selected European scope and civilizational judgments are contestable, and he is not the sole origin of criticism.
representative_people.works: History of the Popes (1834–1836; Austin translation 1840); 1824 historical preface; lectures on epochs (1854); selected World History reflections

representative_people.context: Salmon explicitly recalls his teaching on judging an author by the purpose of a work. Placement in this broad critical-scholarship entry does not establish Ranke transmission.
representative_people.works: Classroom instruction recalled in Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia vi

representative_people.context: Her critical pedagogy and expanded range of evidence supply a comparison with document-based scholarship; a single Ranke-derived genealogy is not claimed.
representative_people.works: “The Teaching of History in Academies and Colleges” (1893); The Newspaper and the Historian (1923), institutionally documented; Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

representative_people.context: Explicitly adopts Ranke’s interest in historical truth while acknowledging that complete reconstruction remains beyond reach and insisting on staying within evidence.
representative_people.works: “In Search of History,” publisher excerpt in Practicing History (consulted 1982 edition)

representative_people.context: Diplomatics tests material and textual characteristics of records. Ecclesiastical scholarship predates university archival history; the current evidence is a scholarly abstract, not a complete Latin treatise.
representative_people.works: De re diplomatica (1681)

representative_people.context: A contributor to debates about genuine and spurious early documents; represents contested authentication practices rather than a simple prehistory of Ranke.
representative_people.works: Propylaeum antiquarium in Acta sanctorum Aprilis II (1675), identified in Head’s references

representative_people.context: Coauthor of a methodological program separating source operations, interpretive meaning and factual assessment. Their contextual reading rules and critical judgments of earlier manuals are explicit, not a claim that documents explain themselves.
representative_people.works: Introduction aux études historiques (1898); Berry English translation (consulted 1904), authors’ preface and Book II chapter VI

representative_people.context: Coauthor of a methodological program separating source operations, interpretive meaning and factual assessment. Their contextual reading rules and critical judgments of earlier manuals are explicit, not a claim that documents explain themselves.
representative_people.works: Introduction aux études historiques (1898); Berry English translation (consulted 1904), authors’ preface and Book II chapter VI

representative_people.context: A German methodological resource acknowledged but criticized by Langlois and Seignobos; their assessment does not substitute for his own argument. Distinct from the physician Hippolyte Bernheim.
representative_people.works: Lehrbuch der historischen Methode (1894 edition discussed by Langlois and Seignobos)

representative_people.context: Langlois and Seignobos credit his attention to changing historical vocabulary and methodological teaching. Their mediated account supplies this selection; no sole origin or direct Ranke transmission is asserted. The same authors criticize his practice and credulity; their praise does not certify his historical conclusions.
representative_people.works: La Monarchie franque; Recherches sur quelques problèmes d’histoire; L’Alleu et le domaine rural, passages identified in Langlois/Seignobos II.6 notes 132–139

representative_people.context: Source search, criticism and interpretation cooperate. Material remains, accounts and monuments are not interchangeable; neither authentic documents nor individual intentions alone yield a complete historical explanation.
representative_people.works: Grundriss der Historik (public edition 1867; consulted Andrews English 1893), §§1–11, 20–24, 28–41

representative_people.context: Appreciates Droysen’s philosophical questions while contesting source categories treated as things outside historical thought. His recognition of preservation’s usefulness prevents a caricature of idealism as indifference to evidence.
representative_people.works: Theory & History of Historiography (consulted 1921 translation), I.1

representative_people.context: Challenges the priority of individual-centered explanation while distinguishing Ranke’s achievement from later disciples; an attributed polemic about method.
representative_people.works: What Is History? (1905), lecture I, selected pp. 16–23

nodes.scope_note: Ranke is an exemplar within older critical practices. Archival scholarship is neither exclusively political nor simply positivist. Mabillon, Droysen and the French methodologists expose different practices and disagreements. Ranke’s theological and exclusionary claims are not atlas assumptions; critical inquiry has non-European histories beyond this selected European genealogy.

strands.title: Document authenticity and archival authority
strands.focus: Material/textual comparison and the authority claimed for sovereign archives provide different grounds of documentary proof. Older practices have their own controversies; no single line of descent is assumed.
strands.works: De re diplomatica (1681); Propylaeum antiquarium (1675), through Head’s scholarly abstract

strands.title: Close sources and historical relations
strands.focus: Ranke’s strict factual ambition coexists with synthesis, political/religious interdependence and ideas. The research program is not merely accumulation of facts.

strands.title: Epochs, progress and theological judgments
strands.focus: Ranke resists a uniform ladder of moral or artistic improvement and values periods in themselves. His theological grounding and civilizational exclusions qualify any universal reading.

strands.title: Criticism, conditions and interpretation
strands.focus: Droysen treats authentication as preparation for interpretation, acknowledges gaps and the historical value of falsification, and limits access to personality while examining wider conditions.
strands.works: Outline of the Principles of History (1893), selected §§20–41

strands.title: Historical language and the meaning of a source
strands.focus: Meaning varies with usage, time, author and surrounding text. Establishing what a source says differs from deciding whether its claims are true; hidden allusions remain conjectural.
strands.works: Introduction to the Study of History, II.6

strands.title: Teaching, manuals and critical disagreement
strands.focus: Methodological instruction and published manuals supply resources through explicit acknowledgment, criticism and adaptation. Bernheim’s and Fustel’s reception differs from Tyler’s instruction recalled by Salmon.
strands.works: Langlois/Seignobos preface; Salmon, Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

strands.title: Critiques of documentary sufficiency
strands.focus: Croce questions abstract source categories; Lamprecht contests explanatory priorities. Their different objections do not establish that authentic documents are useless or that all critical scholars share one doctrine.

nodes.label: Historical materialism
nodes.date_label: Marx’s preface 1859 · Capital I 1867 · later Marxists · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Modes of production, relations of exploitation, class struggle, and historically specific capitalism. Later Marxists disagree over determinism, agency, and culture. Marx’s 1859 developmental propositions coexist with his 1877 rejection of a universal path. Later debates concern political action, imperial accumulation, dialectical and analytical explanation, and reproduction of material life.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Karl Marx (1818–1883), Capital I (1867); developed in critical engagement with political economy, philosophy, and socialist movements.

representative_people.context: Analyzes historically specific production and exploitation. The 1859 preface advances strong forces/relations propositions; the 1877 Russian letter rejects exporting the Western-European expropriation account as a universal path. These claims require comparison, not silent harmonization.
representative_people.works: Capital I (1867); preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859); Russian editorial-board letter (1877)

representative_people.context: A specific historical use of capitalism, wage labor and family dependence to explain sexual identity; not an assertion of formal school membership or a universal cause.
representative_people.works: “Capitalism and Gay Identity” (1983)

representative_people.context: Translation, annotation and selection make Marxist texts available in particular political and pedagogical settings; editorial mediation is a substantive contribution.
representative_people.works: Marx–Engels Selected Correspondence (English translation, 1934); supplementary notes to Capital I (1938); Marx on China (introduction and notes, 1951)

representative_people.context: Uses Capital’s production and rent categories in a contested historical explanation; his reply recognizes varied forms and limits in his own evidence.
representative_people.works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); reply to Sweezy in “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), pp. 157–167

representative_people.context: A contested philosophical rereading of Marx: problematics, overdetermination and the relation of knowledge to its object. His own later foreword qualifies theoreticism.
representative_people.works: For Marx and Reading Capital (1965); revised Reading Capital foreword (1968/1970)

representative_people.context: Contributor to the five-author Reading Capital; the consulted abridged edition retains Althusser and Balibar while omitting Rancière, Macherey and Establet. Coauthorship does not imply identical positions or later agreement.
representative_people.works: Reading Capital (1965), authorship and edition history in the revised foreword (1968/1970)

representative_people.context: Contributor to the five-author Reading Capital; the consulted abridged edition retains Althusser and Balibar while omitting Rancière, Macherey and Establet. Coauthorship does not imply identical positions or later agreement.
representative_people.works: Reading Capital (1965), authorship and edition history in the revised foreword (1968/1970)

representative_people.context: Contributor to the five-author Reading Capital; the consulted abridged edition retains Althusser and Balibar while omitting Rancière, Macherey and Establet. Coauthorship does not imply identical positions or later agreement.
representative_people.works: Reading Capital (1965), authorship and edition history in the revised foreword (1968/1970)

representative_people.context: Contributor to the five-author Reading Capital; the consulted abridged edition retains Althusser and Balibar while omitting Rancière, Macherey and Establet. Coauthorship does not imply identical positions or later agreement.
representative_people.works: Reading Capital (1965), authorship and edition history in the revised foreword (1968/1970)

representative_people.context: Althusser explicitly credits Martin for the concept of the problematic. This is a named conceptual resource in an authorial acknowledgment, not an independently read Martin text or claim of founding a school.
representative_people.works: Acknowledgment in Althusser, For Marx, introduction (1965), section II

representative_people.context: Collaborates with Marx. His Bloch letter rejects an economic-only explanation and gives political struggles and individual wills effects, while retaining economic determination in the last instance.
representative_people.works: Letter to Joseph Bloch (21–22 September 1890); collaboration described in Marx’s 1859 preface

representative_people.context: Presents dialectical method and historically conditioned facts as central, with theory/practice inseparable. His criticism of Engels and strong claims for dialectical truth distinguish this program from generic pluralism.
representative_people.works: What is Orthodox Marxism? (1919), in History and Class Consciousness (1923), opening and sections 1–2

representative_people.context: Treats political violence and exchanges with noncapitalist settings as ongoing aspects of accumulation. Her disagreement with Engels and her collapse thesis remain specific, contestable positions.
representative_people.works: The Accumulation of Capital (1913), chapter 31

representative_people.context: Develops an account of monopoly, finance and imperial conflict, with an explicit political purpose and a censorship history. The 1920 preface’s predictions are his arguments, not a consensus of all Marxists.
representative_people.works: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1916/1917), 1920 French/German preface and book introduction

representative_people.context: Offers an analytical reconstruction, distinguishing what Marx held about productive-force primacy from reasons to defend it; functional explanation is part of the proposed account. The 2000 edition adds reservations.
representative_people.works: Karl Marx’s Theory of History: A Defence (1978; expanded 2000), description and displayed chapter openings

representative_people.context: Reworks Marxian categories for gender and production/reproduction of material life. This selection records the stated feminist project; its specific mechanism awaits a body-passage check.
representative_people.works: Marxism and the Oppression of Women: Toward a Unitary Theory (1983), publisher description

representative_people.context: Marx retrospectively identifies critical reexamination of Hegel’s philosophy of law as a step toward his investigation of material relations. This is a specified critical resource, not adherence to the whole Hegelian system.
representative_people.works: Philosophy of law, discussed in Marx’s 1859 preface

representative_people.context: Investigates class as a historical relationship made through activity and experience; the previously checked preface resists treating workers only as industrial inputs.
representative_people.works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963), preface

representative_people.context: Distinguishes materialist method from conclusions about nineteenth-century Europe and asks how to investigate African histories in their own time and place.
representative_people.works: Marxism and African Liberation (1975 speech)

representative_people.context: Reworks materialist resources in the history of slavery and revolution. His later lectures name Marx, Lenin and Trotsky as readings; retrospective chronology retains its limits.
representative_people.works: The Black Jacobins (1938); Lectures on The Black Jacobins (1971)

representative_people.context: Political-class account discussed critically in Gramsci’s inquiry into intellectual functions.
representative_people.works: Elementi di scienza politica (expanded edition1923), Gramsci author noteA

representative_people.context: An explicitly compared theorist; this selection does not imply Marxist affiliation.
representative_people.works: Theory of elites, compared in Gramsci’s Intellectuals author noteA

representative_people.context: Editorial and translation work enables a particular English selection; translated history, education and politics.
representative_people.works: Selections from the Prison Notebooks (1971), co-editor/translator, prefaceix–xv

representative_people.context: Translated intellectuals, Fordism and philosophy; editorial arrangement differs from notebook sequence.
representative_people.works: Selections from the Prison Notebooks (1971), co-editor/translator, prefaceix–xv

nodes.scope_note: Marx’s historical materialism must be distinguished from the competing historical programmes of later Marxists. Neither Marx’s late qualification nor Engels’s acknowledgment of political effects cancels their stronger causal claims. Lukács, Luxemburg, Lenin, Althusser, Cohen and feminist reworkings offer distinct arguments; shared materialist resources do not establish one doctrine or a verified world chronology.

strands.title: Translation, annotation and historical use
strands.focus: Torr’s editions mediate Marxist writings; Dobb’s reply applies and debates particular rent/production categories. Making texts available and accepting every historical interpretation are different activities.
strands.works: Selected Correspondence (1934); Capital I notes (1938); Dobb reply (1950); Marx on China (1951)

strands.title: Problematics and a disputed epistemological break
strands.focus: Althusser distinguishes changing theoretical questions from merely changing words, credits Martin and Bachelard, and disputes rival periodizations of Marx.

strands.title: Collective reading and theoretical self-criticism
strands.focus: The 1965 seminar produces distinct incomplete readings. Later abridgment and a qualification of theoreticism should not be projected backward as a unified original position.
strands.works: Reading Capital (1965), revised foreword and selected Part I (1968/1970)

strands.title: Overdetermination and political circumstances
strands.focus: Althusser gives political and ideological circumstances explanatory force while retaining economic determination in the last instance. Gramsci is a named resource; reductionism and agency remain disputed.

strands.title: Production relations and the scope of historical claims
strands.focus: Marx’s 1859 preface advances developmental propositions; the 1877 letter restricts the expropriation account to Western Europe and requires comparison of different outcomes. The tension remains visible.

strands.title: Political struggle and economic determination
strands.focus: Engels gives politics, law, theory and individual wills causal effects while maintaining economic determination in the last instance. This qualification is neither economic-only causation nor abandonment of materialism.

strands.title: Dialectical method and historical practice
strands.focus: Lukács treats facts as historically conditioned and connects theory with practice; criticism of Engels coexists with strong claims for dialectical truth.
strands.works: What is Orthodox Marxism? (1919/1923), opening and sections 1–2

strands.title: Different accounts of accumulation and imperial power
strands.focus: Luxemburg’s noncapitalist relations/violence argument and Lenin’s monopoly/finance framing are distinct. Their revolutionary predictions remain attributed propositions rather than independently established historical laws.
strands.works: Accumulation of Capital, chapter 31 (1913); Imperialism, 1920 preface

strands.title: Analytical reconstruction and revision
strands.focus: Cohen separates textual interpretation from defending productive-force primacy and presents functional explanation as part of his reconstruction. The 2000 edition’s reservations qualify its relation to 1978.
strands.works: Karl Marx’s Theory of History (1978/2000), displayed chapter openings

strands.title: Gender and reproduction of material life
strands.focus: Vogel’s stated project reworks Marxian categories to investigate women’s oppression. D’Emilio’s separately checked historical inquiry concerns wages, family dependence and sexual identity; these are distinct uses.
strands.works: Marxism and the Oppression of Women (1983), description; Capitalism and Gay Identity (1983)

strands.title: Situated histories of class, slavery and liberation
strands.focus: Thompson, James and Rodney bring agency, enslavement, revolution and historical specificity to materialist inquiry. European conclusions cannot simply substitute for investigation of other histories.
strands.works: Making preface (1963); Black Jacobins lectures (1971); Marxism and African Liberation (1975)

strands.title: Intellectual functions, consent and organization
strands.focus: Gramsci distinguishes social intellectual functions from professional labels; organic is not a synonym for radical or morally preferable.

strands.title: Subaltern organization and historical traces
strands.focus: Gramsci proposes variable research dimensions, interrupted activity and difficult archival work; later colonial adaptations require separate evidence.

nodes.label: Social facts & collective life
nodes.date_label: Division of Labour 1893 · Rules 1895 · Elementary Forms 1912 · later school · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Social facts, causes and functions, solidarity, ritual and collective thought provide distinct sociological questions. Hubert, Mauss, Simiand, Halbwachs and Meillet develop particular inquiries; historical and anthropological recipients adapt them selectively.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Émile Durkheim (1858–1917), The Division of Labour in Society (1893); influence on Bloch is substantial but selective and critical.

representative_people.context: Defines a sociological object, distinguishes causes from functions, and investigates conditions of solidarity and collective thought. His arguments and ethnographic assumptions require separate assessment.
representative_people.works: De la division du travail social (1893); Les Règles de la méthode sociologique (1895); Les Formes élémentaires de la vie religieuse (1912)

representative_people.context: Collaborative research on sacrifice and later work on gifts examine ritual relations and obligations; the two projects are not interchangeable.
representative_people.works: With Henri Hubert, “Essai sur la nature et la fonction du sacrifice” (1899); “Essai sur le don” (1925)

representative_people.context: Coauthors a provisional comparative theory of sacrifice that distinguishes participants, consecration and mediation. His contribution is not absorbed into Mauss’s later gift essay.
representative_people.works: With Marcel Mauss, “Essai sur la nature et la fonction du sacrifice” (1899)

representative_people.context: Pursues the methodological relation between historical evidence and social science. Annales explicitly reprints his intervention in 1960 as part of its continuing dialogue.
representative_people.works: “Méthode historique et science sociale” (1903; Annales reprint, 1960)

representative_people.context: Develops the social frameworks of remembering as a distinct inquiry. Later critical reuse and his intellectual formation are separate evidentiary questions.
representative_people.works: Les Cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); On Collective Memory (edited English collection, 1992)

representative_people.context: Explicitly applies Durkheim’s social-fact definition to language and investigates social conditions of semantic change.
representative_people.works: “Comment les mots changent de sens” (1906)

representative_people.context: A selective historical recipient and interlocutor, not a doctrinal adherent. His acknowledgment of Durkheim is documented in the scholarly introduction cited here.
representative_people.works: Feudal Society (1939–40); contextual reception study: Susan W. Friedman, Marc Bloch, Sociology and Geography

nodes.scope_note: Durkheim and selected collaborators, recipients and interlocutors, not a membership register. Collective explanation does not imply that all institutions are useful or all differentiation creates solidarity. Colonial-era categories and ethnographic generalizations remain claims to assess. Bloch’s engagement is selective; modernization and Bourdieu links still need more precise reception passages.

strands.title: Social facts and institutional resistance
strands.focus: Durkheim’s examples include obligations, signs and monetary practices. Externality and coercive capacity distinguish his object; mere statistical commonness does not suffice.

strands.title: Origins, functions and critical antecedents
strands.focus: Chapter V disputes Comte’s and Spencer’s utility-based explanations: identifying a use does not explain an institution’s origin, and functions can change.

strands.title: Differentiation and failures of solidarity
strands.focus: Division of labor can produce conflict and anomie. Durkheim’s discussion of crises and capital/labor antagonism qualifies any automatic equation of differentiation with cohesion.
strands.works: Division of Labour (1893), book III chapter I

strands.title: Religious life and collective categories
strands.focus: Sacred practices and collective membership are distinguished from a purely private belief. The proposed social formation of categories is an argument to assess, not an established origin of all thought.
strands.works: Elementary Forms (1912), introduction and religion definition

strands.title: Sacrifice, participants and mediation
strands.focus: Hubert and Mauss build on and revise earlier comparative scholarship. Their provisional model distinguishes ritual participants and movement between sacred and profane.
strands.works: “Essai sur la nature et la fonction du sacrifice” (1899)

strands.title: Historical evidence and social science
strands.focus: Simiand’s methodological challenge and Bloch’s selective historical reception are different forms of engagement; Annales’ later reprint makes one continuing exchange explicit.
strands.works: “Méthode historique et science sociale” (1903; reprinted 1960); Bloch reception in Sociology and Geography

strands.title: Social frameworks of remembering and language
strands.focus: Halbwachs’s memory inquiry and Meillet’s semantic history develop different objects from social relations. Shared vocabulary alone does not establish identical methods.
strands.works: Les Cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); “Comment les mots changent de sens” (1906)

nodes.label: Interpretive historical sociology
nodes.date_label: Weber’s Protestant Ethic 1904–05 · later comparative inquiry · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Interpretive understanding, ideal types, legitimate domination, rationalization, and comparative histories of capitalism and religion. Meaningful interpretation requires causal evidence. Historical questions are selected through cultural concerns, while their answers remain open to public assessment; editorial and translational mediation shape later readings.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Max Weber (1864–1920), The Protestant Ethic (1904–05). Later modernization theory selectively appropriates Weber; his own view of modernity is more ambivalent.

representative_people.context: Connects meaningful action with causal testing and compares historical configurations. The Protestant Ethic conclusion refuses a one-sided spiritualist replacement for materialism and leaves future outcomes open.
representative_people.works: The Protestant Ethic (1904–05; revised 1920), conclusion; Objectivity (1904), excerpt; methodological foundations of sociology, sections 1–11

representative_people.context: A Neo-Kantian interlocutor for concept formation and value relevance. The checked scholarly account stresses Weber’s selective reception, without making him a follower of Rickert’s whole metaphysics.
representative_people.works: Concept/value problems discussed in Kim’s Max Weber, section 2.1

representative_people.context: Historical economics and the Verein für Sozialpolitik provide a research milieu; Kim identifies Schmoller’s mentorship and the agrarian inquiry. This is a bounded institutional connection.
representative_people.works: Verein agrarian investigation, discussed in Kim’s Max Weber, section 1

representative_people.context: Author of a comparative legal-history inquiry into women’s status and a situated feminist critic. She also edits Max Weber’s posthumous writings and writes his biography; these are distinct intellectual activities.
representative_people.works: Ehefrau und Mutter in der Rechtsentwicklung (1907); posthumous Economy and Society edition (1921–22); Max Weber: Ein Lebensbild (1926)

representative_people.context: His 1930 translator’s preface specifies the revised German text used. His 1964 institutional comparison explicitly cites Weber’s bureaucracy analysis; translation and later appropriation have different purposes.
representative_people.works: Protestant Ethic translator’s preface (1930), xxv–xxvii; Evolutionary Universals in Society (1964), selected pages

representative_people.context: Uses Weber for democracy, legitimacy and method. His conclusion invokes Weber through Pipes to deny that capitalist development guarantees political liberty.
representative_people.works: Some Social Requisites of Democracy (1959), selected pages, especially 103–104

representative_people.context: Adapts comparative resources for authority and citizenship. Existing publisher support identifies Weber engagement; no new complete Bendix-book reading is claimed.
representative_people.works: Nation-Building and Citizenship (1964; enlarged editions), checked description

nodes.scope_note: Interpretive sociology, capitalist development, and theories of domination travel through different readers and intermediaries. Ideal types are analytical constructions, not averages or stages every society must traverse. Marianne Weber contributes independent legal-historical research and posthumous editing; Parsons and Lipset make particular later uses. Weber’s qualified defense of materialist inquiry prevents a simple Marx-versus-ideas binary.

strands.title: Meaning and causal evidence
strands.focus: A plausible interpretation of motives is a hypothesis requiring evidence. Understanding does not demand personal empathy, and rational idealization is not a claim that people always act rationally.

strands.title: Ideal types and collective action
strands.focus: Types clarify comparison without serving as averages or compulsory stages. States and organizations matter through actions and meaningful orientations; methodological individualism does not entail individualistic political values.

strands.title: Value relevance and public validity
strands.focus: Cultural concerns select questions; this does not make the validity of answers arbitrary. General regularities help explain particular histories but cannot alone supply a complete account of a specific constellation.

strands.title: Religious conduct and capitalist constraints
strands.focus: The Protestant Ethic conclusion considers ascetic conduct and institutions whose operation outlives religious motivations. It calls for further inquiry into reciprocal conditions and rejects one-sided spiritual causation.
strands.works: Protestant Ethic, printed 119–125 in Parsons translation

strands.title: Legal history and editorial mediation
strands.focus: Marianne Weber’s independent inquiry into women’s legal position belongs alongside her posthumous editing and biography. The unity and arrangement of Economy and Society remain questions in reception.
strands.works: Ehefrau und Mutter (1907); posthumous editions (1921–22); Lebensbild (1926)

strands.title: Different comparative and institutional receptions
strands.focus: Parsons’s translation and institutional comparison, Lipset’s democracy analysis and Bendix’s authority/citizenship inquiry select different resources. No single modernization reading exhausts Weber.

nodes.label: Historical economics
nodes.date_label: Roscher’s programme 1843 · Schmoller’s methodological review 1883 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Historical economists investigate the changing institutions and conditions within which economic claims hold. German programmes, British disciplinary formation, and empirical price research overlap but differ. Their debates concern how to combine explanation and historical evidence: Toynbee values conditional deduction, while Schmoller disputes Menger’s account of abstraction. Earlier disputes also separate Jones’s comparative tenures, Roscher’s contextual programme, Hildebrand’s critique of opposed specialization schemes and Knies’s objections to Roscher’s method. Leslie’s account emphasizes policy differences within historical inquiry.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Gustav Schmoller; William Ashley; William Cunningham; Arnold Toynbee. Thorold Rogers supplies a related empirical tradition in prices and wages. Contextual readings now distinguish Roscher’s 1843 programme, Schmoller’s 1883 methodological review, Cunningham’s textbook, Ashley’s medieval studies, Toynbee’s lectures, Rogers’s wage research and Menger’s criticism.

representative_people.context: Connects economic explanation with law, custom and institutions; defends grounded abstraction in replying to Menger.
representative_people.works: “Zur Methodologie der Staats- und Sozialwissenschaften” (1883; English translation 2021)

representative_people.context: Studies medieval economic institutions and doctrine; his later edition of Mill also documents engagement with theoretical economics.
representative_people.works: An Introduction to English Economic History and Theory (1888–1893); editor, Mill’s Principles of Political Economy (1909)

representative_people.context: Makes economic history a distinct subject through a textbook and university teaching.
representative_people.works: The Growth of English Industry and Commerce (1882; subsequently expanded)

representative_people.context: The nineteenth-century economic historian, not Arnold J. Toynbee. Combines the Industrial Revolution with critical use of conditional economic reasoning.
representative_people.works: Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England (posthumous, 1884), especially the introductory lecture

representative_people.context: Uses wages and commodity prices together to investigate labourers’ purchasing power, while acknowledging uneven evidence.
representative_people.works: Six Centuries of Work and Wages: The History of English Labour (1884)

representative_people.context: An earlier German historical programme preceding Schmoller’s generation. His preface compares institutional development across peoples and values contextual policy judgment while retaining use of Ricardo’s results.
representative_people.works: Grundriss zu Vorlesungen über die Staatswirthschaft nach geschichtlicher Methode (1843)

representative_people.context: An interlocutor who defends the distinct tasks of theoretical inquiry and historical research; his inclusion records a dispute.
representative_people.works: Investigations into the Method of the Social Sciences (1883), Book I, chapters 1–2

representative_people.context: Uses contrasting tenures to question the universal reach of Ricardian rent theory; Ashley later invokes his historical inquiry.
representative_people.works: An Essay on the Distribution of Wealth (1831), preface

representative_people.context: Interprets and criticizes German economic writing for an English-language readership; distinguishes historical inquiry from uniform policy.
representative_people.works: The History of German Political Economy (1875)

representative_people.context: Proposes historical developmental inquiry and questions both exclusive national and exclusive international specialization.
representative_people.works: Die Nationalökonomie der Gegenwart und Zukunft (1848), preface and78–87

representative_people.context: Contests Roscher’s account of method from within historical economics; also critically receives Hildebrand.
representative_people.works: Die politische Oekonomie vom Standpunkte der geschichtlichen Methode (1853), especially31–33

representative_people.context: Uses Knies to examine logical problems of historical economics; explicitly disclaims a complete historical assessment.
representative_people.works: Roscher und Knies, second article (1905), opening

nodes.scope_note: German historical economics, British institutional history, and empirical price studies overlap without forming one school. Roscher’s earlier programme and Schmoller’s generation differ. Menger is shown as a critic, and Toynbee explicitly rejects exclusive reliance on historical investigation. National and civilizational categories in these texts are historical claims to examine, not a globally representative framework. Jones’s providential harmony and Hildebrand’s national-capacity judgments are not adopted as findings.

strands.title: German historical programmes
strands.focus: Compare an earlier historical programme with Schmoller’s institutional and methodological inquiry.

strands.title: British teaching, institutions and historical interpretation
strands.focus: Textbooks, medieval inquiry and Industrial Revolution lectures establish different routes into economic history.

strands.title: Wages, prices and living standards
strands.focus: Compare money wages with the goods they could buy, and ask how gaps in surviving records affect the conclusion.
strands.works: Rogers, Six Centuries of Work and Wages (1884)

strands.title: Disputes over theory and historical method
strands.focus: Schmoller and Menger disagree over explanation; Toynbee argues for combining historical inquiry and deduction. These are distinct positions.

strands.title: Tenures and the limits of general rent theory
strands.focus: Jones grounds comparison in different arrangements between owners and cultivators; his social-harmony conclusions remain contestable.

strands.title: Historical inquiry and policy plurality
strands.focus: Leslie describes conservative and liberal positions within German historical inquiry; Hildebrand questions opposing models of specialization. Neither yields one policy for every historical economist.

strands.title: Disagreement within historical economics
strands.focus: Knies argues that Roscher’s programme confuses method with its subject and intended results. Their shared historical commitments do not settle how explanation should work.

strands.title: Selective reception and disciplinary argument
strands.focus: Ashley invokes Jones and Leslie in defending economic history; Weber uses Knies to isolate logical problems. These are distinct acts of reception.

nodes.label: Political economy & economic theory
nodes.date_label: Smith 1776 · Ricardo 1817 · Mill 1848 · Marshall 1890 · later adaptations · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: A contested body of explanation about production, distribution and exchange. Smith’s division of labour, Ricardo’s distribution problem, Mill’s institutional distinctions, Marshall’s treatment of markets and time, and Menger’s account of theory offer different resources. Historians adapt and criticize these arguments rather than inheriting one uniform model.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Adam Smith is an eighteenth-century precursor; Ricardo, Mill, and Marshall represent different nineteenth-century developments. This is not a single unchanging paradigm. Read Smith (1776), Ricardo (1817/1821), Mill (1848), Marshall (1890/1920), and Menger’s methodological intervention (1883) as differing arguments, not a linear succession.

representative_people.context: Makes division of labour and its effects on productive capacity an explanatory question.
representative_people.works: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776), Book I, chapter 1

representative_people.context: Makes distribution among rent, profit and wages central, while revising and criticizing earlier political economy.
representative_people.works: On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817; third edition 1821)

representative_people.context: Distinguishes production constraints from distribution governed by social laws and customs; assesses alternative arrangements of property.
representative_people.works: Principles of Political Economy with some of their Applications to Social Philosophy (1848), especially Book II, chapter 1

representative_people.context: Analyzes supply, demand and price through provisional assumptions, with different time periods and historically situated conduct.
representative_people.works: Principles of Economics (1890; eighth edition 1920), prefaces

representative_people.context: Defends theoretical explanation as a distinct task that historical investigation alone cannot replace.
representative_people.works: Investigations into the Method of the Social Sciences (1883), Book I, chapters 1–2

representative_people.context: Challenges Smith’s account of an original propensity to barter and treats the market-regulated economy as historically specific.
representative_people.works: The Great Transformation (1944), chapter IV

representative_people.context: Questions the international distribution of technical gains and proposes industrialization supported by trade and capital imports.
representative_people.works: El desarrollo económico de la América Latina y algunos de sus principales problemas (1949), selected introduction

representative_people.context: Distinguishes multiplier mechanisms; Furtado explicitly invokes Keynes when interpreting Brazilian coffee policy retrospectively.
representative_people.works: The General Theory (1936), chapter10; Furtado (1959/2005), chapter XXXI

representative_people.context: Adapts income and demand analysis to Brazil’s coffee crisis and changing domestic market; the historical interpretation receives contemporary criticism.
representative_people.works: Formação econômica do Brasil (1959), chapter XXXI in2005edition

representative_people.context: Lipset’s1959 comparison explicitly draws on Schumpeter’s procedural definition of democracy; this selection concerns that documented use.
representative_people.works: Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942;1947edition cited by Lipset), through Lipset (1959),71

representative_people.context: Criticizes Wakefield’s scheme for producing wage dependence through restricted land access; Mill endorses this scheme in a separately checked text.
representative_people.works: Capital I (1867), chapter33

representative_people.context: Uses Mill’s capital propositions to challenge colonial claims about investment and to explain the drain of India’s resources.
representative_people.works: Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901),55–56

nodes.scope_note: Classical political economy and neoclassical modelling have different chronologies; North’s later institutional revisions add another distinction. This selection foregrounds earlier resources for historical inquiry, not a complete history of twentieth-century economics. Mill’s institutional argument and Marshall’s qualified assumptions prevent a blanket equation of theory with timeless laws. Polanyi appears as a later critic of a specific classical account, extending the selection’s historical reception without turning it into a complete history of twentieth-century theory. Earlier resources remain central, now joined by selected twentieth-century historical uses: Furtado’s Keynes reference, Block/Somers’s Polanyi reception and Lipset’s Schumpeter definition. These do not constitute comprehensive coverage of modern economics. Mill’s property qualifications coexist with colonial and civilizational assumptions; Marx’s Wakefield critique also retains a settler frame. Naoroji adds an Indian appropriation of Mill, not a globally representative roster.

strands.title: Production and distribution in classical political economy
strands.focus: Smith’s productive specialization and Ricardo’s distribution question identify different explanatory priorities.
strands.works: Wealth of Nations (1776); Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817/1821)

strands.title: Mill: institutions and distribution
strands.focus: Compare rules of property and distribution while distinguishing them from the constraints of production.
strands.works: Principles of Political Economy (1848), Book II, chapter 1

strands.title: Marshall: markets, assumptions and time
strands.focus: Holding some conditions constant makes analysis possible; its conclusions depend on the problem and period considered.

strands.title: Menger: the tasks of theory and history
strands.focus: Distinguish general explanation from the investigation of particular historical phenomena without making either dispensable.

strands.title: Multiplier analysis in historical explanation
strands.focus: Keynes’s conditional account becomes an explicit resource in Furtado’s retrospective reading of Brazil’s coffee crisis. This is not evidence that1931policymakers read a1936book.

strands.title: Polanyi’s historical-sociological reception
strands.focus: Block and Somers explicitly bring Polanyi into historical sociology while resisting assimilation to a single classical tradition. Their chapter opening supports this bounded reception claim.

strands.title: Economic theorists as resources for political comparison
strands.focus: Lipset uses Schumpeter’s definition of democracy in comparative inquiry. The documented conceptual use differs from importing a complete economic system.

strands.title: Property qualifications and colonial wage labour
strands.focus: Mill distinguishes land from produced property and condemns slavery while defending owner compensation. His endorsement of Wakefield’s land scheme can be read beside Marx’s critique of the wage dependence that it creates.
strands.works: Mill, II.2§§5–7 and V.11§14; Marx, Capital I,33

strands.title: Political economy against colonial assurances
strands.focus: Naoroji uses Mill’s arguments about capital to dispute automatic benefits of imperial investment. Colonial criticism here adapts a theoretical resource.

nodes.label: Geography & environmental inquiry
nodes.date_label: 1800s roots · Marsh 1864 · Vidal 1903 · Sauer 1925 · later inquiries · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Several traditions ask how human activity and physical environments shape landscapes. Vidal investigates regional individuality; Marsh examines human environmental modification; Sauer relates physical and cultural forms; Leopold joins ecological observation with ethical concern. Their later uses differ, including Annales geography and environmental historians’ landscape inquiry. Critical and feminist geography add questions about capital, mobility, gender and contested place histories; Hayden and the History Workshop journal show specific historical uses. Driver examines the practices and disagreements of imperial geographical inquiry. Sauer’s historical reconstruction, Cosgrove’s criticism of visual neutrality and Febvre’s geographical collaborations reveal further disagreements within landscape inquiry.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Paul Vidal de la Blache influences Febvre and Bloch; George Perkins Marsh, Man and Nature (1864), is an environmental precursor, not an Annales founder. Additional readings: Sauer, “The Morphology of Landscape” (1925); Leopold, A Sand County Almanac (1949).

representative_people.context: Investigates how human activity forms a region’s geographical individuality; engages Michelet’s national framing. His human geography is a resource for Annales, with the reception limits retained in the connection note.
representative_people.works: Tableau de la géographie de la France (1903)

representative_people.context: Studies human modification of physical environments; a precursor to environmental inquiry, not an Annales founder.
representative_people.works: Man and Nature; or, Physical Geography as Modified by Human Action (1864)

representative_people.context: Treats landscapes as related physical and cultural forms with histories; challenges rigid explanations from physical conditions alone.
representative_people.works: “The Morphology of Landscape” (1925)

representative_people.context: Conservationist whose ecological observation and teaching supplied one model for reading landscapes; Cronon later recalls workshops modeled on his course.
representative_people.works: A Sand County Almanac (1949)

representative_people.context: Uses local political boundaries and population distribution to examine ratification.
representative_people.works: The Geographical Distribution of the Vote (1894)

representative_people.context: Studies biological conditions of human geography; Canguilhem explicitly discusses the project.
representative_people.works: Les fondements biologiques de la géographie humaine (1943)

representative_people.context: Examines capitalist restructuring and place identity; Hayden draws on his account while Massey disputes its treatment of tradition.
representative_people.works: The Condition of Postmodernity (1989), 302–304; From Space to Place and Back Again (1991), through Hayden

representative_people.context: Differentiates power over mobility and contests fixed place identities and feminist exclusions; intervenes in historical debate.
representative_people.works: A Global Sense of Place (1991); Flexible Sexism (1991); Places and Their Pasts (1995)

representative_people.context: Uses and critically receives geographical arguments in collaborative urban public history.
representative_people.works: The Power of Place (1995), selected passages

representative_people.context: Studies contested geographical knowledge and imperial exploration; collaborates with Samuel on a spatial-history editorial.
representative_people.works: Geography’s Empire (1992); Hints to Travellers article (issue 1998); with Samuel, Rethinking the Idea of Place (1995)

representative_people.context: In Febvre’s recollection, encouraged his geographical book and enlisted Vidal’s support while committed to the Asian volumes of Géographie universelle.
representative_people.works: Asian volumes of Géographie universelle; collaboration recalled in Febvre’s Combats pour l’histoire (1953)

representative_people.context: Febvre explicitly credits notes and suggestions for specified parts of his geographical introduction to history.
representative_people.works: Contributions to La Terre et l’évolution humaine (1922), acknowledged in the author’s notice

representative_people.context: Uses Vidal’s geographical method in historical inquiry while resisting explanation by physical conditions alone; Sauer receives this intervention critically.
representative_people.works: La Terre et l’évolution humaine (1922), selected passages

representative_people.context: Historically questions landscape’s apparent visual neutrality and its relations to property and power; explicitly discusses Sauer’s morphology.
representative_people.works: “Prospect, perspective and the evolution of the landscape idea” (1985), selected sections

representative_people.context: Named coauthor of a collaborative place-history article in the journal’s 1995 spatial-history section. Publication establishes participation, not founding membership or a shared universal theory.
representative_people.works: Kooramindanjie: Place and the Postcolonial (1995), with the other two named collaborators

representative_people.context: Named coauthor of a collaborative place-history article in the journal’s 1995 spatial-history section. Publication establishes participation, not founding membership or a shared universal theory.
representative_people.works: Kooramindanjie: Place and the Postcolonial (1995), with the other two named collaborators

representative_people.context: Named coauthor of a collaborative place-history article in the journal’s 1995 spatial-history section. Publication establishes participation, not founding membership or a shared universal theory.
representative_people.works: Kooramindanjie: Place and the Postcolonial (1995), with the other two named collaborators

representative_people.context: Links historical inquiry to ecological adaptation; Worster acknowledges this resource while disputing Malin’s Dust Bowl explanations.
representative_people.works: “Ecology and History” (1950); “Dust Storms” (1946), through Worster (1986)

representative_people.context: Historical geography of dispersed commercial farming supplies a specifically cited resource to Worster and, through McDean’s account, Hurt.
representative_people.works: The Suitcase-Farming Frontier: A Study in the Historical Geography of the Central Great Plains (1973), cited by later historians

nodes.scope_note: Vidal’s human geography and Marsh’s environmental inquiry are different resources; neither defines all later environmental history. This is a selective set of resources for historians, not a complete history of geography. Sauer and Leopold supply distinct approaches; national framing, ecological care and landscape morphology are not a single programme. Harvey and Massey disagree within critical inquiry; neither stands for the whole discipline. Colonial frameworks are investigated as historically situated practices with internal conflicts. This expanded selection still does not represent global geography comprehensively.

strands.title: Human activity and regional individuality
strands.focus: Vidal asks how human activity gives a region unity, within an explicitly French national frame.
strands.works: Tableau de la géographie de la France (1903)

strands.title: Human modification of physical environments
strands.focus: Marsh brings historical human action into inquiry about forests, waters and land; later historians recognize this precursor.

strands.title: Physical and cultural landscape forms
