strands.focus: Sauer examines associations of landscape forms and their histories, resisting a rigid physical determinism.

strands.title: Ecological observation and landscape reading
strands.focus: Leopold’s observation and teaching connect ecological processes with human conduct; Cronon recalls a specific teaching inheritance.
strands.works: A Sand County Almanac (1949); Cronon’s retrospective afterword

strands.title: Human ecology and medical geography
strands.focus: Sorre’s project supplies a named geographical resource for conceptual inquiry.

strands.title: Mobility and unequal power
strands.focus: Massey asks who moves, who controls movement and how gender and colonial histories differentiate experience.

strands.title: Place, tradition and historical change
strands.focus: Massey disputes the necessary association of place identity with fixed tradition; Harvey allows valuable local resistance while questioning its sufficiency.

strands.title: Geographical resources in public history
strands.focus: Hayden uses Harvey while citing Massey’s feminist criticism in a project joining urban landscapes and public memory.

strands.title: Imperial networks and contested observation
strands.focus: Driver examines conflicting standards, instruments and observer credibility; colonial support did not make all geographical knowledge uniform.
strands.works: Geography’s Empire (1992); Hints to Travellers article (issue 1998)

strands.title: Reconstructing changing cultural landscapes
strands.focus: Sauer proposes reconstructing past cultural landscapes and their succession. His organic analogy is a working method rather than a literal biological law; claims of neutral observation and culture cycles remain open to criticism.

strands.title: Landscape as a historically situated way of seeing
strands.focus: Cosgrove explicitly challenges the neutrality of the areal concept and links visual conventions with property and power. His criticism of static chorology is placed beside Sauer’s own reconstruction of change, preserving disagreement.

strands.title: Historical inquiry, geographical resources and criticism
strands.focus: Vidal supplies methodological resources to Febvre; Sion encourages the project and Bataillon contributes notes. Sauer praises its criticism of environmentalism but questions its representation of geographical thought.
strands.works: La Terre et l’évolution humaine (1922); Sauer (1925); Febvre’s retrospective Combats essay

strands.title: Collaborative place history
strands.focus: The 1995 spatial-history section includes Rita and Jackie Huggins with Jane M. Jacobs. Verified coauthorship and the public finding aid document collaboration; detailed article interpretation remains limited by access.

strands.title: Dispersed farming as historical geography
strands.focus: Hewes’s suitcase-farming study is used in later agricultural environmental explanation; shared citation does not settle disagreements about capitalism, farming or government.
strands.works: The Suitcase-Farming Frontier (1973), cited in Worster (1986) and discussed by McDean (1986)

nodes.label: Earlier cultural history
nodes.date_label: Burckhardt’s Renaissance 1860 · Huizinga’s Autumn 1919 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Earlier cultural histories connect political arrangements, individual distinction, emotions, images and collective life in different ways. Burckhardt, Huizinga, Lamprecht and the Warburg setting offer competing questions and methods, with later criticism and adaptation.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Jacob Burckhardt, The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy (1860); Johan Huizinga, The Autumn of the Middle Ages (1919).

representative_people.context: Connects Renaissance political arrangements, individual distinction and cultural forms, while acknowledging that interpretive categories divide a complex process. His claims about medieval consciousness and educated women require critical comparison.
representative_people.works: The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy (1860), especially I.1, II.1 and V.6

representative_people.context: Interprets late-medieval emotional and artistic forms as endings as well as beginnings; asks how surviving images distort our view and later treats play as a meaningful social activity.
representative_people.works: The Autumn of the Middle Ages (1919; adapted English The Waning of the Middle Ages, 1924); Homo Ludens (1938)

representative_people.context: Investigates Renaissance images and mnemonic practices through textual and visual reconstruction. The comparison with Burckhardt/Huizinga remains qualified.
representative_people.works: The Art of Memory (1966); Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (1964), its background explicitly discussed in the 1966 preface

representative_people.context: Discusses and criticizes Yates’s drafts and mediates Warburg’s questions about images.
representative_people.works: Draft discussions acknowledged in The Art of Memory (1966), preface xiv

representative_people.context: Offers scholarly help and later recalls both the strengths and evidential risks of Yates’s reconstruction.
representative_people.works: Acknowledgment in The Art of Memory (1966); “On Frances Yates” (1983)

representative_people.context: Discusses Renaissance problems, reads manuscripts and checks some translations for Yates.
representative_people.works: Manuscript and translation work acknowledged in The Art of Memory (1966), preface xiv

representative_people.context: Reads chapters and helps revise and draw reconstructions; the proposed Globe plan is largely her work, according to Frances.
representative_people.works: Plans and sketches, especially Camillo’s theatre and the proposed Globe reconstruction, The Art of Memory (1966)

representative_people.context: Questions about images reach Yates through Bing. No personal contact between Yates and Warburg is claimed.
representative_people.works: Image problems as recalled through Bing in The Art of Memory (1966), preface xiv

representative_people.context: Connects verse and visual culture with political imagination. This extends cultural inquiry without establishing descent from Burckhardt or Huizinga.
representative_people.works: Poetry and Politics under the Stuarts (1960)

representative_people.context: Critically distinguishes life-serving and harmful uses of the past and explicitly quotes Burckhardt on Renaissance culture. This does not equate their cultural or political positions.
representative_people.works: On the Use and Abuse of History for Life (1874), preface and §§2–3

representative_people.context: Advocates a distinct social-psychological history of collective conditions. His developmental rankings and claims of explanatory supremacy are contested propositions, not the method of all cultural history.
representative_people.works: What Is History? (1905), preface and lecture I selections

representative_people.context: Lamprecht explicitly credits his attention to collective historical life; this is a mediated intellectual resource, not an original Herder reading or an exclusive origin claim.
representative_people.works: Ideas concerning the History of Mankind, as cited in Lamprecht, What Is History? (1905), pp. 19–21

representative_people.context: Challenges Burckhardt’s equality claim and asks how period boundaries change with women’s historically differentiated positions.
representative_people.works: “Did Women Have a Renaissance?” (1977)

representative_people.context: Appreciates Huizinga while questioning whether the proposed emotional contrasts distinguish the period adequately.
representative_people.works: “La sensibilité et l’histoire” (1941), collected in Combats pour l’histoire (1953)

nodes.scope_note: A teaching grouping of distinct projects, not one school or an immature stage inevitably superseded by a cultural turn. National, social and cultural inquiry overlap. Period contrasts, elite claims, developmental rankings and the uneven survival of sources require scrutiny; collective psychology here is not psychoanalysis.

strands.title: Images, mnemonic arts and collaborative reconstruction
strands.focus: Yates’s textual and visual inquiry draws on Bing, Gombrich, Walker and R. W. Yates. This is a distinct research setting, not a single doctrine shared with Burckhardt and Huizinga. Warburg’s Florentine archival and image-survival questions provide an institutional background, with methods differing among collaborators.
strands.works: The Art of Memory (1966); Gombrich, “On Frances Yates” (1983)

strands.title: Uses of the past and their dangers
strands.focus: Nietzsche distinguishes monumental, antiquarian and critical uses, each with capacities and risks; Burckhardt supplies an explicit Renaissance example. These are not three exclusive historical schools.
strands.works: On the Use and Abuse of History for Life (1874), §§2–3

strands.title: Political arrangements and individuality
strands.focus: Burckhardt links distinctiveness to republics and despotisms; his interpretive categories and medieval/modern contrast are open to challenge.
strands.works: The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy (1860), I.1 and II.1

strands.title: Gender and the boundaries of a Renaissance
strands.focus: The claim of equality draws on educated elites; Kelly changes the question through differentiated social positions and periodization.

strands.title: Forms of feeling and the end of an age
strands.focus: Huizinga asks how ritual, sound and public forms organize experience; Febvre appreciates the inquiry and questions its period contrast.
strands.works: The Waning of the Middle Ages, preface and chapter I; Febvre (1941)

strands.title: Art in life and uneven survival
strands.focus: Huizinga contrasts the impressions produced by chronicles and surviving art, asking about lost secular objects and practical settings. This does not establish that written sources survive without distortion.
strands.works: The Waning of the Middle Ages, chapter XIX opening

strands.title: Play as a meaningful cultural activity
strands.focus: Huizinga examines absorption, voluntary activity and the shifting relation to seriousness; play is not reduced to leisure or a biological utility.
strands.works: Homo Ludens (1938), chapter I pp. 1–9 in English reprint

strands.title: Collective conditions and social psychology
strands.focus: Lamprecht’s program and reading of Herder differ from Burckhardt’s synthesis; his insistence on collective explanatory priority remains contested.

nodes.label: Biographical & literary traditions
nodes.date_label: Ancient roots · Carlyle’s On Heroes 1841 · Strachey 1918 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: A selective range of life-writing practices: ancient character portraits, private particulars and conversation, heroic interpretation, concentrated literary portraits and debates about evidence and invention. Literary experiments and editorial selection also supply resources for later historical methods.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Thomas Carlyle, On Heroes (1841); Lytton Strachey, Eminent Victorians (1918). Biography does not originate with either writer.

representative_people.context: The opening Heroes lecture gives creative individuals and practical belief a large explanatory role. This is one nineteenth-century strand, not biography’s origin or all Carlyle’s historical writing.
representative_people.works: On Heroes (1841), Lecture I opening (5 May 1840)

representative_people.context: Selects compact portraits using French eloges models and existing biographies. Woolf later praises one royal biography while criticizing another; neither authorial impartiality nor a uniform critical verdict is assumed.
representative_people.works: Eminent Victorians (1918), preface; Queen Victoria and Elizabeth and Essex, evaluated by Woolf (1939)

representative_people.context: Uses minor acts and a portrait analogy to explain a life’s selective treatment of character. One ancient practice, not the origin or entirety of biography.
representative_people.works: Alexander, opening paragraph; archive translation credited to Dryden

representative_people.context: Argues that private particulars can make many lives instructive, while proximity and friendship can both supply and distort information. His moral premise remains situated.
representative_people.works: The Rambler 60 (1750)

representative_people.context: Interweaves letters, recollected conversations and narrative, explicitly adapting Mason’s example. Claims candid portrayal rather than pure praise; actual completeness is not established by that claim.
representative_people.works: Life of Johnson (1791), opening selection in Osgood abridgment (1917)

representative_people.context: Examines verifiable evidence, invention and changing biographical conventions. Differentiates Strachey’s books and asks why failures and humble lives should be excluded; her restricted English canon is not universalized.
representative_people.works: “The Art of Biography” (1939)

representative_people.context: Boswell explicitly names his arrangement of Gray’s life as a model to adapt and enlarge. This records Boswell’s stated debt, not independent reading of Mason.
representative_people.works: Memoirs of Gray, named in Boswell’s opening

representative_people.context: Strachey explicitly values the French eloge tradition as a model for biographical writing. The original eloges were not read in this review.
representative_people.works: Biographical eloges, acknowledged in Eminent Victorians (1918), preface

representative_people.context: Strachey explicitly values the French eloge tradition as a model for biographical writing. The original eloges were not read in this review.
representative_people.works: Biographical eloges, acknowledged in Eminent Victorians (1918), preface

representative_people.context: Strachey acknowledges indispensable information from Cook’s Nightingale biography while using a different scale and angle.
representative_people.works: Life of Florence Nightingale, acknowledged in Strachey’s 1918 postscript

representative_people.context: His abridgment deliberately removes much correspondence, commentary and conversation. Editorial selection changes which Boswell later readers encounter.
representative_people.works: Abridged Life of Johnson, preface dated 28 June 1917

representative_people.context: Bourdieu explicitly uses his challenge to conventionally coherent lives without adopting all his philosophy. The cited literary text remains mediated.
representative_people.works: Le Miroir qui revient (1984), p. 208, cited by Bourdieu (1986)

representative_people.context: Levi uses dialogic and discontinuous literary narration to question a uniformly coherent historical subject. This is a named resource in his 1989 methodological argument, not proof that the novel founded microhistory.
representative_people.works: Tristram Shandy, discussed by Levi (1989)

representative_people.context: Levi uses dialogic and discontinuous literary narration to question a uniformly coherent historical subject. This is a named resource in his 1989 methodological argument, not proof that the novel founded microhistory.
representative_people.works: Jacques le fataliste, discussed by Levi (1989)

nodes.scope_note: Earlier roots and literary practices overlap with modern historical biography without forming one origin story. Plutarch is one ancient example; Johnson’s private lives precede Carlyle’s Heroes. Strachey names particular models and sources, and Woolf distinguishes his achievements and failures. Her English canon is not a universal history of biography. Translations and abridgments mediate the texts encountered here; named literary resources do not by themselves establish a school’s founding.

strands.title: Character and selective lives
strands.focus: Plutarch’s portrait analogy privileges revealing particulars over a full campaign narrative. This is a specific ancient practice, not a timeless division of genres.

strands.title: Private particulars, conversation and narrative
strands.focus: Johnson defends instructional private detail; Boswell arranges documents and conversation, explicitly adapting Mason. Neither proximity nor a claim to candor guarantees accuracy.
strands.works: Rambler 60 (1750); Life of Johnson (1791), selected opening

strands.title: Creative individuals and historical belief
strands.focus: Carlyle’s lecture opening connects great individuals with historical creation and religious conviction. It does not define all nineteenth-century life writing, or all his own writing.

strands.title: Compact portraits and acknowledged models
strands.focus: Strachey chooses concentrated portraits, invokes French eloges and uses Cook’s research. Selection is a stated artistic procedure, not representative sampling of the whole age.

strands.title: Checkable evidence and invention
strands.focus: Woolf’s contrasting judgments of Strachey’s royal biographies test how documentary limits constrain imaginative form. Her conclusions remain criticism, not a settled law of biography.

strands.title: Discontinuous narration and the coherent self
strands.focus: Levi and Bourdieu use named literary experiments to question retrospective coherence. The novels are resources for later arguments, not automatic origins of historical schools.

strands.title: Abridgment and later readers
strands.focus: Osgood explains what his Boswell selection removes. A widely accessible edition is a particular editorial construction of the work.

nodes.label: Strategic & military scholarship
nodes.date_label: Earlier roots · Clausewitz’s On War 1832 · Delbrück’s volumes 1900–20 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Brings strategic reasoning, critical campaign scholarship and the editing of military texts into view. Clausewitz, Jomini, Delbrück, Mahan, Corbett and the translated Sun Tzu tradition pose different questions about judgment, evidence and the purposes of war. Professional education and academic inquiry overlap without being identical.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Carl von Clausewitz, On War (1832); Hans Delbrück joins source criticism to analysis of warfare.

representative_people.context: Examines political purpose, passion, chance and friction in an unfinished, posthumously edited work. Strategic reasoning differs from empirical verification of particular campaigns.
representative_people.works: On War (1832); selected passages in Graham translation with later editorial apparatus

representative_people.context: Joins philological criticism to checks of practical possibility, using population evidence and documentary research. Explicitly acknowledges Ranke and Beloch; possible reconstructions are not automatically established events.
representative_people.works: Geschichte der Kriegskunst im Rahmen der politischen Geschichte, four volumes (1900–1920); first preface (1900)

representative_people.context: Proposes explaining sea power within general history and its social, political and economic surroundings. His naval-professional perspective and selected Europe/America scope are explicit.
representative_people.works: The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783 (1890), preface

representative_people.context: Treats naval operations within wider maritime coordination of armies, fleets and political purposes. Theory aids education and deliberation; this is a situated British imperial perspective.
representative_people.works: Some Principles of Maritime Strategy (1911), introduction

representative_people.context: Organizes posthumous publication and describes intellectual companionship and assistance from others. Her modest prefatory disclaimer does not make editorial work intellectually empty.
representative_people.works: Preface to On War, 30 June 1832

representative_people.context: Defends strategic principles while insisting that war also turns on morale, judgment and contingencies. His conclusion qualifies a wholly mechanical characterization.
representative_people.works: The Art of War, Mendell/Craighill translation (1862), conclusion

representative_people.context: Traditional attribution of a Chinese strategic text that prioritizes overcoming resistance and preserving forces over repeated destructive combat. Neither a fixed composition date nor a uniform Chinese tradition is asserted.
representative_people.works: The Art of War, Giles translation (1910), chapter III §§1–8

representative_people.context: Makes translation, paragraph arrangement and selective Chinese commentary part of the English text’s reception; his criticism of predecessors remains a contested editorial judgment.
representative_people.works: The Art of War (1910), translator’s preface and commentary

representative_people.context: Proposes and collaborates with Howard on a new Clausewitz translation. Strachan later assesses its modernization; translating does not simply transmit an unchanged meaning.
representative_people.works: With Michael Howard, On War (1976), translation; collaboration documented by Strachan

representative_people.context: Challenges Keegan’s culture/politics opposition while valuing The Face of Battle. Later web corrections are distinguished from the original polemic.
representative_people.works: “John Keegan and the Grand Tradition of Trashing Clausewitz” (1994)

representative_people.context: Collaborates with Paret on translating Clausewitz; readable modern vocabulary is also an object of later interpretive criticism.
representative_people.works: With Peter Paret, On War (1976), translation

representative_people.context: Questions Clausewitz through a cultural account of warfare, as represented in Bassford’s opposing reception. This is distinct from the combat-reconstruction method of his earlier book.
representative_people.works: A History of Warfare (1993), mediated by Bassford (1994)

representative_people.context: Delbrück explicitly credits demographic groundwork while correcting individual estimates. A named methodological resource, not acceptance of every army figure.
representative_people.works: Die Bevölkerung der griechisch-römischen Welt (1886), acknowledged in Delbrück’s 1900 preface

nodes.scope_note: A selective teaching umbrella, weighted toward European and Anglophone scholarship, with a Chinese text and its mediated reception distinguished. Delbrück explicitly uses Ranke, Beloch and biographical research; these roots are not independent of every other historical tradition. Theory does not guarantee successful action. Marie’s editing and later translations are substantive mediation. Corbett writes for an imperial setting; neither that perspective nor Mahan’s national judgments is universalized. Bassford’s later online corrections are not assigned to his 1994 argument.

strands.title: Strategic principles, uncertainty and judgment
strands.focus: Clausewitz’s friction and variable tendencies and Jomini’s qualified rules frame different questions. Neither makes war wholly mechanical.
strands.works: On War (1832), selections; The Art of War (1862 translation), conclusion

strands.title: Editing and translating strategic texts
strands.focus: Marie’s posthumous work and Howard/Paret’s translation expose mediation and interpretive choices, rather than a single transparent text.

strands.title: Chinese strategic writing and its translation
strands.focus: Giles’s selection and commentary mediate the attributed Sun Tzu text. Overcoming resistance is not synonymous with winning repeated battles; wider Chinese traditions and textual dating need separate inquiry.
strands.works: The Art of War, Giles translation (1910), preface and III §§1–8

strands.title: Documents and practical possibility
strands.focus: Delbrück combines textual criticism with population and physical constraints, explicitly using Beloch and acknowledging Ranke. Possible alternatives remain distinct from proven events.

strands.title: Sea power and maritime coordination
strands.focus: Mahan proposes integrating sea power with general history; Corbett distinguishes naval operations from wider maritime strategy. This juxtaposition does not itself establish direct transmission.
strands.works: The Influence of Sea Power (1890), preface; Some Principles (1911), introduction

strands.title: Culture, politics and disputed reception
strands.focus: Keegan’s 1993 challenge and Bassford’s response are an exchange about interpreting Clausewitz. Bassford also values Keegan’s earlier work and acknowledges limits to strategic theory.
strands.works: A History of Warfare (1993), mediated; Bassford polemic (1994)

nodes.label: Anthropology & ethnography
nodes.date_label: 1800s roots · Tylor 1871 · Boas 1896 · later revisions · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Ethnographic observation, comparison, historical reconstruction and interpretation generate different accounts of social life. Exchanges with historians involve particular works and methods; colonial knowledge, research authority and the representation of cultures are contested within and beyond the discipline.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Distinct stages include Tylor and Frazer, Boasian historical particularism, and later interpretive anthropology associated with Geertz. These do not form one continuous theory.

representative_people.context: Studies acquired culture through comparative stages and survivals; the hierarchy is his proposition, not the atlas’s classification of peoples.
representative_people.works: Primitive Culture (1871; consulted 1920 edition)

representative_people.context: Reconstructs the Nemi priesthood by comparisons of rituals and beliefs, while acknowledging that inference is not demonstration.
representative_people.works: The Golden Bough: A Study in Comparative Religion (1890; consulted 1894 printing)

representative_people.context: Challenges the inference of identical causes from similar customs; retains comparison after historical investigation establishes comparability.
representative_people.works: “The Limitations of the Comparative Method of Anthropology” (1896)

representative_people.context: Interprets situated public meanings; thick description requires context and argument, not mere descriptive abundance.
representative_people.works: The Interpretation of Cultures (1973), especially “Thick Description”; “Deep Play” (1972); Negara (1980)

representative_people.context: Scott explicitly takes up her emphasis on the meanings of women’s activities within social interaction.
representative_people.works: “The Uses and Abuses of Anthropology: Reflections on Feminism and Cross-Cultural Understanding” (1980)

representative_people.context: Māori scholarship joins historical interpretation and material-culture research; an earlier trajectory distinct from later methodological manifestos.
representative_people.works: The Coming of the Maori (1949)

representative_people.context: Anthropologist and collaborator in a southern Yukon life-history project; the elders are knowledge producers, not anonymous source material.
representative_people.works: Life Lived Like a Story, with Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned (1990)

representative_people.context: Connects close observation, social organization and recorded statements to an account of participants’ perspectives.
representative_people.works: Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922), introduction

representative_people.context: Asks how recurrent activities sustain social relations; functional unity is offered as a working hypothesis.
representative_people.works: “On the Concept of Function in Social Science” (1935); Structure and Function in Primitive Society (1952)

representative_people.context: Connects historical understanding and anthropological translation; this position had critics within anthropology.
representative_people.works: The Sanusi of Cyrenaica (1949); Essays in Social Anthropology (1962)

representative_people.context: Gift obligations connect social relations, law and economy; the reading should retain the essay’s publication context.
representative_people.works: “Essai sur le don” / The Gift (1925)

representative_people.context: A major contextual reading in comparative cultural inquiry; later feminist reassessments examine her place in the canon.
representative_people.works: Patterns of Culture (1934)

representative_people.context: Investigates adolescent life and cultural upbringing in Samoa; the listed evidence does not settle later disputes about her findings.
representative_people.works: Coming of Age in Samoa (1928)

representative_people.context: Develops questions about ritual, liminality and communitas through Ndembu research.
representative_people.works: The Ritual Process (1969)

representative_people.context: Relates structures and events through Pacific histories; particular interpretations remain debated.
representative_people.works: Islands of History (1985)

representative_people.context: Studies colonial knowledge practices; his earlier exchange with social historians is documented separately from the 1996 collection.
representative_people.works: Colonialism and Its Forms of Knowledge (1996); Cohn’s earlier intervention discussed by Medick (1987)

representative_people.context: Historicizes religion and the conditions that authorize symbolic practices; his specific Geertz engagement is not a dismissal of the entire corpus.
representative_people.works: Genealogies of Religion (1993), chapter 1

representative_people.context: Coedits a collection investigating ethnographic writing, authority and political conditions; its essays offer differing positions.
representative_people.works: With George E. Marcus, ed., Writing Culture (1986)

representative_people.context: Coedits the ethnographic writing debate; joint editorship does not make every chapter a shared argument.
representative_people.works: With James Clifford, ed., Writing Culture (1986)

representative_people.context: Questions how research discourse places interlocutors in another time despite the shared time of communication.
representative_people.works: Time and the Other (1983)

representative_people.context: Coedits feminist experiments and histories of the anthropological canon.
representative_people.works: With Deborah A. Gordon, ed., Women Writing Culture (1995)

representative_people.context: Coedits inquiry into gender, race, nationality and the valuation of ethnographic work.
representative_people.works: With Ruth Behar, ed., Women Writing Culture (1995)

representative_people.context: Florida and Louisiana folklore supplies a distinct literary/ethnographic reading; feminist historians of anthropology later revisit her work.
representative_people.works: Mules and Men (1935)

representative_people.context: Village economy and social change are followed through research in China and subsequent returns; his retrospective documents both local initiatives and LSE supervision.
representative_people.works: Peasant Life in China (1939); Chinese-edition retrospective preface (1985)

representative_people.context: Uses historical transformations in Kachin political forms to question models of social equilibrium.
representative_people.works: Political Systems of Highland Burma (1954)

representative_people.context: Adapts relational analysis while explicitly considering historical evidence.
representative_people.works: Structural Anthropology (1958; English 1963); The Savage Mind (1962; English 1966)

representative_people.context: Historical anthropology connects peoples usually separated from accounts of European expansion.
representative_people.works: Europe and the People Without History (1982)

representative_people.context: With economist Baron Isherwood, examines goods as social communication.
representative_people.works: With Baron Isherwood, The World of Goods (1979)

representative_people.context: Questions the social-bandit model through power and patronage. Hobsbawm’s later response acknowledges this objection; Blok’s full original article remains unread.
representative_people.works: “The Peasant and the Brigand: Social Banditry Reconsidered” (1972); response in Hobsbawm, Bandits, revised edition (2000)

representative_people.context: Research on Greek tragedy connects historical-cultural interpretation and semantic ambiguity; the consulted evidence is Barthes’s explicit use, not a reading of Vernant’s entire program.
representative_people.works: Greek-tragedy research as invoked in Barthes, “The Death of the Author” (1967)

representative_people.context: Geertz explicitly invokes later Wittgenstein when explaining public meaning. That selective use does not make all interpretive anthropology Wittgensteinian.
representative_people.works: Philosophical Investigations (1953); Geertz, Thick Description (1973), pp. 12–13

representative_people.context: Geertz adapts the distinction between outwardly similar actions with different meanings. Ryle’s philosophical lecture has its own inquiry into thinking and accomplishment.
representative_people.works: The Thinking of Thoughts (1968); Geertz, Thick Description (1973), pp. 5–7

representative_people.context: Challenges civilizational accounts of bodily shame; a critic, not an Elias adherent.
representative_people.works: Nacktheit und Scham (1988)

representative_people.context: Provides a historian’s explicit use of Kopytoff within Appadurai’s collection.
representative_people.works: “Sacred Commodities” (1986),169,188

representative_people.context: Compares kinship and marriage historically while distinguishing his questions from demographic classifications.
representative_people.works: The Development of the Family and Marriage in Europe (1983),8–9

representative_people.context: Edits comparative local population studies; his later review questions broad inference from uneven evidence.
representative_people.works: Chinese Historical Microdemography (1995); retrospective review of Lee/Wang (2003)

strands.title: Evolutionary comparison and reconstruction
strands.focus: Tylor’s stages and survivals differ from Frazer’s ritual reconstruction; their assumptions require criticism.

strands.title: Historical particularism and comparison
strands.focus: Comparable appearances do not establish common causes; investigate particular histories before generalizing.

strands.title: Relations and transformations
strands.focus: A qualified adaptation of phonology; structural explanation still uses history.

strands.title: Public meaning and interpretation
strands.focus: Situated interpretation differs from both formal structures and private mental contents.

strands.title: Observation, statements and everyday practice
strands.focus: Different kinds of evidence enter sustained ethnographic inquiry.

strands.title: Function and social continuity
strands.focus: Relations and recurrent activities are studied through a hypothesis about the continuity of social organization.

strands.title: Culture, upbringing and comparative inquiry
strands.focus: Benedict and Mead are distinct readings; neither a homogeneous culture nor uncontested findings are assumed.
strands.works: Patterns of Culture (1934); Coming of Age in Samoa (1928)

strands.title: Gifts, obligations and goods
strands.focus: Mauss’s gift questions and Douglas/Isherwood’s consumption project supply different approaches to social exchange.
strands.works: The Gift (1925); The World of Goods (1979)

strands.title: Ritual and social process
strands.focus: Turner’s liminality and communitas frame a distinct inquiry into ritual and hierarchy.

strands.title: Historical inquiry and transformations
strands.focus: Evans-Pritchard, Leach and Sahlins take different routes between ethnography and history.
strands.works: The Sanusi (1949); Highland Burma (1954); Islands of History (1985)

strands.title: Connected histories and political economy
strands.focus: Historical anthropology connects European expansion and the histories of affected peoples.
strands.works: Europe and the People Without History (1982)

strands.title: Knowledge, authority and historical categories
strands.focus: Cohn’s colonial practices and Asad’s religion argument differ in objects and methods.
strands.works: Colonialism and Its Forms of Knowledge (1996); Genealogies of Religion (1993)

strands.title: Ethnographic writing and authority
strands.focus: A collection of arguments about ethnography’s literary and political conditions.

strands.title: Shared time and temporal distancing
strands.focus: Fabian distinguishes research communication from discourse that places its subjects in another time.

strands.title: Feminist criticism and histories of the canon
strands.focus: Rosaldo’s conceptual intervention and the later edited collection are separate projects.

strands.title: Situated scholarship and collaboration
strands.focus: Hurston’s folklore, Buck’s Māori scholarship and the Yukon collaboration have distinct research positions.
strands.works: Mules and Men (1935); The Coming of the Maori (1949); Life Lived Like a Story (1990)

strands.title: Chinese village economy and repeated inquiry
strands.focus: Fei’s retrospective connects local research initiatives, scholarly exchange and subsequent returns.

strands.title: Greek tragedy and interpretive ambiguity
strands.focus: Barthes’s named use of Vernant concerns words heard differently by characters and spectators. It establishes a specific exchange, not full verification of the historical-anthropological program.
strands.works: Vernant research discussed in “The Death of the Author” (1967)

strands.title: Shame and civilizational comparisons
strands.focus: Duerr disputes the historical and cross-cultural scope of civilization theory; the dispute remains open.

strands.title: Biographies and changing status
strands.focus: Kopytoff proposes inquiry into objects’ changing uses and statuses. Geary applies the person/thing problem to relics, while preserving uncertainty about their reception.

strands.title: Kinship and demographic comparison
strands.focus: Goody’s historical kinship questions intersect with Hajnal’s measures without being identical to them. He challenges an exclusive European category while retaining the need to explain particular differences.
strands.works: The Development of the Family and Marriage in Europe (1983),8–9

nodes.scope_note: A selective teaching map of sociocultural anthropology and ethnography, not all anthropology. Evolutionary, historical, functional, structural, interpretive, feminist and critical inquiries overlap without forming a single succession. Chinese research, Māori scholarship and collaborative histories have distinct trajectories. These approaches and rosters neither establish exclusive membership nor turn anthropology into one transferable theory.

nodes.label: National & imperial narratives
nodes.date_label: 1800s–1900s · nation-building, empire and counter-histories · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: National and imperial histories join source work to competing accounts of peoples, states, liberty and civilization. Michelet, Macaulay and Bancroft differ in method and purpose; colonial hierarchies, liberation histories and critiques of nationalist exclusions remain in tension.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: A broad context of historical production, not one school: nation-building, colonial institutions, and resistance generate different and often conflicting projects.

representative_people.context: Interweaves archives, geography, cultural life and a self-forming French people. The 1869 preface admires and disputes Thierry, credits Vico and reflects on the historian’s participation. His revolutionary history later becomes Barthes’s narrative example.
representative_people.works: Histoire de France (1833–1867), preface of 1869; Histoire de la Révolution française (1847–1853); later analysis in Barthes (1968)

representative_people.context: Connects constitutional settlement, commerce, empire and everyday manners while acknowledging crimes and failures. His education minute argues for a hierarchy of knowledge and English-trained imperial intermediaries. Distinct from Catharine Macaulay.
representative_people.works: The History of England from the Accession of James II, volume I, chapter I; “Minute on Indian Education” (2 February 1835)

representative_people.context: Combines comparative documentary criticism with a story of liberty developing from colonial institutions. His professed impartiality does not establish equal representation of all inhabitants.
representative_people.works: History of the United States / History of the Colonization of the United States, volume I (first-edition preface 1834; consulted 17th edition 1859)

representative_people.context: Uses Michelet and Thierry to question narrative transparency and examine how writing signifies historical reality. These readings do not dismiss all national histories or independently refute their factual claims.
representative_people.works: “The Discourse of History” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968)

representative_people.context: Michelet admires his national narrative while criticizing an explanatory commitment to the permanence of races; this is an attributed reception, not a reading of Thierry’s original work.
representative_people.works: Histoire de la Conquête de l’Angleterre par les Normands (1825), as discussed by Michelet and Kaplan

representative_people.context: Michelet names his account of humanity making itself as a central resource; this does not derive all national history from Vico.
representative_people.works: Scienza nuova, translated by Michelet in 1827 and recalled in his 1869 preface

representative_people.context: Michelet quotes him against explanations resting on fixed innate differences, in favor of investigating social and moral circumstances. Original Mill passage uncollated.
representative_people.works: Passage quoted in Michelet, preface to History of France (1869), p. 142

representative_people.context: Questions both colonialist and bourgeois-nationalist elitism, while recognizing overlap between popular and elite politics.
representative_people.works: “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India” (1982)

representative_people.context: Questions modular accounts of nationalism and distinguishes colonial material and spiritual domains through a particular Bengal argument.
representative_people.works: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986); The Nation and Its Fragments (1993), “Whose Imagined Community?”

representative_people.context: Attacks colonial claims to civilization and examines damage to the colonizer; distinct from an economic explanation of abolition.
representative_people.works: Discourse on Colonialism (1950; revised 1955)

representative_people.context: Recasts the Haitian Revolution through enslaved people, leadership and revolutionary conflict; national emancipation is not a uniform explanatory model.
representative_people.works: The Black Jacobins (1938)

representative_people.context: Reinterprets slavery and abolition through capitalism and empire; his specific economic propositions remain disputed.
representative_people.works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944)

representative_people.context: Regional reconstruction and a collaborative continental history provide alternatives to one national master narrative; African historical production does not begin with postwar institutions.
representative_people.works: History of the Southern Luo I (1967); “Description of the Project,” General History of Africa I (1981)

representative_people.context: Examines national consciousness, statehood and power. Paddock’s specific criticism questions organic unity and the centrality of the state; the original books remain uncollated here.
representative_people.works: Weltbürgertum und Nationalstaat (1907); Die Ideen der Staatsräson (1924); Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936), through Paddock

nodes.scope_note: A teaching umbrella, not a single national or imperial doctrine. Cultural and documentary inquiry coexist with narratives of progress. Colonial policy, anticolonial histories, subaltern criticism and collective African projects have different aims; no universal nationalist origin or automatic emancipation is implied.

strands.title: National narratives and the appearance of reality
strands.focus: Michelet’s revolutionary history becomes an object of Barthes’s analysis of detail and signification; this later reading is distinguished from original research and bibliography.
strands.works: Histoire de la Révolution française (1847–1853); Barthes (1967–1968)

strands.title: Reconstructing a people and its historical life
strands.focus: Michelet combines geography, documents, ideas and customs, proposing that France makes itself; admiration and criticism of Thierry coexist.

strands.title: Constitutional settlement, commerce and empire
strands.focus: Macaulay’s prospectus links liberties and prosperity to imperial power but also names crimes, Irish oppression and failures. Manners and material life form part of his project.
strands.works: History of England, volume I, chapter I opening

strands.title: Documentary criticism and republican beginnings
strands.focus: Bancroft seeks contemporary accounts and comparison of witnesses while reading early institutions as the beginnings of national liberty.

strands.title: Historical authority and imperial education
strands.focus: Macaulay’s minute connects public funding, language hierarchy and intermediary elites. The stated policy argument does not prove its implementation or the inferiority of other knowledge traditions.

strands.title: Different critiques of imperial narratives
strands.focus: James, Williams and Césaire contest empire through revolutionary agency, economic explanation and a critique of civilizing claims. Their arguments do not collapse into one national-liberation doctrine.
strands.works: The Black Jacobins (1938); Capitalism and Slavery (1944); Discourse on Colonialism (1950/1955)

strands.title: Nationalist exclusions and alternative scales
strands.focus: Guha and Chatterjee question elite and modular national accounts; Ogot’s regional and collaborative continental work illustrates other scales without claiming the same theoretical position.

strands.title: Historical individuality and national statehood
strands.focus: Meinecke’s historical philosophy crosses into national narration. The connection between particular development and state power requires scrutiny rather than acceptance as an organic necessity.
strands.works: Weltbürgertum und Nationalstaat (1907), through Paddock’s selected criticism

nodes.label: Economic history
nodes.date_label: 1800s roots · Economic History Society founded 1926 · multiple paradigms · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Competing explanations investigate institutions, prices and incomes, class relations, growth, households, slavery and empire. Serial history and cliometrics use different questions and models. North’s incentives differ from Polanyi’s historically specific market society; Gerschenkron questions repeated industrial paths; de Vries connects household labor and demand; Pomeranz combines regional comparison with global resource relations.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Nineteenth-century roots include classical political economy and the German historical school (e.g. Schmoller); twentieth-century examples include R. H. Tawney, Eileen Power, and Douglass North. Further approaches include Polanyi, The Great Transformation (1944); Gerschenkron, Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection); de Vries’s industrious-revolution article (1994); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000). E. A. Wrigley: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988).

representative_people.context: Treats institutions, law and custom as part of economic explanation; his dispute with Menger concerns how abstraction should proceed.
representative_people.works: “Zur Methodologie der Staats- und Sozialwissenschaften” (1883; English translation 2021)

representative_people.context: Agrarian reconstruction tests legal and economic explanations against regional and documentary differences; religion/capitalism adds ethical and causal questions.
representative_people.works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912); Religion and the Rise of Capitalism (1926)

representative_people.context: Combines medieval institutional research with personal reconstruction; distinguishes kinds of evidence and acknowledges editorial and documentary collaboration.
representative_people.works: Medieval English Nunneries (1922); Medieval People (1924)

representative_people.context: Develops institutional explanations involving rules, incentives, learning and historical paths; revises assumptions of earlier neoclassical economic history.
representative_people.works: “Economic Performance through Time” (1993 Nobel lecture)

representative_people.context: Counts paid and unpaid production while distinguishing household forms, class and marital position. Her account of capitalist change retains maternalist assumptions and contested medieval comparisons.
representative_people.works: Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century (1919), preface, introduction and conclusion

representative_people.context: Explains changes in women’s work and wages through training, household organization and industrial/agrarian change. Her qualified optimistic interpretation differs from Clark’s longer decline account.
representative_people.works: Women Workers and the Industrial Revolution, 1750–1850 (1930); reprint preface (1969, signed 1968)

representative_people.context: Production relations and class conflict shape the effects of trade. The reply to Sweezy preserves interaction, contested historical stages and a concession about insufficient evidence.
representative_people.works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); reply to Sweezy in “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), pp. 157–167

representative_people.context: Differential movements of prices, production and income support conjunctural inquiry. His 1956 introduction stresses uneven crises; later debate tests the model’s conditions and distinguishes his experiments from serial routines.
representative_people.works: Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France au XVIIIe siècle (1933); La crise de l’économie française à la fin de l’Ancien Régime et au début de la Révolution (1944); “Panoramas de la crise” (1956)

representative_people.context: Sociologist and economist whose methodological polemic challenged conventional historical explanation.
representative_people.works: “Méthode historique et science sociale” (1903)

representative_people.context: Comparative and economic historian in dialogue with the founders.
representative_people.works: “De la méthode comparative en histoire” (1923)

representative_people.context: Quantitative economic historian whose later research connects population, nutrition, physiology and growth. The cited lecture does not verify his earlier slavery estimates.
representative_people.works: “Economic Growth, Population Theory, and Physiology: The Bearing of Long-Term Processes on the Making of Economic Policy” (1993 Nobel lecture)

representative_people.context: Treats the market-regulated economy as historically specific; uses anthropology to examine reciprocity and redistribution and challenges Smith’s barter narrative.
representative_people.works: The Great Transformation (1944), especially chapter IV, “Societies and Economic Systems”

representative_people.context: Argues that later industrialization can differ in technology, scale, banks and state action; England’s path is not an automatic template.
representative_people.works: Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective: A Book of Essays (1962), title essay

representative_people.context: Relates expanding demand to household labor and resource reallocation before industrialization; considers negotiation and unequal interests within households.
representative_people.works: “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” (1994)

representative_people.context: Compares developed Eurasian regions and connects European divergence with coal and overseas resources, including coercive colonial relations. These are contested explanations.
representative_people.works: The Great Divergence: China, Europe, and the Making of the Modern World Economy (2000)

representative_people.context: Distinguishes arguments about industrial finance and abolition; both remain contested.
representative_people.works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944)

representative_people.context: Challenges the decline thesis in abolition debates; his position is not a consensus of the field.
representative_people.works: Econocide: British Slavery in the Era of Abolition (1977)

representative_people.context: Distinguishes material life, ordinary markets and capitalism while allowing overlap. His world-economy chronology and reading of Weber are arguments within debate.
representative_people.works: Afterthoughts on Material Civilization and Capitalism (1977), especially pp. 44–53, 65–67, 81–83

representative_people.context: With his co-author, critically rereads Labrousse’s experimental construction of evidence and its narrowed serial reception. This is neither rejection of every model nor unqualified defense.
representative_people.works: Grenier and Lepetit, “L’Expérience historique. À propos de C.-E. Labrousse” (1989; abstract consulted)

representative_people.context: With his co-author, critically rereads Labrousse’s experimental construction of evidence and its narrowed serial reception. This is neither rejection of every model nor unqualified defense.
representative_people.works: Grenier and Lepetit, “L’Expérience historique. À propos de C.-E. Labrousse” (1989; abstract consulted)

representative_people.context: Responds to objections to the ancien-régime crisis model by seeking conditions for theoretical justification; the checked opening does not establish the later proof.
representative_people.works: “La crise d’Ancien Régime: un essai de justification théorique” (1992), opening p. 231

representative_people.context: Investigates market conduct and crowd protest through customary norms, legitimacy and material pressures. Hunger alone does not explain the form of action.
representative_people.works: “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd in the Eighteenth Century” (1971)

representative_people.context: Questions the definition of feudalism and transfer of evidence between regions; his account permits money and instability while disputing their transformative effects.
representative_people.works: “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), critique; opening pp. 134–137 consulted

representative_people.context: A Japanese intervention develops the social form of labour and questions Dobb’s geographical coverage. The essay explicitly limits this discussion to Western Europe.
representative_people.works: “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism: A Contribution to the Sweezy-Dobb Controversy” (1952 English translation; opening consulted)

representative_people.context: Peasant research is a named resource in Dobb’s reply and Hilton’s later synthesis. The 1956 work is the Hilton context; it is not projected backward as a publication read by Dobb in 1950.
representative_people.works: Studies in the Agrarian History of England in the Thirteenth Century (1956), cited by Hilton (1973); earlier peasant interpretation cited by Dobb (1950)

representative_people.context: Craft differentiation and corporate organization offer historical resources. Dobb tentatively recalls Unwin’s contribution to his guild interpretation; the precise source of that recollection is not established.
representative_people.works: Industrial Organization in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries (1904)

representative_people.context: Comparative peasant movements join production, conflict, political organization and belief; outcomes and evidence differ across periods. Acknowledges Bloch while criticizing particular Power and Duby emphases.
representative_people.works: Bond Men Made Free (1973); “Warriors and Peasants” (1974; opening consulted)

representative_people.context: Legal and agrarian scholarship informs Tawney’s reconstruction; the introduction distinguishes legal explanations from wider economic change.
representative_people.works: Research discussed in Tawney, The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912), introduction

representative_people.context: Tawney credits research on enclosures and its revision of earlier evidence; quantitative uncertainty and interpretation remain visible.
representative_people.works: Research discussed in Tawney, The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912), introduction

representative_people.context: Tawney identifies Savine’s agrarian research among resources for revising the historical problem; this contextual record does not summarize his whole career.
representative_people.works: Research discussed in Tawney, The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912), introduction

representative_people.context: Clark credits sustained research direction; Pinchbeck credits early guidance and use of materials. These acknowledgments document teaching, not identical conclusions.
representative_people.works: Research supervision acknowledged in Clark (1919) and Pinchbeck (1930), original prefaces

representative_people.context: His 1963 preface identifies editorial reconstruction of Power’s unfinished material; it distinguishes her draft from the published wording.
representative_people.works: Preface to the tenth edition of Power, Medieval People (1963)

representative_people.context: Power credits discussion and criticism; his separate general preface sets out the series’ evidentiary policy. That preface is not her authorial statement.
representative_people.works: General preface to Power, Medieval English Nunneries (1922)

representative_people.context: Provides transcripts/translations of Alnwick’s register and reads manuscript/proofs; Power uses documentary comparison in evaluating injunctions.
representative_people.works: Alnwick register materials acknowledged and discussed in Power, Medieval English Nunneries (1922)

representative_people.context: Treats domestic service as labor connected to industrial change, rather than only a private relationship between mistress and maid.
representative_people.works: Domestic Service (1897), preface and chapters I–II; Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

representative_people.context: Compares Chinese and European economic/state trajectories, using and testing historical categories.
representative_people.works: China Transformed (1997), selected chapter openings

representative_people.context: Explains coffee-surplus destruction as support for income and employment and links crisis to the domestic market; this is retrospective historical analysis.
representative_people.works: Formação econômica do Brasil (1959), chapters XXXI–XXXII opening in2005edition

representative_people.context: Welcomes Furtado’s income-flow analysis but asks for structural explanation of wage labour and Brazil’s place in the formation of capitalism.
representative_people.works: Review of Formação econômica do Brasil (1961),277–279

representative_people.context: Explains managerial enterprise through coordination at greater throughput; the selected opening contrasts earlier market specialization with later institutional change.
representative_people.works: The Visible Hand (1977), selected Part I and chapter1 opening

representative_people.context: Distinguishes technological novelty, adoption and incremental improvement while treating invention as socially and economically situated.
representative_people.works: “The New Economic History and the Industrial Revolution” (1999), selected passages

representative_people.context: Compares changing artisanal industries in colonial India with other industrializing regions; distinguishes employment totals, organization, productivity and uneven outcomes.
representative_people.works: Traditional Industry in the Economy of Colonial India (1999), introduction

representative_people.context: Her study of older British manufactures provides a directly cited resource for Roy’s account of productivity and organization beyond spectacular inventions.
representative_people.works: The Age of Manufactures, 1700–1820, second edition (1994),40, through Roy (1999),8/note12

representative_people.context: Questions what railroad social-saving measures establish and how their counterfactual cost assumptions work.
representative_people.works: “Railroads, American Growth, and the New Economic History: A Critique” (1968), opening and notes

representative_people.context: Co-author with Temin of a methodological criticism within quantitative economic history.
representative_people.works: Comment on Fogel and Engerman (1979),213–214

representative_people.context: With David, challenges inference from revenue comparisons to technical efficiency.
representative_people.works: Comment on Fogel and Engerman (1979),213–214

representative_people.context: Fogel’s collaborator in contested slavery productivity research and subsequent replies.
representative_people.works: “Explaining the Relative Efficiency of Slave Agriculture” (1977), opening; Reply (1980), metadata only

representative_people.context: His household involution argument is disputed by Pomeranz; later criticism distinguishes rising output from returns to labor.
representative_people.works: The Peasant Family and Rural Development in the Yangzi Delta,1350–1988 (1990), through Pomeranz (2000) and Huang’s2002 review

representative_people.context: Treats household consumption as both economic and social; inventory totals are incomplete measures of wealth.
representative_people.works: Consumer Behaviour and Material Culture (1988/1996), preface and introduction

representative_people.context: Provides a named challenge about whether apparent occupational or urban ownership patterns reflect wealth.
representative_people.works: The Pre-industrial Consumer (1990), discussed by Weatherill (1996),xviii–xix

representative_people.context: Investigates agricultural labour through colonial records while distinguishing caste labels from actual occupation.
representative_people.works: Land and Caste in South India (1965), opening extracts I,IV,X

representative_people.context: Economic historian of industrialization, growth and population change. This complements his demographic, quantitative and social-history work; these are overlapping practices.
representative_people.works: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988)

strands.title: Historical economics and disciplinary institutions
strands.focus: Historical specificity and institutional research; formation of a field does not establish one doctrine.
strands.works: Schmoller’s methodological review (1883); Cunningham’s textbook (1882); Ashley and disciplinary institutions

strands.title: British economic and social history
strands.focus: Economic life studied through social relations, belief, households, and women’s work.
strands.works: Tawney, Religion and the Rise of Capitalism; Power, Medieval People; Clark and Pinchbeck on women’s labour

strands.title: French serial and conjunctural history
strands.focus: Simiand and Labrousse investigate different economic movements. Later rereadings distinguish construction of evidence, causal conditions and routine series; uneven crises need not fit one automatic sequence.
strands.works: Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France au XVIIIe siècle (1933); La crise de l’économie française à la fin de l’Ancien Régime et au début de la Révolution (1944); “Panoramas de la crise” (1956); Grenier/Lepetit (1989); Simonin (1992)

strands.title: Capitalist development and contested production relations
strands.focus: Coercion, markets, wage labour and the state are related explanatory problems. Dobb’s reply acknowledges uncertainty about one accumulation hypothesis; Sweezy and Takahashi pose different challenges.
strands.works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); reply to Sweezy in “The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism” (1950), pp. 157–167; Takahashi (1952); Unwin (1904)

strands.title: Cliometrics and historical measurement
strands.focus: Economic models and quantitative evidence; neither all economic history nor all quantitative history.
strands.works: Fogel, “Economic Growth, Population Theory, and Physiology” (1993); North, “Economic Performance through Time” (1993)

strands.title: Institutions and economic change
strands.focus: Rules, incentives, learning, and historical paths; overlaps with cliometrics without being identical to it.

strands.title: Slavery, empire, and unequal development
strands.focus: Different arguments about capitalist development and colonial power; Drescher contests the decline explanation for British slave-trade abolition.
strands.works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944); How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972); Econocide (1977)

strands.title: Market society and nonmarket economic relations
strands.focus: Polanyi distinguishes a market-regulated economy from reciprocity and redistribution; his broad historical claims are arguments to examine, not settled descriptions of every society.

strands.title: Different paths of later industrialization
strands.focus: Compare technology borrowing, industrial scale and the roles of banks and states; later industrializers need not repeat England’s sequence.
strands.works: Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962 collection)

strands.title: Household labor, demand and industrious change
strands.focus: Changes in household resource allocation can increase market labor and demand together. Household members’ interests differ, and the proposed pattern is not universal.
strands.works: “The Industrial Revolution and the Industrious Revolution” (1994)

strands.title: Regional comparison and global divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz compares developed regions within Eurasia and connects divergence with coal and overseas resources, avoiding an undifferentiated Europe-versus-Asia contrast.

strands.title: Material life, markets and capitalism
strands.focus: Braudel distinguishes overlapping economic activities and geographically centered world-economies. His disagreement with Weber and selective Wallerstein dialogue are attributed arguments, not a settled universal history.
strands.works: Afterthoughts on Material Civilization and Capitalism (1977)

strands.title: Market norms and popular action
strands.focus: Thompson asks how customary expectations authorize or constrain protest and exchange; Mintz supplies a named anthropological resource. This is a situated inquiry into English crowds, not a universal premarket economy.
strands.works: “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

strands.title: Agrarian change and documentary comparability
strands.focus: Tawney distinguishes regional and temporal patterns, tenant and landlord activity, legal forms and economic pressures. His introduction treats incomplete statistics and incompatible records as problems of inference.
strands.works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912), introduction

strands.title: Women’s work, household forms and economic change
strands.focus: Clark and Pinchbeck distinguish home production from wages, while differing over the timing and consequences of economic change. Their acknowledgments make research guidance and shared materials part of this scholarship.
strands.works: Working Life of Women (1919); Women Workers (1930)

strands.title: Domestic service as an economic question
strands.focus: Salmon connects household employment with industrial specialization and challenges its reduction to a private complaint. Her historical model and proposed remedies are arguments to assess, not a universal account of women’s experience.
strands.works: Domestic Service (1897), chapters I–II; Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

strands.title: Brazilian income flows and structural criticism
strands.focus: Furtado’s coffee-crisis argument connects demand and historical change; Novais asks how wage labour and capitalism’s formation explain the transformation. Their exchange keeps macroeconomic analysis open to historical criticism.

strands.title: Managerial coordination and the scale of activity
strands.focus: Chandler’s selected opening links new energy, transport and communication capacities to the conditions for administrative coordination. Earlier growth and specialization could remain compatible with owner-managed firms and market exchange.
strands.works: The Visible Hand (1977), Part I and chapter1 opening

strands.title: Artisans and uneven industrialization in India
strands.focus: Roy examines five crafts rather than treating textile decline as universal. His introduction distinguishes family work, wage labour, markets and organizational change, while acknowledging that adaptation did not yield development comparable to Europe or Japan.
strands.works: Traditional Industry in the Economy of Colonial India (1999), introduction

strands.title: Firms, inventions and forms of work
strands.focus: Compare Chandler’s American enterprise scale, Mokyr’s British technological change and Roy’s Indian artisanal reorganization. These explanations concern different units and periods; none supplies a universal sequence from household to large factory.
strands.works: Chandler (1977); Mokyr (1999); Roy (1999), selected primary passages

strands.title: Railroads and the meaning of social saving
strands.focus: McClelland contests identifying measured transport savings with the railroad’s entire contribution to growth. His notes question the relation between observed freight prices and marginal costs under altered traffic and competition.
strands.works: Railroads and American Economic Growth (1964); McClelland (1968), opening and notes

strands.title: Slavery productivity and a contested inference
strands.focus: Fogel and Engerman’s opening specifies a total-factor-productivity index. David and Temin argue that national-price aggregation across differing crop mixes need not rank technical efficiency: climate, prices and risk complicate the inference.

strands.title: Household production and disputed divergence
strands.focus: Pomeranz challenges Huang’s involution thesis and compares household labor with industrious change. Huang’s later review argues that output growth can conceal diminishing returns to work; Pomeranz’s reply opening rejects one necessary path to development.
strands.works: Pomeranz (2000),17; Huang and Pomeranz (2002), selected retrospective passages

strands.title: Coal, constraints and competing explanations
strands.focus: Pomeranz links accessible energy and colonial resources to relief of land constraints. Huang questions whether coal availability explains divergence or industrial demand explains coal development. The exchange leaves causal weights open to examination.

strands.title: Wealth and the measurement of goods
strands.focus: Weatherill acknowledges Shammas’s challenge: ownership patterns associated with occupation or towns may reflect wealth. Their different data constructions ask different questions.

strands.title: Agrarian labour and recorded categories
strands.focus: Kumar’s southern Indian inquiry combines documentary interpretation with quantitative reconstruction. Her stated caste/occupation assumptions must remain visible when discussing estimates.
strands.works: Land and Caste in South India (1965), opening extracts I,IV,X

strands.title: Population and the character of industrial growth
strands.focus: Wrigley investigates population change and the contingent character of industrial growth. This bounded summary follows the Economic History Society account; the two books have not been reread here.
strands.works: People, Cities and Wealth (1987); Continuity, Chance and Change (1988)

nodes.scope_note: Distinguish the relevant historians, evidence, and mechanisms before claiming an influence. A subject shared with Annales or Marxism is not itself an explanation. Institutional approaches are not interchangeable, and consumption does not replace production. Household interests can conflict. Gerschenkron’s European comparison and Pomeranz’s Eurasian argument have distinct scales; neither is a universal development law. Furtado’s demand analysis and Novais’s structural criticism offer a Brazilian exchange, with primary-edition and numerical verification limits retained.

nodes.label: Military history
nodes.date_label: Earlier roots · Howard 1961 · Keegan 1976 · multiple paradigms · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Studies campaigns and combat alongside institutions, societies, maritime power, gender and remembrance. Howard’s contextual reconstruction, Keegan’s critical study of battle and debates over military revolutions supply different methods and explanations. Source access, narrative framing and geographic scope shape their claims.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Distinct roots include Clausewitz, On War (1832), and Hans Delbrück; later examples: Michael Howard, John Keegan, and Joanna Bourke.

representative_people.context: Examines political purpose, passion, chance and friction in an unfinished, posthumously edited work. Strategic reasoning differs from empirical verification of particular campaigns.
representative_people.works: On War (1832); selected passages in Graham translation with later editorial apparatus

representative_people.context: Joins philological criticism to checks of practical possibility, using population evidence and documentary research. Explicitly acknowledges Ranke and Beloch; possible reconstructions are not automatically established events.
representative_people.works: Geschichte der Kriegskunst im Rahmen der politischen Geschichte, four volumes (1900–1920); first preface (1900)

representative_people.context: Combines campaign reconstruction, wider social context and war-studies teaching. Archival loss/access constrained the 1961 study; later Ultra disclosure exposed limits of official Grand Strategy records.
representative_people.works: The Franco-Prussian War (1961); Grand Strategy, IV (1972); War in European History (1976)

representative_people.context: Studies combat experience through critically assessed testimony, documents and physical possibility. Sandhurst teaching, Delbrück/Burne and scholarly/library assistance inform the work; his battle definition leaves much colonial and guerrilla experience outside its frame.
representative_people.works: The Face of Battle (1976), available opening excerpt; A History of Warfare (1993), separate argument mediated by Bassford

representative_people.context: Studies bodily injury, disease and masculinity in Britain during and after the Great War.
representative_people.works: Dismembering the Male (1996)

representative_people.context: Builds the opening-war narrative around decisions and circumstances. Her methodological excerpt insists on documented detail; the full Guns of August source apparatus remains to be collated.
representative_people.works: The Guns of August (1962); “In Search of History,” publisher excerpt in Practicing History (consulted 1982 edition)

representative_people.context: Combines campaigns, diplomacy and narrative; her German-centered framing of the Thirty Years War attracts criticism.
representative_people.works: The Thirty Years War (1938); “The Strategy of the Great Civil War” (1945)

representative_people.context: Cultural history of Great War mourning complicates a simple rupture in forms of remembrance.
representative_people.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995)

representative_people.context: An early recovery of Black service and exclusion from national remembrance.
representative_people.works: The Colored Patriots of the American Revolution (1855)

representative_people.context: Expands the military-revolution debate around fortifications and chronology. Separately criticizes Wedgwood’s framing, as reported by Woolrych; original cited book passages remain unread.
representative_people.works: “The ‘Military Revolution,’ 1560–1660—a Myth?” (1976; revised 1979); The Military Revolution (1988); The Thirty Years War (1984), pp. xv, 216–217, mediated by Woolrych

representative_people.context: Proposes explaining sea power within general history and its social, political and economic surroundings. His naval-professional perspective and selected Europe/America scope are explicit.
representative_people.works: The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783 (1890), preface

representative_people.context: Treats naval operations within wider maritime coordination of armies, fleets and political purposes. Theory aids education and deliberation; this is a situated British imperial perspective.
representative_people.works: Some Principles of Maritime Strategy (1911), introduction

representative_people.context: Proposes and collaborates with Howard on a new Clausewitz translation. Strachan later assesses its modernization; translating does not simply transmit an unchanged meaning.
representative_people.works: With Michael Howard, On War (1976), translation; collaboration documented by Strachan

representative_people.context: Challenges Keegan’s culture/politics opposition while valuing The Face of Battle. Later web corrections are distinguished from the original polemic.
representative_people.works: “John Keegan and the Grand Tradition of Trashing Clausewitz” (1994)

representative_people.context: Keegan uses Inherent Military Probability with caution about assuming armies act alike across time.
representative_people.works: Inherent Military Probability, discussed in The Face of Battle (1976) excerpt

representative_people.context: Named colleague and source of a recounted practical drill experiment; a resource for asking what combat descriptions physically imply.
representative_people.works: Acknowledgments and drill experiment in The Face of Battle (1976) excerpt

representative_people.context: Sandhurst librarian acknowledged by Keegan; library work joins interlibrary loans and other research assistance in producing the book.
representative_people.works: Research/library assistance acknowledged in The Face of Battle (1976)

representative_people.context: Proposes tactical change with wider institutional effects; the opening is read directly, later argument mediated by Rogers.
representative_people.works: “The Military Revolution, 1560–1660” (1955 lecture; 1956 publication; revised 1967)

representative_people.context: Argues for multiple episodes of military change and edits the competing interpretations.
representative_people.works: “The Military Revolutions of the Hundred Years’ War” (1993); The Military Revolution Debate (1995), editor

representative_people.context: Questions the conventional chronology, emphasizing continuity and later change; mediated by Rogers.
representative_people.works: A Military Revolution? Military Change and European Society (1991)

representative_people.context: Tests army-growth claims and challenges a fortification-led explanation; mediated by Rogers.
representative_people.works: “Recalculating French Army Growth” (1994; revised 1995)

representative_people.context: Examines finance and political concessions, qualifying automatic state centralization; mediated by Rogers.
