representative_people.works: Data contribution credited in Ferrie (1996 manuscript), note10 and Table1

representative_people.context: Makes assumptions and category changes explicit in estimates of nineteenth-century agricultural labour in southern India.
representative_people.works: Land and Caste in South India (1965), opening extracts I,IV,X

representative_people.context: Coauthors the parish-register research programme and its requirement for a deliberately sampled national inquiry.
representative_people.works: With Louis Henry, “Pour connaître la population de la France depuis Louis XIV” (1958),663–665

representative_people.context: Coauthors the inventory of surviving parish registers with Fleury and Henry.
representative_people.works: “Inventaire par sondage des registres paroissiaux de France” (1960), coauthorship checked

representative_people.context: Lee and Wang explicitly credit his collaborative publications and intellectual and editorial contributions.
representative_people.works: Contributions acknowledged in One Quarter of Humanity (1999)

strands.title: Serial evidence and collective patterns
strands.focus: Prices and incomes support conjunctural and social questions without requiring neoclassical theory.
strands.works: Esquisse du mouvement des prix et des revenus en France au XVIIIe siècle (1933)

strands.title: Population reconstruction
strands.focus: Family linkage and aggregate reconstruction differ in units and assumptions; missing mobile families are a methodological problem Henry explicitly identifies.
strands.works: Anciennes familles genevoises (1956); The Population History of England (1981)

strands.title: Cliometrics
strands.focus: Fogel’s counterfactual railroad comparison and North’s institutional development are different uses of economic reasoning; neither stands for all quantitative history.
strands.works: Railroads and American Economic Growth (1964); “Economic Performance through Time” (1993)

strands.title: Electoral groups and competing explanations
strands.focus: Compare economic interests with ethnic and religious affiliations in New York voting; Benson’s categories overlap and his argument is not a universal law of elections.

strands.title: Occupations, property and social mobility
strands.focus: Separate occupational change from property accumulation through linked local records; Thernstrom’s use of Weber broadens class beyond a single occupational ranking.

strands.title: Slavery: estimates, coercion and interpretation
strands.focus: Read the cliometric study alongside Gutman’s criticism of its labor/cooperation interpretation; neither efficiency estimates nor a book’s polemical reception alone describe enslaved people’s lives.
strands.works: Time on the Cross (1974); Slavery and the Numbers Game (1975)

strands.title: Estimating the Atlantic slave trade
strands.focus: Reconstruct the scale of forced migration from uneven evidence. Curtin’s influential estimates were later revised; totals do not substitute for histories of violence and agency.
strands.works: The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census (1969)

strands.title: Household surveys and the limits of response
strands.focus: Salmon combines employer and worker returns, bureau tabulation and wage comparisons. Distribution through college and association networks, reluctance to reply and uneven knowledge qualify her representativeness claims.

strands.title: Counterfactual assumptions and sensitivity
strands.focus: McClelland’s criticism makes alternative transport capacity, pricing and cost assumptions explicit questions. Critiquing a model’s inference is itself quantitative historical work.

strands.title: Revenue and technical efficiency
strands.focus: David and Temin distinguish revenue from producing the same outputs with fewer inputs. Their specific objection should be read with the authors’ reply; the reply is located here, but its body remains unchecked.

strands.title: Who remains visible in mobility records?
strands.focus: Ferrie questions findings based on local stayers and late observation after arrival. Linking migrants expands observation, but selective linkage and occupational coding still constrain inference.

strands.title: Caste, occupation and colonial counts
strands.focus: Kumar states the assumptions needed to estimate earlier agricultural labour from later caste counts. Changing census categories and officials’ conflation of caste with occupation limit comparison.
strands.works: Land and Caste in South India (1965), opening extracts IV,X

strands.title: Sampling parishes and their surviving records
strands.focus: The Fleury–Henry programme requires more than a collection of convenient local studies. Its later implementation changes sampling to meet practical constraints and treats earlier, poorer records separately.

strands.title: Fertility measures and their denominators
strands.focus: Lee and Wang distinguish synthetic total fertility from fertility within marriage and state adjustments to several underlying estimates. Interpreting those measures requires more than comparing the resulting totals.
strands.works: One Quarter of Humanity (1999), Table6.1 notes and86–90

nodes.scope_note: Serial history, demographic reconstruction, and cliometrics use numbers differently. A quantitative method does not establish a common theory. Counting, source linkage and formal modeling require different assumptions. Recorded categories, missing people and units of comparison shape conclusions; neither criticism nor narrative history ended quantitative research.

nodes.label: Contextual intellectual history / Cambridge School
nodes.description: Reads arguments as interventions in historically specific linguistic and political contexts. Skinner emphasizes what authors were doing in writing; Pocock reconstructs political languages. The Cambridge School is a grouping of related projects, not a uniform method or a synonym for every contextual history. Dunn joins philosophical precision to reconstructing historical acts; Laslett’s textual editing and later inquiries into rights extend the grouping without supplying one shared doctrine.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Quentin Skinner, “Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas” (1969); J. G. A. Pocock.

representative_people.context: Asks what an author could be doing in a historically situated intervention. Social conditions matter, but cannot alone identify its intended force; his selective Collingwood reception includes explicit criticism.
representative_people.works: Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas (1969)

representative_people.context: Studies historically available levels of argument and political languages. The Machiavellian Moment selects republican fragility in time and a proposed Atlantic continuation, acknowledging multiple resources and collaboration with Skinner.
representative_people.works: The Ancient Constitution and the Feudal Law (1957; bibliography checked); The history of political thought: a methodological inquiry (1962; selected reprint); The Machiavellian Moment (1975), introduction vii–x

representative_people.context: Skinner explicitly recalls his changing questions and question/answer logic. This is selective reception alongside analytical philosophy and does not establish uniform Cambridge idealism.
representative_people.works: An Autobiography (1939), reception in Skinner’s 2002 interview

representative_people.context: Skinner recalls reading the Investigations and making use, purpose and public intelligibility central to his questions. This is his particular reception, not a description of every Cambridge historian.
representative_people.works: Philosophical Investigations (1953; Skinner recalls his revised 1958 edition), reception in On Encountering the Past (2002)

representative_people.context: Skinner explicitly recalls Austin’s account of doing things with words as a resource for asking what historical authors were doing. The interview documents reception; Austin’s full lectures remain separately uncollated.
representative_people.works: How To Do Things with Words (1962), reception through Skinner’s 2002 interview

representative_people.context: Joins philosophical precision to historical acts, distinguishing propositions from what a person does in making a statement. He acknowledges exchanges with Laslett and Skinner without claiming complete agreement.
representative_people.works: The Identity of the History of Ideas (1968), selected pp. 85–104

representative_people.context: Critical editing of Locke is an important contextual project. Dunn acknowledges discussion; later scholarship questions a straightforward Laslett-to-Skinner methodological succession.
representative_people.works: John Locke, Two Treatises of Government, edited with introduction by Laslett (1960; edition metadata and reception checked)

representative_people.context: Skinner and Dunn explicitly draw on problems of perceptual expectations and interpretation. This is a specified resource, not evidence that all contextual historians adopted Gombrich’s art history.
representative_people.works: Art and Illusion (1960), cited by Skinner (1969), p. 7, and Dunn (1968), notes

representative_people.context: Skinner invokes the priority of paradigms in interpreting evidence; Dunn also acknowledges the work among methodological resources.
representative_people.works: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), chapter V, reception in Skinner (1969), p. 7

representative_people.context: Dunn discusses reconstructing Plato’s intellectual activity through Ryle’s philosophical-historical interpretation. This is distinct from Ryle’s knowing-how argument.
representative_people.works: Plato’s Progress (1966), reception in Dunn (1968), p. 94 and note 20

representative_people.context: Pocock uses the vocabulary of political traditions while questioning whether its philosophical statement adequately explains a historian’s method.
representative_people.works: Political Education (1956), reception in Pocock’s methodological inquiry (1962), reprint pp. 3–5

representative_people.context: Pocock explicitly identifies Baron’s civic-humanist interpretation as an important and controversial resource. This records reception, not independent verification of Baron’s whole thesis.
representative_people.works: Civic-humanist interpretation acknowledged in The Machiavellian Moment (1975), introduction

representative_people.context: Skinner acknowledges practical-syllogism analysis when separating intentional action from a merely external causal account.
representative_people.works: Intention (1957), reception in Skinner (1969), p. 44

representative_people.context: Investigates ius across varied scholastic philosophical contexts, questioning a single simplified origin of individual rights. Scope here follows the book description; body chapters remain uncollated.
representative_people.works: Liberty, Right and Nature: Individual Rights in Later Scholastic Thought (1997)

representative_people.context: Combines historical and critical political inquiry around Locke, including property, toleration and Aboriginal rights. Listed subjects do not establish the conclusions of unread chapters.
representative_people.works: An Approach to Political Philosophy: Locke in Contexts (1993)

representative_people.context: Traces natural-rights arguments from medieval roots into seventeenth-century debates. This is his proposed inquiry, not a claim that Brett or Tully share all its conclusions.
representative_people.works: Natural Rights Theories: Their Origin and Development (1979)

nodes.scope_note: Skinner’s interventions and Pocock’s political languages are related but not identical; the Cambridge School is narrower than all contextual interpretation. Public conventions constrain possible interventions; historical context is neither a complete causal deduction of a text nor recovery of a private intention without evidence. Later accounts dispute simple Laslett-to-Skinner founding narratives. Named philosophical resources are particular receptions, not school membership.

strands.title: Skinner’s philosophical resources
strands.focus: His retrospective account joins changing questions in Collingwood with language use in Wittgenstein and doing things with words in Austin. This records an acknowledged combination in Skinner’s work, not their doctrinal identity.
strands.works: On Encountering the Past (2002), answers 1 and 6 about earlier work

strands.title: Interventions, conventions and intended force
strands.focus: Skinner separates what words mean from what an author is doing with them. Public conventions and evidence constrain interpretation; a social setting alone does not determine the complete meaning of an intervention.

strands.title: Historically available levels of argument
strands.focus: Pocock asks at what level people actually formulated political ideas. A maximally coherent philosophical reconstruction and a history of thinking are legitimate but different inquiries; ideas remain historical events even when not the sole cause of action.
strands.works: The history of political thought: a methodological inquiry (1962), reprint pp. 3–11

strands.title: Republican fragility, virtue and corruption
strands.focus: Pocock’s introduction selects the problem of a republic’s existence in time, then proposes English and Atlantic continuations involving property, arms and commerce. It acknowledges Baron’s controversial resource and Skinner’s collaboration; this is a selected argument, not an exhaustive Atlantic narrative.

strands.title: Philosophical precision and historical acts
strands.focus: Dunn distinguishes a proposition’s logical identity from a historical statement’s activity, including irony and polemic. Reconstructing the act requires evidence of the person’s available situation; philosophical and historical problems cannot simply replace one another.
strands.works: The Identity of the History of Ideas (1968), selected pp. 85–104

strands.title: Critical editions and disputed methodological succession
strands.focus: Laslett’s Locke edition and discussions with Dunn belong to contextual inquiry. They do not establish that Skinner inherited a complete method from him; Furuta’s later argument explicitly contests such a simple sequence.
strands.works: Two Treatises of Government, Laslett edition (1960); Dunn (1968); Furuta (2021), abstract

strands.title: Rights across philosophical and political contexts
strands.focus: Tuck traces natural-rights theories, Brett differentiates scholastic uses of ius, and Tully joins historical with critical inquiry around Locke. These projects extend the range of questions without forming one origin story; the present selections rely on scoped descriptions.
strands.works: Natural Rights Theories (1979); Locke in Contexts (1993); Liberty, Right and Nature (1997)

nodes.label: Dependency / world-systems
nodes.description: Related but distinct approaches explain development and underdevelopment through historically unequal relations of capitalism, empire, and exchange. Marxist concepts are reworked alongside other resources; dependency theory has non-Marxist as well as Marxist strands, and world-systems analysis is not simply British Marxist social history enlarged. Prebisch’s industrialization strategy, Frank’s metropolitan–satellite hypotheses, dos Santos’s internal/external constraints, Cardoso and Faletto’s political alliances, and Wallerstein’s system-level unit require separate readings. Industrial growth and dependence are not mutually exclusive in all these accounts.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: André Gunder Frank; Walter Rodney, How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972); Immanuel Wallerstein (1974).

representative_people.context: Proposes that metropolitan–satellite relations historically produce underdevelopment, with hypotheses about export ties and their weakening; this is a contested account, not an earlier national stage.
representative_people.works: The Development of Underdevelopment (1966), reprint pp. 86–93

representative_people.context: African historical explanation in a wider political project.
representative_people.works: How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972)

representative_people.context: Practitioner and theorist of world-systems historical analysis. Uses a world-economy’s division of labor as the unit, combining historical sources with theory. His definition includes coerced labor and is explicitly disputed with Dobb’s production-relations account. The role describes his practice in this selection, not an exclusive disciplinary credential or affiliation with every dependency programme.
representative_people.works: The Modern World-System I (1974); The Rise and Future Demise of the World Capitalist System (1974), selected pages

representative_people.context: Distinguishes colonial, financial-industrial and technological-industrial dependence, connecting external constraints with internal production and class relations.
representative_people.works: The Structure of Dependence (1970)

representative_people.context: With Faletto, makes political processes and internal/external alliances central; dependent development is not synonymous with no industrialization.
representative_people.works: With Enzo Faletto, Dependency and Development in Latin America (English 1979; Spanish original 1969)

representative_people.context: Coauthors the historical-political inquiry into dependency and development; national struggles and alliances matter alongside external relations.
representative_people.works: With Fernando Henrique Cardoso, Dependency and Development in Latin America (English 1979; Spanish original 1969)

representative_people.context: Argues that technical gains are distributed unequally; industrialization requires primary exports and capital imports. A structuralist resource and later target, not identical to Marxist dependency.
representative_people.works: El desarrollo económico de la América Latina y algunos de sus principales problemas (1949), selected introduction

representative_people.context: Frank selectively uses his Brazilian economic history while disputing broader conclusions. This contextual reception does not make Furtado an adherent of every Frank hypothesis.
representative_people.works: Formação econômica do Brasil (1959), cited in Frank’s 1966 note 6

representative_people.context: Develops a Marxist dependency inquiry centered on production and labor exploitation; the archive identifies his central work, while its full mechanism and polemical exchanges remain to be checked.
representative_people.works: Dialéctica de la dependencia (1973)

representative_people.context: Defends a distinct Marxist current and examines foreign capital within domestic domination, while identifying unfinished empirical research on states. Her claim of theoretical vindication remains contestable.
representative_people.works: El capitalismo dependiente latinoamericano (1974); O capitalismo dependente latino-americano e sua teoria crítica (1986 conference)

representative_people.context: Studies peripheral social formations and uneven accumulation. The checked description supports a related project, without making it identical to Frank or Wallerstein.
representative_people.works: Unequal Development (English 1976; French original 1973)

representative_people.context: Studies successive configurations of accumulation and state power; this is a distinct historical-sociological account within the wider systemic discussion.
representative_people.works: The Long Twentieth Century (1994)

strands.title: Frank’s metropolitan–satellite hypotheses
strands.focus: International, national and local relations historically produce underdevelopment in Frank’s argument; export decline and weak ties figure in hypotheses requiring further research.

strands.title: African underdevelopment
strands.focus: A historical argument centred on Africa and colonial relations, not interchangeable with every dependency model.

strands.title: World-systems analysis
strands.focus: The division of labor defines the historical unit, with external arenas distinguished from internal exchange. Coerced labor can belong to capitalism in Wallerstein’s contested account.
strands.works: The Modern World-System I; The Rise and Future Demise (1974)

strands.title: Structuralist development and its critics
strands.focus: Prebisch advocates industrialization through an expanded trade relationship; dos Santos uses ECLA research but contests the sufficiency of its policies.

strands.title: Internal structures and external constraints
strands.focus: Dos Santos distinguishes historical forms of dependence; industrial expansion can reproduce technological and financial constraints.

strands.title: Political alliances and dependent development
strands.focus: Cardoso and Faletto’s project gives historical political processes a central role; it cannot be collapsed into a universal stagnation thesis.
strands.works: Dependency and Development in Latin America (1969/1979)

strands.title: Marxist dependency and internal disagreement
strands.focus: Bambirra defends a Marxist current including Marini while recognizing research gaps; her attacks on rival currents remain attributed arguments.
strands.works: Bambirra (1986); Marini, Dialéctica de la dependencia (1973)

strands.title: Peripheral accumulation and changing world powers
strands.focus: Amin’s peripheral formations and Arrighi’s accumulation/state-power inquiry provide related but distinct projects, not one common cycle model.
strands.works: Unequal Development (1973/1976); The Long Twentieth Century (1994)

nodes.scope_note: Dependency theories, Rodney’s African history, and Wallerstein’s world-system are related but cannot share every incoming or outgoing claim. Structuralist precursors are not automatically Marxist dependentistas. Bambirra’s defense of one Marxist current is a situated intervention; neither it nor Wallerstein’s disputed definition of capitalism settles the umbrella’s boundaries.

nodes.label: New cultural history
nodes.description: Meaning, symbols, rituals, representation, and practices help constitute social life. Draws on anthropology and multiple historical traditions.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Natalie Zemon Davis; Clifford Geertz as an influence; Lynn Hunt, The New Cultural History (1989).

representative_people.context: Class is a historical relationship formed through material experience and culture; the Making preface explicitly restricts its study to English developments.
representative_people.works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963); “Time, Work-Discipline, and Industrial Capitalism” (1967); “The Moral Economy of the English Crowd” (1971)

representative_people.context: Compares Glikl, Marie de l’Incarnation and Merian without making them one universal female trajectory. An explicitly imagined prologue tests her categories; stories, religious difference, colonial power and textual mediation shape interpretation.
representative_people.works: Women on the Margins (1995), prologue, selected Glikl opening, conclusion and acknowledgments

representative_people.context: Brings plural cultural approaches into debate while investigating political symbols and practices alongside a sociology of revolutionary politics.
representative_people.works: Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution (1984); The New Cultural History (1989), editor and introduction author

representative_people.context: An anthropological resource, not a historian’s membership in a school.
representative_people.works: The Interpretation of Cultures (1973)

representative_people.context: Reading depends on material forms and differentiated practices. Collective representations help explain social divisions; critical fidelity to Annales includes disagreement with Braudel’s hierarchy.
representative_people.works: “Le monde comme représentation” (1989); Lectures et lecteurs dans la France d’Ancien Régime (1987, contextual reference cited in the article)

representative_people.context: Uses cricket and autobiographical social experience to investigate culture and aesthetics.
representative_people.works: Beyond a Boundary (1963)

representative_people.context: Chartier explicitly uses McKenzie’s account of the meanings produced by textual forms; conceptual resource, not membership in one historical school.
representative_people.works: Bibliography and the Sociology of Texts (1986; Panizzi Lectures 1985), cited by Chartier (1989)

representative_people.context: Chartier uses Marin’s analysis of signs and representation in examining the relation between absent objects, present images and conventions of recognition.
representative_people.works: La critique du discours: Étude sur la Logique de Port-Royal et les Pensées de Pascal (1975), discussed by Chartier (1989)

representative_people.context: The meeting of text and reader supplies Chartier a resource; he also differentiates historically situated appropriation from a universal account of self-understanding.
representative_people.works: Temps et récit, vol. III, Le temps raconté (1985), pp. 228–263 as cited by Chartier (1989)

representative_people.context: Interpretive communities help Chartier specify differentiated reading practices, without making all readers in a society identical.
representative_people.works: Is There a Text in This Class? The Authority of Interpretive Communities (1980), pp. 1–17, cited by Chartier (1989)

representative_people.context: Interprets unusual documents as entry points into historical meanings; the reader can contest his interpretations, and he explicitly disclaims a representative sample.
representative_people.works: The Great Cat Massacre (1984), introduction

representative_people.context: Investigates preindustrial popular culture; his later historiographical reflection questions a simple succession of cultural approaches.
representative_people.works: Popular Culture in Early Modern Europe (1978); “From Cultural History to Histories of Cultures” (undated electronic essay)

representative_people.context: Feminist analysis supplies a formative cultural-history resource in Hunt’s account and a directly acknowledged social/textual resource for Spiegel.
representative_people.works: “The Body Politic” (1989), draft and p. 101 cited by Spiegel (1993)

representative_people.context: Treats gender and experience as historical questions, joining cultural and institutional interpretation.
representative_people.works: “Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis” (1986); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

representative_people.context: Examines historical uses of Foucault. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Michel Foucault’s History of Culture, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Reconsiders community and ritual through conflict and gender. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Crowds, Community, and Ritual in the Work of E. P. Thompson and Natalie Davis, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: An anthropologist comparing interpretive resources and structure/event questions. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Local Knowledge, Local History: Geertz and Beyond, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Distinguishes literary resources in White and LaCapra. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Literature, Criticism, and Historical Imagination: The Literary Challenge of Hayden White and Dominick LaCapra, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Reads parades as changing representations of social divisions. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: The American Parade: Representations of the Nineteenth-Century Social Order, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Investigates narratives that make suffering a humanitarian concern. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Bodies, Details, and the Humanitarian Narrative, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Studies visual attention beyond a simple language analogy. Context follows Hunt’s introduction; chapter body remains unread.
representative_people.works: Seeing Culture in a Room for a Renaissance Prince, in Hunt, ed., The New Cultural History (1989)

representative_people.context: Compares connoisseurship prescriptions with administrative classifications of possessions.
representative_people.works: Superfluous Things (1991), chapter 2 excerpt

representative_people.context: Studies contested authentication and the narratives accompanying transferred relics.
representative_people.works: “Sacred Commodities” (1986),186–190

nodes.scope_note: Anthropological interpretation, historical representations, and class/cultural experience are distinct resources; culture does not arrive after material explanation ends.

strands.title: Class, conflict and cultural experience
strands.focus: Culture helps constitute social relationships in early Marxist and Caribbean inquiries; later cultural history does not inaugurate attention to meaning.

strands.title: Anthropological interpretation and its disputes
strands.focus: Historical interpretation adapts anthropology while debating coherence, differences and what documents permit.
strands.works: The Great Cat Massacre (1984); The New Cultural History (1989)

strands.title: Gender, community and conflict
strands.focus: Gender contributes to cultural inquiry and complicates unified pictures of communities and rituals.
strands.works: Gender (1986); The Body Politic and Desan chapter (1989)

strands.title: Material texts and differentiated readers
strands.focus: Textual form, circulation and appropriation help explain meanings and social divisions.

strands.title: Political symbols and public performance
strands.focus: Symbols, practices and public displays enter political and social explanation.
strands.works: Politics, Culture, and Class (1984); The American Parade (1989)

strands.title: Narrative, criticism and humanitarian concern
strands.focus: Narrative form is both a problem of historical writing and a historical object.
strands.works: Kramer and Laqueur chapters (1989); Rethinking Intellectual History (1983)

strands.title: Visual practice and attention
strands.focus: Seeing and situated attention need examination beyond a simple analogy between images and language.
strands.works: Seeing Culture in a Room for a Renaissance Prince (1989)

strands.title: Popular cultures and historical plurality
strands.focus: Popular culture is a historical subject with variable practices, not one timeless folk essence.
strands.works: Popular Culture in Early Modern Europe (1978)

strands.title: Objects and textual categories
strands.focus: Clunas asks how prescriptions and inventories classify objects. Their categories shape what historians can reconstruct; surviving museum objects alone cannot supply the whole material world.

nodes.label: Linguistic turn / poststructuralism
nodes.description: Examines how language, narrative, discourse, and power shape historical knowledge and subject formation. Narrative theory, structuralist inheritances, and poststructuralist critiques overlap but are not interchangeable. This node groups debates rather than identifying one school.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Michel Foucault; Jacques Derrida; Hayden White, Metahistory (1973).

representative_people.context: Discourse, genealogy and subject formation are related, changing inquiries; institutional and practical relations enter the account. Historians adapt and criticize them in different ways.
representative_people.works: The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969); “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History” (1971); “The Subject and Power” (1982)

representative_people.context: Questions conceptual hierarchies and conditions of signification through close reading and institutional questions; no mechanical rule permits arbitrary interpretation.
representative_people.works: Of Grammatology (1967); “Letter to a Japanese Friend” (1983); Archive Fever (1994/1996)

representative_people.context: Historical narrative theory; not every position under the linguistic turn.
representative_people.works: Metahistory (1973)

representative_people.context: Reworks signification and unconscious interpretation; the linguistic turn is not a uniform Lacanian program.
representative_people.works: “Le stade du miroir” (1949); “L’instance de la lettre” (1957); Écrits collection (1966)

representative_people.context: Theorizes material ideology and the constitution of subjects; reception is specifically documented through Hall and cultural-studies debates.
representative_people.works: “Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses” (1970); Hall, “Cultural Studies: Two Paradigms” (1980)

representative_people.context: An interlocutor in historians’ reception of Foucault, organizing debate across theoretical and empirical approaches. The edited volume is not one uniform Foucauldian program.
representative_people.works: Foucault and the Writing of History, edited collection (1994); Console and Classify (1987)

representative_people.context: Derrida examines the relation of writing to the historicity of ideal objects through Husserl’s geometry. This is a particular critical engagement, not Husserl’s membership in a later historical turn.
representative_people.works: Husserl’s Origin of Geometry as discussed in Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967), chapter 2 opening

representative_people.context: Derrida explicitly identifies Destruktion and Abbau as resources that he adapts; the acknowledgment does not imply endorsement of Heidegger’s whole philosophy or politics.
representative_people.works: Derrida, “Letter to a Japanese Friend” (1983); Of Grammatology (1967), selected chapter 2

representative_people.context: Derrida explicitly draws on signs and interpretants while questioning a final meaning outside signification. This contextual use does not equate pragmatism with deconstruction.
representative_people.works: Peirce passages discussed in Derrida, Of Grammatology (1967), corrected English edition pp. 48–50

representative_people.context: An explicit resource in Foucault’s genealogy and Barthes’s discussion of facts and meaning; their appropriations are distinct from Nietzsche’s full argument.
representative_people.works: Genealogy (1887), selected passages; Foucault’s genealogy essay (1971); Barthes’s history essay (1967)

representative_people.context: Moves among myth analysis, historical discourse and a challenge to authorial closure. His trajectory is not a single timeless structuralist method.
representative_people.works: Mythologies (1957); “The Discourse of History” and “The Death of the Author” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968)

representative_people.context: Explicitly cited for dialogue among texts and paragrammatism in Barthes’s historical-discourse analysis. The original article is not newly read and the acknowledgment does not establish identical positions.
representative_people.works: “Bakhtine, le mot, le dialogue et le roman” (1967), cited in Barthes’s “The Discourse of History,” note 3

representative_people.context: Barthes invokes his research on ambiguous words in Greek tragedy to distinguish characters’ understanding from the spectator’s. This is a named scholarly resource, not a formal linguistic-turn affiliation.
representative_people.works: Research on Greek tragedy as invoked in “The Death of the Author” (1967), final paragraph

representative_people.context: A historian and translator who makes rhetorical analysis usable for historiography while retaining questions about sources and reference.
representative_people.works: Barthes translation (1981); “Analysing the discourse of history” (1983/1990)

representative_people.context: Reads texts as situated social acts with distinct discursive forms; manuscript and patronage evidence changed her initial hypothesis.
representative_people.works: Romancing the Past (1993), introduction, acknowledgments and notes

representative_people.context: Historicizes gender categories and the production of experience while retaining institutional relations and historical inquiry.
representative_people.works: “Gender” (1986); “The Evidence of Experience” (1991)

representative_people.context: Questions the political idioms through which class receives meaning; this is a particular historical intervention.
representative_people.works: Languages of Class (1983), selected introduction opening

representative_people.context: Reconsiders textual interpretation and the meaning of context through literary criticism and philosophy.
representative_people.works: Rethinking Intellectual History (1983)

representative_people.context: Investigates laboring people’s understandings of social order across politics, work, language and art.
representative_people.works: Visions of the People (1991)

representative_people.context: An interlocutor whose article explicitly frames meaning and experience as a historiographical problem; detailed argument remains to be checked.
representative_people.works: “Intellectual History after the Linguistic Turn” (1987)

representative_people.context: Spiegel explicitly credits her draft argument and sustained manuscript reading in developing a social/textual historical method.
representative_people.works: “The Body Politic” (1989), cited in Romancing the Past (1993), introduction note 7

representative_people.context: Socially situated discourse is an explicitly cited resource for Spiegel, not a formal affiliation with a later historians’ school.
representative_people.works: The Dialogic Imagination (English 1981), p. 259 cited by Spiegel (1993)

representative_people.works: Anatomy of Criticism (1957)

representative_people.context: Named rhetorical resource in White’s introduction; distinct from Peter Burke and Edmund Burke III.
representative_people.works: A Grammar of Motives (edition cited by White1969)

representative_people.works: Mimesis, cited by White in Metahistory (1973),2n1

representative_people.works: “Feminist History after the Linguistic Turn” (1994), 374–379

strands.title: Discourse and genealogy
strands.focus: Archaeology examines rules connecting actual statements and the formation of objects; genealogy traces contingent descent and emergence. Social and institutional relations enter these inquiries.
strands.works: The Archaeology of Knowledge (1969), three chapters; “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History” (1971), pp. 139–152

strands.title: Deconstruction
strands.focus: Critical work through conceptual hierarchies and differential relations, with an explicitly adapted Heidegger resource. The 1983 letter rejects a mechanical method and includes institutions and translation.
strands.works: Of Grammatology (1967), selected chapter 2; “Letter to a Japanese Friend” (1983)

strands.title: Narrative theory
strands.focus: Emplotment and tropes concern the forms of historical explanation.

strands.title: Signification and divided subjectivity
strands.focus: Lacan’s changed sign diagram and reading of dream-work distinguish his appropriation from literal repetition of Saussure. Historians debate its capacity to explain changing gender relations.

strands.title: Ideology, practices and subjects
strands.focus: Althusser’s interpellation operates through material practices. His apparatuses include contradiction and resistance; Hall’s adoption and criticism remain a specific reception.

strands.title: Subject formation, action and resistance
strands.focus: Foucault distinguishes power relations from capacities and communication while studying their interconnections; freedom and resistance enter action upon actions. Goldstein provides a historically situated interlocutor.
strands.works: “The Subject and Power” (1982); Foucault and the Writing of History (1994)

strands.title: Writing, ideal objects and historicity
strands.focus: Derrida’s critical reading of Husserl asks how writing enters the historical transmission of ideal objects. It is distinct from a claim that historical evidence has no constraints.

strands.title: Interpretants and a critique of presence
strands.focus: Peirce is a named resource in Derrida’s account of signification; this particular use neither subsumes all pragmatism nor equates arbitrariness with individual caprice.
strands.works: Of Grammatology, corrected English edition (1997), pp. 44–50

strands.title: Madness, reason and discursive practice
strands.focus: Derrida questions the language of an archaeology of silence; Foucault disputes his reading of Descartes and the reduction of discursive practices to textual traces. Each criticism remains attributed.
strands.works: “Cogito and the History of Madness” (lecture 1963); “My Body, This Paper, This Fire” (English 1979)

strands.title: Genealogical questions and perspectival knowledge
strands.focus: Nietzsche’s distinction between origins and uses, and his account of multiple perspectives, enter different later arguments in Foucault and Barthes. Their readings are not interchangeable.
strands.works: Genealogy II.12–13 and III.12; Foucault (1971); Barthes (1967)

strands.title: Myth and the naturalization of history
strands.focus: Barthes’s two-level account asks how historically produced meanings appear natural. He links formal analysis with historical criticism, rather than treating semiology as sufficient by itself.

strands.title: Authorship, textual plurality and the reader
strands.focus: The 1967 essay questions the author as final explanatory authority and invokes Vernant’s tragic ambiguity. Its theoretical reader must be distinguished from research on actual readers.
strands.works: “The Death of the Author” (1967), Richard Howard translation

strands.title: Historical utterance, reference and narrative detail
strands.focus: Barthes distinguishes acts of uttering, content units and signification, drawing on Jakobson and Kristeva. Bann’s adoption and qualification keep historical practice within the debate.
strands.works: “The Discourse of History” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968); Bann (1983/1990)

strands.title: Social sites and textual action
strands.focus: Spiegel combines attention to form with documentary and patronage inquiry; texts act in social settings and are not transparent reflections.

strands.title: Gender categories and historical experience
strands.focus: Scott makes experience something to explain and connects meanings with institutions and subjectivity.

strands.title: Class and political idioms
strands.focus: Different historical inquiries question how social identities receive political meaning.
strands.works: Languages of Class (1983); Visions of the People (1991)

strands.title: Texts, contexts and debates over experience
strands.focus: LaCapra’s textual/contextual project and Toews’s explicitly titled meaning/experience intervention are distinct; detailed agreement is not presumed.
strands.works: Rethinking Intellectual History (1983); Intellectual History after the Linguistic Turn (1987)

strands.title: Literary taxonomies and historical events
strands.focus: White distinguishes narrative arrangement from invented events and treats plot classifications as revisable analytical choices.

nodes.scope_note: Structural linguistics, discourse, deconstruction, and narrative theory differ. A historical concern with language alone does not identify a poststructuralist.

nodes.label: Microhistory / everyday life
nodes.description: Italian microstoria reconstructs relations and tests categories through close inquiry; German Alltagsgeschichte studies everyday practices and power. Neither is defined by small places alone, and their intellectual exchanges do not erase their differences.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Carlo Ginzburg, The Cheese and the Worms (1976); Giovanni Levi; Alf Lüdtke.

representative_people.context: Reconstructs Menocchio’s reading through inquisitorial records; later argues that narrative construction can coexist with evidentiary claims.
representative_people.works: The Cheese and the Worms (Italian 1976); “Microhistory: Two or Three Things That I Know about It” (1993)

representative_people.context: Reconstructs social relations and individual strategies at close range; Ginzburg’s account stresses their relation to wider contexts. His own methodological essays examine choices within conflicting norms and question fixed cultural contexts in interpretive history.
representative_people.works: Inheriting Power: The Story of an Exorcist (English 1988); I pericoli del geertzismo (1985); Les usages de la biographie (1989)

representative_people.context: Alltagsgeschichte researcher examining workers’ everyday practices, criticizing some structural priorities and drawing on Mann’s power networks.
representative_people.works: “Polymorphous Synchrony: German Industrial Workers and the Politics of Everyday Life” (1993)

representative_people.context: Examines occupational classification in Turin; Ginzburg identifies her relational reconstruction alongside Levi’s.
representative_people.works: La Ville et les métiers (1990)

representative_people.context: Microanalytical interlocutor whose formulation about exceptional evidence informs Ginzburg’s account of comparison.
representative_people.works: “Micro-analisi e storia sociale” (1977), discussed by Ginzburg (1993)

representative_people.context: Engages anthropology critically and collaboratively, including a working group with Lüdtke, Sabean and others.
representative_people.works: “Missionaries in the Row Boat”? (1987); with David Sabean, eds., Interest and Emotion (1984)

representative_people.context: Retrospective methodological interlocutor: Ginzburg praises his treatment of historical scale while explicitly denying known influence on microhistory’s emergence.
representative_people.works: History: The Last Things before the Last (1969), discussed by Ginzburg (1993), pp. 26–27

representative_people.context: An edited EHESS collection investigates changes of observational scale and generalization; it neither equates all small studies with microstoria nor makes small intrinsically superior. His own scale essay treats changed observation as changing the object and relationships available for analysis.
representative_people.works: Jeux d’échelles (editor, 1996); Micro-analyse et construction du social (1996)

representative_people.context: A critic of Alltagsgeschichte’s conceptual and explanatory claims who also acknowledges its cultural and experiential contributions.
representative_people.works: Alltagsgeschichte: Königsweg zu neuen Ufern oder Irrgarten der Illusionen? (1980s versions)

representative_people.context: Mexican local historian combining archives, conversations and lived experience for a local readership. This microhistoria is a distinct project, not a presumed branch of Italian microstoria.
representative_people.works: Pueblo en vilo (1968; revised edition consulted, 1979)

representative_people.context: González credits her corrections, proposed changes and preparation of the manuscript; the credited collaboration exceeds typing.
representative_people.works: Editorial collaboration on Pueblo en vilo, acknowledged in its preface

representative_people.context: Her preserved correspondence, association papers and long series of household accounts supplied González’s local history.
representative_people.works: Private archive and household expense notebooks used in Pueblo en vilo

strands.title: Italian microstoria
strands.focus: A varied research programme connecting intensive cases to larger questions; cultural and social-relational inquiries overlap.

strands.title: Alltagsgeschichte
strands.focus: Lüdtke studies workers’ situated practices and power, using Mann as well as questioning structural priorities.
strands.works: “Polymorphous Synchrony” (1993); The History of Everyday Life (English 1995)

strands.title: Social relations and changing categories
strands.focus: Close reconstruction examines how relations and classifications are made through action.
strands.works: Levi, Inheriting Power; Cerutti, La Ville et les métiers

strands.title: Exceptional evidence and historical inference
strands.focus: An unusual case can expose assumptions without statistically representing a population.

strands.title: History and anthropology in working exchange
strands.focus: Critical engagement with Cohn and collaborative research complicate a one-way borrowing model.

strands.title: Moving between historical scales
strands.focus: Results at one scale cannot simply be transferred to another; retrospective affinity is distinguished from transmission.

strands.title: Everyday history, concepts and explanation
strands.focus: Wehler values the recovery of culture and experience but disputes claims to a replacement explanatory framework. Lüdtke challenges the reduction of everyday history to an illustrative supplement, while accepting some criticism of romanticization and insisting on reconstructing connections between traces. Both positions are internally qualified.

strands.title: Testing context through close interpretation
strands.focus: Levi argues that small episodes should revise the explanatory context, criticizing Darnton’s assumed cultural patterns while distinguishing Geertz’s accomplishments from mechanical applications.
strands.works: I pericoli del geertzismo (1985; Portuguese translation 1999)

strands.title: Choices within conflicting norms
strands.focus: Levi’s biography essay examines limited room for action and the formation of groups within contradictory normative systems; his disagreement with Bourdieu is one of emphasis.

strands.title: Varying scale changes the object of inquiry
strands.focus: Revel distinguishes changes of analytical scale from merely magnifying an unchanged object; no scale has an automatic privilege. Relational inquiry makes collective formation a problem to explain.
strands.works: Micro-analyse et construction du social (1996), sections 3–4

strands.title: Mexican microhistoria and local readership
strands.focus: González explains local events alongside regional and national pressures, combining documentary records, informal conversations and personal recollection. His claims to typicality and his treatment of uncorroborated memory are methodological choices open to criticism.

strands.title: Archives, informants and editorial collaboration
strands.focus: González’s preface credits Josefina’s archive, his father’s recollections, other informants and Armida’s revisions. These contributions make the local history a collaborative production despite its single-author title page.

nodes.scope_note: Italian microstoria and German Alltagsgeschichte have distinct origins and aims; scale alone is not membership in either project. Evidence, narrative and generalization remain contested within this umbrella. Kracauer is a retrospective comparison, not a claimed founder. González’s Mexican microhistoria is included as a distinct local-history project; shared terminology does not establish transmission from Italian or German programmes.

nodes.label: Environmental history
nodes.description: Explains historical relations among people and the nonhuman world through ecological exchange, agriculture, property, commodity flows, conservation and cultural ideas of nature. These approaches disagree about causal emphasis. Cases from New England, the Great Plains, Mexico, India, colonial islands and South Africa connect ecological processes with power without supplying one universal model. Bullard’s environmental-justice inquiry and Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life histories broaden comparison toward unequal burdens, displacement and authority over historical accounts. Dust Bowl debates distinguish agricultural capitalism, technology and soils, federal intervention, regional scale and household survival; primary criticism and later social history complicate a single causal summary.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred Crosby; Donald Worster; Carolyn Merchant; William Cronon. ASEH founded 1977. Expanded contextual readings include Leopold’s precursor essays, Melville’s Mexican study, Gadgil and Guha’s Indian history, Grove’s colonial conservation and Carruthers’s South African park history.

representative_people.context: Argues that organisms accompanying Europeans helped transform environments and sustain settler expansion, particularly in temperate regions.
representative_people.works: Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986)

representative_people.context: Connects the Dust Bowl with agricultural capitalism as well as environmental conditions; this is a contested explanation, not the field’s unanimous account.
representative_people.works: Dust Bowl: The Southern Plains in the 1930s (1979); “The Dirty Thirties: A Study in Agricultural Capitalism” (1986)

representative_people.context: Brings feminist history of science into environmental inquiry; argues that mechanical conceptions of nature support new forms of control and capitalist development.
representative_people.works: The Death of Nature: Women, Ecology, and the Scientific Revolution (1980)

representative_people.context: Links colonial property and ecological change, city–hinterland commodity flows, and cultural ideas of wilderness. His later afterword criticizes schematic capitalism and uneven treatment of Indigenous and colonial sources in his first book.
representative_people.works: Changes in the Land (1983); Nature’s Metropolis (1991); “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995)

representative_people.context: Ecological observation and conservation ethics precede the field’s later consolidation; Cronon identifies a landscape-training model drawn from Leopold.
representative_people.works: A Sand County Almanac (1949)

representative_people.context: With ecologist Madhav Gadgil, examines changing resource use, social conflict and resistance in Indian environmental history. Distinct from Ranajit Guha.
representative_people.works: With Madhav Gadgil, This Fissured Land: An Ecological History of India (1992; UC Press edition 1993)

representative_people.context: Ecologist collaborating with Ramachandra Guha on resource-use systems and their social and political conflicts in India.
representative_people.works: With Ramachandra Guha, This Fissured Land: An Ecological History of India (1992; UC Press edition 1993)

representative_people.context: Traces conservation ideas through colonial island settings and scientific networks; his geographical emphasis differs from histories of mainland African conservation.
representative_people.works: Green Imperialism: Colonial Expansion, Tropical Island Edens and the Origins of Environmentalism, 1600–1860 (1995)

representative_people.context: Examines South African conservation through the politics of Kruger National Park, racial power and Afrikaner nationalism.
representative_people.works: The Kruger National Park: A Social and Political History (1995)

representative_people.context: Adapts Crosby’s biological-conquest question to introduced grazing animals and social change in Mexico’s Valle del Mezquital, emphasizing places with continuing Indigenous populations.
representative_people.works: A Plague of Sheep: Environmental Consequences of the Conquest of Mexico (1994)

representative_people.context: Supplies a documented teaching resource: Cronon’s 1994 graduate environmental-history syllabus assigns his 1941 essay. This is a specific use, not a field-wide genealogy.
representative_people.works: “Foreword to Historical Geography” (1941), assigned in Cronon’s History 901 (1994)

representative_people.context: Studies unequal pollution burdens and the political capacity to resist them; his Alsen account preserves disagreement about compensation and continuing health needs.
representative_people.works: Dumping in Dixie (1990), introduction and Alsen excerpts

representative_people.context: Her life narrative offers a situated account of displacement from Country and community relationships, voiced alongside her daughter rather than reduced to anonymous testimony.
representative_people.works: With Jackie Huggins, Auntie Rita (1994); with Jackie Huggins and Jane M. Jacobs, Kooramindanjie (1995)

representative_people.context: Historian and collaborator in her mother’s life narrative; the relationship between oral testimony and official histories is visible in Heiss’s contemporary review.
representative_people.works: With Rita Huggins, Auntie Rita (1994); Sister Girl (1998), through Heiss’s review

representative_people.context: Criticizes geographical generalization and competing accounts of government and capitalist culture; his preference for Hurt is a position within the debate.
representative_people.works: “Dust Bowl Historiography” (1986)

representative_people.context: Reviews Hurt favorably while asking historians to include northern Plains experiences; his desired scale differs from McDean’s later emphasis.
representative_people.works: Review of Hurt’s The Dust Bowl (1983)

representative_people.context: An ecological-history resource whom Worster both acknowledges and criticizes for explanations through natural dust storms and adaptation after pioneering.
representative_people.works: “Ecology and History” (1950); “Dust Storms” series (1946), through Worster’s 1986 discussion

representative_people.context: Emphasizes farmers’ endurance and criticizes federal intervention; McDean disputes his account while recognizing his description of farming practices.
representative_people.works: The Dust Bowl: Men, Dirt, and Depression (1979), through McDean and Fite

representative_people.context: Studies farming technology, soils, drought and conservation; McDean and Fite praise the book but emphasize its causal balance differently.
representative_people.works: The Dust Bowl: An Agricultural and Social History (1981), through contemporary reviews

representative_people.context: Examines families who remained in southwestern Kansas, work and assistance, and social adaptation alongside environmental change.
representative_people.works: Rooted in Dust (1994); contents identify oral-history and agricultural-census appendices

representative_people.context: Guha uses his analysis of Orientalist representations to question deep ecology’s selective appropriation of Asian traditions.
representative_people.works: “Orientalist Constructions of India” (1986), received in Guha (1989)

representative_people.context: Responds to Guha by defending wilderness protection and biocentrism informed by social analysis; this selection rests on the author abstract.
representative_people.works: “The Relevance of Deep Ecology to the Third World” (1990), abstract

representative_people.context: Challenges Cronon’s treatment of wilderness through conservation biology and ecocentric ethics; his wider accusations remain contested interpretations.
representative_people.works: “Reinventing Nature, The End Of Wilderness?” (1996)

representative_people.context: A named interlocutor in disputes about Bacon, experiment and domination of nature; this is a focused criticism, not a rejection of environmental history.
representative_people.works: “Wrestling with Proteus” (1999), author abstract

nodes.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship. A bounded second-pass addition now compares Bullard and the Huggins collaboration; primary-excerpt, publisher-description and metadata limits remain distinct, and neither selection represents every community.

strands.title: Organisms, conquest and ecological exchange
strands.focus: Compare Crosby’s temperate settler environments with Melville’s explicit adaptation to grazing animals, land and continuing Indigenous populations in Mexico.
strands.works: Ecological Imperialism (1986); A Plague of Sheep (1994)

strands.title: Agricultural capitalism and environmental crisis
strands.focus: Worster connects the Dust Bowl to agricultural capitalism. Compare that argument with competing explanations instead of treating it as settled consensus.

strands.title: Gender, science and the control of nature
strands.focus: Merchant’s feminist intervention joins history of science with environmental questions; her mechanical-order argument concerns ideas, power and material change.

strands.title: Colonial property and ecological change
strands.focus: Property concepts help Cronon explain changes in New England. Read with his later self-criticism about source asymmetry, spirituality and schematic capitalism.
strands.works: Changes in the Land (1983; retrospective afterword 2003)

strands.title: Cities, commodities and hinterlands
strands.focus: Follow lumber, grain and meat between rural production and urban processing and markets; follow capital back toward the countryside.
strands.works: Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (1991)

strands.title: Resource use and social conflict in India
strands.focus: Changing resource-use systems, state interventions and resistance connect ecological and social histories without making precolonial society uniformly harmonious.

strands.title: Conservation, colonial science and racial power
strands.focus: Grove studies colonial conservation networks and islands; Carruthers studies a South African park’s racial and national politics. These distinct scales complicate a purely benevolent conservation story.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Wilderness as a historical cultural idea
strands.focus: Cronon examines the pristine-wilderness ideal and Indigenous removal, while defending care for nonhuman nature in inhabited places.

strands.title: Historical geography in environmental-history teaching
strands.focus: Cronon’s 1994 syllabus assigns Sauer’s 1941 essay among several resources for bringing nature into history. Assignment demonstrates use without establishing assent or an exclusive intellectual ancestry.

strands.title: Unequal pollution burdens and collective action
strands.focus: Bullard joins environmental distribution with race, class and organizing capacity. The Alsen case distinguishes partial gains from unresolved health concerns and internal disagreement.
strands.works: Dumping in Dixie (1990), selected reprinted excerpts

strands.title: Country, displacement and historical voice
strands.focus: Read Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life-history project beside conservation and settler-landscape narratives. Publisher descriptions support this bounded comparison; their full books and place article remain unread.
strands.works: Auntie Rita (1994); Changes in the Land (1983); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Agricultural culture, technology and regional causes
strands.focus: Worster argues for interacting natural and cultural forces while emphasizing agricultural capitalism. McDean criticizes his generalization, contests Bonnifield’s federal-policy account and favors Hurt’s regional specificity. These are competing interpretations.
strands.works: Worster (1986); McDean (1986), discussing books of 1979 and 1981

strands.title: Ecological adaptation and the promise of development
strands.focus: Worster acknowledges Malin’s ecological history but disputes explanations through natural storms and a passing pioneering stage. He distinguishes rival cultural values and varied regional entrepreneurial intensity.

strands.title: Regional boundaries and histories of staying
strands.focus: Compare McDean’s insistence on a specific Dust Bowl region, Fite’s call for northern Plains coverage, and Riney-Kehrberg’s household survival study in southwestern Kansas. Causal explanation, geographical scale and lived experience pose different questions.

strands.title: Wilderness, livelihood and different political contexts
strands.focus: Guha targets American deep ecology’s universal claims and conservation’s unequal costs in India, while acknowledging Naess’s concern about inequality. Cronon studies American sublime/frontier ideals and everyday responsibility, explicitly citing Guha in note28. Shared concerns about exclusion do not erase their different contexts or Cronon’s support for protected wild lands.

strands.title: Can biocentrism incorporate social criticism?
strands.focus: Johns’s abstract disputes Guha’s equation of deep ecology with wilderness protection and defends biocentrism joined to critical social theory against overconsumption and militarism. This is a named response; the article’s detailed reasoning is not newly verified.

strands.title: Cultural criticism and habitat protection
strands.focus: Sessions objects that Cronon underweights biodiversity and connected wild habitat. His claim that cultural construction conflicts with independent nature is a critical interpretation: Cronon explicitly defends nonhuman autonomy and wild-land protection.

strands.title: Material change, ideas and gendered nature
strands.focus: Merchant retrospectively clarifies that ecological and economic changes made some ideas more plausible rather than mechanically causing them. Her socialist ecofeminism addresses production and reproduction and challenges an essentialist identification of women with nature.
strands.works: The Death of Nature (1980); Radical Ecology (1992), discussed in Merchant’s 2006 retrospective

strands.title: Colonial conservation: knowledge, power and benefits
strands.focus: Carruthers’s review welcomes Grove’s island settings and exchanges of knowledge, while questioning parts of his synthesis. Her Kruger prologue and epilogue emphasize changing political coalitions, racial exclusion and allocation of benefits. Scientific conservation and unequal power can coexist; these works ask different questions at different scales.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995), reviewed by Carruthers (1996); The Kruger National Park (1995), prologue and epilogue

nodes.label: Subaltern Studies
nodes.description: Critiques colonial and elite nationalist histories; begins with subordinate groups’ politics and develops debates over representation and historical knowledge.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Ranajit Guha; Shahid Amin; Dipesh Chakrabarty. Neither all South Asian history nor all postcolonial thought.

representative_people.context: Proposes an autonomous domain of popular politics while recognizing overlap with elites and variable regional social positions.
representative_people.works: “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India” (1982); Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983)

representative_people.context: Combines judicial archives and local interviews to examine peasant politics and competing national memories.
representative_people.works: Event, Metaphor, Memory: Chauri Chaura, 1922–1992 (1995)

representative_people.context: Revises universalizing class narratives through Bengal labor; later investigates historians’ translations of subordinate pasts.
representative_people.works: Rethinking Working-Class History: Bengal 1890–1940 (1989); “Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts” (1997); Provincializing Europe (2000)

representative_people.context: Addresses the relationship between colonial nationalism and cultural difference within a changing collective.
representative_people.works: Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986); The Nation and Its Fragments (1993)

representative_people.context: Critically engages Guha’s autonomy claim and the gendered limits of recovering subaltern consciousness.
representative_people.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988)

representative_people.context: Historicizes communalism as a category and explores contested political communities.
representative_people.works: The Construction of Communalism in Colonial North India (1990)

representative_people.context: Examines science as both imperial authority and a resource for national emancipation.
representative_people.works: Another Reason: Science and the Imagination of Modern India (1999)

representative_people.context: Credits early research while contesting later priorities and identifying tensions within the initial project.
representative_people.works: “The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies,” in Writing Social History (1997)

representative_people.context: Recognizes Chakrabarty’s theoretical intervention while questioning static cultural categories and the treatment of gender.
representative_people.works: Review of Rethinking Working Class History (1990), 96–99

nodes.scope_note: The collective changes across time; subordinate agency, colonial archives, and representation must not become a single unchanging postcolonial theory. Guha’s autonomy thesis, Spivak’s representation problem and Sarkar’s internal criticism are not interchangeable. Religion, gender, labor, local memory and colonial knowledge remain distinct questions; the present roster is geographically selective.

strands.title: Popular politics and elite historiography
strands.focus: Autonomy is an argued distinction, with interaction and regional variation built into the early statement.

strands.title: Local events, archives and remembrance
strands.focus: Different records and recollections complicate national narratives of Chauri Chaura.

strands.title: Labor and historical difference
strands.focus: Bengal’s jute workers prompt criticism of universal class narratives that leave culture residual.

strands.title: Historical translation and its limits
strands.focus: Religious accounts of agency pose a problem for the secular historian’s narration.

strands.title: Nation, community and colonial categories
strands.focus: Nationalism and communalism receive distinct historical critiques; political communities are not timeless givens.
strands.works: The Nation and Its Fragments (1993); The Construction of Communalism (1990)

strands.title: Gender and the recovery of consciousness
strands.focus: Representation remains necessary and difficult; adding women to a list does not settle the problem.

strands.title: Science and national imagination
strands.focus: Scientific reason acquires different political uses under empire and nationalism.

strands.title: Disputing the project’s changing priorities
strands.focus: Sarkar defends research into subordinate social groups while questioning community-centered explanations.
strands.works: “The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies” (1997)

nodes.label: Gender history
nodes.description: Examines gender as a historically changing organization of social relations, identities and power. Research on work, family, masculinity, bodies and colonial settings connects gender to class, race and other relations without reducing these to one framework. Some feminist historians develop and criticize British Marxist social history; this is one route among several.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Joan Wallach Scott, “Gender” (1986); Leonore Davidoff and Catherine Hall, Family Fortunes (1987); Evelyn Brooks Higginbotham, “The Metalanguage of Race” (1992); Anna Clark, The Struggle for the Breeches (1995).

representative_people.context: Gender as historical analysis.
representative_people.works: Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis (1986)

representative_people.context: Feminist historical inquiry developing and reassessing class history.
representative_people.works: Eve and the New Jerusalem (1983)

representative_people.context: Gender-history contribution: connects family, religion, economic opportunity and English middle-class formation.
representative_people.works: With Leonore Davidoff, Family Fortunes: Men and Women of the English Middle Class, 1780–1850 (1987)

representative_people.context: Integrates work, family and radical rhetoric in a gendered account of British class formation.
representative_people.works: The Struggle for the Breeches (1995)

representative_people.context: A historical resource extended and criticized; not represented as adopting all later gender theories.
representative_people.works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963)

representative_people.context: Gender-history contribution: connects family, religion, economic opportunity and English middle-class formation.

strands.title: Psychoanalytic subjectivity and historical variation
strands.focus: Scott values constructed subjectivity while questioning universal antagonism; her discussion of Alexander identifies a historical feminist use without establishing consensus.

nodes.scope_note: Gender history is a distinct research field with competing explanations and methods. Women’s history remains independent and is not superseded. Racial formation and intersectional analysis have their own entries; connections express specific arguments rather than membership in a combined school. Historical differences of class, race, caste, place and sexuality remain integral questions within gender history.

nodes.label: Sexuality & queer history
nodes.description: Studies changing sexual categories, identities, practices, and norms. Queer approaches challenge stable or transhistorical identities.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Jeffrey Weeks; John D’Emilio; Foucault as an influence; George Chauncey, Gay New York (1994).

representative_people.context: British sexual politics and changing sexual meanings; D’Emilio names Weeks as a predecessor while pursuing a different material explanation.
representative_people.works: Coming Out (1977); Sexuality and Its Discontents (1985)

representative_people.context: Connects identity formation to wage labor and family change, alongside a history of organizations and political struggle; a historically situated argument, not a universal origin of same-sex desire.
representative_people.works: “Capitalism and Gay Identity” (1983); Sexual Politics, Sexual Communities (1983)

representative_people.context: Urban social history questions a uniformly closeted past through changing places, categories and policing.
representative_people.works: Gay New York (1994)

representative_people.context: D’Emilio explicitly acknowledges a resource for historicizing identity while seeking a different explanation. Stoler also uses and criticizes Foucault; neither project stands for the entire field.

representative_people.context: Coauthored Buffalo lesbian community history built through interviews; class, race and butch-fem practices remain situated.

nodes.scope_note: Histories of sexuality, gay/lesbian recovery, queer theory and trans interventions overlap without a single succession or uniform Foucauldian position. Material explanation, interviewing, literary analysis and colonial research differ; historical practices do not automatically establish a timeless modern identity. Geographic coverage remains selective.

strands.title: Chinese histories and textual traditions

strands.title: Intersectional criticism of queer politics

nodes.label: Postcolonial history / critique
nodes.date_label: 1970s roots · expansion from the 1980s · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Questions imperial knowledge, Eurocentric universals, and the assumption that all societies follow Europe’s historical path.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Edward Said, Orientalism (1978); Gayatri Spivak (1988); Dipesh Chakrabarty, Provincializing Europe (2000).

representative_people.context: Studies imperial authority through texts and institutions, combining discourse analysis with hegemony and attention to particular writers.
representative_people.works: Orientalism (1978)

representative_people.context: Questions intellectual representation through colonialism, labor and gender; uses deconstruction critically.
representative_people.works: “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988)

nodes.scope_note: Said, Spivak, and Chakrabarty address different problems; literary critique and historical scholarship interact without becoming the same discipline. Feminist critiques, colonial archival research and theories of ambivalence introduce further disagreements. These selections do not make postcolonial thought synonymous with South Asian history, literary theory or all anti-colonial politics.

strands.title: Representation and intellectual responsibility

strands.focus: Bengal supplies the setting for a disputed account of cultural autonomy and political modernity.

strands.title: Mimicry, ambivalence and hybridity

strands.focus: Neither women’s situations nor feminist scholarship form a single homogeneous subject.

nodes.label: Memory studies
nodes.description: Studies remembering, commemoration and forgetting through social relations, narratives, bodies and cultural forms. Recollection is evidence requiring interpretation; memory and history are connected in different, contested ways.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Maurice Halbwachs (1925) as a precursor; Pierre Nora, Les Lieux de mémoire (1984–92).

representative_people.context: Social frameworks make remembering a relational process; later English selections are distinct from the original French works. The original French conclusion also addresses changes in traditions through relations between groups.
representative_people.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); On Collective Memory, ed. and trans. Lewis Coser (1992 selections)
