nodes.scope_note: Halbwachs’s social frameworks, Nora’s commemorative sites, and Samuel’s popular uses of the past are distinct projects. Communicative and cultural memory are the Assmann project’s distinctions, not a universal taxonomy. War mourning, Holocaust memorials and feminist subjectivity require different historical explanations; this selection remains weighted toward European debates. Jelin’s Argentina project adds a pre-2000 case beyond Europe; it does not represent all Latin American memory work.

strands.title: Social frameworks of remembering
strands.focus: Family, religious and class contexts organize recollection; a collective framework is not proof of one identical group memory.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925); English selections (1992)

strands.title: Sites of memory and historical reconstruction
strands.focus: Sites combine material, symbolic and functional dimensions, extending beyond monuments alone.

strands.title: Habit, bodies and ceremony
strands.focus: Remembering includes bodily competence, not only recalled propositions or pictures.

strands.title: Communication and cultural objectivation
strands.focus: Everyday recollection and durable cultural forms operate differently; Assmann revises rather than merely repeats Halbwachs.

strands.title: Media and uses of cultural memory
strands.focus: Writing, images and monuments organize what can be stored and recalled.

strands.title: Mourning and cultural continuities after war
strands.focus: Traditional and modern forms overlap in Great War mourning; this is not a template for every subsequent catastrophe.
strands.works: Sites of Memory, Sites of Mourning (1995)

strands.title: Holocaust memorials and their contexts
strands.focus: Memorial forms and meanings vary across places and institutions.

strands.title: Popular practices of historical knowledge
strands.focus: Family research, images and reenactment make historical work visible outside professional writing.

strands.title: Life histories, gender and subjectivity
strands.focus: Fascist everyday life and feminist psychoanalytic inquiry are distinct routes into interpreted recollection.

strands.title: Archival authority, access and inscription
strands.focus: Combe’s inquiry into access supplies a named resource to Derrida. His account differentiates archives from spontaneous memory and examines institutional authority and technical inscription.

strands.title: Urban landscapes and public memory
strands.focus: Hayden’s collaborative practice links historical interpretation to lived places.

strands.title: Traditions in contact and conflict
strands.focus: Halbwachs explains revisions of collective remembering through contact with other groups and their traditions; social frameworks are not an assurance of a unanimous or unchanging past.
strands.works: Les cadres sociaux de la mémoire (1925), final concluding subsection

strands.title: Memorial production and public disagreement
strands.focus: Young’s Saarbrücken account follows a covert art project into public controversy and political recognition. His interpretation makes the memorial’s production and reception part of its meaning.

strands.title: Argentina: rights, remembrance and generations
strands.focus: Jelin examines competing public memories and tensions within human-rights activism. Her conclusion questions both political forgetting and repetition that prevents younger generations from reinterpreting the past.

strands.title: Vichy’s afterlife and historical inquiry
strands.focus: Rousso distinguishes memory as an object of research, as a preliminary examination of inherited representations, and as a way to extend an event’s historical study into its aftermath.

strands.title: Jewish remembrance and historiography
strands.focus: Yerushalmi’s prologue asks why concern with historical meaning and remembrance need not give professional historical writing the central role. This is a situated historical question, not a timeless definition of Jewish people.

strands.title: Resources for studying forgetting
strands.focus: Jelin’s 1994 analysis explicitly draws on Yerushalmi’s transmission argument and Loraux’s treatment of amnesty and mourning. Their Spanish 1989 essays are distinct from Zakhor.
strands.works: Usos del olvido essays (1989), as used by Jelin (1994)

nodes.label: Freudian psychoanalysis
nodes.date_label: 1890s onward; divergent later schools · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: A clinical practice and family of theories concerning unconscious conflict, development, sexuality, interpretation and relationships. Freud’s changing methods, later child-analysis disputes, psychosocial history, linguistic rereading and feminist adaptations require distinct accounts.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Sigmund Freud; later adaptations include Erik Erikson’s historical psychobiography and Jacques Lacan’s rereading through language. Historical interpretation must address evidence and context rather than assume access to an unrecorded inner life.

nodes.scope_note: This is a tradition entry, not an individual Freud node. Clinical claims and normative sexual classifications are historically situated. Breuer treated Anna O.; Freud’s account is not an independent outcome audit. Klein, Anna Freud, Erikson, Lacan and feminist interpreters pursue divergent questions. Historical motive inference requires documentary criticism; neither clinical access nor a uniform Freudian school can be assumed. Primary readings here cover the Clark lectures and selected Group Psychology chapters, not Freud’s entire career.

strands.title: Catharsis, repression and changing methods
strands.focus: Freud distinguishes Breuer’s earlier practice, hypnotic experiments and his developing use of association. His retrospective narrative does not establish clinical outcomes.

strands.title: Association, dreams and indirect expression
strands.focus: Manifest and latent dream material, condensation, displacement and everyday errors form different routes in Freud’s interpretation. Psychic determination remains a theoretical premise to examine.

strands.title: Development, transference and sublimation
strands.focus: Freud’s sexuality extends beyond reproduction; transference and sublimation connect his developmental and clinical account. Its normative sexual classifications are historical judgments.

strands.title: Individual relations and group bonds
strands.focus: Group Psychology starts with relations already present in individual life and questions suggestion as a sufficient explanation, proposing libidinal attachments.

strands.title: Child analysis and divergent developments
strands.focus: Klein’s play interpretation differs from other early child-analysis practices. Anna Freud and Klein are not interchangeable extensions of Freud; support here is a retrospective institutional profile.

strands.title: Psychosocial and historical adaptations
strands.focus: Erikson examines identity in historical orders; Gay argues for a place within contextual history. Neither position represents all psychoanalytic traditions.

strands.title: Feminist questions and subjectivity
strands.focus: Mitchell’s published program and Alexander’s historical work show productive feminist uses with different source support. These do not imply feminist consensus.
strands.works: Psychoanalysis and Feminism (1974); Becoming a Woman (1994/1995)

strands.title: Translation, context and historical inference
strands.focus: Schapiro’s Leonardo criticism tests an application against historical knowledge while retaining the possibility of psychological inquiry. Unrecorded motives are not directly accessible clinical facts.

strands.title: Identification and the signifier
strands.focus: The mirror-stage argument concerns identification and misrecognition; the later linguistic essay reformulates dream-work through metaphor and metonymy. This is a changing program, not the whole history of psychoanalysis.

strands.title: Archives and technical models of memory
strands.focus: Derrida reworks Freud’s destruction drive and Mystic Pad while asking whether changing recording technologies alter a model or its object. These are philosophical questions, not clinical findings.

nodes.label: History of science
nodes.date_label: Earlier roots · History of Science Society founded 1924 · later approaches · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Studies scientific knowledge, practices, instruments, institutions, and their historical settings. Histories of ideas, social and cultural histories, and material approaches coexist. The field predates Kuhn and STS, which transform parts of its questions without founding or exhausting it.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: George Sarton; Alexandre Koyré, Études galiléennes (1939); Robert K. Yates and Foucault provide additional, distinct contributions; they do not substitute for these historians and programmes. Further approaches include Metzger’s history of chemistry (1923), Maier’s medieval natural philosophy (1949), Fleck’s scientific fact (1935), Needham’s collaborative Chinese science project (from 1954), Rossiter’s Women Scientists in America (1982), and Merchant’s The Death of Nature (1980).

nodes.scope_note: Kuhn is a central reorientation, not the field’s sole founder. Sarton, Koyré, Merton, and historians of experimental practice distinguish important approaches; Yates and Foucault are additional contributions. Chinese science and women’s scientific work expand this selection; it still needs fuller coverage of other regions and material practices. Named Chinese-series contributors and Daston/Galison’s image and instrument studies deepen the selection. Publication credits do not replace primary argument checks; wider regional coverage remains selective. Arabic mathematics, colonial Indian science, African healing and a Beninese knowledge programme are separate selected projects, not regional proxies or exhaustive coverage.

nodes.label: Hayden White / narrative theory
nodes.description: Examines how emplotment, argument, and tropes organize historical accounts. Narrative form helps constitute an interpretation rather than merely decorating established facts. His work raises disputes about historical explanation and representation; it should not be reduced to the claim that evidence is irrelevant.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Metahistory: The Historical Imagination in Nineteenth-Century Europe (1973). White’s analysis of historical narrative is a distinct contribution within debates grouped here as the linguistic turn.
nodes.scope_note: Metahistory’s formalist reading of selected nineteenth-century European works is one project; the1999 afterword also affirms a Marxian commitment. Narrative construction does not erase the distinction between historical and invented events. The1992 Holocaust essay is represented only by a short course extract, not its full argument.

nodes.label: Thomas Kuhn
nodes.description: Explains scientific development through normal science, disciplinary commitments, crises, and revolutions. Paradigms organize problems and standards of inquiry. Later sociologists adapt these arguments, sometimes in ways Kuhn disputes; this is not a universal law that all intellectual history moves through discrete paradigms. His preface acknowledges Koyré, Metzger, Maier and Fleck as distinct resources. The later distinction between shared disciplinary commitments and exemplary solutions makes “paradigm” more precise. In his 1970 exchange, Kuhn stresses substantial agreement with Popper while distinguishing tests of puzzle solutions from challenges to basic theory. Popper accepts that normal research exists but disputes its educational desirability; Lakatos later proposes appraisal of research programmes through novel predictions. Their accusations of irrationalism are criticisms of Kuhn, not his own stated position. Skinner, Dunn and deMause use Kuhn for different historical purposes.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962; expanded second edition 1970). Distinguish his analysis of scientific communities from loose uses of paradigm to mean any school of historical writing. Read the 1962 preface alongside the 1969 postscript included in the second edition: sources of the argument and later clarification are different evidence.

nodes.label: Bruno Latour / laboratory studies
nodes.description: Studies the practical work through which scientific claims become established facts, including experiments, inscriptions, instruments, and relations among researchers. Laboratory ethnography offers a route into science studies that should not be collapsed into textual interpretation or into Bloor’s programme. The Pasteur study extends his inquiry into historical scientific change and distinguishes that analysis from an explanation by social forces alone. Bloor’s1999response contests the treatment of sociological explanation in the Pasteur case. Law’s1986edited volume provides a particular publication context shared with Callon; collaboration does not establish agreement.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: With Steve Woolgar, Laboratory Life: The Social Construction of Scientific Facts (1979). The revised 1986 edition drops Social from the subtitle. Latour is one contributor within a wider field. Les Microbes: guerre et paix, suivi de Irréductions (1984; translated as The Pasteurization of France, 1988) joins historical investigation to a separate theoretical argument.

nodes.label: Sociology of scientific knowledge / SSK
nodes.description: Investigates how scientific beliefs become accepted within social practices and institutions. The Edinburgh Strong Programme seeks causal explanations of both accepted and rejected knowledge using the same kinds of explanation. SSK includes different programmes; it is neither all sociology of science nor all STS. Collins’s replication studies and Pinch’s work on controversies expose additional empirical programmes; these differ from treating SSK as only Bloor’s principles. Bloor explicitly includes material causes and rejects equating symmetry with equal credibility. His disagreement with Latour concerns the analytical roles of objects and society.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: David Bloor, Knowledge and Social Imagery (1976; second edition 1991); Barry Barnes. The symmetry principle is a rule for explanation, not a claim that all scientific assertions have equal evidential merit. Barnes, Bloor and Henry, Scientific Knowledge (1996); Collins, Changing Order (1985); Pinch and Bijker, “The Social Construction of Facts and Artefacts” (1984).

nodes.label: Science and technology studies / STS
nodes.description: An interdisciplinary field examining how knowledge, technologies, institutions, and social arrangements develop together. Historical, sociological, ethnographic, and policy-oriented inquiries coexist. SSK and laboratory studies contribute to STS but do not define its entire scope. Knorr Cetina’s comparative laboratory cultures, Harding’s feminist epistemology, and Sussex/Cornell institution building add distinct approaches and histories.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Sheila Jasanoff, Gerald E. Markle, James C. Petersen, and Trevor Pinch, eds., Handbook of Science and Technology Studies (1995); Bruno Latour and Steve Woolgar, Laboratory Life (1979). Hughes, Bijker and Pinch distinguish systems and constructionist technology research (1987); Jasanoff examines regulatory advice (1990); Haraway examines situated objectivity (1988).

nodes.label: Conceptual history / Begriffsgeschichte
nodes.description: Traces changing political and social concepts in relation to historical experience, conflict, and expectations. Koselleck links conceptual change to different temporalities and to the emergence of modern historical consciousness. This overlaps with contextual intellectual history while asking different questions about semantic change across time. Collective German lexicon work, French studies of polemical usages and Richter’s comparisons represent distinct programs. Concepts can register and help shape social processes without exhausting those processes.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Reinhart Koselleck, Vergangene Zukunft (1979), translated as Futures Past (1985; Columbia edition 2004). The German conceptual-history tradition is related to, but not a branch of, Skinner and Pocock’s Cambridge School.

representative_people.context: German conceptual history; not a branch of the Cambridge School. Separates words from concepts, concepts from social reality and analytical categories from historical actors’ vocabulary; experience and expectation organize questions rather than determine their answers.
representative_people.works: Vergangene Zukunft (1979); Futures Past (1985)

representative_people.context: A coeditor of the German historical-concepts lexicon whose program differs from Koselleck’s. Tribe discusses criticism of his earlier völkisch framing and later revisions; original editions are not collated here.
representative_people.works: Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe, collective editorial project; discussion in Tribe’s Futures Past introduction (2004), pp. x–xiv

representative_people.context: A coeditor of the German lexicon with a distinct social-historical program; editorial collaboration does not establish one shared analytical method.
representative_people.works: Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe, collective editorial project; Koselleck’s preface and Tribe’s introduction to Futures Past

representative_people.context: Explicitly compares German conceptual history, the French Handbuch and Cambridge political-thought programs. The checked abstracts support comparative questions, not every judgment in the unread chapters.
representative_people.works: The History of Political and Social Concepts (1995), chapters 4 and 6, abstracts

representative_people.context: Coedits the French Handbuch and, with Gumbrecht, examines philosophe as a social role with competing pragmatic uses. This is a separate empirical program, not an unaltered copy of the German lexicon.
representative_people.works: Handbuch politisch-sozialer Grundbegriffe in Frankreich 1680–1820, Heft 3 (1985); with Gumbrecht, Philosophe, Philosophie, pp. 7–14

representative_people.context: Named coeditor of the 1985 French Handbuch volume. Editorial responsibility is documented; the checked preview does not establish sole authorship of its methodological article.
representative_people.works: Handbuch politisch-sozialer Grundbegriffe in Frankreich 1680–1820, Heft 3 (1985), title/imprint

representative_people.context: Coauthors the French study of philosophe, distinguishing changing social roles and pragmatic oppositions from dictionary definitions alone.
representative_people.works: With Rolf Reichardt, Philosophe, Philosophie (1985), selected pp. 7–14

representative_people.context: Koselleck explicitly invokes the difficulty of defining concepts that contain a history. This particular quotation does not establish adherence to Nietzsche’s entire philosophy.
representative_people.works: On the Genealogy of Morality (1887), quoted in Futures Past, chapter 5, p. 85

representative_people.context: Koselleck uses Weber’s legitimacy typology as an example of historical vocabulary becoming an analytical category. Olsen disputes a general Weber-based founding genealogy; the narrower example is preserved.
representative_people.works: Legitimacy typology discussed in Futures Past, chapter 5, p. 92

representative_people.context: Koselleck’s preface invokes the plurality of times as a resource for differentiating historical temporalities. This is a quoted resource, not a complete account of Herder’s history.
representative_people.works: Passage on plural times quoted in Koselleck’s preface to Futures Past, pp. 1–5

representative_people.context: Reconstructs competing uses of public opinion in constitutional argument; included for this practice without claiming membership in a German school.
representative_people.works: “Libertad de imprenta, opinión pública y debate constitucional” (2000), 15–20

nodes.scope_note: Koselleck’s conceptual change and historical time differ from reconstructing a particular author’s intervention. Brunner, Conze and Koselleck’s editorial association does not imply identical methods or political commitments. Experience and expectation are formal research categories with variable contents; the proposed modern temporal transformation is neither a universal timetable nor a prediction of particular events.

strands.title: Words, concepts and overlapping semantic layers
strands.focus: The same word can persist while conceptual content changes; a concept can carry multiple historical layers. Koselleck combines synchronic usage with diachronic comparison without treating every word as a key historical concept.

strands.title: Concepts as indicators and factors
strands.focus: Concepts register social relations and can help act upon them, but social events are not identical with their linguistic conceptualization. Historians must also distinguish actors’ terms from their own justified analytical categories.

strands.title: Experience, expectation and unequal temporalities
strands.focus: These formal categories direct questions about remembered pasts and anticipated futures. Their asymmetry does not independently predict contents; Koselleck’s modernity thesis recognizes simplification, unequal social temporalities and recurring structures.
strands.works: Futures Past, preface and selected chapter 14 pp. 255–264, 271–275

strands.title: Collective lexicon, distinct programs and political criticism
strands.focus: Brunner, Conze and Koselleck participate in one editorial project with different research emphases. Criticism of Brunner’s political framing and textual revisions must be attributed and assessed through evidence, without assigning a uniform position to all editors and contributors.
strands.works: Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe; Koselleck’s preface and Tribe’s selected introduction

strands.title: French social roles and opposing uses
strands.focus: Gumbrecht and Reichardt investigate philosophe as a social role. Opponents can use similar semantic contents with opposed force; dictionaries participate in polemics instead of neutrally settling every usage. Their court discussion explicitly draws on Elias.

strands.title: Comparing conceptual history and political languages
strands.focus: Richter’s 1995 comparison makes differences among the German lexicon, French Handbuch and Skinner/Pocock programs explicit. Shared historical vocabulary questions do not establish one method or an origin of one school in another.
strands.works: The History of Political and Social Concepts (1995), chapters 4 and 6, abstracts

strands.title: Public opinion and contested sovereignty
strands.focus: Goldman distinguishes appeals to an enlightened general will from the divergent opinions of provinces. The meaning of public opinion changes within struggles over who can speak for a sovereign people.
strands.works: “Libertad de imprenta” (2000), 15–20; earlier joint presentation acknowledged in note 26

nodes.label: Psychohistory / psychoanalytic history
nodes.date_label: Earlier roots; postwar growth · 1950s–80s · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: A contested range of historical uses of psychological interpretation: psychosocial life studies, psychoanalytically informed contextual history and theories of childrearing and collective fantasy. Disagreements concern sources, explanatory scale, historical variability and retrospective inference.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Erik H. Erikson, Young Man Luther: A Study in Psychoanalysis and History (1958); Peter Gay, Freud for Historians (1985). These projects should not be treated as straightforward applications of Lacan.

representative_people.context: Connects individual development with historical social orders, and asks that the identity-crisis concept itself face historical scrutiny. His later Luther formulation remains his interpretation.
representative_people.works: Young Man Luther (1958), existing metadata; “Autobiographic Notes on the Identity Crisis” (1970), selected primary passages

representative_people.context: Argues for psychoanalytic interpretation alongside external historical circumstances and distances his work from reductionist versions of psychohistory.
representative_people.works: Freud for Historians (1985); The Bourgeois Experience; methodological interview (1997)

representative_people.context: Challenges Freud’s Leonardo interpretation through translation, source context and alternative explanations. Faulty application is distinguished from disproof of all psychoanalysis.
representative_people.works: “Leonardo and Freud: An Art-Historical Study” (1956), selected passages

representative_people.context: Proposes an autonomous science linking childrearing with group fantasies. His causal theory and progressive narrative are contested, including by Pollock.
representative_people.works: Foundations of Psychohistory (1982), preface; “On Writing Childhood History” (1988), selected passages

representative_people.context: Questions deMause’s source selection and broad narrative of improvement. His later criticism of her 1983 book concerns inferences from diary silence; the exchange remains unresolved here.
representative_people.works: The Forgotten Children (1981 thesis), pp. 93–94; Forgotten Children (1983), discussed by deMause (1988)

representative_people.context: Gay values the integration of psychological and contextual explanation in his witchcraft study while disputing their relative weight. This is reception evidence.
representative_people.works: Entertaining Satan, discussed in Gay’s 1997 interview

representative_people.context: Gay recalls the 1950/1951 Freud reading circle as an impetus to his interests. Neumann’s wife also participated; the account does not name her.
representative_people.works: Freud reading circle recalled by Gay (1997)

representative_people.context: Gay recalls the 1950/1951 Freud reading circle as an impetus to his interests. Neumann’s wife also participated; the account does not name her.
representative_people.works: Freud reading circle recalled by Gay (1997)

nodes.scope_note: Erikson, Gay and deMause have different explanatory ambitions; they are not interchangeable applications of Lacan. Schapiro’s art-historical criticism supplies a methodological interlocutor, not blanket rejection of psychoanalysis. Pollock’s thesis and deMause’s later response address distinct texts and disputed evidential procedures. Original case books and wider political, religious and regional applications remain selective research limits; theoretical or clinical assertions are not established diagnoses of past people.

strands.title: Psychosocial lives and historical orders
strands.focus: Erikson places identity within somatic, ego and social orders; his later discussion relates Luther’s personal crisis to transformation. This is an attributed interpretation.
strands.works: Young Man Luther (1958); retrospective account (1970), p. 750

strands.title: Psychoanalytic resources within contextual history
strands.focus: Gay insists on external circumstances and inner life together; his qualified judgment of Demos shows disagreement about explanatory weight.

strands.title: Childrearing, group fantasy and causal ambition
strands.focus: deMause proposes an independent explanatory science. His progressive model and reductionist commitment differ from other approaches represented in this umbrella.

strands.title: Childhood sources, selection and silence
strands.focus: Pollock questions selected evidence and sweeping change; deMause disputes inferences from unrecorded punishment. The thesis, later book and reply are distinct texts, without independent diary collation here.
strands.works: Pollock thesis (1981), pp. 93–94; deMause (1988), selected reply

strands.title: Psychobiography and historical knowledge
strands.focus: Schapiro examines translation and contextual evidence in Freud’s Leonardo interpretation. His particular criticism neither dismisses every psychobiography nor directly rebuts Erikson.

strands.title: Historicizing psychological concepts
strands.focus: Erikson asks for historical scrutiny of identity crises and the categories used to describe them. Retrospective self-interpretation itself becomes evidence requiring criticism.

nodes.label: Frantz Fanon
nodes.description: Analyzes colonial domination through racialized experience, psychic injury, and struggles for liberation. A psychiatrist and political theorist whose work supplies historians with questions about subject formation, violence, and the limits of national liberation; his arguments are not confined to individual psychology.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Black Skin, White Masks (French original 1952); The Wretched of the Earth (French original 1961). Later English editions have different publication dates.
nodes.scope_note: Black Skin, White Masks (1952) treats racialized experience through psychological and social explanation; its introduction names Freud while insisting on sociogeny. The Wretched of the Earth (1961) combines liberation strategy, criticism of elite nationalism and psychiatric cases. These are connected inquiries, not one invariant doctrine or membership in psychohistory. Gendered and regional generalizations require critical reading.

nodes.label: Walter Rodney
nodes.description: Explains underdevelopment through historically unequal relations of slavery, colonial extraction and capitalism. Regional African research, Guyanese labor history and popular education give his work distinct scales and audiences. His account of systemic constraints also investigates changing societies; dependency analysis captures only part of his scholarship and politics.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Groundings with My Brothers (1969); How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972).
nodes.scope_note: A History of the Upper Guinea Coast, 1545–1800 (1970, from a 1966 thesis) reconstructs regional change; The Groundings with My Brothers (1969) concerns political education; How Europe Underdeveloped Africa (1972) offers a didactic synthesis. A History of the Guyanese Working People, 1881–1905 (posthumous, 1981) examines labor and racial divisions. His 1975 Marxism lecture distinguishes method from fixed European conclusions. James’s later strategic criticism coexists with formative intellectual exchange.

nodes.label: C. L. R. James
nodes.description: Places enslaved people’s revolutionary action at the center of the Haitian Revolution and reworks Marxist historical explanation through the Caribbean. His writing also investigates colonial society, race, and cultural life through cricket and autobiography.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Black Jacobins (1938; revised 1963); Beyond a Boundary (1963). The two editions of The Black Jacobins should not be treated as an unchanged argument.
nodes.scope_note: The Black Jacobins (1938; revised 1963) and the 1971 lectures distinguish successive historical perspectives. James later sought closer study of rank-and-file leaders and praised Du Bois’s attention to political imagination. His recollections identify Trotsky, Lenin and Marx among resources, alongside Caribbean projects. Beyond a Boundary (1963) examines social divisions through clubs and treats cricket as an art. These connections do not make him a disciple of postwar British social history.

nodes.label: Eric Williams
nodes.description: Argues that slavery and slave-trade wealth contributed to British capitalist development, and that changing economic interests helped explain abolition. These are related but distinguishable theses whose mechanisms, timing, and weight remain debated. His work challenges accounts centered on European benevolence.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Capitalism and Slavery (1944). Distinguish the original book from later editions and from subsequent arguments about capitalism and slavery.
nodes.scope_note: The 1944 preface separates slavery’s contribution to industrial finance from industrial capitalism’s role in abolition; the conclusion gives economic forces explanatory priority. Williams names Ragatz, Pitman, Herskovits, Burch and Harlow among scholarly helpers. Drescher’s 1977 challenge concerns decline and the 1807 slave-trade abolition, not a refutation of every slavery/capitalism claim. From Columbus to Castro (1970) is a later Caribbean synthesis, here checked only bibliographically.

nodes.label: Antonio Gramsci
nodes.description: Hegemony, common sense, subaltern groups, and intellectuals help explain domination through consent as well as coercion. Later historians and cultural theorists adapt these concepts differently. Anglophone reception predates the widely used 1971 Selections and does not follow a single timetable.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Antonio Gramsci (1891–1937); Selections from the Prison Notebooks (1971). Guha’s Subaltern Studies and Hall’s cultural studies are distinct adaptations.
nodes.scope_note: Unfinished and revised prison writings reach readers through editorial selections and translations. Intellectuals are defined by social functions, common sense is historically layered, and subaltern inquiry includes organization and autonomous activity. Gramsci’s broad geographical and linguistic hierarchies are open to criticism; later adaptations are distinct projects.

nodes.label: Historicism & idealist philosophies of history
nodes.date_label: 1800s roots · Dilthey 1883 · Croce 1917 · Meinecke 1936 · Collingwood 1946 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Groups related arguments for historical specificity and interpretive understanding. German Historismus and British and Italian idealism are not one doctrine: Collingwood’s re-enactment is a particular account of historical thought, not a method shared by everyone here. This usage differs from Popper’s criticism of predictive laws of historical development. Approaches separate documentary interpretation, the human sciences, living historical questions, developmental individuality and rethinking past arguments; their disagreements concern evidence, values, political power and historical context.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Wilhelm Dilthey; Benedetto Croce, Theory and History of Historiography (1917); Friedrich Meinecke, Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936); R. G. Collingwood, The Idea of History (1946, posthumous).

representative_people.context: Develops a foundation for human sciences encompassing history, theory and practical judgments. Later attention to expression and shared historical worlds qualifies an account based only on individual psychology; the later primary text remains separately scoped.
representative_people.works: Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883), chapters 1, 2, 6; The Formation of the Historical World in the Human Sciences (1910), through editors’ introduction and SEP

representative_people.context: Historical thought responds to present questions while drawing on preserved documents. His distinction between living history and chronicle is idealist, not a distinction between important and trivial subjects or an instruction to disregard evidence.
representative_people.works: Theory and History of Historiography (Italian 1917; consulted 1921 Ainslie translation from 1919 edition), I.1

representative_people.context: Studies individuality and development in a selected genealogy of historicism. His account of national statehood and power receives a specific, attributed criticism from Paddock; neither the definition nor the criticism represents every historicism.
representative_people.works: Weltbürgertum und Nationalstaat (1907); Die Ideen der Staatsräson (1924); Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936), through publisher and scholarly selections

representative_people.context: Re-enactment reconstructs an intelligible act of thought through evidence, not its original sensations or total immediacy. Skinner later credits changing questions and question/answer logic while emphasizing other philosophical resources.
representative_people.works: An Autobiography (1939), reception through Skinner; The Idea of History (1946, posthumous), Epilegomena §4, selected paragraphs

representative_people.context: Combines interpretive understanding with a critical method and a conception of the moral historical world. His approach bridges documentary scholarship and philosophical reflection without becoming identical to Dilthey or Croce.
representative_people.works: Grundriss der Historik (public edition 1867; consulted 1893 English translation)

representative_people.context: Provides an earlier comparison for historical individuality and the value of epochs. His theology and documentary practice differ from later philosophies; no backward influence is implied.
representative_people.works: 1824 preface; lectures on epochs (1854); selected World History reflections

representative_people.context: Dilthey expands the critical project toward historical reason and embodied human experience. This identifies a named philosophical resource, not agreement with every Kantian premise.
representative_people.works: Critique of Pure Reason; Dilthey’s Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883) as a documented reworking

representative_people.context: Dilthey contests speculative system-building while adapting objective spirit to shared historical forms. A productive appropriation with disagreement; the original Hegel corpus is not independently collated here.
representative_people.works: Objective spirit; Dilthey’s Die Jugendgeschichte Hegels (1906) and later Formation project as documented reception

representative_people.context: Hermeneutics and religious life become objects of Dilthey’s editorial, biographical and philosophical work; the intellectual setting extends beyond a private psychological portrait.
representative_people.works: Hermeneutical writings and letters; Dilthey’s 1860 hermeneutical study and Leben Schleiermachers, volume I (1870) as reception

representative_people.context: A resource in Dilthey’s expanded critical perspective and an author central to Meinecke’s selective genealogy. These distinct receptions do not establish one unbroken school.
representative_people.works: Historical philosophy; Meinecke’s Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936), through Paddock’s account

representative_people.context: An explicitly documented recipient of Collingwood’s question/answer logic, with substantial analytical-philosophical commitments. Placement records selective reception and does not label the Cambridge approach idealist.
representative_people.works: “Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas” (1969), reception discussed in the 2002 interview

nodes.scope_note: German historicism, Italian idealism, and Collingwood’s re-enactment are not one doctrine; neither is this Popper’s usage of historicism.

strands.title: Understanding through historical investigation
strands.focus: Droysen makes interpretable traces, interdependent critical operations and wider conditions central; neither bare testimony nor complete psychological access suffices.
strands.works: Outline of the Principles of History (1893), selected sections

strands.title: Human sciences, theory and practical judgment
strands.focus: The 1883 program distinguishes historical assertions, theoretical uniformities and evaluations/rules. Its broad remit includes humanities and social sciences, rather than forbidding every explanatory generalization.
strands.works: Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883), chapters 1, 2 and 6

strands.title: Expressions and shared historical worlds
strands.focus: Later Dilthey situates understanding in meaningful expressions, institutions and common historical life. Hegel’s objective spirit is appropriated with different commitments; individual introspection is insufficient.
strands.works: Formation of the Historical World (1910) and related drafts, through editors and SEP

strands.title: Present questions and preserved records
strands.focus: Croce distinguishes historical thinking from preserved chronicle without rejecting preservation. His explicit engagement with Droysen joins appreciation to criticism of abstract source categories.

strands.title: Individuality, development and state power
strands.focus: Meinecke’s genealogy privileges historical development and particularity. Paddock challenges its treatment of national statehood and supposed breaks in the author’s outlook; that is an attributed interpretation based on selected passages.
strands.works: Weltbürgertum und Nationalstaat (1907); Die Entstehung des Historismus (1936), mediated readings

strands.title: Re-enactment, context and changing questions
strands.focus: Rethinking an argument differs from reliving its sensations. Skinner’s particular reception stresses questions and answers while drawing heavily on analytical philosophy; this is not the shared method of everyone in the umbrella.
strands.works: The Idea of History, Epilegomena §4; An Autobiography through Skinner’s interview

nodes.label: Explanation & objectivity debates
nodes.date_label: Earlier roots · Becker address 1931 · Hempel 1942 · Carr 1961 · Elton 1967 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Disputes concern general laws, understanding actions, historical facts, and the possibility of objectivity. Analytic philosophy’s covering-law debate overlaps with historians’ arguments about evidence and interpretation without being identical to them. Narrative theory enters a discussion already under way.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Becker’s 1931 address (published 1932); Hempel, “The Function of General Laws in History” (1942); Dray, Laws and Explanation in History (1957); Carr, What Is History? (1961); Elton, The Practice of History (1967).

representative_people.context: Connects everyday inquiry, social memory and changing interpretation while retaining critical checks.
representative_people.works: Everyman His Own Historian (address 1931; publication 1932)

representative_people.context: Proposes testable laws and initial conditions, allowing probability and incomplete explanation sketches.
representative_people.works: The Function of General Laws in History (1942)

representative_people.context: Challenges reducing all historical explanations to a covering-law model; rational action and pragmatic questions are distinct concerns.
representative_people.works: Laws and Explanation in History (1957)

representative_people.context: Treats selection, interpretation and research as reciprocal while rejecting equal validity for every account.
representative_people.works: What Is History? (1961)

representative_people.context: Addresses research, imagination, writing and teaching; Mink cites his insistence on immersion in a period.
representative_people.works: The Practice of History (1967)

representative_people.context: Historian of evidence who distinguishes origins from explanation and treats traces as answers to questions under evidential constraints.
representative_people.works: Apologie pour l’histoire ou Métier d’historien (1949)

representative_people.context: Combines rhetorical analysis of historiography with attention to source-based construction; adopts Barthes while questioning a uniform disappearance of concern with reality.

representative_people.context: Historical thought responds to present questions while drawing on preserved documents. His distinction between living history and chronicle is idealist, not a distinction between important and trivial subjects or an instruction to disregard evidence.

representative_people.context: Re-enactment reconstructs an intelligible act of thought through evidence, not its original sensations or total immediacy. Skinner later credits changing questions and question/answer logic while emphasizing other philosophical resources.

representative_people.context: Dilthey contests speculative system-building while adapting objective spirit to shared historical forms. A productive appropriation with disagreement; the original Hegel corpus is not independently collated here.

nodes.scope_note: Covering laws, understanding action, historical facts, and objectivity are different disputes; participants do not form a shared school. Hempel’s probabilistic sketches, Dray’s challenge, Carr’s reciprocal research and Mink’s comprehension are distinct. Primary readings and publisher-only contexts are explicitly separated.

strands.title: Genealogy, values and historical explanation
strands.focus: Nietzsche’s critique asks both how moral judgments arise and what they are worth; Rée and Schopenhauer are distinct interlocutors. Origin and later function must not be conflated.

strands.title: Rhetoric, reference and historical achievement
strands.focus: Barthes analyzes the presentation of reality; Bann uses that analysis while questioning its scope and preserving source-based scrutiny. Formal analysis alone does not decide a historical claim’s truth.

strands.title: The historian, surviving sources and the historical picture
strands.focus: Michelet’s account of reciprocal formation and Huizinga’s warning about surviving art raise different questions about historical knowledge; they do not deny the need for evidence.

strands.title: Evidence, understanding and the historical question
strands.focus: Droysen, Dilthey, Croce and Collingwood offer different accounts of what inquiry does with traces, thought, context and practical concerns. These are explicit conceptual resources, not a common doctrine or a proved genealogy of later debate.

strands.title: Language use and following rules
strands.focus: Wittgenstein examines varied activities and similarities rather than one essence of language. Following a rule involves a practice; an interpretation cannot supply its own application without limit.

strands.title: Knowing how, action and accomplishment
strands.focus: Ryle distinguishes competent action from both an automatic movement and a performance governed by an endless series of prior theoretical decisions. A richer action description identifies purpose and circumstances.
strands.works: The Concept of Mind, II.1–3; The Thinking of Thoughts

strands.title: Narrative and historical understanding
strands.focus: White identifies particular philosophical interlocutors rather than responding to one undifferentiated philosophy of history.

strands.title: Laws, probability and explanation sketches
strands.focus: Hempel’s demand for testable relations permits incomplete research proposals and probabilistic accounts.

strands.title: Action and the limits of one explanatory model
strands.focus: Dray’s challenge includes reasons, uniqueness and pragmatic questions; it is not a ban on all generalization.
strands.works: Laws and Explanation (1957); Nature of Historical Explanation (1952)

strands.title: Selection, relevance and revisable interpretation
strands.focus: Becker and Carr preserve evidence while disputing self-interpreting facts; they do not offer identical positions.

strands.title: Historical craft, imagination and instruction
strands.focus: Elton’s research/writing/teaching agenda and Skinner’s apprenticeship reading identify practices of training.

strands.title: Narrative comprehension and truth
strands.focus: Mink separates grasping relations from truth tests and disputes both Gallie’s following and Hardy’s lived-narrative account.

strands.title: Knowledge of the past and speculative historical systems
strands.focus: Walsh’s scope distinguishes questions about inquiry from philosophies of the whole historical process.

nodes.label: Frankfurt School / critical theory
nodes.date_label: 1920s roots · Benjamin · Adorno · Habermas · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Critical theorists draw differently on Marx, Weber, and Freud to examine domination, culture, and rationality. Benjamin’s reflections on historical time and Habermas’s public sphere offer distinct resources for historians. Benjamin’s association with the Institute and Habermas’s later work should not imply a single institutional position or doctrine.

strands.focus: Standardization is linked to capital and power, not treated as an autonomous law of technology.

Empirical projects, exile institutions, Freudian debates and feminist/public-sphere criticisms are distinguished. Roster critics and historians are not thereby Institute members.

nodes.label: Practice theory
nodes.date_label: Bourdieu · de Certeau · Sewell · 1970s–90s development · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Examines how embodied dispositions and situated activities reproduce or alter social relations. Bourdieu’s habitus and strategies, de Certeau’s tactics, and Sewell’s account of structure offer different ways to connect agency, constraint, and meaning. These are several resources for reassessing cultural history, not a single replacement paradigm.

nodes.scope_note: Bourdieu, de Certeau, and Sewell offer distinct accounts. Practice theory is not a unified successor to cultural history. Collaborative everyday research, cultural repertoires and Ortner’s plural orientation broaden this selection. Strategy has different meanings across these authors.

nodes.label: Norbert Elias
nodes.description: Links changes in manners and affect to interdependence and state formation. Historians adapt and contest his account of the relations between social constraint and self-restraint. The approach raises questions about historical scale and variation rather than supplying a universal ladder of civilization.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Über den Prozeß der Zivilisation (1939), known in English as The Civilizing Process; The Court Society (German 1969). Distinguish original publication, translations, and later reception.
nodes.scope_note: Interdependence, manners, and state formation are historical questions; comparison with Weber or Freud is not automatically demonstrated borrowing. His retrospective interview names psychoanalytic and Durkheimian readings. Collaborative projects and Duerr’s criticism qualify the range of this inquiry; book bodies and reception are checked separately.

nodes.label: British cultural studies
nodes.date_label: Hoggart · Williams · Hall · CCCS 1964 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Examines culture as lived and contested, including popular forms, class, media, race, and gender. Debates among culturalist, structuralist, feminist, and antiracist projects reshape the field. It exchanges ideas with historical scholarship while retaining distinct institutional and disciplinary histories.

nodes.scope_note: Hoggart, Williams, Thompson and Hall have distinct trajectories. Birmingham is one institutional center; feminist, antiracist, ethnographic and media projects revise its questions. Culturalist/structuralist distinctions are debated, not successive closed schools. Contributors listed as theoretical resources are not thereby CCCS members. Exchanges with history do not make the fields identical.

nodes.label: Progressive & consensus historiography (US)
nodes.date_label: Contrasting frameworks prominent in the 1890s–1950s · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: A paired comparison of influential US approaches, not one school or the whole profession. Progressive interpretations emphasize economic interest and conflict; postwar consensus interpretations emphasize shared commitments across political divisions. The labels are contested and do not capture every argument of the writers grouped under them.

strands.title: Progressive interpretations
strands.focus: Economic conflict, sectional patterns and literary interpretation are distinct inquiries.
strands.works: An Economic Interpretation of the Constitution; Turner’s frontier essay

strands.title: Consensus interpretations

strands.works: The American Political Tradition; The Liberal Tradition in America

strands.title: Collaborative synthesis and distinct women’s-history questions
strands.focus: Charles and Mary Beard’s joint histories require recognition of both authors. Mary’s archival work and challenge to the subject-sex tradition cannot be reduced to Charles’s constitutional interpretation.
strands.works: The Rise of American Civilization (1927); Woman as Force in History (1946)

strands.title: Sectional mapping and proxies
strands.focus: Libby explains how delegate votes stand for local constituencies and where corrections enter.
strands.works: The Geographical Distribution of the Vote (1894)

strands.title: Multiple hypotheses and changing questions
strands.focus: Turner advocates disciplinary exchange and challenges history used merely to illustrate a prior law.

strands.title: Literary ideas and political conflict
strands.focus: Parrington declares his standpoint and treats literary debate within social and economic histories.

strands.title: Critical political portraits
strands.focus: Hofstadter’s selected leaders reveal shared premises; this is not comprehensive biography.

strands.title: Liberal assumptions and conformity
strands.focus: Hartz treats unanimity as a danger and insists on comparative inquiry; his national generalization is disputed.

strands.title: Disagreement about national homogeneity
strands.focus: Higham differentiates Boorstin, Hartz and Potter and questions the minimization of ideological conflict.
strands.works: The Cult of the American Consensus (1959)

nodes.scope_note: Progressive and consensus interpretations are contrasting positions. Attribute criticisms and economic explanations to the relevant side. Hofstadter’s critical portraits, Hartz’s fear of conformity and Boorstin’s appraisal must remain distinct. Frontier/free-land and civilizational hierarchies in older texts are historical claims, not this atlas’s categories.

nodes.label: New Left & radical history (US)
nodes.description: Challenges consensus interpretations through studies of class, race, capitalism, and empire. Radical diplomatic, labour, and slavery histories overlap with new social history but differ in politics and method. Their engagements with Black history do not supply that field’s independent origins. Gutman’s cultural labor history also criticizes some New Left institutional accounts. Alice and Staughton Lynd make organizer testimony and participant review part of research practice; Zinn’s selective Marxian commitments differ from Genovese’s paternalism interpretation.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: William Appleman Williams, The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959)—a different writer from Eric Williams; Staughton Lynd; Eugene Genovese, Roll, Jordan, Roll (1974); Herbert Gutman, Work, Culture, and Society (1976); Radical History Review (1973).

representative_people.context: Revisionist diplomatic history linking ideology, political economy and expansion; a different historian from Eric Williams.
representative_people.works: The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959)

representative_people.context: Investigates radical intellectual traditions and, with Alice Lynd, edits working-class organizers’ accounts with explicit participant correction and selection limits.
representative_people.works: Intellectual Origins of American Radicalism (1968); with Alice Lynd, eds., Rank and File (1973)

representative_people.context: Interprets slavery through class, culture and paternalism as contested domination. His preface’s national-culture framing and later criticism remain visible; paternalism is not a claim of benign slavery.
representative_people.works: Roll, Jordan, Roll (1974), preface, acknowledgments and opening paternalism discussion

representative_people.context: Studies work discipline and differentiated working-class cultures; explicitly adapts British methods and criticizes some New Left labor history. His 1973 article excludes nonwhite and bound workers from its detailed scope.
representative_people.works: Work, Culture, and Society (1976); Work, Culture, and Society in Industrializing America, 1815–1919 (1973 article)

representative_people.context: Coedits organizer testimony with Staughton Lynd; editing and participants’ correction are explicit features of the method.
representative_people.works: With Staughton Lynd, eds., Rank and File (1973), introduction

representative_people.works: Beyond Equality (1967), cited by Gutman; The Fall of the House of Labor (1987)

representative_people.works: The Mechanics and the Jeffersonians: New York, 1789–1801 (1964)

representative_people.context: Gutman distinguishes his sailors-and-revolution study from corporate-liberalism-centered New Left labor history. This selection follows that specific contrast.
representative_people.works: Jack Tar in the Streets: Merchant Seamen in the Politics of the American Revolution (1968)

representative_people.context: Writes popular radical history and defends selective Marxian insights while rejecting dogmatic authority; this differs from one uniform Marxist program.
representative_people.works: A People’s History of the United States (1980); Je Ne Suis Pas Un Marxiste (1988)

representative_people.context: Reinterprets Progressive-era business regulation as shaped by business leaders; the claim belongs to his revisionist project, not all radical historians.
representative_people.works: The Triumph of Conservatism (1963)

representative_people.context: Genovese explicitly credits his slavery scholarship and source work; acknowledgment establishes a resource, not complete theoretical agreement.
representative_people.works: From Sundown to Sunup; The American Slave, acknowledged in Roll, Jordan, Roll (1974)

representative_people.context: Shares ideas and material with Genovese during research on slavery and culture; the specific collaboration does not assign all his work to a single movement.

representative_people.works: Research exchange acknowledged in Roll, Jordan, Roll (1974)

nodes.scope_note: Radical diplomatic history, labour history, and slavery history differ. William Appleman Williams is not Eric Williams. This is a US teaching grouping, not the British New Left or a single party line. Collaborators and interlocutors are selected by particular work, without imputing all of an author’s later politics to it. Edited testimony, cultural analysis and quantitative resources can coexist.

strands.title: Diplomacy, ideology and expansion
strands.focus: William Appleman Williams links ideology and political economy in US expansion; his 1959 work must be distinguished from later Vietnam-era revisions.

strands.title: Business power and reform
strands.focus: Kolko attributes important regulatory initiatives to business leadership; this revisionist argument is distinct from a blanket rejection of all reform.

strands.title: Work discipline and differentiated cultures
strands.focus: Gutman adapts British methods while criticizing narrow US labor history, including some New Left accounts; Montgomery connects workplace and political organization.

strands.title: Artisans, sailors and radical traditions
strands.focus: Young, Lemisch and Lynd pose different questions about popular participation and radical political ideas. Their subjects do not imply a single class consciousness.

strands.title: Organizers’ accounts and shared editing
strands.focus: The Lynds combine interviews, written accounts and speeches in a selective collection whose participants read and correct the edited accounts.

strands.title: Slavery, culture and paternalism
strands.focus: Genovese’s interpretation of domination and negotiated claims remains disputed. Acknowledged cultural, documentary and quantitative resources do not establish unanimous agreement.
strands.works: Roll, Jordan, Roll (1974); retrospective Johnson review (2001)

strands.title: Popular radical history and selective Marxism
strands.focus: Zinn values alienation, class and internationalism while rejecting doctrinal authority; this is a particular stance within a diverse radical historiography.
strands.works: A People’s History (1980); Je Ne Suis Pas Un Marxiste (1988)

nodes.label: History Workshop movement
nodes.description: Develops collaborative history from below through adult education, labour movements, and historical scholarship. Its socialist and feminist projects involve worker-historians alongside academic historians. Oral testimony, women’s history, and later work on popular memory reshape its concerns.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Raphael Samuel; History Workshop Journal (1976 onward); Sheila Rowbotham, Hidden from History (1973); Samuel, Theatres of Memory (1994); Gareth Stedman Jones, Languages of Class (1983), a contested reorientation in British social history.

representative_people.context: Ruskin collaboration, a journal intervention on oral history and later popular-past research form related but distinct projects. His methodological essay argues for interaction between oral and written evidence while examining the selection and silences of both.
representative_people.works: “Local History and Oral History” (1976); Theatres of Memory (1994)

representative_people.context: Feminist participation challenges the movement’s priorities as well as expanding its historical subjects.
representative_people.works: Hidden from History (1973)

representative_people.context: Questions how class acquires political meaning in particular idioms; a contested reorientation, not an undifferentiated Workshop doctrine. In the Chartism chapter he distinguishes political language from an automatic expression of distress while retaining the relevance of social conditions.
representative_people.works: Languages of Class (1983)

representative_people.context: Founding journal editor whose feminist historical work joins labor, sexual difference and subjectivity.
representative_people.works: Becoming a Woman (1994); Ruskin pamphlet on St Giles’s Fair, recalled in the Davin interview

representative_people.context: Founding editor, pamphlet collaborator and teacher; studies gender, empire and poor children’s lives. Her 1978 essay connects imperial population concerns with the redefinition of motherhood and the displacement of attention from poverty and environment.
representative_people.works: “Imperialism and Motherhood” (1978); Growing Up Poor (1996)

representative_people.context: Contributes a specific argument about competing place histories to the journal’s 1995 spatial-history section; publication does not establish founding membership.
representative_people.works: Places and Their Pasts (1995)

representative_people.works: With Raphael Samuel, Rethinking the Idea of Place (1995)

strands.title: Adult education and collaborative history
strands.focus: Ruskin students’ research and cheaply produced pamphlets connect participation, audiences and publication.

strands.title: Contested linguistic reorientation
strands.focus: Stedman Jones questions class’s assumed political meaning; this is one intervention within a heterogeneous movement.

strands.title: Oral history in publication and teaching
strands.focus: The 1976 journal article supplies an early venue; Taylor’s recollection documents Davin teaching oral history in 1998.
strands.works: Samuel (1976); Davin’s teaching, recalled by Becky Taylor (2025)

strands.title: Gender and the domestic history of empire
strands.focus: Davin’s study of motherhood connects metropolitan gender questions to imperial politics.
strands.works: “Imperialism and Motherhood” (1978), discussed retrospectively by its author

strands.title: Feminist history and psychoanalytic questions
strands.focus: Sexual difference and subjectivity open questions about historical actors and the historian’s interpretation.

strands.title: Popular historical practices
strands.focus: Samuel examines historical knowledge made through everyday cultural activity.

strands.title: Spatial history and contested places
strands.focus: Driver and Samuel’s editorial accompanies Massey’s intervention on changing place identities and histories.

strands.title: Collaborative place history
strands.focus: The 1995 spatial-history section includes Rita and Jackie Huggins with Jane M. Jacobs. Verified coauthorship and the public finding aid document collaboration; detailed article interpretation remains limited by access.

strands.title: Oral and documentary evidence in interaction
strands.focus: Samuel treats local history as an inquiry shaped by available sources and questions. Oral evidence can expose archival omissions but has its own silences and retrospective distortions.
strands.works: Local History and Oral History (1976), selected reprint passages

strands.title: Empire, class and definitions of motherhood
strands.focus: Davin examines how imperial concerns and professional authority made mothers responsible for population health. Her account differentiates pressures on women across class positions.
strands.works: Imperialism and Motherhood (1978), opening and research credits

strands.title: Worker history and union authority
strands.focus: Douglass examines tensions between miners, employers and union officials, connecting historical disputes with his own experience of workplace representation.
strands.works: Pit Life in Co. Durham (1972), attributed excerpt

strands.title: Chartist language and class explanations
strands.focus: Stedman Jones questions explanations that derive political mobilization directly from hardship. Kirk accepts attention to language but disputes its relative autonomy and the marginalization of anti-capitalist ideas.
strands.works: Rethinking Chartism (1983); In Defence of Class (1987), selected passages

nodes.scope_note: Adult education, socialist research, feminist criticism, and linguistic debates interact; no single turn describes the whole movement. The Ruskin workshops, later itinerant meetings and journal are related institutions with distinct histories. Retrospective participant accounts supply evidence about earlier practice without extending this map beyond 2000.

nodes.label: Historical demography & history of the family
nodes.date_label: Henry · Cambridge Group · 1950s–70s expansion · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Combines related inquiries into population, households, childhood and intimate relations. Henry’s family reconstitution and Cambridge’s aggregate and household studies differ from Ariès’s historical concepts and Stone’s family interpretation. Pollock’s criticism questions evidence and sweeping changes in parental care. Lee and Wang’s Chinese population study challenges received Malthusian comparisons without making the field’s regional patterns uniform.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Louis Henry; Cambridge Group for the History of Population and Social Structure (1964); Peter Laslett, The World We Have Lost (1965); Wrigley and Schofield, The Population History of England (1981); Philippe Ariès (1960); Lawrence Stone (1977). Additional selections: Hajnal (1965); Laslett and Wall (1972); Pollock (1981/1983); Wrigley, Davies, Oeppen and Schofield (1997); Lee and Wang (1999).

representative_people.context: Develops historical family reconstitution at INED; his Geneva study explains why mobile urban and elite families require documents beyond one locality’s parish registers.
representative_people.works: Anciennes familles genevoises: Étude démographique, XVIe–XXe siècle (1956)

representative_people.context: Cambridge Group co-founder; household composition studies question a simple industrial origin of nuclear households. Household form does not measure affection.
representative_people.works: The World We Have Lost (1965); with Richard Wall, ed., Household and Family in Past Time (1972)

representative_people.works: L’Enfant et la vie familiale sous l’Ancien Régime (1960); Centuries of Childhood (English 1962)

representative_people.context: Examines family relations, marriage and affective individualism; Pollock disputes the explanation of change and selective use of personal documents. This is not a universally established household trajectory.
representative_people.works: The Family, Sex and Marriage in England, 1500–1800 (1977)

representative_people.works: With E. A. Wrigley, Ros Davies and Roger Schofield, English Population History from Family Reconstitution 1580–1837 (1997)

representative_people.context: Co-author of Cambridge’s collaborative reconstruction of preindustrial population from parish-register families.
representative_people.works: With E. A. Wrigley, Jim Oeppen and Roger Schofield, English Population History from Family Reconstitution 1580–1837 (1997)

representative_people.context: Collaborates on comparative household history, a different evidential question from changes in intimate feelings.
representative_people.works: With Peter Laslett, ed., Household and Family in Past Time (1972)

representative_people.works: “European Marriage Patterns in Perspective” (1965)

representative_people.works: The Forgotten Children (PhD thesis, 1981); Forgotten Children: Parent-Child Relations from 1500 to 1900 (1983)

representative_people.works: With Wang Feng, One Quarter of Humanity: Malthusian Mythology and Chinese Realities, 1700–2000 (1999)

representative_people.works: With James Z. Lee, One Quarter of Humanity: Malthusian Mythology and Chinese Realities, 1700–2000 (1999)

representative_people.works: “Women’s Work and the Family in Nineteenth-Century Europe” (1975); Women, Work, and Family (1978)

nodes.scope_note: Family reconstitution and aggregate reconstruction differ from histories of childhood or family meanings; Henry, Annales, and Cambridge are not interchangeable. Household composition, marriage behavior, concepts of childhood and parental conduct are different objects of study. England and France are prominent in this selection; Chinese comparative research broadens the questions without representing all non-European family histories. Later institutional webpages are retrospective sources, not an extension beyond 2000.

strands.title: Reconstituting families from historical records
strands.focus: Link records of family events while examining who disappears from observation; Henry flags mobility and social differences, and Cambridge’s 1997 study is explicitly collaborative.
strands.works: Anciennes familles genevoises (1956); English Population History from Family Reconstitution (1997)

strands.title: Reconstructing aggregate population
strands.focus: Use historical demographic observations to estimate population and vital rates; a national reconstruction is distinct from following the observed life of one family.
strands.works: The Population History of England 1541–1871: A Reconstruction (1981)

strands.title: Households and comparative marriage patterns
strands.focus: Compare household composition and marriage patterns without inferring feelings from household size or treating one region as universal.
strands.works: Household and Family in Past Time (1972); “European Marriage Patterns in Perspective” (1965)

strands.title: Childhood concepts, conduct and evidence
strands.focus: Ariès examines childhood as a historical concept; Pollock questions broad change narratives through personal documents. Affection and recognition of a separate life stage are not identical claims.
strands.works: Centuries of Childhood (1962); The Forgotten Children (1981); Forgotten Children (1983)

strands.title: Marriage, intimacy and disputed change
strands.focus: Stone’s affective-individualism interpretation meets criticism of its explanation and evidential selection. Neither prescriptive literature nor diary writers transparently represent everyone.
strands.works: The Family, Sex and Marriage in England (1977); Pollock’s thesis, pp. 96–98 and 143–144 (1981)

strands.title: Chinese population and Malthusian comparisons
strands.focus: Lee and Wang argue for forms of population regulation missed by received China/West contrasts. Their fertility and marriage claims remain arguments to test against evidence and regional variation.

strands.title: Patterns, exceptions and explanation
strands.focus: Hajnal distinguishes late marriage from remaining unmarried, acknowledges regional variation and separates identifying a pattern from explaining it. Goody questions its uniqueness and the scale of comparison.

strands.title: Local monographs and collective sampling
strands.focus: Fleury and Henry credit Goubert and other researchers, but argue that chosen parish monographs cannot simply be added into a national sample. Biraben joins their subsequent register inventory.

strands.title: Population totals and family subsets
strands.focus: Henry’s survey account distinguishes aggregate reconstruction from the smaller rural sample used for family reconstitution. Changes in sampling and uneven record quality constrain what each can establish.

strands.title: Observed fertility and deliberate control
strands.focus: Lee and Wang interpret delayed first births, longer intervals and earlier stopping as marital restraint. Harrell’s later review questions source completeness, regional reach and whether these patterns establish intentional control.
strands.works: One Quarter of Humanity (1999),86–90; Harrell review (2003),543

strands.title: Local evidence and collaborative reconstruction
strands.focus: Harrell’s collection brings local demographic studies together; Lee and Wang acknowledge Campbell’s contributions. A broad comparative argument still requires attention to differences among local sources.
strands.works: Chinese Historical Microdemography (1995); One Quarter of Humanity (1999), opening acknowledgment

strands.title: Family change, social differences and source selection
strands.focus: Stone qualifies affective individualism with reversals and overlapping patterns across social groups, while making a debatable assumption about surviving documents. Pollock separates childhood concepts, affection and discipline and questions how family histories generalize from their sources.
strands.works: Stone, abridged edition (1979), 21–29; Pollock, Forgotten Children (1983), 1–10

strands.title: Italian residence and marriage patterns
strands.focus: Kertzer and Hogan report patrilocal residence without the expected combination of early female marriage, large spousal age differences and low nonmarriage. Similar marriage ages among wage workers and sharecroppers complicate a simple account of proletarianization.
strands.works: “Reflections on the European Marriage Pattern” (1991), Casalecchio, 1861–1921

nodes.label: Revival of narrative / debate over quantification
nodes.description: Stone diagnoses renewed interest in narrative, individuals, and culture amid dissatisfaction with some structural and quantitative explanations. Hobsbawm contests the diagnosis. This contemporary debate concerns historians’ practices; it differs from White’s earlier analysis of narrative form and does not establish that quantitative history ended.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Lawrence Stone, “The Revival of Narrative” (1979); Eric Hobsbawm, “The Revival of Narrative: Some Comments” (1980). Compare with Metahistory (1973), which predates both.

representative_people.context: The 1979 revival diagnosis and the earlier 1978 Tuchman review are distinct interventions. In the review he praises communication while questioning the selection of events and explanatory depth. The 1979 essay restricts its diagnosis to a prominent minority and acknowledges continuing quantitative work.

representative_people.context: Questions whether changed subjects and presentation establish a retreat from explanation; small-scale inquiry can serve larger analytical questions.
representative_people.works: “The Revival of Narrative: Some Comments” (1980), pp. 3–8

representative_people.works: The Guns of August (1962); A Distant Mirror and its 1978 reception; “In Search of History,” publisher excerpt

representative_people.context: Her sustained narrative practice precedes 1979. Prefatory explanations defend attention to uncertainty without claiming to answer every historical question.

strands.title: Historical subjects, explanation and presentation
strands.focus: Hobsbawm questions Stone’s diagnosis by separating changing topics and narrative presentation from the abandonment of analytical explanation. Cited small-scale studies need not share one method or political interpretation.

strands.title: Narrative, crisis and competing standards of explanation
strands.focus: Stone questions Tuchman’s selected events and modern parallels while admiring her narrative. Fox-Genovese challenges his professional and progress assumptions; defense does not mean agreement with every historical claim.

strands.title: A limited diagnosis and continuing plurality

strands.title: Story, argument and explanation
strands.focus: Stone includes analysis within narrative; Hobsbawm disputes the claimed larger retreat from explanation.

strands.title: Events and cases as analytical resources

strands.works: Bouvines (1973); The Cheese and the Worms (1976)

strands.title: Cultural subjects and different forms
strands.focus: Brown’s portrait and Zeldin’s themes prevent a simple equation of cultural interest with storytelling.
strands.works: The World of Late Antiquity (1971); France (1973–1977)

strands.title: Selection, typicality and court records
strands.focus: Stone asks what exceptional cases can reveal and what prosecution counts actually measure.

strands.title: Narrative continuity and readers
strands.focus: Earlier Tuchman and Wedgwood work and critical exchanges situate the later diagnosis.

nodes.label: Comparative historical sociology
nodes.date_label: Comparative programmes · 1960s–90s · earlier resources · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Compares how states, rights, class relations and collective struggles change. Moore studies agrarian routes; Skocpol combines state breakdown with class and international relations; Tilly follows contention; Mann maps intersecting power networks. Bendix, Goldstone, Somers and Block supply different questions about authority, demography, citizenship and economic institutions. Sewell’s exchange with Skocpol makes ideology an explicit debate.
