nodes.scope_note: A field of competing comparisons, not one state-centered theory. Cases range beyond Europe, but this selection is uneven and does not exhaust regional traditions. Cultural and institutional explanations can be combined; political outcomes are not inevitable stages.

strands.title: Agrarian relations and political routes
strands.focus: Class alliances and rural power produce divergent, often violent paths rather than a smooth democratic sequence.

strands.title: States and revolutionary transformations
strands.focus: State organizations, agrarian classes and international competition enter a combined explanation.

strands.title: Contention and repertoires
strands.focus: Historically specific performances link local claims to wider transformations.
strands.works: Tilly, The Contentious French (1986); political-performances essay (1993–1994)

strands.title: Overlapping networks of power
strands.focus: Forms and reach of power are differentiated rather than enclosed in one homogeneous society.
strands.works: Mann, The Sources of Social Power I (1986)

strands.title: Comparative Marxian transitions
strands.focus: European transitions and divergent state forms frame a contested comparative synthesis.

strands.title: Authority, law and citizenship
strands.focus: Bendix compares authority; Somers examines how local relations and national law shape rights. Their methods are distinct.

strands.title: Reconsidering Polanyi
strands.focus: A specific collaborative engagement with economic institutions broadens the field’s conceptual resources.

strands.title: Population, institutions and state crises
strands.focus: Demographic pressures acquire political effects through institutions and elite relations, not population alone.

strands.title: Ideology within structural explanation
strands.focus: Sewell criticizes a restricted account of ideology; Skocpol acknowledges a problem and responds. Her reply’s opening also questions Sewell’s anonymous conception of culture; the exchange contains disagreement in both directions.

strands.title: Interdependence and group power
strands.focus: Court settings and community exclusion are distinct research scales.
strands.works: The Court Society (1969); The Established and the Outsiders (1965)

strands.title: Sport and regulated excitement
strands.focus: Sport opens a further historical problem of affect and interdependence.

strands.title: Comparing crises and their different outcomes
strands.focus: Goldstone compares England and the Fronde, then distinguishes Castile from the Spanish monarchy’s rebellious peripheries. Similar pressures need not produce identical outcomes. Perry values the comparison but questions how far its claims travel across different societies and periods.

strands.title: Empire formation and conflicting political aims
strands.focus: Eisenstadt’s prefaces distinguish social conditions from the emergence of leaders able to organize an imperial polity. Rulers seek resources less bound to traditional groups while trying to control those resources themselves. This comparison retains structural-functional and evolutionary assumptions that his retrospective introduction discusses rather than simply disowns.
strands.works: The Political Systems of Empires (1963), selected prefaces

strands.title: Questioning the units of comparison
strands.focus: Eisenstadt takes up Rokkan’s attention to cultural and territorial settings and questions exporting European state categories. Subrahmanyam separately uses Eurasian circulation to challenge autonomous-state and ideological partitions. These are distinct arguments, not a demonstrated intellectual lineage between the authors.
strands.works: Eisenstadt, Stein Rokkan Lecture (1985); Subrahmanyam, Connected Histories (1997)

nodes.label: West German historical social science / Sonderweg
nodes.date_label: Wehler · Kocka · 1960s–90s debates and extensions · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Historical social science investigates German politics through social and economic structures. Wehler’s Empire interpretation, Kocka’s industrial and bourgeois research, and Frevert’s gender history address different questions. Blackbourn/Eley contest Sonderweg assumptions; Kocka revises parts while defending comparison. Lüdtke questions structural priorities through everyday practices. Fischer’s war-aims controversy is a related precursor.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Hans-Ulrich Wehler, Das deutsche Kaiserreich (1973); Jürgen Kocka; Geschichte und Gesellschaft (1975); David Blackbourn and Geoff Eley, The Peculiarities of German History (1984). Fritz Fischer’s 1961 intervention is a related precursor.

representative_people.context: Explains Imperial German politics through social and economic power structures; his interpretation provokes criticism and revision.
representative_people.works: Das deutsche Kaiserreich 1871–1918 (1973; English 1985)

representative_people.works: Industrial Culture and Bourgeois Society in Modern Germany (1999); “German History before Hitler” (1988)

strands.title: Historical social science
strands.focus: Wehler’s structural political explanation and Kocka’s organizational/social comparisons differ within a broader programme.
strands.works: Wehler, Das deutsche Kaiserreich (1973); Kocka, Industrial Culture (1999)

strands.title: Sonderweg criticism
strands.focus: Critics contest the western yardstick and bourgeois-failure thesis; Kocka accepts revisions while defending qualified comparison.

strands.title: War aims and a related controversy
strands.focus: An archival intervention about First World War aims supplies context for later revisionist questions.

strands.title: Gender, rights and bourgeois society
strands.focus: Women’s opportunities and restrictions enter the history of German society and its political arrangements.

strands.title: Everyday practices and structural priorities
strands.focus: A specific critical exchange about workplace relations keeps actors’ practices visible alongside structures. The separately checked Lüdtke–Wehler exchange contests explanatory priorities while acknowledging some benefits and weaknesses on both sides.

strands.title: A journal as a research and discussion venue
strands.focus: The four authors of the 1975 foreword proposed combining historical interpretation with social-scientific analysis. Thematic issues, research reports and a discussion forum would connect specialists and wider readers. This is an announced programme, not proof that all editorial practice fulfilled it.

strands.title: Structural questions within inherited historical methods
strands.focus: Schieder reads Ranke, Droysen and other earlier historians as already addressing relations between individuals and larger forces. His call to revise inherited methods complicates an absolute divide between traditional history and structural inquiry; his portraits of rival traditions remain contestable.
strands.works: Strukturen und Persönlichkeiten, section I (1968 edition)

strands.title: Mentorship and political accountability
strands.focus: Wehler’s retrospective account combines intellectual gratitude to Schieder with discussion of Nazi-era writings and silence. The 1999 scholarly debate examines postwar continuities and the limits of earlier scrutiny. Methodological innovation and a liberal teaching style do not by themselves settle political responsibility.
strands.works: Wehler interview; Schulze, Helm and Ott on the historians’ debate (1999)

strands.title: Class membership and gendered self-description
strands.focus: Frevert reads the Pringsheim/Mann family’s descriptions of education, occupation and beauty against definitions of bourgeois membership. Her argument differentiates women’s and men’s positions within a class.
strands.works: Classe et genre dans la bourgeoisie allemande du XIXe siècle (1991)

nodes.scope_note: A teaching umbrella spanning a research programme, a contested German-path argument and critics. Historical social science is broader than Sonderweg; neither is synonymous with the later Historikerstreit. Long-term conditions are not inevitable causes of Nazism, and gender history broadens the programme without making all contributors doctrinal adherents. Innovation also coexisted with inherited teaching relationships and politically contested continuities across 1945; the 1998–1999 debate over historians’ Nazi pasts is a distinct episode.

nodes.label: Holocaust historiography
nodes.description: Investigates the persecution and murder of European Jews through policies, institutions, ideology, perpetrators, victims, and testimony. Intentionalist and functionalist debates intersect with disputes about representation and remembrance. Survivor scholarship and documentation have earlier roots; these concerns coexist rather than replacing one another in a fixed sequence.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Raul Hilberg, The Destruction of the European Jews (1961); Martin Broszat; Hans Mommsen; Christopher Browning, Ordinary Men (1992); Saul Friedländer, ed., Probing the Limits of Representation (1992); the Goldhagen controversy (1996).

representative_people.context: Studies the administrative machinery of destruction; this major synthesis is distinct from earlier Jewish documentation and its account of victims is contestable.
representative_people.works: The Destruction of the European Jews (1961; revised editions)

representative_people.context: Interrogates the development of extermination policy while criticizing Irving’s manipulation of sources and retaining Hitler’s ideological role.
representative_people.works: “Hitler and the Genesis of the ‘Final Solution’” (German 1977; English 1979)

representative_people.context: Investigates the development of genocidal policy; his particular chapter remains a reading route within the intentionalist/functionalist debate.
representative_people.works: “The Realization of the Unthinkable” (1986)

representative_people.context: Combines ideological and situational explanations of participation; uses testimony critically when disputing uniform perpetrator motivations.
representative_people.works: Ordinary Men (1992); response to Goldhagen (1996)

representative_people.context: Historical explanation and representation.
representative_people.works: Probing the Limits of Representation (1992), editor

representative_people.works: Hitler’s Willing Executioners (1996); symposium presentation (1996)

nodes.scope_note: Persecution, perpetrators, victims, representation, and memory coexist. Intentionalist/functionalist disputes do not exhaust the field or precede all survivor scholarship. Wartime documentation, daily-life inquiry and rescue research complicate a perpetrator-centered canon. Explanation of radicalization is not exculpation, and disagreement over representation is not equivalent to Holocaust denial. The selection does not cover every occupied country or persecuted population.

strands.title: Jewish documentation during persecution
strands.focus: Collective source creation precedes postwar academic debates; archival survival and selection shape later knowledge.

strands.title: Administrative processes of destruction
strands.focus: Institutions and documentary reconstruction illuminate perpetration; victims’ diverse responses require distinct investigation.
strands.works: The Destruction of the European Jews (1961)

strands.title: Ideology, decisions and radicalization

strands.works: Ordinary Men (1992); Hitler’s Willing Executioners and symposium (1996)

strands.title: Jewish daily life, family and gender

strands.title: Testimony, listening and interpretation
strands.focus: Witnessing raises literary and psychoanalytic questions as well as problems of historical evidence.

strands.title: Narrative and the limits of representation

strands.title: Memorial forms and public remembrance
strands.focus: Later sites of remembrance have their own forms and historical contexts.

nodes.label: Nationalism studies
nodes.date_label: Modernist debates · 1983 landmark works · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Makes the formation of nations and traditions an object of historical explanation. Anderson, Gellner, and Hobsbawm offer different modernist accounts; ethno-symbolist and postcolonial critics question their premises. Treating national identity as historical does not require assuming that every tradition is a recent invention.

representative_people.works: Imagined Communities (1983)

Hroch’s comparative phases, Billig’s everyday reminders and Yuval-Davis’s gender analysis address different questions. Nations, states and nationalist movements are not interchangeable; European typologies require testing beyond their original cases.

strands.focus: Language and circulating print help make unfamiliar people imaginable as a community.

strands.title: Modern mobility and literate culture

strands.title: Historically produced traditions
strands.focus: Rituals and claims of continuity have specific histories in national and imperial settings.

strands.title: Ethnic ties, myths and memories
strands.focus: Earlier cultural inheritances help explain particular nationalisms without making all nations timeless.

strands.title: Comparing national movements

strands.title: Routine reproduction of nationhood

strands.title: Gender, citizenship and national projects
strands.focus: Gender relations organize national reproduction and membership across, within and beyond state boundaries.

nodes.description: Postwar institutions challenge colonial denials of African historical agency while building on older African historical knowledge and writing. Oral traditions, documentary criticism, archaeology, and linguistics support diverse inquiries. Nationalist, Marxist, social, and cultural projects overlap and contend; their institutional expansion is not the beginning of African historical thought.

nodes.scope_note: The node concerns postwar institutions, not the beginning of African historical knowledge. Nationalist, Marxist, oral, and other methods require distinct contexts. Ibadan, Dar es Salaam and UNESCO are distinct institutional settings. Earlier Yoruba writing, West African spoken knowledge, East African reconstruction, women’s histories and labor inquiry are not one nationalist programme. Northern Africa and further African intellectual traditions still require expansion.

nodes.label: History of technology
nodes.description: Studies technological systems, invention, maintenance, use, and social change. Develops distinct institutions while exchanging questions with histories of science, economy, environment, and gender. Systems approaches and feminist studies of household technology show the range of its explanations. Wajcman’s feminist social-shaping questions and Bray’s Chinese domestic technologies broaden the field’s material and geographical examples.

nodes.label: Consumption & material culture
nodes.description: Examines commercial promotion, household demand, goods’ changing value, taste, gender and provisioning. McKendrick, Brewer and Plumb distinguish commercial and social changes; de Vries connects consumption with household labor; Mintz links diets to colonial production. Anthropological and feminist approaches ask how objects acquire meanings and how consumer roles depend on unequal social relations.

nodes.scope_note: Demand, taste, provisioning, commodities, and material objects are not one theory; gender and empire connect consumption to production. Commodity circulation, cultural biography and goods as communication are distinct questions. De Vries acknowledges conflicting household interests; feminist research does not reduce women to consumers. Much of this selection concerns Europe and the United States; Mintz’s colonial production connects regions but does not make the coverage global in every respect.

strands.title: Whose consumption becomes visible?
strands.focus: Clunas’s selected texts privilege elite men. Rules assigning objects to women do not directly recover women’s own meanings; subsistence consumers also remain poorly represented. Pagani highlights this limit while praising the method.

strands.title: Relics and changing value
strands.focus: Geary follows transfers and renewed authentication of relics. Their careers may change how communities value them; price equivalences and the relative frequency of different transfers remain uncertain.

strands.title: Specific historical uses of theory
strands.focus: Vickery explicitly uses Bourdieu and Douglas/Isherwood; Geary cites Kopytoff. These establish particular uses with different evidence and questions, without proving uniform reception across consumption history.

nodes.label: Historians’ responses to postmodernism
nodes.description: Brings together disputes about evidence, narrative, realism, and social explanation. Defences of historical knowledge, postmodern arguments, and revisions of cultural history are competing positions rather than a consensus or final resolution. Hunt participates in several of these reassessments, making them useful companions to her later global-era argument.

representative_people.works: The Practice of History (1967); Return to Essentials (1991)

representative_people.context: Acknowledged reader of the jointly authored manuscript; its conclusions are not assigned to him.
representative_people.works: Detailed reading of Telling the Truth about History manuscript, acknowledged in 1994 book

representative_people.context: Different interventions are used by Jenkins and Evans; neither citation defines all History Workshop participants.
representative_people.works: Grand Narratives (1990); Reading the Signs II (1992), cited by Jenkins/Evans

representative_people.context: Comments on the editors’ introduction and participates in the conference exchanges.
representative_people.works: Introduction to Beyond the Cultural Turn (1999), acknowledged comments

nodes.scope_note: Defences, critiques, and revisions of historical knowledge conflict. A collection with White’s afterword cannot stand for unanimous rejection of him. Primary introductions distinguish skeptical interpretation, practical realism, disciplinary criticism and empirical reassessments. Exact source notes separate the editors’ descriptions of essays from reading the essays themselves.

strands.title: Facts and interpretive significance
strands.focus: Jenkins accepts an actual past while disputing that facts determine a single interpretation.

strands.title: Practical realism and public inquiry
strands.focus: The coauthors link tentative knowledge, archival inquiry and democratic discussion; their social history of knowledge remains an argument.
strands.works: Telling the Truth about History (1994), introduction and chapter 7

strands.title: Historical practice and outside scrutiny
strands.focus: Evans values practical experience while accepting White’s objection to a disciplinary monopoly on understanding it.

strands.title: Evidence and the limits of representation
strands.focus: The Ginzburg intervention and the Holocaust volume remain distinguishable from a claim that all interpretations are equally sustainable.

strands.title: Culture, practice and comparison
strands.focus: The editors distinguish Sewell’s system/practice tension from Biernacki’s comparative testing and Jacob’s questions about situated science.

strands.title: Narrative, categories and embodied practice
strands.focus: Citizenship, murder narratives and African healing pose different questions about how knowledge is organized.

strands.title: Gender, bodies and selfhood
strands.focus: Rose’s recurring moral discourse, Bynum’s mortality and Seigel’s dimensions of selfhood are distinct inquiries.

strands.title: An unfinished and internally divided reassessment
strands.focus: White’s Marxian and deconstructive commitments accompany a volume whose editors explicitly acknowledge disagreement.
strands.works: Beyond the Cultural Turn (1999), introduction 24–25; afterword 315–318

nodes.label: Ivy Pinchbeck
nodes.description: Reconstructs women’s work before and during industrialization through household production, wages, training and agricultural change. She emphasizes unequal disruption while arguing for eventual benefits, a position distinct from Clark’s account of capitalist development.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Women Workers and the Industrial Revolution, 1750–1850 (1930; new preface in the 1969 reprint). The original preface acknowledges Eileen Power’s direction of the research and Lilian Knowles’s earlier guidance.
nodes.scope_note: The complete 1930 introduction distinguishes paid visibility from productive work itself and separates married women, single women and workers supporting families. Power directs the acknowledged research; Knowles gives early guidance and Dorothy George supplies specific evidence. The 1969 preface, signed 1968, calls for later occupational research without supplying it. The broad optimistic conclusion remains an attributed argument; most occupational chapters and the original conclusion are unread.

nodes.label: Alice Clark
nodes.description: Studies women’s paid and unpaid production through overlapping household and capitalist arrangements. Differences of class and marital position shape her account of changing work, training and authority; her chronology and assumptions about earlier households remain contested.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century (1919). Compare with Pinchbeck’s later-period study to examine how historians explain the relationship between economic change and women’s autonomy.
nodes.scope_note: The 1919 preface credits Schreiner, Knowles and Power’s unpublished research. Introduction and conclusion distinguish production for use, family enterprise and individual wages, while admitting conjectural medieval comparisons and incomplete causal evidence. Maternal and racial assumptions belong to Clark’s historical position. Erickson’s 1992 introduction values unpaid-work analysis while disputing chronology and household equality. Main occupational cases are not newly read; neither timeless equality nor a uniform decline for all women is established.

nodes.label: Mary Ritter Beard
nodes.description: Argues that women helped make historical institutions and events, and that histories must investigate their activity rather than assume universal passivity. Her work combines historical argument, collaborative synthesis and efforts to preserve and teach women’s records.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Woman as Force in History: A Study in Traditions and Realities (1946); work supporting women’s documentary collections, including the Sophia Smith Collection. Her account of agency remains open to criticism about differences among women and structures of power.
nodes.scope_note: Woman as Force in History (1946) challenges the subject-sex tradition through legal and other historical inquiry; its preface does not establish that agency cancels subordination. WCWA (1935–1940) and Smith collecting depended on Schwimmer, Grierson, donors and other collaborators. Voss-Hubbard documents Black women’s limited authority and funding within WCWA. Cott’s 1991 editorial recovery uses letters preserved by correspondents. Mary’s distinct work coexists with collaboration with Charles; legal cases and specific later theoretical criticism remain to be checked.

nodes.label: Julia Cherry Spruill
nodes.date_label: Women’s social history in colonial America · 1938
nodes.description: Investigates women’s everyday life, institutions, work and public activity in the colonial South through varied documentary evidence. Later reissues and public interpretation renew use of her work while exposing limits in whose lives become sustained research questions.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Women’s Life and Work in the Southern Colonies (1938); later reissues associated with Anne Firor Scott show that the field’s expansion also involved renewed attention to earlier scholarship.
nodes.scope_note: Richter’s complete 1999 review mediates Spruill’s shift from attitudes to empirical groundwork and her distinction between prescribed reading and actual behavior. The book examines status and regional differences, but mentions Black and Native women without sustained questions about their life and work, in Richter’s assessment. Scott’s 1972 and 1998 introductions are editorial reception; Colonial Williamsburg use is documented, while Richter’s own proposed slavery research remains an intention. Earlier methods are not membership in postwar social history, and friendship with Beard does not prove transmission.

nodes.label: Lucy Maynard Salmon
nodes.description: Brings domestic employment, everyday evidence and critical teaching into historical inquiry. Domestic Service combines questionnaires, statistical comparison and historical explanation, treating household work as connected to wider economic change. Her practice depends on respondents, students, librarians and statistical collaborators.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Domestic Service (1897); teaching and research at Vassar, including work with cookbooks and household material evidence. Connects histories of women’s work to a wider reconsideration of what counts as a historical source.
nodes.scope_note: The 1897 preface and opening chapters explain response limits and distinguish facts from proposed remedies; the 1901 edition adds European inquiry. Distribution through college and association networks is not established probability sampling, despite Salmon’s claim to representativeness. The 1906 Apologia recalls Tyler’s teaching and describes disciplinary boundaries from her own perspective. Underhill’s manuscript and index work is acknowledged. Vassar documents later source criticism and pedagogy; original newspaper studies and contemporary reviews remain unchecked. Her earlier inquiry is not postwar social-history membership.

nodes.label: Eleanor Flexner
nodes.date_label: Women’s rights, labour, and political struggle · 1959
nodes.description: Reconstructs women’s rights organizing alongside labor, education, abolition and Black women’s activity before the 1960s. Her account makes the boundaries of a movement a historical question: contemporary and later readers disagree about its suffrage emphasis, structural explanation and exclusions.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Century of Struggle: The Woman’s Rights Movement in the United States (1959; later revised and enlarged editions). Publication, reception, and subsequent revision belong to different moments.
nodes.scope_note: The 1959 publication, 1975 revision and later editions are separate moments. James praises expanded coverage but calls for a private-property explanation; Ostrander questions integration of other reforms while recognizing the book’s narrower declared purpose. Rupp values archival reach and race/class breadth but questions absent other women of color and private relationships. Her 1992 account mediates Flexner’s use of Schomburg, Howard, Terrell and Women’s Trade Union League records. Original prefatory and archival passages remain to be collated; this is neither an exhaustive history of women nor proof that later feminist history begins with a single book.

nodes.label: Barbara W. Tuchman
nodes.description: Builds historical narratives around decisions, personalities and political circumstances, combining readable prose with documentary reconstruction. Her accounts of research identify specialist help, conflicting evidence and uncertain inference. Critical reception asks how narrative selection relates to wider social and institutional explanation.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Guns of August (1962). A useful case for asking how narrative pace, characterization, and the selection of events support or constrain an explanation.
nodes.scope_note: The Guns of August (1962) precedes the 1979 revival diagnosis. In “In Search of History” Tuchman explicitly invokes Ranke’s historical truth and Bowen’s reader principle while rejecting invented detail. A Distant Mirror (1978) uses Coucy as a narrative vehicle and acknowledges an unanswered initial causal question, selection bias and debts to editors, chroniclers and sociological medievalists. Stone’s 1978 criticism and Fox-Genovese’s defense are distinct interpretations, not a simple narrative-versus-analysis divide. Specialist assistance does not mean agreement with every conclusion; Tuchman is not placed in women’s history solely because she is a woman, or in Marxism because a Marxist defended her.

nodes.label: Eileen Power
nodes.description: Combines medieval institutional inquiry with reconstruction of individual lives for wider audiences. Her work examines women, households and economic relations through varied sources, while teaching, shared research and editorial collaboration connect projects and generations.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Medieval English Nunneries, c. 1275 to 1535 (1922); Medieval People (1924); economic history at LSE and educational work with Rhoda Power. Pinchbeck’s 1930 preface acknowledges Power’s research direction.
nodes.scope_note: Medieval English Nunneries (1922) separates rules from visitation evidence and warns that recorded faults are incomplete accounts. Medieval People (1924) uses personal reconstruction and explicit source notes. Power shares unpublished material with Clark and directs Pinchbeck’s research. Postan’s 1963 preface identifies reconstructed wording in a posthumous addition. These projects, later editing and Hilton’s particular periodization criticism should remain distinct; original cases and the criticized Cambridge chapter are not fully audited.

nodes.label: C. V. Wedgwood
nodes.description: Combines narrative craft with political, military, biographical and cultural history for broad audiences. She reconstructs participants’ motives and uncertainty, while revising judgments when documents and scholarship change. Her sustained practice gives historical narrative a place during the expansion of social-scientific approaches.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Cicely Veronica Wedgwood; The Thirty Years War (1938); The King’s Peace and The King’s War; biographical work on William the Silent. These are contributions to political, military, and biographical history.
nodes.scope_note: The King’s Peace (1955) and The King’s War (1958) defend attention to sequence and contemporary experience without answering every causal question. Woolrych documents the 1961 revaluation of Strafford and criticizes occasional eulogy and weak explanation of social/regional allegiance; Parker’s war criticism is mediated through that memoir. Her cultural work includes verse and political imagination. Narrative continuity precedes the 1979 debate; original prefaces and cases are not fully collated here.

nodes.label: Frances A. Yates
nodes.date_label: Renaissance culture and arts of memory · 1960s–70s
nodes.description: Investigates mnemonic techniques, images and Renaissance intellectual culture through textual and visual reconstruction. The Art of Memory distinguishes traditions of remembering and argues that their transformations matter to the history of knowledge. Named collaborators and critics help expose both the resources and risks of this inquiry.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Art of Memory (1966), including its treatment of Renaissance memory systems and questions about scientific method. Her historical interpretations are arguments for assessment, not a single uncontested model of Renaissance thought.
nodes.scope_note: The complete preface and concluding chapter distinguish classical rhetoric, medieval prudence, Lullism and Renaissance occult memory. Yates uses Rossi without claiming identical approaches; Bing mediates Warburg’s image questions, and Walker and R. W. Yates contribute specific work. Leibniz and secret-transmission arguments retain their hypothetical or contested status. Mnemonic arts differ from collective commemoration; Yates is not assigned a Skinner-derived method or Cambridge School membership.

nodes.label: Helen Maud Cam
nodes.date_label: Liberties and Communities 1944 · Law-finders and Law-makers 1962
nodes.description: Reconstructs medieval government through local institutions, legal records and parliamentary representation. Her research examines the making and editing of evidence as well as the relations between communities and central authority. Her contribution also includes teaching, scholarly editing and histories of historians.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Liberties and Communities in Medieval England (1944); studies of legal and constitutional history. IHR identifies local sources and medieval political history as central to her work.
nodes.scope_note: Studies in the Hundred Rolls (1921) and later collections distinguish documents from the institutions they disclose. Cam’s 1948 Stubbs opening combines appreciation with revision; Cheney identifies Maitland, Vinogradoff and documentary training, while questioning some juristic deductions and larger claims of legal progress. His memoir is a situated assessment, not a substitute for her full cases. Women’s place in scholarship is not confined to women’s-history subjects; the Ranke comparison remains undirected.

nodes.label: Dorothy Thompson
nodes.date_label: Class, women, and popular politics · postwar–1990s
nodes.description: Reconstructs women’s participation in popular radical politics while examining class, family, and community. A critical participant in a Marxist intellectual tradition, she questions both histories that overlook women and approaches that isolate them from shared political relations. Her career connects postwar labour history with debates reshaped by the women’s movement.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “Women and Nineteenth-Century Radical Politics: A Lost Dimension,” in Juliet Mitchell and Ann Oakley, eds., The Rights and Wrongs of Women (1976); The Chartists: Popular Politics in the Industrial Revolution (1984); Outsiders: Class, Gender and Nation (1993). Her interview reflects critically on class and women’s history.
nodes.scope_note: Chartist documentary and monographic research, the 1976 women’s-politics essay, Queen Victoria (1990) and Outsiders (1993) address related but distinct questions. Her interview describes Torr’s tutoring, adult education, reciprocal work with Edward, and objections to class reduction and inflated claims for a new attention to language. Biography’s gender/power argument receives a specific contemporary criticism. The full interview is checked; monograph claims remain scoped to descriptions and scholarly accounts.

nodes.label: E. P. Thompson
nodes.description: Makes culture, experience, and agency central to the historical formation of class, contributing to an early cultural reorientation within Marxist social history. He retained materialist explanation while disputing other uses of culture and theory. Feminist historians developed resources from his work while criticizing its handling of gender; he resisted some of their extensions and criticisms. This is an intertwined history of inheritance and disagreement, not a simple replacement of class by culture.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Making of the English Working Class (1963); The Poverty of Theory, or an Orrery of Errors (1978). Edward Palmer Thompson has an individual entry here alongside Dorothy Thompson, whose research and arguments remain distinct.
nodes.scope_note: Making (1963) examines English class formation, explicitly limiting Scottish, Welsh and Irish coverage. Essays on time discipline (1967) and moral economy (1971) add distinct problems and named Annales/anthropological resources. Whigs and Hunters (1975) examines law and property; its current support is a selected review. Dorothy’s intellectual contribution is acknowledged in the Making preface; their separate authorship and reciprocal collaboration remain distinct. Primary preface and selected essay passages are checked, not all monographs or every later reception.

nodes.label: Marc Bloch
nodes.description: Comparative historian of social relations, sacred kingship and historical evidence. His Apologie distinguishes causes from beginnings and interrogates traces through questions, using present observation without collapsing historical differences.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Royal Touch (1924); Feudal Society (1939–40).
nodes.scope_note: The Royal Touch and Feudal Society provide distinct historical objects; the unfinished, posthumously published Apologie (1949) addresses method. Pirenne, Maitland and Simiand appear as specific resources, not interchangeable schools. Primary methodological passages are checked; the historical books retain narrower description/metadata support and unresolved questions about generalization.

nodes.label: Lucien Febvre
nodes.date_label: La Terre 1922 · Problem of Unbelief 1942 · Combats 1953
nodes.description: Problem-led historian of geography, belief and socially organized feelings, and collaborator in book history. He challenges anachronistic ideas about Rabelais, critically adapts cultural and psychological resources, and prompts both productive reception and objections.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Problem of Unbelief in the Sixteenth Century (1942).
nodes.scope_note: The Unbelief polemic (1942), sensitivity essay (1941) and Febvre–Martin book project are distinct inquiries. Historical conditions of thought should not become an unquestioned assertion that dissent was impossible. Walker’s appreciative criticism preserves that dispute. Wallon and Blondel are specific psychological resources; Martin’s substantial drafting and research are separately credited.

nodes.label: Fernand Braudel
nodes.description: Historian of multiple durations, material life, markets and capitalism. His models require historical testing and have finite lifespans. He borrows from Lévi-Strauss, engages Wallerstein and criticizes Weber’s explanation of capitalist origins.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Mediterranean (1949); “Histoire et sciences sociales: La longue durée” (1958).
nodes.scope_note: The Mediterranean (1949), the duration essay (1958) and the 1977 economic synthesis have distinct objects. Febvre’s commission and Labrousse’s conjunctures are named resources. Braudel’s market/capitalism distinction permits overlap; his Weber polemic and differing world-economy chronology remain attributed positions. Chartier later questions his hierarchy of explanation. Selected methodological and economic passages are checked; the Mediterranean monograph is not newly read in full.

nodes.label: Ernest Labrousse
nodes.date_label: Prices and incomes study 1933 · French economic crisis study 1944
nodes.description: Investigates differential prices, incomes and conjunctures to explain social tensions and revolutionary crises. His collective inquiry recognizes uneven sectoral movements; later historians debate the construction of his evidence and the conditions of his causal model.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Studies of prices, incomes, and the crisis of the ancien régime.
nodes.scope_note: Esquisse (1933), the unfinished La Crise (1944) and “Panoramas de la crise” (1956) are distinct projects. Simiand and Hamilton are retrospectively identified resources; Braudel’s appreciative use includes reservations about short duration. Perrot’s supervised strike research combines serial training with attention to lived action. Primary 1956 opening and selected scholarly reception are checked; full monographs, interview body and later mathematical defense remain unread.

nodes.label: Maurice Dobb
nodes.date_label: Studies in the Development of Capitalism 1946 · transition debate 1950
nodes.description: Explains capitalist development through changing production relations and class conflict, while allowing trade to interact with those relations. His historical synthesis prompts international debate over feudalism, labour, the state and accumulation.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946).
nodes.scope_note: Studies (1946) and the 1950 reply to Sweezy are distinct texts. The reply explicitly uses Marx, Tawney and other historians; it concedes weak evidence for one accumulation hypothesis. Sweezy challenges definition and regional transfer; Takahashi adds a Japanese intervention focused on Western Europe. The primary reply is read in full, not the monograph or all later comparisons. His Asia and historical-stage claims remain attributed positions.

nodes.label: Rodney Hilton
nodes.date_label: Medieval peasantries · Bond Men Made Free 1973
nodes.description: Examines medieval peasant society, collective action and class relations through comparative historical inquiry. Economic conditions interact with political organization and belief; his study of 1381 distinguishes defeat, limited gains and longer-term consequences.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Studies of medieval peasantries and debates over the transition from feudalism.
nodes.scope_note: Bond Men Made Free (1973) names Bloch and several economic historians as resources; specific Power/Duby criticisms coexist with productive exchange. Contemporary Genet criticism questions period and state differentiation. Selected primary passages reveal mediation and limits on transferring medieval conclusions to other times; full case evidence is not independently audited. Birrell, Dyer, Hill and Razi are explicitly credited draft readers, not inferred coauthors.

nodes.label: Dona Torr
nodes.date_label: Editorial work 1930s–50s · Tom Mann and His Times, vol. 1, 1956
nodes.description: Combines labour biography, translation, annotation, tutoring and collaborative historical publication. Her work connects individual lives with radical political traditions, while testimony and criticism reveal differences over interpretation, group organization and party commitments.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Tom Mann and His Times; Historians’ Group projects.
nodes.scope_note: Tom Mann and His Times, vol. 1 (1956), was prepared with help from Hill and Morton; the second volume remained unfinished, with fragments later edited by E. P. Thompson. Archive descriptions distinguish drafts from published chapters. Editions of Marx/Engels provide another form of intellectual contribution. Murphy’s contemporary review challenges biographical framing. Primary testimony/review and archival descriptions are checked; the original monograph, notebooks and translations are not read in full.

nodes.label: Eric Hobsbawm
nodes.date_label: Labouring Men 1964 · The Invention of Tradition, coedited, 1983
nodes.description: Studies labour, popular protest, capitalist transformation and national identifications across different scales. Cultural evidence and explanatory synthesis coexist; his responses to criticism revise some claims while retaining others.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Labouring Men (1964); with Terence Ranger, The Invention of Tradition (1983); response to Stone on narrative (1980).
nodes.scope_note: The 1980 narrative reply, Bandits in its revised 2000 form, and Nations and Nationalism (1990/1992) distinguish debate, self-revision and historical synthesis. Later concessions about myth and political power are not projected into 1969. Colombian interlocutors and European comparative models supply named resources. Labouring Men and the main nationalism cases remain unread; selected primary support does not audit his entire career or generalizations.

nodes.label: Christopher Hill
nodes.date_label: The English Revolution 1940 · The World Turned Upside Down 1972
nodes.description: Examines the English Revolution through social conflict, religious arguments and unrealized radical alternatives. His changing projects and exchanges with collaborators and critics expose questions about evidence, categories and comparative explanation.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The World Turned Upside Down (1972).
nodes.scope_note: The original 1940 pamphlet, its 1955 revision preface and The World Turned Upside Down (1972) are distinct. Hill credits Dobb, Hilton, Yates and other resources; a 1986 review values Barg’s Soviet comparisons. The Ranter debate distinguishes organized sect, milieu and hostile labeling, with disagreement on several sides. Introductions and selected exchanges are read; the full cases, Davis’s monograph and Hill’s later response remain follow-ups.

nodes.label: R. H. Tawney
nodes.date_label: The Agrarian Problem 1912 · Religion and the Rise of Capitalism 1926
nodes.description: Relates agrarian institutions, economic change and religious ethics through historically differentiated inquiry. His acknowledged debts coexist with criticism of one-sided explanations and attention to the limits of documentary and statistical evidence.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Agrarian Problem in the Sixteenth Century (1912); Religion and the Rise of Capitalism (1926); with Eileen Power, Tudor Economic Documents (1924).
nodes.scope_note: The Agrarian Problem (1912) and Religion and the Rise of Capitalism (1926) address related but distinct problems. Ashley, Weber and named agrarian historians provide resources; Tawney’s Weber criticism concerns causal weight and religious differences. Dobb’s reception does not make Tawney a Marxist. Preface, introduction and selected notes/concluding passages are checked; detailed cases and the later 1936 preface remain unread. Tutorial discussion and credited research assistance belong to the work’s production.

nodes.label: Roger Chartier
nodes.date_label: Representations and social practices · Le monde comme représentation 1989
nodes.description: Explains how textual forms, reading practices and collective representations shape social differences. His programme joins material bibliography to differentiated appropriation, critically reworks Annales and uses conceptual resources without accepting every formulation.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “Le monde comme représentation” (1989).
nodes.scope_note: The 1989 article explicitly engages McKenzie, Ricœur, Fish, Marin, Durkheim/Mauss, Elias, Ginzburg, Certeau and Foucault. Productive Foucault use coexists with a different account of appropriation; criticism of Braudel concerns an explanatory hierarchy. Social divisions include gender, generation, religion and education as well as class. The primary article is checked, but its cited works and historical examples do not thereby receive independent verification.

nodes.label: Public history
nodes.date_label: Earlier public practices · US training discussions 1975 · The Public Historian 1978 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Historical research and interpretation undertaken with public institutions, communities and audiences. Professional service, collaborative authorship, preservation and popular uses of the past pose different questions about who sets the agenda and controls its presentation.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Robert Kelley: “Public History” (1978); G. Wesley Johnson: UCSB public-history training discussions (1975), documented by Kelley (1978); Michael Frisch: A Shared Authority (1990); Dolores Hayden: The Power of Place (1995); Roy Rosenzweig: The Presence of the Past (1998); David Thelen: The Presence of the Past (1998); Luli Callinicos: “The People’s Past” (1986); Raphael Samuel: “Local History and Oral History” (1976).

representative_people.context: Articulates a US programme of historical work in government, business and public institutions.
representative_people.works: “Public History” (1978)

representative_people.context: Co-develops the UCSB training initiative described by Kelley; this is a programme role, not sole authorship of public history.
representative_people.works: UCSB public-history training discussions (1975), documented by Kelley (1978)

representative_people.context: Examines editing and mediation between oral interviews and public presentation.
representative_people.works: A Shared Authority (1990)

representative_people.context: Connects urban landscapes with collaborative public interpretation.
representative_people.works: The Power of Place (1995)

representative_people.context: Co-studies everyday engagement with the past in the United States.
representative_people.works: The Presence of the Past (1998)

representative_people.context: Co-studies participation and historical authority beyond professional institutions.
representative_people.works: The Presence of the Past (1998)

representative_people.context: Discusses South African popular history, worker education and community struggle.
representative_people.works: “The People’s Past” (1986)

representative_people.context: Offers a British local/oral-history interlocutor; not a derivative of US professional training.
representative_people.works: “Local History and Oral History” (1976)

nodes.scope_note: The US professional programme is one formation. British local/oral practice and South African worker education enter as distinct interlocutors. Neither all public memory nor every popular historical product is equated with professional public history. Museum practice, Indigenous authority and non-Anglophone formations need fuller treatment.

strands.title: Professional practice and commissioning
strands.focus: Kelley foregrounds historical questions posed by public and private organizations.

strands.title: Oral sources and public authority
strands.focus: Editing, documentary forms and audiences mediate historical testimony.

strands.title: Place and collaborative interpretation
strands.focus: Urban landscapes support public interpretation of differentiated social pasts.

strands.title: Everyday uses of the past
strands.focus: A US survey asks how people participate in historical activity and evaluate authority.

strands.title: Worker education and community history
strands.focus: Callinicos connects popular historical writing to unions, resistance, language and audiences in South Africa.

nodes.label: Medical & health history
nodes.date_label: Earlier medical scholarship · social-medicine interventions 1930s · later social histories · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Studies medicine, illness, healing and health in their historical settings. Practitioner scholarship, institutional histories, patient perspectives, public health and colonial or gendered experience coexist and contest what should count as medical knowledge and whose records matter.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Henry E. Sigerist: Socialized Medicine in the Soviet Union (1937); Roy Porter: “Lay Medical Knowledge” (1985); Dorothy Porter: Health, Civilization and the State (1999); Barbara Duden: The Woman Beneath the Skin (English edition 1991); Megan Vaughan: Curing Their Ills (1991); Steven Feierman: The Social Basis of Health and Healing in Africa (1992); John M. Janzen: The Social Basis of Health and Healing in Africa (1992).

representative_people.context: Combines medical historical scholarship with contested social-medicine and insurance advocacy before the postwar social-history expansion.
representative_people.works: Socialized Medicine in the Soviet Union (1937)

representative_people.context: Investigates lay knowledge and action within eighteenth-century medical encounters.
representative_people.works: “Lay Medical Knowledge” (1985)

representative_people.context: Studies public health through institutions, social conflict and citizenship.
representative_people.works: Health, Civilization and the State (1999)

representative_people.context: Historicizes women’s embodied experience through a physician’s records.
representative_people.works: The Woman Beneath the Skin (English edition 1991)

representative_people.context: Examines colonial medical discourse and power in African settings.
representative_people.works: Curing Their Ills (1991)

representative_people.context: Co-edits historical and social inquiries into health and therapeutic practices in Africa.
representative_people.works: The Social Basis of Health and Healing in Africa (1992)

representative_people.context: Co-edits interdisciplinary studies of African healing institutions and practices.
representative_people.works: The Social Basis of Health and Healing in Africa (1992)

representative_people.context: Rogaski traces changes in weisheng through imperial encounters, state power and racialized standards of modernity. Rogaski uses Tianjin to connect bodily practice, the built environment and projects of national modernity. Selected introduction only; retain the changing Chinese concept rather than equating it with timeless Western hygiene. Introduction pp. 1–3; one treaty-port inquiry, not a proxy for all Chinese or Asian medical historiography.
representative_people.works: Hygienic Modernity: Meanings of Health and Disease in Treaty-Port China

representative_people.context: McCallum examines how scholarship on starvation, experimentation, segregation and trauma sharpens the analysis of colonialism in Canadian Indigenous health history. Author abstract only; this is a historiographical framing, not new clinical evidence or a universal model of Indigenous experience.
representative_people.works: Starvation, Experimentation, Segregation, and Trauma: Words for Reading Indigenous Health History

representative_people.context: Wynter, Campbell, Chaney and Marks historicize changing explanations of mental illness while tracing the persistence of racialized assumptions. Wynter and coauthors widen the history of antiracist psychiatry by examining Frederick Hickling, Aggrey Burke and Suman Fernando alongside better-known figures. Version-of-record opening pp. 2–3 checked; attribution to this historical analysis, not clinical guidance or endorsement of historical racial categories. Selected programme passage pp. 2–3; clinicians are subjects of the 2025 study, not its coauthors. Their careers are not dated 2025.
representative_people.works: The persistence of history: Racism, anti-Blackness, and the causes of mental ill health, c.1800–2020

nodes.label: Intellectual history

nodes.description: Studies thought, concepts, arguments and their production, circulation and interpretation in historical settings. Social and cultural settings matter without reducing texts to reflections of social position. Women’s intellectual histories and African, Islamic, South Asian and Latin American traditions still need much fuller coverage.

nodes.scope_note: Institutional histories, Marxist cultural analysis, feminist inquiry and colonial labour studies coexist and disagree. Thompson’s work already contains a cultural reorientation; later gender analysis involves productive inheritance as well as criticism. This selection includes Britain, the United States, France, South Asia and Africa but does not constitute global coverage. Labour institutions and historical scholarship about them have different chronologies. Fuller Latin American, Caribbean, East Asian and Indigenous labour historiographies remain priorities.

strands.title: Class formation, culture and work discipline

strands.title: Workplace power and differentiated cultures

strands.title: Strikes, serial research and workers’ voices
strands.focus: Perrot’s French strike research extends beyond counting events to gestures and testimony.

strands.title: Women’s work, gender and household economies
strands.focus: Alice Clark’s earlier research, Tilly/Scott’s work-family inquiry and Anna Clark’s gendered class history have different questions and evidence.

strands.title: Colonial labour, culture, caste and criticism
strands.focus: Kumar scrutinizes categories; Chakrabarty’s Bengal interpretation receives Nair’s criticism; Cooper studies African labour politics. These cases do not share one model.

strands.title: Workers as narrators and historical collaborators
strands.focus: Alice and Staughton Lynd’s editorial practice raises questions about testimony, selection and rank-and-file perspectives.

strands.title: Military labour and recruitment systems
strands.focus: Lucassen and Zürcher compare recruitment arrangements and household strategies without treating them as a universal sequence.

nodes.label: Ethnohistory
nodes.date_label: Earlier interdisciplinary work · Great Lakes–Ohio Valley project 1953 · Lurie 1961 · continuing regional programmes · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Combines historical and anthropological inquiry through archives, material evidence, language, oral traditions and situated cultural interpretation. North American claims research, Wendat/Huron historical reconstruction, Nahua documentary studies and Andean historical anthropology form distinct programmes. Ethnohistory studies historical change rather than assigning some peoples to an unchanging ethnographic past.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Erminie Wheeler-Voegelin: Great Lakes–Ohio Valley Ethnohistorical Research Project reports (project begun 1953); Nancy Oestreich Lurie: “Ethnohistory: An Ethnological Point of View” (1961); Bruce G. Trigger: The Children of Aataentsic (1976; later preface 1987); James Lockhart: The Nahuas After the Conquest (1992); John V. Murra: Anthropological History of Andean Polities (coeditor, 1986); Nathan Wachtel: Anthropological History of Andean Polities (coeditor, 1986); Jacques Revel: Anthropological History of Andean Polities (coeditor, 1986); Julie Cruikshank: Life Lived Like a Story (1990), with Angela Sidney, Kitty Smith and Annie Ned; Angela Sidney: Life Lived Like a Story (1990), collaborative volume; Kitty Smith: Life Lived Like a Story (1990), collaborative volume; Annie Ned: Life Lived Like a Story (1990), collaborative volume; Angela Cavender Wilson: “American Indian History or Non-Indian Perceptions of American Indian History?” (1996); Silvia Rivera Cusicanqui: “El potencial epistemológico y teórico de la historia oral” (1987); Jan Vansina: Oral Tradition as History (1985).

nodes.scope_note: The field overlaps with Indigenous history but does not automatically confer Indigenous authority, community consent or decolonizing method. Claims research could serve governments as well as claimants. Indigenous authors appear here as qualified interlocutors and critics, not as members of an externally assigned school. Lurie herself disputes restricting the approach to particular peoples. The Americas dominate this initial selection; Vansina provides a comparison with African oral-tradition methodology, not proof that African history descends from US ethnohistory.

strands.title: Claims research and commissioned archives
strands.focus: Wheeler-Voegelin’s project reconstructs locations and migrations for Justice Department cases; sponsorship matters to interpretation.

strands.title: Ethnological reading and documentary criticism
strands.focus: Lurie questions special-people definitions and examines the conditions under which documents were produced.

strands.title: Archaeology and histories across contact
strands.focus: Trigger’s Wendat/Huron inquiry examines precontact change as well as European encounters.

strands.title: Nahua texts and colonial mediation
strands.focus: Lockhart’s documentary programme makes Indigenous-language writing central; notarial conventions and scribal selection still require criticism.

strands.title: Andean historical anthropology
strands.focus: Murra and Wachtel question static reconstructions and combine fieldwork, historical records and language; Revel shares the editorial project.

strands.title: Collaboration and Indigenous historical authority
strands.focus: The Yukon collaboration, Wilson’s criticism and Rivera’s account of collective practice pose different questions about who interprets and controls knowledge.
strands.works: Life Lived Like a Story (1990); Wilson (1996); Rivera (1987)

strands.title: Oral tradition as a comparative methodological problem
strands.focus: Vansina’s analysis of transmission supplies a comparison with documentary interpretation; oral traditions and retrospective interviews are not identical sources.

nodes.label: Joan Wallach Scott
nodes.description: Develops gender as a historical analysis of social relationships and power. Her 1986 formulation connects symbols, normative claims, institutions and subjectivity while insisting on historical variation.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis (1986).
nodes.scope_note: Existing cross-field presence warrants a visible argument, not just another name in a roster. This entry covers the 1986 intervention; later experience and secularism arguments need their own claims.

nodes.label: Natalie Zemon Davis
nodes.description: Uses contrasting seventeenth-century lives to investigate religion, writing and relations of power across Europe and its colonial outposts. Women on the Margins makes individual lives a route into broader historical questions.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Women on the Margins: Three Seventeenth-Century Lives (1995).
nodes.scope_note: Comparative biography provides a connection beyond gender history. This entry is supported by a newly checked book description; its methodological interpretation still needs a fresh body-text check. Other career contributions remain in the preserved contexts.

nodes.label: Lynn Hunt
nodes.description: Reassesses the explanatory models of social history in her introduction to The New Cultural History. She recognizes turns toward culture within Marxist and Annales histories while questioning the priority assigned to social experience.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Introduction: History, Culture, and Text (1989).
nodes.scope_note: Connects the cultural turn to disputes within social explanation. Hunt authored this introduction and edited the collection; she did not author all its essays. Her political-culture work remains a separate inherited context.

nodes.label: Catherine Hall
nodes.description: With Leonore Davidoff, relates English middle-class formation to gender, family, religion and economic life in Family Fortunes. Class identities and gender relations are investigated together rather than in separate historical accounts.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Family Fortunes: Men and Women of the English Middle Class 1780–1850 (1987). Joint work; retain all coauthor credits.
nodes.scope_note: Equal coauthor credit with Davidoff. The 1987 work is distinct from Hall’s later introduction and later imperial history. Newly checked evidence is the indexed prologue abstract and publisher description of a later edition.

nodes.label: Leonore Davidoff
nodes.description: With Catherine Hall, makes family and gender central to the history of English middle-class formation in Family Fortunes. The study connects social identities with institutions, economic opportunities and domestic relations.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Family Fortunes: Men and Women of the English Middle Class 1780–1850 (1987). Joint work; retain all coauthor credits.
nodes.scope_note: Equal coauthor credit with Hall; both resolve to one work. Do not infer that either scholar wrote a particular passage alone. The original intervention dates to 1987, not the reissue consulted here.

nodes.label: Evelyn Brooks Higginbotham
nodes.description: Argues that race structures the meanings of gender, class and sexuality. Her 1992 intervention challenges insufficient racial analysis in feminist theory and develops an account of race as socially constructed, contested power.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: African-American Women’s History and the Metalanguage of Race (1992).
nodes.scope_note: A theoretical contribution within Black history as well as feminist historiography. Her opening acknowledges useful feminist resources and earlier Black scholarship; it does not license an indiscriminate critique edge to every cited theorist.

nodes.label: Linda Tuhiwai Smith
nodes.description: Places research within colonial histories and Indigenous struggles over knowledge and self-determination. Decolonizing Methodologies addresses the responsibilities, community relationships and authority involved in research with Indigenous peoples.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Decolonizing Methodologies: Research and Indigenous Peoples (1999).
nodes.scope_note: Connects Indigenous historical authority with the politics of research. This is a situated methodological programme, not a claim that Indigenous research is uniform or that every Western method is rejected.

nodes.label: Lorraine Daston
nodes.description: With Peter Galison, investigates changing scientific ideals of objectivity through images and atlas-making. Their 1992 article distinguishes mechanical objectivity from other historically formed components of the concept.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Image of Objectivity (1992). Joint work; retain all coauthor credits.
nodes.scope_note: Adds a substantive history-of-science contribution beyond gender history. Galison retains equal authorship and argument credit. Their historical analysis does not assert that scientific objectivity is simply impossible.

nodes.label: Racial formation
nodes.date_label: Earlier roots · Omi–Winant 1986 / revised 1994 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Investigates how racial categories and meanings are produced and contested through social, political and economic relations. Omi and Winant’s programme treats race as historically specific and consequential, not as a biological essence or a simple expression of another social category.
nodes.scope_note: A distinct theoretical programme relevant to histories of racialization, not a synonym for Black history or all scholarship about race. Original 1986 and revised 1994 editions remain distinct. The checked course extract is labelled second edition; its retyped pagination and edition attribution have not been independently authenticated. Intersectional analysis connects racial inquiry with gender, class and sexuality without being identical to racial-formation theory.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Michael Omi and Howard Winant, Racial Formation in the United States (1986; second edition 1994).

representative_people.context: Joint account of racial categories as historically formed through social and political relations; separate from Scott’s gender project.
representative_people.works: Racial Formation in the United States (1986; second edition 1994)

representative_people.context: Joint account of racial categories as historically formed through social and political relations; separate from Scott’s gender project.
representative_people.works: Racial Formation in the United States (1986; second edition 1994)

strands.title: Racial formation
strands.focus: Race is historically produced through political and social processes; this is not the same programme as Scott’s gender analysis.
strands.works: Racial Formation in the United States (1986; second edition 1994)

nodes.label: Intersectional analysis
nodes.date_label: Earlier Black feminist roots · Crenshaw 1989 · Cohen 1997 · coverage through 2000
nodes.description: Examines how relations of race, gender, class and sexuality interact in specific structures of power. Crenshaw challenges single-axis frameworks that obscure Black women; Cohen brings an explicit intersectional critique to queer politics. The approach connects distinct fields without merging their objects or methods.
nodes.scope_note: An analytical approach with Black feminist and other intellectual and political roots, not a single school founded from nothing in 1989. Crenshaw’s legal critique and Cohen’s political intervention are distinct. Connections to gender, racial formation and queer history do not establish that every practitioner adopts this approach, or a direct Crenshaw–Omi/Winant borrowing.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Kimberlé Crenshaw, “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989); Cathy J. Cohen, “Punks, Bulldaggers, and Welfare Queens” (1997). Earlier Black feminist resources are explicitly acknowledged by these authors.

representative_people.context: Legal scholar whose critique centers Black women excluded by single-axis approaches.
representative_people.works: “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989)

representative_people.context: Critiques single-oppression queer politics and argues for analysis of intersecting systems of power; a situated political-theoretical intervention, not a verdict on every sexuality historian.
representative_people.works: “Punks, Bulldaggers, and Welfare Queens: The Radical Potential of Queer Politics?” (1997)

strands.title: Intersectional criticism
strands.focus: Crenshaw challenges single-axis frameworks that obscure Black women’s experiences; this legal intervention is not a claim to invent all Black feminist analysis.
strands.works: “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989)

strands.title: Intersectional criticism of queer politics
strands.focus: Cohen challenges a simple heterosexual/queer division of power and calls for attention to race, gender, class and sexuality together. Political critique is not equivalent to a rejection of all queer history.
strands.works: “Punks, Bulldaggers, and Welfare Queens: The Radical Potential of Queer Politics?” (1997)

edges.relationship: Later Wittgenstein supplies a resource for Geertz’s public meaning
edges.evidence_note: “Thick Description,” pp. 12–13, explicitly invokes Wittgenstein in explaining why meaning cannot be reduced to private mental contents. This is a bounded borrowing. Selected Investigations sections now supply primary context for varied use and shared practices; they do not make all meaning a single formula.

edges.relationship: Geertz explicitly borrows Ryle’s thick-description distinction
edges.evidence_note: Primary pp. 5–7 use the twitch/wink example to distinguish acts that outwardly resemble one another. More detail alone does not supply the relevant interpretation. The complete reproduced 1968 lecture now supplies the original distinction’s philosophical context, including purpose, competence and exploration; original-edition wording remains uncollated.

edges.relationship: Geertz invokes Weber for an interpretive account of culture
edges.evidence_note: Primary p. 5 explicitly invokes Weber while presenting meaning as the object of interpretation. This does not make every part of Geertz’s work Weberian.

edges.relationship: provides the disciplinary setting for interpretive anthropology
edges.evidence_note: Disciplinary location is not an upstream intellectual event. Interpretive anthropology is a project within anthropology.

edges.relationship: Geertz’s interpretation of symbolic practices becomes a resource for cultural history
edges.evidence_note: Hunt’s primary 1984 p. 87 supplies a named reception example; the existing political-history edge specifies that use. Davis remains an earlier proposed example whose direct reception is not established by the passages checked here. Darnton’s original acknowledgments now add a specific Princeton co-teaching mechanism with Geertz; his introduction names Lévi-Strauss and acknowledges archival mediation. This does not certify Davis’s direct reception or all anthropological routes.

edges.relationship: Geertzian interpretation and microhistory invite comparison as well as methodological disagreement
edges.evidence_note: Compare contextual interpretation; do not assume Ginzburg or Italian microstoria simply adopted Geertz’s method. Ginzburg 1993 note 69 cites Levi’s “I pericoli del geertzismo”; that essay was not read, so its detailed critique is a follow-up, not an asserted directed influence.

edges.relationship: Lévi-Strauss adapts Jakobson’s and Trubetzkoy’s phonological resources
edges.evidence_note: Structural Anthropology pp. 31–36 and notes 8–14 identify the resources and warn against literal transfer of phonemic analysis to kinship. Saussure’s node is a broader linguistic tradition, not a claim of direct collaboration.

edges.relationship: Barthes adapts linguistic distinctions and proposes reversing the semiology hierarchy
edges.evidence_note: Elements of Semiology introduction explicitly invokes the Course but proposes making semiology part of linguistics. The categories are a provisional research programme, not an unchanged transfer or a summary of Barthes’s later work. Myth Today adapts the sign as a second-level signifier; the history essay also explicitly uses Jakobson’s shifters. These passages extend rather than erase the earlier scoped 1964 reading.

edges.relationship: Lacan transforms Saussurean signification and explicitly uses Jakobson’s linguistic resources
edges.evidence_note: Primary 1957 PDF pp. 3–4 visually checked: Lacan acknowledges S/s is not exactly a Cours diagram and substitutes matching doors for the tree illustration. Notes 3/10 credit Jakobson; appropriation does not establish identity between linguistic and psychoanalytic theories.
edges.map_label: The sign diagram, metaphor and metonymy

edges.relationship: Lacan explicitly uses Lévi-Strauss on symbolic efficacy and language/social laws
edges.evidence_note: Mirror-stage note 1 cites “L’efficacité symbolique” (1949); Function and Field PDF p. 27/note 18 cites “Language and the Analysis of Social Laws” (1951), alongside symbolic exchange on p. 24. These primary receptions replace the earlier generic evidence; original printings and Lévi-Strauss articles are not newly collated.

edges.relationship: provides a distinct structuralist project within the discipline
edges.evidence_note: Structural anthropology is situated within the discipline. A containing field is not itself a dated transmitter.

edges.relationship: Durkheimian scholarship and Mauss provide acknowledged resources
edges.evidence_note: The dedication acknowledges Durkheim and the Année sociologique; chapter 2 opens with Mauss’s call to learn from linguistics. These passages strengthen named antecedents without independently verifying every proposed exchange/classification mechanism.

edges.relationship: Derrida questions the speech/writing hierarchy while working through differential relations
edges.evidence_note: Corrected 1997 English pp. 27–35 and 44–50 distinguish nonnatural signification from private caprice and question the exclusion of writing. This is neither rejection of every linguistic insight nor a claim that Saussure assigns fixed meanings to isolated words. This edition is identified; the separate MIA excerpt’s exact witness remains unresolved.

edges.relationship: Derrida questions nature/culture and the grounds of structural analysis
edges.evidence_note: The consulted English transcription engages the incest-prohibition problem and bricolage. Derrida recognizes Lévi-Strauss’s own questioning while disputing its conceptual limits; criticism does not imply that Lévi-Strauss naively ignored them.

edges.relationship: helps form an intellectual context that decenters the subject
edges.evidence_note: Shared intellectual setting is not evidence of a direct Saussure-to-Foucault borrowing. Preserve Foucault’s separate epistemological and genealogical routes.

edges.relationship: Foucault explicitly situates Canguilhem and conceptual histories among his resources
edges.evidence_note: The available 1985 opening names Canguilhem, Bachelard, Cavaillès and Koyré and explains the significance of medicine and biology. This is Foucault’s selective retrospective account, distinct from structural linguistics; the original Canguilhem works and full revised preface are not newly read.
edges.map_label: Canguilhem and histories of scientific concepts

edges.relationship: Foucault reworks Nietzsche’s descent and emergence as genealogical questions
edges.evidence_note: The 1971 essay, English pp. 139–152, explicitly examines changing Nietzschean terms, documentary detail and struggles over rules. It opposes teleological recovery of a pure origin; Foucault’s historical and biological interpretations remain attributed, with cited originals uncollated. Nietzsche’s own preface and II.12–13 are now separately read, including the distinction between genesis and later utility; this does not establish identity with Foucault’s whole interpretation.
edges.map_label: Descent, emergence and struggles over rules

edges.relationship: Barthes contributes distinct analyses of myth, historical discourse and authorial authority
edges.evidence_note: Primary selections differentiate naturalized meanings, uttering/utterance, narrative detail and the theoretical reader. Bann supplies a particular historical adaptation and qualification; these do not define every linguistic approach or prove that past events are imaginary.
edges.map_label: Myth, historical discourse and authorial authority

edges.relationship: Lacan contributes a linguistically constituted, divided subject as a contested conceptual resource
edges.evidence_note: The 1949 and 1957 primary selections distinguish identification and signifying mechanisms. Scott’s 1986 response supplies a particular historical reception and limitation; the linguistic turn is not uniformly Lacanian.

edges.relationship: Foucault contributes historical inquiries into discourse, practices and subjects
edges.evidence_note: The three archaeology chapters relate actual statements and objects to institutional practices; the genealogy essay and 1982 subject account distinguish further questions about contingent formation and action. Goldstein’s profile documents one empirical reception. These do not define all language-centered history or reduce material relations to text.

edges.relationship: Derrida contributes critical readings of hierarchies and conditions of signification
edges.evidence_note: Selected Grammatology passages and the complete 1983 letter distinguish differential relations and contextual translation from arbitrary interpretation or a mechanical method. Scott supplies a specific historical use of deconstruction; historians do not all adopt one program.

edges.relationship: informs analysis of power and subject formation
edges.evidence_note: Power and historical categories are resources for some gender analyses, not a sole origin of gender or racial-formation scholarship. Scott explicitly proposes Foucault’s dispersed conception of power on p. 1067; this is a named use, not an origin claim.

edges.relationship: Foucault supplies a named resource that sexuality historians adapt and question
edges.evidence_note: D’Emilio’s 1983 note 1 explicitly acknowledges Foucault, McIntosh and Weeks while arguing that a wage-labor explanation remains necessary. Stoler’s 1995 project critically extends Foucault into colonial history. This supports specific reception, not a sole origin of the field.

edges.relationship: Said adopts Foucault’s discourse analysis while retaining individual authors’ effects
edges.evidence_note: This compressed link concerns Said’s use and revision of discourse analysis, not every postcolonial historian. The checked introduction explicitly states both debt and disagreement.

edges.relationship: Spivak uses and tests Derridean deconstruction in a critique of representation
edges.evidence_note: This route concerns Spivak’s critical use of deconstruction; it does not define every postcolonial approach. The checked conclusion explicitly distinguishes this use from treating deconstruction as feminism in itself.
