edges.evidence_note: Metahistory (1973) precedes Stone (1979). Stone note 2 explicitly cites it through Starn; a separate directed contribution records that reception. This undirected comparison preserves the difference between theory of form and diagnosis of practice.

edges.relationship: Anderson adapts historical materialism to comparative transitions and state forms
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Anderson’s publisher describes an explicitly Marxist programme; this specifies one contributor without making Skocpol’s state analysis reducible to class.
edges.map_label: Anderson: historical materialism and divergent states

edges.relationship: Bendix adapts Weber’s comparative resources to authority and citizenship
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Publisher biographical evidence explicitly identifies Bendix’s Weber engagement; the new support specifies Bendix rather than certifying every inherited Skocpol claim.

edges.relationship: Moore’s divergent political routes and Bendix’s comparisons challenge a uniform modernization sequence
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. The checked work descriptions support multiple routes and alternatives to neo-evolutionary assumptions. This is not a rejection of all modernization questions. Lipset’s own 1959 conclusion already denies automatic democratization, and Eisenstadt’s 2000 program explicitly disputes convergence. Moore/Bendix criticism must therefore target particular assumptions rather than refute a unanimity that never existed.

edges.relationship: Tilly’s contention, Skocpol’s state/revolution comparisons and Somers’s citizenship inquiry offer distinct political explanations
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Tilly’s own essay p. 9 explicitly describes the relations explored by The Contentious French. This strengthens his part of the field link, not all claims about Skocpol. Skocpol’s primary conclusion specifies state breakdown and international pressures; Somers’s primary abstract names law and regional associations. Earlier Tilly qualifications remain.

edges.relationship: compares state-centered and world-system units of explanation
edges.evidence_note: Replaces a specific claim about Skocpol’s 1977 critique with comparison. The cited 1979 and 2004 books do not document that article as such. Wallerstein’s own division-of-labor argument now specifies the systemic side; Skocpol’s 1977 critique remains unread, so the edge stays an undirected comparison. Second-pass check (2026-09-13): the 1977 article’s primary opening is now read in its 1994 reprint, but not its later critique. Its favorable framing of the world-historical project qualifies any simple opposition. This comparison remains undirected; no additional Skocpol–Wallerstein critique is asserted on opening evidence alone.

edges.relationship: shares comparative questions across regions while differing in methods and scale
edges.evidence_note: No direct Skocpol → Pomeranz genealogy is asserted. Wong73 quotes Tilly’s definition while distinguishing paths; Subrahmanyam758–759 directly contests Goldstone’s model. The broad comparison remains undirected, alongside a separately recorded specific critique.

edges.relationship: Kocka adapts Weberian concepts to industrial organization and bourgeois society
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. The 1999 publisher description explicitly names Weber and Marx; Kocka’s 1988 response also identifies Weber among earlier critical resources.

edges.relationship: Western modernization comparisons frame a disputed German-path argument
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Kocka’s 1988 pp. 7, 9, 11–12 explicitly examine the yardstick, accept revisions and defend a qualified comparison. Neither inevitable Nazism nor a uniform West is asserted.

edges.relationship: Wehler’s structural interpretation challenges political explanation detached from social and economic power
edges.evidence_note: Targets later disciplinary priorities associated with the tradition, not source criticism itself or every aspect of Ranke’s scholarship. The checked publisher describes his analysis and Fischer-controversy setting. Direct reception of Ranke’s original work remains unproven. The 1975 journal programme explicitly combines historical-hermeneutic and social-scientific approaches. Schieder’s earlier section on structures and personalities also claims resources within older historiography. These primary texts qualify any reading of this criticism as an absolute methodological rupture; they do not verify direct Wehler reception of Ranke.
edges.map_label: Wehler: social structures in political explanation

edges.relationship: Blackbourn and Eley contest the Sonderweg yardstick and bourgeois-failure account
edges.evidence_note: Applies to specific critics, not a uniform Marxist position on German history. OUP contents distinguish their arguments and Kocka’s reply accepts significant changes without endorsing all conclusions. The inherited historical-left placement remains qualified; this is no verdict by an entire tradition.

edges.relationship: Lüdtke questions structural priorities through everyday practices, including Kocka’s Siemens study
edges.evidence_note: Applies to the Alltagsgeschichte part of the umbrella node. A specific Lüdtke–Wehler exchange remains a bibliographic gap. The 1993 primary note 27 now identifies Kocka’s 1969 study and its limited treatment of delimitation from below. This fills a concrete example; the earlier named Lüdtke–Wehler exchange remains unread. Second-pass direct exchange now checked: Lüdtke’s 1989 sections 3–4 and note 26 explicitly engage Wehler’s polemic, contest the supplementary status assigned to everyday inquiry and admit some methodological weaknesses. Wehler’s own selected text acknowledges cultural/experiential gains while challenging explanatory claims. This fills the earlier named exchange gap; full texts and version collation remain incomplete.
edges.map_label: Lüdtke: workplace practices and structural limits

edges.relationship: intersects in questions about social structures, authoritarianism, and Nazi rule
edges.evidence_note: Does not equate the Sonderweg thesis, intentionalist–functionalist debate, and Historikerstreit.

edges.relationship: Holocaust memorial research makes the forms and contexts of public remembrance an explicit object of study
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Young’s 1993 book adds a specified memorial project to the inherited testimony/representation connection. Publisher support is at book-description level; individual memorial chapters remain unread.

edges.relationship: tests arguments about narrative and representation against the history of genocide
edges.evidence_note: The 1992 volume includes White and his critics. The link identifies a contested test of representation, not a verdict that the linguistic turn licenses denial.

edges.relationship: Holocaust representation debates make evidence and the limits of historical narration central questions
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Broszat’s checked 1977 source criticism supplies an earlier methodological comparison, not a response to postmodernism or evidence of reception by participants in the later debate. The 1992 representation volume remains checked at metadata/contents level; its individual arguments require primary follow-up.
edges.map_label: Evidence and the limits of representation

edges.relationship: Holocaust testimony studies and oral history share questions about recollection, listening and evidence
edges.evidence_note: No archive foundation dates are attached to this general reference; dedicated testimony scholarship should supplement it. Felman/Laub add a dedicated witnessing reference, checked at publisher-description level. Kaplan’s interviews and Browning’s explicit Tec use now support a separate directed contribution; no archive founding dates are inferred.

edges.relationship: Holocaust research and social history intersect in situational explanation and Jewish daily-life inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement. Browning’s primary 1996 response combines ideological and situational factors; Kaplan uses personal sources to reconstruct daily life. Neither position defines the whole field.

edges.relationship: Holocaust research and political history intersect in institutions, ideology and constrained choices
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement. Broszat’s primary argument retains ideology while challenging a simple unfolding programme; Bauer’s rescue research supplies a separate political question. This remains a comparison.

edges.relationship: Historical accounts of national formation question claims of timeless national traditions
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Hroch explicitly treats nation formation as contingent and interruptible; Smith’s qualified account of ethnic inheritances also differs from perennial nationalism.
edges.map_label: Historicizing nations without one origin model

edges.relationship: Hobsbawm and Anderson bring distinct questions about capitalism and historical construction into nationalism research
edges.evidence_note: Gellner and the entire field are not classified as Marxist. Anderson’s primary excerpt supplies a specific market/print mechanism. This is not a claim that Gellner, Smith or the whole field belongs to Marxist social history.
edges.map_label: Hobsbawm and Anderson: distinct capitalist histories

edges.relationship: National traditions, ethnic memories and commemorative sites offer distinct accounts of shared pasts
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement. Nora’s situated account supplies a specific comparison; this does not make nations the only memory communities or establish a direct transmission from invented-tradition scholarship. Smith explicitly makes myths and memories part of his explanatory approach. This comparison remains separate from Nora’s project and does not assert their direct transmission.

edges.relationship: Anderson’s account becomes a named interlocutor for Chatterjee’s argument about colonial difference
edges.evidence_note: Chatterjee is a critic and theorist in his own right; postcolonial accounts do not simply extend Anderson. Chatterjee’s primary 1993 pp. 4–7 praise aspects of Anderson while explicitly disputing modular derivation. A new reverse critique records that productive disagreement.

edges.relationship: invites comparison of national frameworks with cross-border historical processes
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement. Duara’s national/local/transnational narratives specify a project for this comparison; the publisher description does not certify all book cases or a direct Anderson influence.

edges.relationship: Gellner connects national belonging to modern mobility and a shared literate culture
edges.evidence_note: Gellner’s own book replaces Anderson as the specific reference; this does not describe every theory of nationalism. The Warwick reply supplies a primary restatement and accepts some premodern cultural continuity; Smith disputes explanatory sufficiency, not the reality of modern transformations.

edges.relationship: Vansina develops critical methods for transmitted traditions, distinct from eyewitness interviews
edges.evidence_note: Oral traditions transmitted across generations and recorded life-history interviews are distinct sources; neither is unique to one region. Primary 1981 pp. 142–144 adds passage support while the 1985 book retains metadata-only verification. Separate primary reading of the 1985 text now supports competing definitions and communal transmission; the older bibliography record retains its original metadata scope.

edges.relationship: National historical projects intersect with African institutions and collective syntheses
edges.evidence_note: National histories are one strand. African historical knowledge and writing predate postwar professionalization and national liberation. Ogot’s programme and Ranger’s recollections demonstrate differing aims; the comparison is not a universal nationalist origin.

edges.relationship: Liberation politics and critiques of colonial knowledge contribute to distinct African historical projects
edges.evidence_note: Decolonization supplies important contexts, not a sole origin of African historiography. Ki-Zerbo’s opening calls for critical reconstruction rather than reversing inherited myths; Ranger recalls institutional variety.

edges.relationship: Rodney connects African history to an account of underdevelopment structured by unequal power
edges.evidence_note: Rodney’s work replaces Vansina as the pertinent theoretical reference; the field is broader than dependency analysis. The primary excerpt strengthens the argument check; neither its generalizations nor dependency theory define the field.

edges.relationship: Attention to social and literary contexts informs Vansina’s criticism of oral traditions
edges.evidence_note: Vansina’s primary methodological chapter pp. 142–144 supports attention to the social and literary contexts of oral tradition. This is a specified methodological resource; direct transmission from a particular anthropological school remains unestablished.

edges.relationship: African oral-source inquiry and Indigenous methodologies invite a qualified comparison
edges.evidence_note: A seminar comparison, not identical sovereign status, common origin or asserted transfer. Smith’s introduction and Wilson’s essay now supply primary methodological support alongside African oral-source readings; differences of historical situation and authority remain.
edges.map_label: Oral evidence and different colonial contexts

edges.relationship: Thornton brings African institutions and cultural actors into Atlantic historical explanation
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. The 1998 publisher description supports the specific intervention; Ogot’s earlier programme also explicitly seeks intercontinental exchange. These are contributions, not a genealogy of all global history.
edges.map_label: Thornton: African actors across the Atlantic

edges.relationship: Du Bois’s double consciousness enters Gilroy’s diaspora argument
edges.evidence_note: Gilroy explicitly identifies this conceptual resource in his preface. Porter Wesley’s Afro-Brazilian bibliography provides a separate material contribution to diaspora research; neither route makes the umbrella a single school.
edges.map_label: Du Bois and diaspora research resources

edges.relationship: James and Williams examine slavery and revolution across imperial boundaries
edges.evidence_note: Earlier transregional scholarship is not retrospectively assigned a single later Atlantic-school identity. Gilroy’s preface acknowledges limited treatment of James and Fanon; it cannot substantiate detailed reception of either. The separately recorded James/Williams contributions retain their own evidence.

edges.relationship: provides an oceanic scale for comparing and connecting historical processes
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement. Altman’s paired localities offer a concrete example for comparing connected and oceanic scales; no transmission to a single global-history school is asserted.

edges.relationship: Curtin’s census contributes quantitative reconstruction of the slave trade
edges.evidence_note: Curtin’s book replaces Gilroy as the reference. Its estimates were subsequently revised; quantitative inquiry did not begin or end with this book. The current Curtin check is bibliographic; numerical series and the later 1999 database still require separate review.

edges.relationship: Gilroy challenges nationally bounded and racially essentialist accounts of identity
edges.evidence_note: Retargeted from postcolonial history as a whole to identity categories, matching the stated object of criticism more closely. The primary preface explicitly rejects racial purity and closed categories while presenting conclusions as provisional. This critique is not directed at every recovery of collective identity.

edges.relationship: shares historical questions while maintaining distinct objects and institutions
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement.

edges.relationship: Hughes’s systems history joins Bijker and Pinch’s technology research in their 1987 edited collaboration
edges.evidence_note: The 1987 edited volume documents a concrete collaboration. Systems history and SCOT remain distinguishable approaches; publisher description checked, not all chapters.
edges.map_label: Hughes, Bijker and Pinch: systems and choices

edges.relationship: Compare Hughes’s systems with Chandler’s coordination, Mokyr’s technological creativity and Roy’s artisanal change
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement. Selected primary passages now distinguish Chandler’s managerial coordination, Mokyr’s invention/adoption and Roy’s artisanal reorganization in India. This remains an editorial comparison across units, periods and scales; it asserts no direct transmission among these three authors. Roy’s specific use of Berg is separately identified within the approaches.

edges.relationship: Cowan connects household technology to gendered labour and social arrangements
edges.evidence_note: Cowan’s specific work replaces a generic SHOT page as the supporting reference.

edges.relationship: Shares questions about infrastructure, commodity movement and transformed environments
edges.evidence_note: Comparison supported by specific historical studies; the unverified Envirotech foundation date is omitted. The added scholarly reception account specifically supports Cronon’s rural–urban commodity relations. The Hughes reference retains its existing verification limits.

edges.relationship: De Vries links household labor and demand; Brewer and Porter collect wider questions about goods and economic life
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement. The comparison remains undirected. The new separate contribution records the particular industrious-revolution argument, not a general direction for every overlap. The comparison now includes primary McKendrick, Weatherill and Vickery passages: acceleration, ownership, household work and material meanings are different outcomes, with unequal evidence coverage.

edges.relationship: Appadurai and Kopytoff examine objects’ value, circulation and changing commodity status
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement. Their primary opening extracts specify the comparison’s questions; this is not proof that new cultural history directly caused their anthropological programmes. Clunas supplies a further specific comparison through Ming connoisseurship texts and an inventory: cultural classifications and consumer distinctions are related questions. Pagani’s1993 review records a contemporary assessment. This addition does not establish transmission from Appadurai or Kopytoff to Clunas. Geary’s1986 relic study adds a historical case of changing status and contested value. This comparison remains undirected; the distinct anthropology contribution records his explicit Kopytoff reference.

edges.relationship: Mintz connects changing sugar consumption with colonial slave production, industrial labor and capitalism
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Publisher description now checked for this specific argument; the full book and reception remain unreviewed.
edges.map_label: Mintz: sugar, colonial labor and changing diets

edges.relationship: Bourdieu relates taste and cultural practices to social position
edges.evidence_note: Distinction is the relevant work, rather than using Outline of a Theory of Practice alone as a proxy. Vickery explicitly cites Distinction in chapter5/note9 when distinguishing differentiation from imitation. This establishes a particular historian’s use; the original Bourdieu argument still awaits primary checking. Revision1.79 supplies the previously missing primary check through selected Distinction conclusion passages. It distinguishes practical classification and struggles over recognition from an automatic equation of taste with conscious imitation; Vickery remains the particular historical-use example.

edges.relationship: De Grazia and Furlough’s edited collection connects gendered consumption with family labor, identity and state definitions
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. The 1996 publisher description supports this edited intervention in European and US history, not every individual chapter’s argument or a universal female consumer. A further specific contribution is Vickery’s1998 inquiry into purchasing work, property and meanings. Her selected cases qualify both stereotyped consumer motives and claims of universal female authority.
edges.map_label: De Grazia and Furlough: gender, labor and consumption

edges.relationship: provokes competing arguments about evidence, narrative, and realism
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Jenkins’s checked discussion and the other books’ primary introductions now document competing responses; broad claims about all postmodernists remain attributed.

edges.relationship: Ginzburg and other critics contest arguments about narrative and historical truth
edges.evidence_note: Criticism is attributed to particular participants, not to every historian or contributor to Beyond the Cultural Turn. Evans’s introduction also explicitly accepts White’s defense of scrutiny from outside the discipline. Jenkins draws on White while distinguishing their uses of discourse; criticism is not this whole entry’s position. Ginzburg 1992 body remains unchecked.

edges.relationship: reassesses cultural history’s relationships with social explanation
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. The editors’ primary preface ix–xi and introduction 12–25 explain this programme through named contributions and explicitly refuse a single alternative paradigm; essay bodies are not newly checked.

edges.relationship: Ginzburg defends evidentiary inference while recognizing the constructed stages of historical research
edges.evidence_note: A contribution by a particular microhistorian, not a position required of every small-scale history. His 1993 p. 32 explicitly joins narrative experiment to opposition to skeptical textual reduction; earlier 1992 context remains.

edges.relationship: revisits how social explanation can incorporate cultural analysis
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. The editors’ primary preface ix–xi and introduction 12–25 explain this programme through named contributions and explicitly refuse a single alternative paradigm; essay bodies are not newly checked.

edges.relationship: connects earlier objectivity disputes to later arguments about historical knowledge
edges.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. These primary interventions distinguish evidence from interpretation and comprehension from truth. They specify earlier conceptual questions; this source addition alone does not prove every later author’s reception. Specific reception now appears in Jenkins’s and Evans’s introductions: both engage Carr and Elton. Appleby/Hunt/Jacob chapter 7 note 1 explicitly cites Novick and Becker. This does not certify every earlier conceptual route.

edges.relationship: Montaillou invites comparison with intensive small-scale historical inquiry
edges.evidence_note: The publisher describes village reconstruction through inquisitorial records. This provides a comparison of scale and evidence, not proof of Italian microstoria membership. The separate directed microhistory-to-Annales contribution concerns the 1988 editorial’s explicit methodological engagement.

edges.relationship: Foucault’s objects, classifications and practices become resources for histories of human sciences
edges.evidence_note: Archaeology’s object-formation chapter connects psychiatric discourse with institutions and practices. Goldstein’s retrospective profile describes a specific historical adaptation attending to professionalization, continuities and actors; her book and original methodological articles remain unread. This is one strand within history of science.

edges.relationship: provides materialist resources reworked in histories of slavery and revolution
edges.evidence_note: Retargeted from the anti-colonial umbrella to James. The feedback’s blanket assertion that both James and Eric Williams write as Marxists is not adopted; their distinct arguments remain visible. James’s 1971 recollection names his reading of Trotsky, Lenin and Marx. It supports a specific resource while leaving exact retrospective chronology open; Williams is not assigned the same theoretical identity.

edges.relationship: offers a comparison of long-duration and transregional historical explanation
edges.evidence_note: Braudel is a point of comparison; the present references do not establish every proposed line of influence to McNeill, Wallerstein, or connected history.

edges.relationship: intersects in historical analyses of meaning and categories of difference
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement. Hunt explicitly identifies Davis, Smith-Rosenberg and Scott as formative cultural-history resources. The comparison remains undirected; a separate contribution records this specific feminist route.

edges.relationship: Cronon’s commodity flows, Worster’s agriculture and Pomeranz’s resource constraints connect economic and environmental questions
edges.evidence_note: Editorial comparison of the cited approaches, not a claim of transmission or agreement. These are concrete, differing explanatory approaches; the comparison still makes no transmission claim. Pomeranz’s introduction adds a distinct comparative resource argument; these authors do not supply a single agreed model.
edges.map_label: Cronon and Worster: markets, land and resources

edges.relationship: Ginzburg contests textual reduction while treating narrative form as part of historical research
edges.evidence_note: A specific intervention in the 1992 volume, not a rejection of every form of linguistic analysis by all microhistorians. The 1993 discussion explicitly names Ankersmit. It cannot stand for all microhistorians or all linguistic approaches.
edges.map_label: Ginzburg: narrative need not erase knowledge

edges.relationship: Braudel borrows structural models while insisting on historical duration and testing
edges.evidence_note: The 1987 reprint, pp. 24–25 and 28–31, supplies the formerly missing named Lévi-Strauss discussion. Braudel explicitly borrows a mechanical/statistical distinction, appreciates the programme and tests models against changing conditions and breakdown. Original 1958 printing uncollated. The individual Braudel link specifies the same exchange, not a second independent transmission.

edges.relationship: participates in reassessments of representation and cultural history
edges.evidence_note: White’s afterword to Beyond the Cultural Turn is a concrete contribution. The unsupported claim that his reception was largely critical is omitted. Complete afterword315–324 reaffirms a Marxian standpoint while disputing claims of ideology-free social science; its closing paragraph retains the possibility of scientific social inquiry.

edges.relationship: Rodney contributes African research and a critique of underdevelopment through unequal power
edges.evidence_note: The earlier Upper Guinea project adds regional research to the 1972 power argument and Ranger’s Dar recollection. Neither the thesis abstract nor the retrospective testimony verifies the full monograph; Dar es Salaam remains intellectually plural.
edges.map_label: Rodney: research, power and Dar es Salaam

edges.relationship: establishes women’s work as a sustained subject of interwar historical inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. The primary introduction distinguishes work from recorded wage employment, training and marital status; eventual gains are her interpretation, not an independently established uniform outcome.
edges.map_label: Work, wages and uneven industrial change

edges.relationship: investigates industrialization through changes in women’s productive work
edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. The primary introduction distinguishes work from recorded wage employment, training and marital status; eventual gains are her interpretation, not an independently established uniform outcome.
edges.map_label: Work, wages and uneven industrial change

edges.relationship: reconstructs ordinary women’s working lives before the later expansion of the field
edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. The primary introduction/conclusion include unpaid production and overlapping forms. Medieval comparisons and broad causation remain qualified; maternal/racial assumptions are not endorsed.

edges.relationship: connects household production and women’s economic position to historical change
edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. The primary introduction/conclusion include unpaid production and overlapping forms. Medieval comparisons and broad causation remain qualified; maternal/racial assumptions are not endorsed.

edges.relationship: invites comparison of periodization and explanations of women’s work
edges.evidence_note: Different historical periods and questions; the comparison does not assert agreement, direct supervision, or a simple causal lineage. Their primary arguments distinguish periods and production forms; Erickson’s later introduction makes the contrast explicit without establishing direct transmission.
edges.map_label: Different periods and judgments of change

edges.relationship: argues for women’s historical agency and supports documentary recovery
edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. The complete 1946 preface supplies the attributed agency argument; Voss-Hubbard reconstructs collaborative archival practice and its institutional/racial limits. Neither proves universal emancipation or sole founding.
edges.map_label: Agency, records and contested archival practice

edges.relationship: invites comparison between earlier agency-centered history and later recovery groupings
edges.evidence_note: An editorial test of Hunt’s grouping, not a claim that Beard adopted the later language of identity politics. Beard questions the historical subject-sex premise and equality as a sufficient guide in her preface. This remains a comparison with later identity questions, not their origin or a shared unified position.
edges.map_label: Historical agency and the category of women

edges.relationship: contributes a documentary history of women in the southern colonies
edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. Richter’s 1999 review documents source use, Scott’s reissues and Colonial Williamsburg interpretation, alongside a specific coverage criticism. Original book passages remain mediated.
edges.map_label: Everyday institutions and later editorial recovery

edges.relationship: provides an earlier case of inquiry into everyday work and social relations
edges.evidence_note: Earlier social history is compared with the later field; no direct influence on every postwar social historian is asserted. Richter describes regional, status, work and family questions and reports Scott’s comparison with later methods. No broad direct influence follows from methodological similarity.
edges.map_label: Earlier social inquiry and uneven coverage

edges.relationship: investigates domestic service and household work before postwar expansion
edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. Original preface and chapters I–II support the concrete labor inquiry; the 1906 Apologia distinguishes its purpose from household panaceas. Evidence limits and acknowledged collective work remain explicit.
edges.map_label: Domestic work, survey evidence and explanation

edges.relationship: offers earlier investigations of ordinary life and social evidence
edges.evidence_note: The Vassar account uses social-history terminology retrospectively; this link does not move Salmon into a school that expanded after her death. The primary opening connects household work with industrial change, while the preface discusses nonresponse. This is an earlier comparison, not postwar movement membership.
edges.map_label: Earlier labor inquiry and evidence limits

edges.relationship: invites comparison through cookbooks, household objects, and everyday evidence
edges.evidence_note: A comparison of evidence and questions, not a direct genealogy from Salmon to the 1980s consumption-history literature. The original chapters consider changing household production; Vassar documents material-source pedagogy. Neither establishes a direct genealogy of the later consumption movement.

edges.relationship: shares critical work with sources while extending the range of evidence and subjects
edges.evidence_note: Not an assertion that her pedagogy derived solely from Ranke; source criticism and social inquiry can coexist. Salmon’s Apologia explicitly names Tyler’s instruction on judging a work’s purpose. This adds a specific interlocutor without reclassifying the existing Ranke comparison as influence.
edges.map_label: Source criticism with named teaching resources

edges.relationship: places women’s rights organizing alongside labor and Black women’s activity before the 1960s
edges.evidence_note: James and Rupp identify broader coverage while offering different criticisms. Later women’s history is neither a uniform continuation nor a field founded by this book alone. Original 1959 text and later editions remain distinct.
edges.map_label: Rights organizing, labor and archival reach

edges.relationship: makes women’s rights organizing an object of political history while exposing disputed movement boundaries
edges.evidence_note: Ostrander questions causal integration of other reforms; Rupp distinguishes historical self-definition from broadened categories. These receptions clarify the political-history contribution without settling the disagreement.

edges.relationship: uses documented narrative detail to reconstruct decisions and the opening of the First World War
edges.evidence_note: Publisher description establishes the work’s focus; Tuchman’s own methodological excerpt insists on evidence and supplies a weather example. The complete Guns of August source apparatus has not been newly checked, and a craft statement does not independently validate every reconstructed decision.
edges.map_label: War decisions and documented narrative detail

edges.relationship: connects diplomatic choices and political circumstances through narrative reconstruction
edges.evidence_note: The Guns of August provides the original context. A Distant Mirror’s foreword and 1978 reception add a distinct case about selecting events and relating individuals to institutions; this is not proof that narrative alone supplies a sufficient explanation.

edges.relationship: shows that prominent narrative history and disputes over its explanation preceded the 1979 revival diagnosis
edges.evidence_note: The 1962 book and 1978 review exchange establish chronology. Stone’s 1979 essay now has selected primary checks, including its recognition of continuing narrative practice; no causal origin or Tuchman endorsement of White is inferred.
edges.map_label: Narrative practice before the revival diagnosis

edges.relationship: investigates medieval women within economic and social history
edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. The nunneries discussion pp. 493–498 differentiates injunctions, recorded findings and the incompleteness of fault-seeking evidence.
edges.map_label: Rules, recorded faults and women’s lives

edges.relationship: contributes medieval research, teaching, and institutional work
edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. Primary prefaces identify documentary help, personal reconstruction and later editorial mediation, which are different contributions.

edges.relationship: offers earlier historical inquiry into ordinary people and everyday relations
edges.evidence_note: Power’s interwar work predates the period assigned to new social history; contribution to social inquiry is not a claim of direct transmission to every later approach. The 1924 preface and Bodo opening now support a particular personal teaching method; this existing comparison remains undirected.

edges.relationship: directs the research acknowledged in Pinchbeck’s original preface
edges.evidence_note: Direct evidence: preface to the first edition, printed p. vi (preview PDF p. 7), thanks Eileen Power for directing the research, discussion, and criticism of the manuscript. This supports research guidance, not agreement on every conclusion.

edges.relationship: reconstructs seventeenth-century political conflict through narrative histories
edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. Woolrych pp. 529–530 quotes the prefaces on uncertainty, motives and narrative explanation, while noting limits concerning allegiance. Original prefaces remain mediated.
edges.map_label: Motives and uncertainty in political narrative

edges.relationship: connects warfare to political and religious conflict in early modern Europe
edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. Woolrych discusses battlefield reconstruction and the relation of campaigns to politics; he also records Parker’s objection to the German-centered framing.

edges.relationship: uses individual political lives alongside wider narratives
edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. Woolrych pp. 523–525 distinguishes early Strafford from the 1961 revaluation prompted by new documents and research.

edges.relationship: provides an earlier example of sustained narrative historical writing
edges.evidence_note: The 1938 work demonstrates narrative continuity, not a narrative practice originating with a 1979 revival. The 1955/1958 prefatory defense, as quoted by Woolrych, supplies a particular methodological comparison. It is not a response to Stone’s later diagnosis.

edges.relationship: invites comparison of Renaissance cultural forms and historical meanings
edges.evidence_note: Affinity in subjects is not proof of direct descent from Burckhardt or Huizinga. The primary preface now documents a distinct Warburg setting and collaborators; no Burckhardt/Huizinga transmission is established.

edges.relationship: investigates connections between memory systems and histories of knowledge
edges.evidence_note: The Art of Memory’s contents include scientific-method questions; this does not equate Yates’s approach with Kuhn, SSK, or STS. Complete chapter XVII pp. 368–389 now supports an attributed argument about mnemonic ordering, combinatory projects and methods. Stronger causal and secret-transmission hypotheses remain unverified.

edges.relationship: contrasts mnemonic arts with collective memory and commemoration
edges.evidence_note: A teaching distinction, not a claim that Yates founded or directly produced the later memory-studies field. The primary preface differentiates several techniques and their intellectual/religious uses; that scope does not establish a direct genealogy of collective-memory scholarship.

edges.relationship: compares Renaissance intellectual inquiry with contextual histories of argument
edges.evidence_note: Different approaches to historical meanings; Yates is not assigned Cambridge School membership or a Skinner-derived method. The primary preface places Bruno historically while using distinct textual/visual resources. Shared contextual concern is an editorial comparison, not membership evidence.

edges.relationship: examines medieval government and institutions through local records
edges.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. Cheney identifies criticism of the Hundred Rolls editions and local administration, then county representation and parliamentary practice. His specific reservations remain attributed.

edges.relationship: invites comparison of documentary criticism and historical institutional inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Cam’s documented interlocutors include Maitland, Stubbs, and Vinogradoff. This is not an invented direct Ranke → Cam influence claim. Cam’s Stubbs opening and Cheney’s account provide named scholarly resources, without changing this comparison into a Ranke influence.

edges.relationship: recovers women’s participation in radical movements through class and community relations
edges.evidence_note: Chase identifies the 1976 essay and its question about changing cooperation. The interview distinguishes women’s organizations, family relations and neglected conflict; it neither dismisses women-only inquiry nor claims to found feminism. Original essay not independently read.

edges.relationship: reconstructs Chartism and popular radical participation
edges.evidence_note: Publisher scope identifies political aims, force and reciprocal responses by radicals and established classes. Interview pp. 15–16 insists on constituencies and contextual language. Monograph evidence is not independently checked.

edges.relationship: connects class formation and political action to families and communities
edges.evidence_note: Interview distinguishes family relations, women’s organizations and class conflict. The Chartists contents connect manufacturing communities, leaders/followers and women; this specific contribution is not a claim to found social history.

edges.relationship: provides a tradition of class analysis that she adopts and critically reassesses
edges.evidence_note: Her retrospective interview describes collective Marxist formation and, at pp. 6–8, neglected gender and ethnic differences. Influence preserves critical affiliation; the reverse critique added here specifies her objections rather than cancelling the inheritance.

edges.relationship: invites comparison of class-centered women’s history with later relational analyses
edges.evidence_note: This comparison concerns gender and class; it does not attribute every later race or gender theory to Thompson.

edges.relationship: contributes an account of working-class formation emphasizing experience, culture, and agency
edges.evidence_note: The primary Making preface defines class through historical relationships and distinguishes conditioned experience from any uniform law of consciousness. His theoretical intervention and later cultural disagreements belong to a contested materialist practice.

edges.relationship: criticizes Althusser’s treatment of experience and historical evidence
edges.evidence_note: The 1978 essay’s opening objections establish the polemic. This records Thompson’s criticism, not a judgment that it settles the dispute. The older umbrella-level edge_027 remains preserved.

edges.relationship: provides approaches to labour, class, culture, and agency developed and reworked by feminist and gender historians
edges.evidence_note: A productive inheritance as well as a disagreement. Concerns particular British Marxist and socialist-feminist strands, not a sole origin of gender history. Anna Clark’s 1995 study supplies a further named integration of class formation, family and radical rhetoric.

edges.relationship: places culture and experience within the historical explanation of class formation
edges.evidence_note: The primary Making preface places cultural formation inside the explanation of class. Its English scope is explicit. Later disputes and feminist criticisms do not erase this contribution or imply abandoning materialist explanation.

edges.relationship: offers historical resources that feminist historians extend while questioning their gendered limits
edges.evidence_note: Taylor describes a concrete feminist development of Thompson’s work. The connection concerns gender history, not every theory discussed in gender history.

edges.relationship: challenges the gendered scope of his account of class and experience
edges.evidence_note: Includes Scott’s criticism and subsequent feminist debate. Thompson resisted some criticism; the disagreement coexists with the productive inheritance recorded in edge_313.

edges.relationship: Co-founds Annales and contributes comparative inquiry into social relations, belief and traces
edges.evidence_note: The 1929 statement directly supports the collaborative programme; selected Apologie passages specify evidential reasoning. Royal Touch and Feudal Society remain differently scoped book references. Individual and group links describe related levels, not independent transmissions.

edges.relationship: Co-founds Annales and contributes historical questions about belief, feelings and material culture
edges.evidence_note: The 1929 statement and 1941 essay substantiate the programme and historical psychology; book-history collaboration has separate institutional evidence. These are distinct contributions within the group, not the definition of all Annales.

edges.relationship: Contributes multiple durations and historically tested models within Annales
edges.evidence_note: The duration essay contains productive structural borrowing and attention to models’ finite validity. This is one programme within Annales; Chartier’s 1989 objection to explanatory hierarchy is represented separately.

edges.relationship: Contributes conjunctural evidence and questions about uneven social crises
edges.evidence_note: The primary 1956 opening differentiates sectors; Grenier/Lepetit’s later abstract distinguishes Labrousse’s experimental intentions from a narrowed serial reception. Neither source makes his programme the whole of Annales.

edges.relationship: provides a historical account of capitalist development debated by the Historians’ Group
edges.evidence_note: The participant memoir identifies collective reception; Dobb’s primary reply specifies production relations, trade interaction and a concession about weak evidence. Takahashi demonstrates a distinct international intervention, not unanimous endorsement.

edges.relationship: contributes medieval peasant history and analysis of feudal class relations
edges.evidence_note: Selected primary Bond Men passages connect class relations with political organization, religion and mediated evidence. The comparative argument does not imply that all peasant movements share outcomes or that later capitalist development was their conscious aim.
edges.map_label: Peasant action, aims and uneven outcomes

edges.relationship: contributes labour history and the organization of collaborative historical inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Participant testimony, archive guide and scholarly accounts specify tutoring, translation and cooperative research. The guide distinguishes Hill/Morton’s published contribution from an unprinted Edward draft; later fragments do not constitute a completed second volume. Morgan also distinguishes draft praise from the published tribute.
edges.map_label: Torr’s tutoring, editing and collective work

edges.relationship: contributes histories of labour, protest, and capitalist transformation
edges.evidence_note: A specific contribution within a heterogeneous field. The individual and group links describe related levels of the same history, not independent evidence of several transmissions. Revised Bandits specifies culture, political power and responses to criticism; the narrative reply distinguishes analysis from presentation.

edges.relationship: contributes an interpretation of revolutionary politics and radical belief
edges.evidence_note: A specific contribution within a heterogeneous field. The individual and group links describe related levels of the same history, not independent evidence of several transmissions. Primary preface/introduction specify Dobb’s resource and religious/radical alternatives; the later Ranter dispute remains an open scholarly disagreement.

edges.relationship: connects economic change to religious ethics and social relations
edges.evidence_note: A specific contribution within a heterogeneous field. The individual and group links describe related levels of the same history, not independent evidence of several transmissions. The complete agrarian introduction adds regional differentiation, legal/economic questions and problems of statistical comparability.

edges.relationship: Reworks Annales through representations, material forms and differentiated appropriation
edges.evidence_note: The primary 1989 article concludes with critical fidelity to Annales. It questions Braudel’s explanatory hierarchy while retaining an account of social divisions; it does not announce the abandonment of social history.

edges.relationship: is acknowledged and critically discussed in Tawney’s work on religion and capitalism
edges.evidence_note: Tawney names Weber in his introduction while explicitly reserving disagreement. Chapter IV note 32 makes the criticism specific: causal weighting, nonreligious thought and Calvinist/Puritan differentiation.

edges.relationship: Ashley’s study of canonist doctrine helps frame Tawney’s historical question
edges.evidence_note: A named debt to Ashley, not a claim that Tawney adopted the entire German historical school.

edges.relationship: offers arguments and historical problems taken up and contested by British Marxist historians
edges.evidence_note: An external interlocutor; shared socialist concerns do not establish Marxist membership. Dobb’s primary reply p. 164 supplies one exact instance of reception; the precise underlying Tawney passage remains unidentified.
edges.map_label: An external resource for Dobb’s inquiry

edges.relationship: provides long-duration questions that Wallerstein adapts and theorizes differently
edges.evidence_note: Applies to Wallerstein, not to every dependency theorist. Braudel’s 1977 text also names Wallerstein and distinguishes their usages and chronologies. The new reverse contribution records this specific reading, without making reciprocal influence claims identical. Wallerstein 1974 p. 388 explicitly uses Braudel’s criticism of rigid historical models. This named primary reception complements the prior retrospective evidence.

edges.relationship: Connects textual manufacture, reading and representations to social differentiation
edges.evidence_note: The 1989 primary article explicitly uses McKenzie, Durkheim/Mauss and other resources. Meaning depends on forms and practices; social classifications are also made through representation. This is one cultural-historical programme, not a uniform mentality.

edges.relationship: Febvre critically receives Huizinga’s account of historical forms of feeling
edges.evidence_note: The 1941 sensitivity essay praises Huizinga while questioning whether the contrasted emotional patterns distinguish the late Middle Ages sufficiently. Productive use and criticism coexist; this does not derive all Annales from earlier cultural history.

edges.relationship: Kuhn acknowledges Koyré, Metzger, Maier and Fleck as resources for his historical account
edges.evidence_note: The 1962 preface identifies named debts; this arrow concerns those works, not every historian of science.

edges.relationship: Pinch and Bijker adapt controversy research to technological alternatives and stabilization
edges.evidence_note: Their 1984 article explicitly combines the two research areas; not a genealogy of all technology history.

edges.relationship: Latour investigates Pasteur’s historical rise and the establishment of microbes as actors
edges.evidence_note: Author’s description supports this contribution; full reception within history of science remains to be researched.

edges.relationship: Rossiter makes women’s scientific careers and institutional barriers central historical questions
edges.evidence_note: A specific contribution through Women Scientists in America (1982), not the origin of the whole science field.

edges.relationship: Merchant connects the history of science with women and environmental questions
edges.evidence_note: Berkeley’s retrospective documents Merchant’s cross-field contribution. The added primary excerpt, reprinted in 1991, supports her account of mechanical order, control of nature and capitalist development. It does not verify every gender claim or adjudicate criticisms of the 1980 book. Selected 2006 retrospective passages now clarify Merchant’s material/ideational argument and her response to named 1990s critics. Pesic’s 1999 author abstract supplies a competing reading of Bacon’s metaphor. These sources document disagreement; they do not settle Bacon’s intentions or independently verify early experimental practices. Later reception is not backdated into the mapped period.

edges.relationship: Haraway contributes a feminist argument for situated and accountable scientific objectivity
edges.evidence_note: Scoped to feminist science studies within the gender-history entry; does not represent all gender historians.

edges.relationship: Toynbee uses classical political economy and conditional deduction to guide historical inquiry
edges.evidence_note: The introductory lecture explicitly describes what historical research gains from economic reasoning; this is compatible with criticizing its misuse.
edges.map_label: Toynbee: theory helps frame historical questions

edges.relationship: Menger challenges the substitution of historical investigation for theoretical explanation
edges.evidence_note: Book I, chapters 1–2 and Schmoller’s contemporary response document this intervention. It concerns Menger’s particular argument, not all economists or a rejection of doing history.

edges.relationship: Ashley edits Mill’s Principles and traces changes across its editions
edges.evidence_note: The 1909 edition’s introduction documents an editorial contribution to the study of economic theory. It does not mean Ashley accepted every Mill argument or that the historical school produced Mill’s original work.

edges.relationship: Vidal explicitly takes up Michelet’s conception of France while asking how human activity forms geographical individuality
edges.evidence_note: The opening of Tableau names Michelet and reworks his national framing as a geographical question. This concerns a specific engagement, not all national traditions or an assertion that France is naturally predetermined.
edges.map_label: Michelet’s France in Vidal’s geographical question

edges.relationship: Cronon draws on anthropology, alongside economics and legal theory, to analyze colonial property
edges.evidence_note: In his 2003 retrospective on the 1983 book, Cronon identifies these resources for the chapter “Bounding the Land.” No particular anthropologist or exclusive disciplinary origin is inferred.

edges.relationship: Cronon historicizes the pristine-wilderness ideal as a cultural formation
edges.evidence_note: The 1995 essay contributes a historical cultural analysis of wilderness, including Indigenous removal and care for inhabited environments. It does not deny nonhuman reality or demonstrate influence on the entire cultural turn.
edges.map_label: Cronon: wilderness as a historical cultural idea

edges.relationship: Carruthers connects South African conservation with racial power and national politics
edges.evidence_note: The 1995 Kruger study is a specific environmental-history contribution to African history. Publisher-level argument support is recorded; no school-wide influence or coverage of all African environments is claimed.
edges.map_label: Carruthers: conservation and South African politics

edges.relationship: Polanyi uses social anthropology to distinguish market regulation from other economic relations
edges.evidence_note: Chapter IV explicitly calls for linking economic history with anthropology and discusses reciprocity and redistribution. This records a concrete intellectual resource, not endorsement of all Polanyi’s historical generalizations.

edges.relationship: Polanyi challenges Smith’s conjectural account of a propensity to barter
edges.evidence_note: The primary chapter names Smith and disputes making barter an original human economic motive. This is Polanyi’s particular critique, not a consensus of economic historians or a rejection of every argument by Smith.
edges.map_label: Polanyi: criticism of Smith’s barter account

edges.relationship: De Vries links expanding demand with household labor and resource reallocation
edges.evidence_note: The 1994 article provides a named demand-and-labor intervention in explanations of industrialization, while qualifying household unity and universal stages. It does not make consumption history the sole source of the argument.
edges.map_label: De Vries: demand and the industrious revolution

edges.relationship: Appadurai and Kopytoff offer distinct analyses of circulating value and changing commodity status
edges.evidence_note: The primary opening extracts document their conceptual contributions. Douglas and Isherwood supply a further, publisher-supported account of goods as communication. No exclusive disciplinary origin or influence on every historian is claimed. Vickery’s chapter5/note9 explicitly uses Douglas/Isherwood and cites Appadurai’s collection. It does not name Kopytoff in the checked passages, so that individual reception is not inferred. Geary explicitly cites Kopytoff169 and proposes object biographies188 in the same1986 collection. This now supplies a particular historian’s use of the person/commodity problem, with his own limits on evidence189–190.
edges.map_label: Circulating value, commodity status and social uses

edges.relationship: Benson tests interpretations of Jacksonian politics through New York voting patterns
edges.evidence_note: Primary chapter openings support a particular electoral investigation and attention to overlapping group categories, not a claim that political history as a whole adopted one method.
edges.map_label: Benson: voting groups and political explanation

edges.relationship: Benson explicitly challenges the economic-determinist interpretation he attributes to Turner and Beard
edges.evidence_note: Chapter VIII opening names both historians. The target is the Progressive side of the paired entry and a specified interpretation; it is not criticism of every argument by them or every consensus historian.
edges.map_label: Benson: criticism of economic-determinist voting history

edges.relationship: Gutman disputes Fogel and Engerman’s account of enslaved people’s labor and cooperation
edges.evidence_note: Publisher support identifies data-based criticism and coercion; the full tables and replies remain unreviewed. Gutman is a named social historian intervening in a particular cliometric controversy, not the voice of an anti-quantitative consensus.
edges.map_label: Gutman: evidence, coercion and Time on the Cross

edges.relationship: Fogel’s railroad counterfactual questions a decisive-innovation account associated with Rostow
edges.evidence_note: The indexed official Nobel committee account explicitly contrasts Fogel with Rostow and Schumpeter. This records a particular challenge to railroad indispensability, not disproof of every modernization argument or independent verification of Fogel’s estimates.

edges.relationship: Thernstrom draws on Weber to distinguish dimensions of social position
edges.evidence_note: The primary opening of Poverty and Progress chapter 5, p. 115, explicitly quotes Weber before examining property/savings alongside occupations. The link records named use in one study, not Weber’s origin of all quantitative history.

edges.relationship: Hunt explicitly uses Geertz’s cultural frame to examine revolutionary political authority
edges.evidence_note: The primary opening of chapter 3, p. 87, names Geertz. This records her particular analytical use, not the origin of all cultural political history.
edges.map_label: Hunt: Geertz and the cultural framing of authority

edges.relationship: Hunt’s French Revolution study joins political symbols, practices and social identities in cultural explanation
edges.evidence_note: Primary chapter openings and the book’s paired poetics/sociology sections support this contribution across fields. It does not make cultural history an exclusively political invention or discard quantitative evidence.
edges.map_label: Hunt: political practice and cultural explanation

edges.relationship: Tilly connects local claim-making with changing repertoires and wider political/economic processes
edges.evidence_note: His 1993–1994 primary essay explains the programme and its Britain/France limits. Movements are not automatically democratic or timeless social organisms.
edges.map_label: Tilly: collective performances and historical change

edges.relationship: Guha treats colonial peasant insurgency as deliberate political action and consciousness
edges.evidence_note: Duke’s description supports the intervention against blind-reaction accounts. Full-book interpretation and the variability of peasant consciousness remain open; this is not the voice of all South Asian history.
edges.map_label: Guha: insurgent peasants as political actors

edges.relationship: Chakrabarty challenges universalizing working-class narratives through Bengal labor history
edges.evidence_note: Publisher support attributes the criticism of reductionist culture/consciousness and universal class categories. The target is a specified model, not all Marxist or social history; the study also retains Marxian questions. The primary preface xi–xv now supports the stated anti-reductionist argument and its continuing commitment to equality. Nair’s 1990 review raises a distinct counter-question about cultural determination, historical reworking and gender; the new reciprocal critique records that response without treating either position as settled.
edges.map_label: Chakrabarty: class categories and colonial labor

edges.relationship: Cooper’s labor history exposes colonial government’s categories and control over social relations
edges.evidence_note: The primary Part I introduction, pp. 23–24, connects classifications of labor with colonial power. This records a particular social-political inquiry, not a claim that labor alone explains decolonization. The Mombasa case (234–241) now supplies a concrete sequence connecting mobilization, wage investigations, differentiated reform and repression.
edges.map_label: Cooper: labor categories and colonial governing

edges.relationship: Davidoff and Hall integrate gender, family, religion and economic opportunity into middle-class history
edges.evidence_note: The publisher description and indexed prologue specify the joint study. This productive contribution coexists with the undirected subject overlap in edge_092; women’s history is not reduced to a postwar social-history subset. The expanded prologue check emphasizes familial support beneath public prominence. Vickery’s specific appreciative criticism (1993, 393–401) keeps the book’s chronology and generalizations open to debate.
edges.map_label: Davidoff and Hall: gender and class formation

edges.relationship: Scott explicitly draws on Foucault’s genealogy when historicizing experience and analytic categories
edges.evidence_note: The 1991 conclusion, p. 796, cites “Nietzsche, Genealogy, History.” The contribution operates through Scott’s particular intervention and is not a claim that Foucault shaped all social historians.
edges.map_label: Scott: genealogy and the history of categories

edges.relationship: Block and Somers bring Polanyi’s economic-institutional questions into historical sociology
edges.evidence_note: Their 1984 chapter is a documented engagement with a specific thinker; it does not make economic history the origin of the entire field.

edges.relationship: Sewell challenges Skocpol’s restricted treatment of ideology within structural revolutionary explanation
edges.evidence_note: The 1985 critique values her comparative analysis; her reply acknowledges a shortcoming. This is a specific exchange, not all cultural historians opposing all sociology. The directly checked reply opening also expresses reservations about Sewell’s proposed conception of culture; acknowledgment is not complete agreement. A separate reciprocal edge records that specific objection.

edges.relationship: Lüdtke uses Mann’s intersecting power networks as a resource for everyday-history inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Lüdtke’s 1993 note 74 explicitly discusses Mann’s 1986 chapter. Applies to Alltagsgeschichte within the paired entry, not a genealogy of Italian microhistory.

edges.relationship: Kocka draws on Marx alongside Weber for industrial and bourgeois social history
edges.evidence_note: Explicit publisher support concerns analytical resources, not doctrinal Marxism or all German historians. This productive use coexists with the historical-left criticism already recorded.
edges.map_label: Kocka: Marx as an analytical resource

edges.relationship: Kocka’s organizational and bourgeois comparisons broaden social-history questions
edges.evidence_note: A named research contribution evidenced by the 1999 collection’s contents; no claim that Bielefeld founded new social history or that all studies share one argument.

edges.relationship: Frevert brings women’s lives and gendered rights into German social history
edges.evidence_note: The work’s contents and her documented Bielefeld context support a specific contribution. This does not imply adherence to every Sonderweg thesis or simple succession of approaches.

edges.relationship: Goldstone combines demographic pressures with institutions and elite relations to explain state crises
edges.evidence_note: Publisher description supports a specific comparative application. It does not establish population as a sufficient cause, consensus among demographers, or the validity of every estimate. Primary preface xxi–xxvi and comparison 156–169 now support the conjunctural argument. Fiscal pressure alone does not explain the contrasting regional cases; Perry’s review questions the breadth of generalization without reducing the book to simple Malthusianism.

edges.relationship: Medick brings a critical engagement with Cohn and collaborative anthropology into historical inquiry
edges.evidence_note: His 1987 introductory note and note 10 document a specific exchange and working group. This addresses historical anthropology and everyday-life research within the umbrella.

edges.relationship: Levi and Cerutti reconstruct social relations and classifications through intensive inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Ginzburg 1993 p. 33 presents their work as reconstructing interaction, not merely as an attack on social explanation. His assessment is a participant interpretation.

edges.relationship: Lüdtke uses Passerini’s work on fascism and everyday self-representation
edges.evidence_note: His 1993 note 49 cites her 1987 pp. 22ff on distancing conduct. Applies to Alltagsgeschichte, without making oral history the origin of Italian microstoria.

edges.relationship: Gluck and Patai’s collection brings feminist methodological questions into oral-history practice
edges.evidence_note: A plural edited intervention, supported at collection-description level; individual essay positions remain to be checked.

edges.relationship: Bozzoli and Nkotsoe’s life-history project contributes to South African women’s history
edges.evidence_note: The primary introduction specifies interviewing and interpretive work alongside social conditions; it does not make one set of lives representative of all women.
edges.map_label: Phokeng: gender, migration and life histories

edges.relationship: Passerini’s work investigates everyday relations with fascist power through memory and other sources
edges.evidence_note: Publisher description and her retrospective discussion support this specific political-history resource, not a general equation of recollection with resistance.

edges.relationship: Feminist participants reshape History Workshop’s subjects, organization and interpretive questions
edges.evidence_note: The archive account identifies Rowbotham, Alexander and Davin in the organizing around the 1970 Ruskin conference; Alexander’s historical work adds a differentiated later contribution. This complements the broad comparison rather than asserting one feminist doctrine.
edges.map_label: Rowbotham, Alexander and Davin: feminist interventions

edges.relationship: Alexander brings psychoanalytic questions into feminist historical inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Her participant interview explicitly discusses Freud; the 1994/1995 collection description places psychoanalytic subjectivity within pre-2000 work. Neither source proves the first date of reception or a movement-wide Freudian commitment.

edges.relationship: Jan Assmann uses Bourdieu in discussing the organization of everyday communication
edges.evidence_note: The primary 1995 note 8 cites Bourdieu’s 1972 Esquisse. The arrow is confined to this documented conceptual resource; it does not claim that all embodied-memory scholarship derives from practice theory.

edges.relationship: Assmann’s account connects remembering to intersecting groups and collective self-images
edges.evidence_note: The 1995 essay supplies a conceptual resource for identity questions; this editorial contribution does not mean it founded identity-based history or that collective memory is homogeneous.

edges.relationship: Chatterjee challenges the modular account associated with Anderson through colonial historical difference
edges.evidence_note: Primary pp. 4–7 formulate the objection while retaining print and language as relevant resources. The critique is not a rejection of all national imagining.

edges.relationship: Yuval-Davis makes gender relations constitutive of national projects and citizenship
edges.evidence_note: Publisher-level support establishes the book’s stated intervention, not every chapter claim.

edges.relationship: Hroch’s comparative inquiry relates national movements to their social settings and participants
edges.evidence_note: His primary 1993 essay explicitly develops comparison through selected dimensions and variable sequences; this is a methodological contribution, not a claim that one sociological school founded his research.

edges.relationship: Billig makes everyday reminders of nationhood a resource for studying routine cultural practices
edges.evidence_note: A bounded conceptual contribution from Banal Nationalism, supported by the publisher description; no general genealogy of cultural history is asserted.

edges.relationship: Kaplan brings women’s and family experiences into the history of Jewish persecution
edges.evidence_note: Her book’s stated method uses varied personal sources and resists assumptions based on hindsight. It is one intervention, not a claim that gender exhausts Jewish experience.
edges.map_label: Kaplan: women, family and daily life

edges.relationship: Personal testimony informs Kaplan’s daily-life inquiry and Browning’s use of Tec’s Rufeisen study
edges.evidence_note: Kaplan’s abstract explicitly includes interviews; Browning’s primary p. 17 uses testimony mediated by Tec. This specific contribution complements the broad comparison and retains source-criticism requirements.
edges.map_label: Kaplan’s interviews; Tec in Browning’s debate

edges.relationship: Said uses hegemony to explain the persistence of Orientalist authority
edges.evidence_note: Explicit primary introduction uptake; this particular use does not define the whole umbrella.

edges.relationship: Spivak and Stoler question different limits of Foucault’s accounts of power
edges.evidence_note: Spivak’s primary essay addresses representation and labor; Stoler’s publisher description identifies empire and race. Their criticisms coexist with productive theoretical use.

edges.relationship: Mohanty and Stoler make gendered colonial relations part of postcolonial inquiry
edges.evidence_note: A gender-history contribution; distinct textual and archival projects.

edges.relationship: Mohanty criticizes scholarship that treats women across the Third World as one homogeneous subject
edges.evidence_note: The revised essay explicitly allows differences within Western feminism and seeks solidarities; this is a targeted criticism, not a rejection of women’s history.

edges.relationship: Spivak questions the gendered recovery of an autonomous subaltern subject
edges.evidence_note: The primary Guha discussion and gender argument supply a bounded intervention; her critique does not equate subalternity with literal voicelessness.

edges.relationship: Amin connects local recollections and judicial archives to national remembrance
edges.evidence_note: Publisher description supports the research design; Chakrabarty’s primary 1997 essay documents contemporary uptake of Amin’s narrative method.
edges.map_label: Amin: local memory and national narratives

edges.relationship: Prakash examines science in imperial classification and national emancipation
edges.evidence_note: A contribution through Another Reason (1999), supported at publisher-description level; no claim that Subaltern Studies founded science history.

edges.relationship: Chakrabarty questions disciplinary inclusion through an explicit engagement with Telling the Truth About History
edges.evidence_note: The primary 1997 essay engages Appleby and her coauthors while distinguishing democratic inclusion from limits of secular narration. The relationship records an intervention, not consensus.

edges.relationship: Cabral reworks questions of production and class through culture and liberation
edges.evidence_note: Primary 1970 lecture supplies explicit conceptual use. This does not assign every anti-colonial thinker to one Marxist programme.

edges.relationship: Cabral makes historically changing culture part of the explanation of liberation
edges.evidence_note: A conceptual contribution to cultural historical questions, not demonstrated reception by every cultural historian.
edges.map_label: Cabral: culture as historical social activity

edges.relationship: Awe’s collection and Bozzoli’s life-history project bring women’s historical questions into African inquiry
edges.evidence_note: The Nigerian repository account and previously checked South African introduction support distinct projects and evidence.
edges.map_label: Awe and Bozzoli: different women’s histories

edges.relationship: Amadiume’s Nnobi study makes colonial change and women’s social positions questions for gender analysis
edges.evidence_note: HRAF summary supports a bounded historical-ethnographic intervention; no continent-wide identity model is inferred.
edges.map_label: Amadiume: gender in a specific historical setting

edges.relationship: Cooper brings labor as a social process into the history of African decolonization
edges.evidence_note: Previously checked primary introduction critiques colonial categories and simple labor dichotomies; publisher description identifies the comparative French/British frame. The Mombasa case (234–241) shows how rural connections supported urban collective action and how official labor reform sought to reshape those relations.

edges.relationship: Rodney adapts materialist method to historical time and place
edges.evidence_note: His 1975 lecture explicitly separates method from conclusions about nineteenth-century Europe. This is his account of a conceptual resource, not a claim that African/Caribbean history derives wholly from European theory.

edges.relationship: Upper Guinea research connects regional change and Atlantic slave trading
edges.evidence_note: The 1966 thesis abstract identifies European and intra-African forces; the 1970 book contributes regional scholarship. This does not certify every argument of the unread book or make Africans a single responding actor.
edges.map_label: Upper Guinea: regional and Atlantic relations

edges.relationship: Guyanese working people become subjects of differentiated labor history
edges.evidence_note: The posthumous 1981 book addresses immigration, race, class, resistance and accommodation. Mapping it here identifies substantive social history, not membership in a unified school. Publisher-level support retains its limits.
edges.map_label: Guyana: labor, race and class divisions

edges.relationship: James criticizes Rodney’s political preparation for taking power
