The 1969 article p. 37 directly cites Investigations §§43 and 79, adding contemporary primary evidence to the retrospective interview.

edges.relationship: Ryle invokes Freud against an assumption of transparent consciousness
edges.evidence_note: The Concept of Mind, p. 14, names Freud’s account of unrecognized impulses as a challenge to an assumption in the official doctrine. This bounded resource does not make Ryle a psychoanalyst or establish agreement with Freud’s whole theory.
edges.map_label: Freud and the limits of conscious self-knowledge

edges.relationship: Both examine intelligible use and action through distinct philosophical projects
edges.evidence_note: The selected primary texts support a comparison of contextual use, competent practice and conceptual confusions. Tanney discusses parallel development and possible reciprocal learning; the current evidence does not warrant choosing one general transmission direction.
edges.map_label: Use, action and distinct philosophical methods

edges.relationship: Skinner and Dunn explicitly use Kuhn among interpretive resources
edges.evidence_note: Skinner (1969), p. 7, invokes the priority of paradigms and chapter V of Structure; Dunn’s notes also acknowledge the work. This bounded methodological use does not derive the entire Cambridge grouping from a theory of scientific revolutions.
edges.map_label: Kuhn as a specified interpretive resource

edges.relationship: Dunn uses Ryle’s reconstruction of Plato’s intellectual activity
edges.evidence_note: Dunn (1968), p. 94 and note 20 p. 103, discusses Plato’s Progress (1966) as a reconstruction from difficult evidence. This is a particular reception in historical-philosophical interpretation, distinct from Geertz’s use of Ryle or the knowing-how argument; the full Ryle book remains unread.

edges.relationship: Skinner criticizes Collingwood’s inference from identifying a problem to solving it
edges.evidence_note: Skinner (1969), pp. 50–51, argues that intelligible attempts may fail to solve their problems. This specific criticism coexists with his acknowledged question/answer resource; it does not reject all contextual interpretation or every historicist position. Collingwood’s original passage remains to be collated.

edges.relationship: Koselleck invokes Nietzsche on historically accumulated concepts resisting definition
edges.evidence_note: Futures Past, chapter 5, p. 85, explicitly quotes the difficulty of defining what has a history. This supports a particular conceptual resource, not a complete Nietzschean genealogy of conceptual history.
edges.map_label: Historical concepts and limits of definition

edges.relationship: Koselleck uses Weber’s legitimacy typology to distinguish analytical categories
edges.evidence_note: Futures Past, chapter 5, p. 92, discusses transformation of historical political vocabulary into a scientific category. This specific example does not establish Weber as a founding inspiration of the entire program; Olsen’s introduction note 9 explicitly disputes that larger genealogy.
edges.map_label: Weber’s typology as an analytical example

edges.relationship: Gumbrecht and Reichardt use Elias for the courtly setting of philosophe
edges.evidence_note: The 1985 French Handbuch article, p. 12 and note 4, cites The Civilizing Process in discussing court interaction and affect regulation. This is documented reception in one French conceptual-history case, not a claim about the origins of all German or French lexicon work.
edges.map_label: Elias in the French philosophe study

edges.relationship: Schmoller and the Verein provide an institutional setting for Weber’s agrarian inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Kim’s scholarly biographical section identifies mentorship and the agrarian commission. This is a specified research setting, not a claim that Weber simply inherits every methodological position of the German historical school.
edges.map_label: Schmoller, the Verein and agrarian research

edges.relationship: Rostow reworks production theory; Lipset uses Schumpeter’s electoral definition
edges.evidence_note: Rostow’s 1960 chapter 2 closes with a dynamic-production account critically related to classical and Keynesian models. Lipset 1959 p. 71 explicitly cites Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy for an electoral definition. These are separate resources, not a single economics-to-modernization genealogy.

edges.relationship: Lipset and Huntington pose distinct historical questions about legitimacy and institutions
edges.evidence_note: Lipset 1959 compares development and legitimacy while rejecting automatic democratization; Huntington 1968 pp. 1–7, 12–13 distinguishes institutionalization from growth and electoral form. This contribution identifies questions and comparative tools, not adoption by every political historian or endorsement of their national typologies.

edges.relationship: Eisenstadt reconstructs comparative inquiry around multiple modern programs
edges.evidence_note: The 2000 article pp. 1–4, 24–26 rejects Western convergence and examines continually reconstructed cultural and institutional programs, including destructive possibilities. Its contribution coexists with the opposite-direction Moore/Bendix criticism; it does not retrospectively attribute the later program to every 1950s theorist.

edges.relationship: Vogel reworks Marxian categories for gender and reproduction of material life
edges.evidence_note: The checked publisher description identifies this specific constructive feminist inquiry in the 1983 book. It does not verify every mechanism in the unread body or identify all gender history with Marxism; the primary-passage limitation is retained.
edges.map_label: Vogel’s feminist reworking of Marxian categories

edges.relationship: Weber defends materialist historical inquiry against a particular juristic refutation
edges.evidence_note: The available Objectivity excerpt rejects the inference that legally regulated economic life must therefore be explained only by conscious legal purposes. Legal forms can persist while their practical social significance changes. This bounded defense is neither wholesale adherence to Marxism nor a complete account of Weber’s disagreements with Marx.
edges.map_label: A qualified defense of materialist inquiry

edges.relationship: Wallerstein contests Dobb’s definition of capitalism and the transitional period
edges.evidence_note: Wallerstein 1974 pp. 393, 399 names Dobb and quotes Capitalism Yesterday and Today. He prefers a world-economy/market-production unit that includes coerced labor. This records disagreement, not a verdict against Dobb’s historical evidence.
edges.map_label: Wallerstein challenges Dobb’s unit and definition

edges.relationship: Dos Santos disputes a comparative-cost account of dependent economies
edges.evidence_note: The Structure of Dependence pp. 235–236 targets free-competition/comparative-cost assumptions and policy sufficiency. Prebisch’s earlier qualified use of trade theory differs; this is not rejection of economics as a whole.
edges.map_label: Dos Santos: comparative costs and dependence

edges.relationship: Prebisch’s structuralism and Polanyi’s exchange analysis provide distinct resources
edges.evidence_note: Dos Santos uses ECLA research while criticizing its policies; Wallerstein 1974 p. 390 explicitly cites Polanyi’s instituted-economy essay. Prebisch’s trade/industrialization argument specifies the structuralist context without making all dependentistas structuralists.
edges.map_label: Structuralist research and Polanyi’s exchange forms

edges.relationship: Alice and Staughton Lynd develop a participatory organizer-history collection
edges.evidence_note: Rank and File (1973), introduction 1–8, explains referrals, editing and participant correction. It combines interviews with written accounts and speeches; the sample is selective and the testimony mediated.
edges.map_label: The Lynds: testimony and participant correction

edges.relationship: Genovese uses Fogel and Engerman’s statistical and analytical work
edges.evidence_note: His acknowledgments explicitly credit their supplied work and Engerman’s manuscript reading. This resource does not imply acceptance of all their conclusions and does not cancel Gutman’s separate criticism of Time on the Cross.
edges.map_label: Fogel and Engerman’s research supplied to Genovese

edges.relationship: Slavery scholarship and source collections provide resources for Genovese
edges.evidence_note: The preface and acknowledgments name Rawick, Levine and Litwack; permissions also identify Du Bois and Black historical source collections. This particular use respects Black history’s independent institutions and does not derive that field from the New Left.

edges.relationship: Feminist historical analysis helps constitute new cultural inquiry
edges.evidence_note: Hunt’s 1989 introduction identifies Davis, Smith-Rosenberg and Scott as formative resources and discusses gender within Desan’s community/ritual inquiry. This particular route does not subsume racial-formation scholarship or make all cultural historians share one feminist position.

edges.relationship: Smith-Rosenberg contributes to Spiegel’s social and textual method
edges.evidence_note: Romancing the Past introduction note 7 cites The Body Politic and thanks Smith-Rosenberg for a draft; acknowledgments credit sustained exchange and her reading every chapter. This is a concrete reciprocal contribution, not gender history receiving theory only from outside.

edges.relationship: Laqueur’s humanitarian-narrative inquiry expands social-historical questions
edges.evidence_note: Hunt’s introduction explicitly presents Laqueur’s chapter as extending social history’s attention to class and power through narrative. This is Hunt’s editorial interpretation; the chapter body and downstream reception are not newly checked.

edges.relationship: McNeill makes world history an explicit problem of evidence and interpretation
edges.evidence_note: The complete1986 address distinguishes source criticism from selection and interpretation, argues that some accounts fit facts and broader experience better, and advocates ecumenical synthesis. His normative program is not a proof of eventual convergence or a claim that all stories are equivalent.
edges.map_label: McNeill: evidence, interpretation and world history

edges.relationship: Subrahmanyam contests Goldstone’s autonomous-state model and ideological partitions
edges.evidence_note: Connected Histories758–759 names Revolution and Rebellion1991, objecting to demographic/fiscal sequencing and an eschatological/cyclical partition in light of circulating ideas. sources.citation: Brian Vickers, ed., Occult and Scientific Mentalities in the Renaissance (Cambridge University Press, 1984).

verification.note: Publisher description and contents, plus primary introduction opening at DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511572999.002, consulted. Description proposes distinct assumptions/methods and questions a simple magic-to-science transition; opening criticizes older dismissals of occult inquiry. Full introduction and cases unread. No direct Vickers-to-Yates critique arrow is inferred from the opening alone; the proposed distinction remains debatable.

sources.title: Austin Woolrych, “Cicely Veronica Wedgwood, 1910–1997,” Proceedings of the British Academy 97 (1998), pp. 521–534.

Volume designated 1997; scan identifies 1998 publication.

sources.title: Mary Ritter Beard, Woman as Force in History: A Study in Traditions and Realities (Macmillan, 1946), preface.
sources.citation: Mary Ritter Beard, Woman as Force in History: A Study in Traditions and Realities (Macmillan, 1946), preface.

verification.note: Complete preface, signed summer 1945, read in Andy Blunden’s transcription. It sets out the subject-sex argument, legal/equity inquiry, criticism of equality as a sufficient guide, and enlarged historical attention. Opening portions of chapters I and X also consulted, not complete chapters. Original printing and legal cases not collated. Transcription adds an article to the title; established bibliographic title retained. Beard’s generalizations are arguments, not independently verified facts.

sources.citation: Anke Voss-Hubbard, “No Documents—No History”: Mary Ritter Beard and the Early History of Women’s Archives, American Archivist 58/1 (Winter 1995), pp. 16–30.

Documents Black women’s marginal authority/funding and organizational disputes alongside achievements. Original letters/reports and Collier-Thomas’s cited 1986 essay are mediated, not independently read. No sole-founder claim or universal claim about women’s archives is adopted.

sources.title: Julie Richter, review of Julia Cherry Spruill, Women’s Life and Work in the Southern Colonies, H-SAWH, March 1999.
sources.citation: Julie Richter, review of Julia Cherry Spruill, Women’s Life and Work in the Southern Colonies, H-SAWH, March 1999.

Book, original preface and Scott introductions remain mediated; friendship with Beard does not establish methodological transmission.

sources.title: Lucy Maynard Salmon, Domestic Service (1897; second edition, Macmillan, 1901), prefaces and chapters I–II.
sources.citation: Lucy Maynard Salmon, Domestic Service (1897; second edition, Macmillan, 1901), prefaces and chapters I–II.

Remaining chapters, original schedules and numerical calculations not audited; historical generalizations remain Salmon’s arguments.

sources.title: Lucy Maynard Salmon, Progress in the Household (Houghton Mifflin, 1906), Apologia, pp. v–xiv.
sources.citation: Lucy Maynard Salmon, Progress in the Household (Houghton Mifflin, 1906), Apologia, pp. v–xiv.

sources.citation: Frances James, “Century of Women’s Struggle,” International Socialist Review 21/1 (Winter 1960), pp. 27–28.

sources.title: Lawrence Stone, “The Worst of Times?” New York Review of Books, 28 September 1978.
sources.citation: Lawrence Stone, “The Worst of Times?” New York Review of Books, 28 September 1978.

verification.note: Complete review of A Distant Mirror read. Stone praises scholarship and narrative communication while criticizing analogy, biographical focus and selection of events over institutional/economic explanation. His uses of Geertz and Veblen are his interventions, not those authors’ direct reviews. His own progress and historical claims remain attributed. This is distinct from his 1979 Past & Present article, whose full text remains unread.

sources.title: Elizabeth Fox-Genovese and Lawrence Stone, “Tuchman and History,” New York Review of Books, 7 December 1978.
sources.citation: Elizabeth Fox-Genovese and Lawrence Stone, “Tuchman and History,” New York Review of Books, 7 December 1978.

verification.note: Complete letter and Stone reply read. Fox-Genovese challenges professional prestige as a criterion and Stone’s crisis/progress assumptions, defending narrative’s treatment of groups and material dislocation while explicitly distinguishing Tuchman from Marxism. Stone defends differences between synthesis and innovative research and qualifies his progress claim. Tuchman is the subject, not an author of this exchange; neither reviewer’s historical claims are independently verified here.

sources.title: John Keegan, The Face of Battle (1976), acknowledgments and opening publisher excerpt; consulted 1983 edition.
sources.citation: John Keegan, The Face of Battle (1976), acknowledgments and opening publisher excerpt; consulted 1983 edition.

Original 1976 date cross-checked with WorldCat 2137107 and Bassford; not confused with this reprint.

Later ideal/absolute-war correction points to work begun in 2016; later trinity-translation note links 2005–2025 work. Neither is assigned to 1994. sources.citation: Hew Strachan, “Michael Howard,” Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the British Academy 20 (2022), pp. 223–244.

Modernization and Cold War emphasis are Strachan’s retrospective assessment, not independent collation. Howard’s Use and Abuse essay remains unread after 403/interstitial failures; do not infer full text from metadata. Post-2000 memoir treats pre-2000 scholarship.

sources.title: Alfred Thayer Mahan, The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783 (1890), preface signed December 1889.
sources.citation: Alfred Thayer Mahan, The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783 (1890), preface signed December 1889.

verification.note: Complete preface and title/edition data read in transcription of twelfth edition, with 1890 and 1918 copyright notices. Supports a proposed integration of maritime power with general history and mutual causal surroundings, and criticism of both land-centered histories and naval chronicles. Historical examples and national comparisons are Mahan’s claims, not independently verified. Main chapters, geographic conditions and later policy reception unread; do not reduce whole book to its preface.

sources.title: Julian Stafford Corbett, Some Principles of Maritime Strategy (1911), introduction, pp. 3–11.
sources.citation: Julian Stafford Corbett, Some Principles of Maritime Strategy (1911), introduction, pp. 3–11.

verification.note: Complete introduction read in Gutenberg transcription with printed-page markers. Theory supplies shared concepts for deliberation and education, not guaranteed execution; maritime strategy coordinates military, naval and political considerations within a British imperial perspective. Later chapters on command of the sea, limited war and operations remain unread. No direct Mahan-to-Corbett transmission inferred from juxtaposition.

sources.title: Antoine-Henri Jomini, The Art of War, G. H. Mendell and W. P. Craighill English translation (1862), translators’ preface and conclusion, pp. 321–325.
sources.citation: Antoine-Henri Jomini, The Art of War, G. H. Mendell and W. P. Craighill English translation (1862), translators’ preface and conclusion, pp. 321–325.

verification.note: Complete translators’ preface (January 1862) and complete conclusion with notes 51–52 read. Jomini distinguishes strategic principles from the uncertainty, morale and judgment of war as a whole; cannot be reduced to mechanical geometry. Translators describe public military education and editorial choices. Remaining chapters and French editions not collated; 1862 is this translation’s date.

sources.title: Clifford J. Rogers, ed., The Military Revolution Debate (1995; consulted Routledge 2018 preview), preface, credits and introduction pp. 1–10; Michael Roberts, opening pp. 13–15.

Other essays are represented through this participant-editor’s account, not independently read. His judgments about Western expansion and theoretical merit remain attributed; no single settled technological explanation is asserted.

sources.title: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Lionel Giles English translation and commentary (1910), preface and chapter III §§1–8.
sources.citation: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Lionel Giles English translation and commentary (1910), preface and chapter III §§1–8.

sources.title: Plutarch, Alexander, opening methodological paragraph; translation credited to John Dryden by the archive.
sources.citation: Plutarch, Alexander, opening methodological paragraph; translation credited to John Dryden by the archive.

sources.title: Samuel Johnson, The Rambler 60 (13 October 1750), transcription following first collected edition (1752), edited by Jack Lynch.
sources.citation: Samuel Johnson, The Rambler 60 (13 October 1750), transcription following first collected edition (1752), edited by Jack Lynch.

sources.title: James Boswell, Life of Johnson (1791), opening selection in Charles Grosvenor Osgood’s abridgment (preface dated 28 June 1917).
sources.citation: James Boswell, Life of Johnson (1791), opening selection in Charles Grosvenor Osgood’s abridgment (preface dated 28 June 1917).

Boswell explicitly names Mason’s Memoirs of Gray and combines documents/conversation with connective narrative. His claims to accuracy/completeness are not independently audited. Osgood omits much commentary, letters and conversation; this is not the full original opening or book. Original 1791 date cross-checked in indexed Google Books title-page metadata, https://books.google.com/books?id=HeINAAAAQAAJ.

sources.title: Thomas Carlyle, On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841), Lecture I, 5 May 1840, opening selection.
sources.citation: Thomas Carlyle, On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841), Lecture I, 5 May 1840, opening selection.

Power’s earlier checked quotation from another Carlyle text does not license reducing all his work to this selection; its original remains uncollated.

sources.title: Lytton Strachey, Eminent Victorians (1918), preface and postscript.
sources.citation: Lytton Strachey, Eminent Victorians (1918), preface and postscript.

verification.note: Complete preface and postscript read. Selection, French eloges models and an explicit debt to Edward Cook’s Nightingale biography support particular claims. Ranke/Gibbon are rhetorical comparisons, not documented personal critics. Incidental Manning opening is not a complete life; Strachey’s claim to impartiality is not an independent audit.

sources.title: Virginia Woolf, “The Art of Biography,” The Atlantic, April 1939.
sources.citation: Virginia Woolf, “The Art of Biography,” The Atlantic, April 1939.

verification.note: Complete sections I–IV read at https://www.literaturecambridge.co.uk/news/Woolf-biography; archive date and sections I–III subsequently checked here. Supports Woolf’s different judgments of Strachey’s Victoria and Elizabeth and Essex, checkable evidence, selection and changing conventions. Her restricted English canon is not a universal history; her praise does not certify all Victoria facts. Cambridge footer’s collection date is unreliable. A Gutenberg Australia transcription repeats typos; Leonard Woolf’s complete editorial note describes posthumous mediation. Original print scan and section IV archive wording uncollated; The New Biography unread.

sources.title: Pierre Bourdieu, “L’illusion biographique,” Actes de la recherche en sciences sociales 62–63 (1986), pp. 69–72, DOI 10.3406/arss.1986.2317.
sources.citation: Pierre Bourdieu, “L’illusion biographique,” Actes de la recherche en sciences sociales 62–63 (1986), pp. 69–72, DOI 10.3406/arss.1986.2317.

sources.title: Giovanni Levi, “Les usages de la biographie,” Annales ESC 44/6 (1989), pp. 1325–1336, translated by Olivier Christin, DOI 10.3406/ahess.1989.283658.
sources.citation: Giovanni Levi, “Les usages de la biographie,” Annales ESC 44/6 (1989), pp. 1325–1336, translated by Olivier Christin, DOI 10.3406/ahess.1989.283658.

Bourdieu disagreement is explicitly one of emphasis; scientific absurdity refers to an individual/society opposition, not all biography. Roche, Venturi and literary works remain mediated. Notes 18/20 identify Chartier’s Italian collection essay, not automatically another French 1989 article.

sources.title: Natalie Zemon Davis, Women on the Margins: Three Seventeenth-Century Lives (1995), consulted third printing/first paperback (1997), selected primary passages.
sources.citation: Natalie Zemon Davis, Women on the Margins: Three Seventeenth-Century Lives (1995), consulted third printing/first paperback (1997), selected primary passages.

verification.note: Public OCR read: title/edition; complete prologue pp. 1–4, conclusion pp. 203–216 and acknowledgments pp. 340–344; selected Glikl opening pp. 6–8 and conclusion notes 1–8/start of 9. Main chapters and remaining notes not fully read. Prologue is an imagined October 1994 dialogue. Certeau and Foucault are explicit resources; editions/translations and collaboration are discussed. Original manuscripts, Glikl editions and clinical work uncollated. Pappenheim was treated by Breuer, not Freud; Davis’s reconstruction of her likely feelings is conjectural. This primary selection supplements, rather than retroactively upgrades, the existing catalogue record.

sources.title: Sigmund Freud, The Origin and Development of Psychoanalysis (1910), Harry W. Chase translation of the September 1909 Clark lectures.
sources.citation: Sigmund Freud, The Origin and Development of Psychoanalysis (1910), Harry W. Chase translation of the September 1909 Clark lectures.

Official Freud Edition metadata confirms lectures in September 1909, original publication 1910: https://www.freudedition.net/en/ueber-psychoanalyse. Introductory Fancher material and later commentary were not completely read. Freud’s clinical outcomes, universal developmental claims and judgments of critics are attributed, not independently validated. Original journal/German witnesses uncollated; contradictory edition dates in notes 15/18 and the Charing Cross etymology are not adopted.

sources.title: Sigmund Freud, Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego (German 1921; James Strachey English translation, 1922), chapters I and IV.

edges.relationship: Founded in 1967 as an institutional home for the emerging social-history programme Peter Stearns sought to establish within the discipline.
edges.evidence_note: Censer’s publisher abstract explicitly connects the founding with Stearns’s effort to establish the field’s disciplinary position. This does not date the origin of all social history or assert that the journal founded the entire field.

edges.relationship: Founded in 1976 by History Workshop activists to advance collaborative, democratic historical work through a journal of socialist historians.
edges.evidence_note: The movement’s institutional account links the 1976 journal to its democratic-history purpose and 1975 manifesto. Feminist commitments developed further; the later subtitle is not projected unchanged onto 1976.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1929 to develop economic and social history across the divisions separating historians and researchers of contemporary societies.
edges.evidence_note: Bloch and Febvre’s first editorial states the interdisciplinary problem motivating the new periodical. The target is the atlas entry that includes this founding project, not a claim that every later Annales approach already existed. This record names the 1929 title rather than assigning its founding date to an unverified modern-title run.

edges.relationship: Hosted Stone’s 1979 Revival of Narrative essay and Hobsbawm’s 1980 comments, providing a concrete entry into the narrative-versus-structural-explanation controversy.
edges.evidence_note: Two publisher records identify the opening essay and named follow-up in adjacent issues. The existing revival entry supplies the qualified debate context. The journal hosted the disagreement; it did not endorse one side, and this exchange did not terminate quantitative history.

edges.relationship: Founded in 1952 through a coalition involving British Marxist historians to advance historical research for readers across periods, regions and specialisms.
edges.evidence_note: The link locates a journal-building initiative within Marxist social history while retaining its generalist purpose and participation beyond Marxism. It does not identify the journal as exclusively Marxist, date the birth of social history to 1952, or replace its separate narrative-debate edge.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1959 following the joint planning of SHOT and its journal, with a programme of bringing disciplines together in the history of technology.
edges.evidence_note: Participant recollections connect the 1958 institutional decision to the first-issue programme. The edge records institutional consolidation and interdisciplinary intent; older histories of technology are not erased and subsequent practice is not inferred from the manifesto.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1975 with a programme connecting historical inquiry and social-scientific analysis through thematic issues, research reports and discussion.
edges.evidence_note: Uses the already reviewed four-author founding foreword. Historical social science is broader than Sonderweg; neither all later journal contents nor every contributor is assigned to a single doctrine. The announced editorial mechanisms are not an audit of implementation.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1916 under Carter G. Woodson and ASNLH to preserve, publish and expand knowledge of Black historical experience and contributions.
edges.evidence_note: Contemporary reception reproduced in volume 1 describes the recovery and documentation programme. This institutional milestone falls within the atlas’s earlier roots; Black historical thought predates the journal. The 1916 original title remains distinct from the 2002 Journal of African American History title.

edges.relationship: Established as a project in 1912 to institutionalize history of science through Sarton’s programme of historical synthesis, set out in the first volume published in 1913.
edges.evidence_note: Preserves the existing 1912 foundation date and explicitly distinguishes 1913 first publication. The initial Sartonian synthesis is one programme within history of science; it does not characterize the entire field or the journal’s later pluralism.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1976 as part of the organizing effort that established an institutional community for environmental history in the United States and produced ASEH in 1977.
edges.evidence_note: The journal and society were planned together to organize an emerging field. This institutional formation is distinct from the later 1990 renaming, 1996 merger and the separate Environment and History launched in 1995. It does not make US institutionalization the origin of all environmental historical thought.

edges.relationship: A sustained interdisciplinary venue for women’s history.
edges.evidence_note: Norberg reviews historical writing across the journal’s first decades, including suffrage research; Smith-Rosenberg’s 1975 essay is an early anchor.
edges.selection_note: Selected for sustained historical contributions within feminist scholarship. This is a women’s-history link, not a claim that every article is historical or that the journal founded the field.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. The endpoint limits this review, not the journal’s later importance.

edges.relationship: A continuing feminist forum publishing women’s history and historical special issues.
edges.evidence_note: Institutional history documents connections with historians; Norberg identifies an enduring historical publishing role.
edges.selection_note: Selected for a sustained historical strand in an interdisciplinary journal, rather than an exclusive disciplinary identity.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A specialist venue for feminist gender history during the 1990s.
edges.evidence_note: Norberg’s retrospective identifies the journal as a dedicated feminist-history outlet from 1989; the earlier institutional-history source supports its launch context.
edges.selection_note: Selected for the gender-history part of the atlas entry. This does not establish equivalent coverage of every racial-formation approach in that broad entry.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A specialist venue connecting women’s history with feminist and gender analysis.
edges.evidence_note: Meade and Rupp trace a continuing forum from its diverse first volume through later methodological debates.
edges.selection_note: Selected for dedicated historical publishing. The retrospective rejects a simple progression from an exclusively white, US-centred beginning; this selection retains that qualification.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A continuing interdisciplinary venue for comparative historical analysis.
edges.evidence_note: The anniversary foreword describes an enduring comparative forum. Wallerstein (1974) and Scott/Tilly (1975) provide dated examples.
edges.selection_note: Selected as a bridge between history and social analysis, with a remit broader than the entry’s state/class comparisons; not an exclusive organ of historical sociology.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A venue for sustained exchanges between anthropological theory and historical inquiry.
edges.evidence_note: Ortner’s 1984 theoretical review and Medick’s 1987 methodological intervention anchor this bounded selection within the journal’s comparative editorial tradition.
edges.selection_note: Selected for the history–anthropology interface, not for all anthropology. The short interval follows the reviewed contributions; wider coverage needs further review.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. The endpoint limits this review, not the journal’s later importance.

edges.relationship: A sustained institutional venue for historical social-science research.
edges.evidence_note: McCants traces continuity of the association journal’s analytical mission across forty years.
edges.selection_note: Selected for the social-science strand within new social history. It does not stand for all forms of social history.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A continuing venue for quantitative work within historical social science.
edges.evidence_note: The retrospective explicitly locates quantitative alongside qualitative methods in the journal’s continuing programme.
edges.selection_note: Selected as an interdisciplinary home for quantitative approaches, without making quantification its sole method or the source of the entire field.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A sustained society journal for economic and social history.
edges.evidence_note: The centenary study follows the Review across several periods rather than relying only on its founding mission.
edges.selection_note: Selected for an enduring disciplinary role; economic history has much earlier intellectual roots.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A continuing venue for social history intertwined with economic inquiry.
edges.evidence_note: The sampled contents document recurring labour, demographic and social-structure research, with changing methods.
edges.selection_note: Selected for the economic/social intersection. Its technical turn does not represent the whole new-social-history movement.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A continuing forum for oral-history method, interpretation and practice.
edges.evidence_note: The retrospective identifies contributions by Haley (1973), Grele (1978), Frisch (1979), feminist methodologists (1987), Portelli (1992) and Yow (1997).
edges.selection_note: Selected for a sustained methodological conversation. The source’s US emphasis limits global representativeness; later articles do not extend this reviewed interval.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. The endpoint limits this review, not the journal’s later importance.

edges.relationship: A sustained venue for quantitative approaches to historical questions.
edges.evidence_note: The editors identify quantification as a continuing contribution across the journal’s five decades.
edges.selection_note: Selected for methodological continuity within a broader interdisciplinary programme; neither all interdisciplinary history nor all its articles are quantitative.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: An interdisciplinary venue for historical population research.
edges.evidence_note: The retrospective highlights population reconstruction and demographic leadership in its publication history.
edges.selection_note: Selected for historical-demographic work. This does not establish equal coverage of every approach to family history in the combined atlas entry.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A sustained institutional and intellectual venue for the history of science.
edges.evidence_note: Holton follows successive generations and changing subject matter through the twentieth century.
edges.selection_note: Selected for continuity across changing programmes. Later pluralism is not assimilated to Sarton’s original vision, and venue publication begins with the 1913 volume.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A dedicated forum consolidating interdisciplinary nationalism studies.
edges.evidence_note: Hutchinson describes an existing field gaining a continuing forum, including early theoretical exchanges and a 1996 symposium.
edges.selection_note: Selected for consolidation and discussion within the atlas’s final decade; not for founding nationalism studies.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A continuing specialist forum for the theory and philosophy of history.
edges.evidence_note: The editor describes successive decades of editorial work and almost annual thematic issues.
edges.selection_note: Selected for sustained disciplinary discussion, wider than the atlas entry’s explanation/objectivity debates. No single philosophical position is attributed to the journal.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A continuing forum for Marxist historical interpretation and debate.
edges.evidence_note: The retrospective follows historical arguments through successive editorial phases, beginning with the British-development theses.
edges.selection_note: Selected for historical contributions within a broader political/theoretical review. British New Left Review is not equated with the atlas’s US New Left entry.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. The endpoint limits this review, not the journal’s later importance.

edges.relationship: A sustained institutional home for new social history.
edges.evidence_note: Censer’s retrospective abstract explicitly describes the journal’s continuing field role and accommodation of methodological changes.
edges.selection_note: Selected on a specific scholarly historical assessment. Full-article details have not been verified; the entry does not claim comprehensive worldwide representation.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A continuing journal associated with the History Workshop movement and its changing practice.
edges.evidence_note: The institutional retrospective and contributions in 1976 and 1995 anchor continuity alongside changes of method and audience.
edges.selection_note: Selected for its direct movement relationship. The journal’s trajectory is not identical to the workshops or to the later digital magazine.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A generalist journal with a sustained role in social-historical research.
edges.evidence_note: The retrospective connects labour, social power and cultural interpretation through articles selected across five decades.
edges.selection_note: Selected for sustained social-historical contributions within a generalist journal. Its authors and methods are broader than one school.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. The endpoint limits this review, not the journal’s later importance.

edges.relationship: A venue for cultural interpretation within historical research.
edges.evidence_note: The editors discuss Davis’s 1981 social-symbolic analysis and Stewart’s 1995 imperial-cultural interpretation and its disputed reception.
edges.selection_note: Selected for a cultural-history strand rather than a separate journal-wide doctrine or founding role.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. The endpoint limits this review, not the journal’s later importance.

edges.relationship: A sustained methodological forum within African history.
edges.evidence_note: Doortmont’s volume survey identifies a continuing niche in source criticism, archival reporting and methodological debate.
edges.selection_note: Selected for method within an already established field. The interval starts with the reported first-volume appearance; the journal did not found African history.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A continuing institutional venue in the development of history of technology.
edges.evidence_note: Participant accounts connect journal editing with the developing scholarly community through Kranzberg’s editorship.
edges.selection_note: Selected for a documented institutional role; this interval ends at the reviewed editorial handover, not the end of the journal’s importance.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. The endpoint limits this review, not the journal’s later importance.

edges.relationship: An institutional forum for world-history research during the 1990s.
edges.evidence_note: The association’s retrospective explicitly identifies a continuing central role under Bentley, who edited it from 1990.
edges.selection_note: Selected for world-history community consolidation, not for founding all global or connected history. Evidence is a scoped indexed extract; full tribute remains unread.

temporal_scope.note: Selected evidentiary interval; neither the field’s lifespan nor a publication start/cessation claim. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.debate_name: Bloor–Latour exchange on symmetry and the sociology of scientific knowledge
edges.relationship: Published Bloor’s Anti-Latour and Latour’s reply in volume 30(1), 1999.
edges.evidence_note: Previously read primary passages establish an explicit exchange at pp. 81–112 and 113–129. Hosting implies no endorsement. Bloor’s final rejoinder remains unread.

edges.debate_name: Warwick debate: Anthony D. Smith and Ernest Gellner
edges.relationship: Published the Smith–Gellner exchange on nations and nationalism in 1996.
edges.evidence_note: The discussion occurred in 1995; this edge dates publication. Smith’s qualified ethno-symbolic position and Gellner’s modernism remain distinct, without assigning either to the journal.

edges.relationship: A collective research forum for Italian microhistory.
edges.evidence_note: Raggio reconstructs collaborative editorial practice through issues on family/community (1976), villages (1981), local conflict (1986) and land markets (1987).
edges.selection_note: Selected for the Italian microhistory strand; it does not represent every form of microhistory or German Alltagsgeschichte. The journal predated this programme.

temporal_scope.note: Evidenced selection interval, not a field lifespan or a claim of journal cessation. Later importance is not assessed by this endpoint.

edges.relationship: A society forum for the development of African historical scholarship in Nigeria.
edges.evidence_note: The study follows changing methods and historical contributions across the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s.
edges.selection_note: Selected for the Nigerian scholarly community and African agency. Nigeria increasingly predominates; the study also identifies limited women’s-history coverage.

temporal_scope.note: Evidenced selection interval, not a field lifespan or a claim of journal cessation. Later importance is not assessed by this endpoint.

edges.relationship: A sustained forum for decolonizing accounts of Africa’s past.
edges.evidence_note: The retrospective traces challenges to colonial narratives and methodological change across the reviewed period.
edges.selection_note: Selected for a Nigerian anti-colonial historiographical strand, not all liberation theories or all African scholarship. Nationalist interpretation and economic relevance remain contested.

temporal_scope.note: Evidenced selection interval, not a field lifespan or a claim of journal cessation. Later importance is not assessed by this endpoint.

edges.relationship: An enduring interdisciplinary venue for historical research on Indigenous peoples, especially in the Americas.
edges.evidence_note: The society history and longitudinal abstract establish continuing publication and changing research scope.
edges.selection_note: Selected as an ethnohistorical interlocutor within this broad entry. Publication about Indigenous peoples does not establish Indigenous control of research or endorsement of decolonizing methods.

temporal_scope.note: Evidenced selection interval, not a field lifespan or a claim of journal cessation. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A sustained French venue for labour history and an expanding social history.
edges.evidence_note: Ceamanos traces four decades of institutionalization and changes in questions, communities and methods.
edges.selection_note: Selected for the French labour/social-history community. The predecessor L’Actualité de l’Histoire is not backdated under this title; no exclusive Marxist affiliation is inferred.

temporal_scope.note: Evidenced selection interval, not a field lifespan or a claim of journal cessation. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A continuing institutional and scholarly home for African American history.
edges.evidence_note: Dagbovie traces the journal’s role across successive editorial generations, beyond Woodson’s initial programme.
edges.selection_note: Selected for sustained African American historical scholarship. The original title applies throughout this interval; the 2002 renaming does not truncate the field’s history.

temporal_scope.note: Evidenced selection interval, not a field lifespan or a claim of journal cessation. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: The early journal forum associated with the Annales movement.
edges.evidence_note: Burke’s previously checked generational history supports this early phase; publisher chronology bounds the original title.
edges.selection_note: Selected for the movement’s early journal community. This supplements the founding edge; it does not imply a uniform doctrine or erase antecedents.

temporal_scope.note: Evidenced selection interval, not a field lifespan or a claim of journal cessation. Later importance is not assessed by this endpoint.

edges.relationship: A sustained postwar journal forum for successive Annales approaches.
edges.evidence_note: The generational history, 1988–1989 editorial reconsideration and Conrad’s transition analysis support the postwar interval.
edges.selection_note: Selected across changing programmes, not as one unchanging school. The ESC title ends in 1993; the publication continues.

temporal_scope.note: Evidenced selection interval, not a field lifespan or a claim of journal cessation. Later importance is not assessed by this endpoint.

edges.relationship: A continuing Annales forum for historical inquiry in dialogue with the social sciences.
edges.evidence_note: Conrad studies the 1990s editorial transition and recurring thematic work; publisher chronology identifies the 1994 subtitle change.
edges.selection_note: Selected for the journal community’s continued, self-critical development. Its refusal of doctrinal closure is retained; this is not an extension of Braudel’s programme unchanged.

temporal_scope.note: Evidenced selection interval, not a field lifespan or a claim of journal cessation. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: An established interdisciplinary forum for science and technology studies.
edges.evidence_note: Sismondo’s retrospective identifies an established field role by the late 1970s and editorial continuity through 2002; the 1984 Pinch–Bijker contribution anchors the technology interface.
edges.selection_note: Selected from 1980, after the documented late-1970s consolidation. Evidence includes a limited indexed retrospective; STS is broader than SSK and no exclusive school allegiance is assigned.

temporal_scope.note: Evidenced selection interval, not a field lifespan or a claim of journal cessation. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A specialist forum for historical studies of sexuality during the 1990s.
edges.evidence_note: Nye’s twenty-year retrospective abstract reviews changing questions, periods and methods, particularly women’s sexuality; the opening identifies the 1990 launch.
edges.selection_note: Selected for sexuality history within the combined sexuality/queer entry, not as a journal uniformly committed to queer theory. Full-text review remains a follow-up.

temporal_scope.note: Evidenced selection interval, not a field lifespan or a claim of journal cessation. 2000 is the atlas coverage boundary.

edges.relationship: A continuing professional forum for public history.
edges.evidence_note: Kelley’s initial programme and NCPH’s institutional account establish its continuing UCSB and society role.
edges.selection_note: Selected for the US professional community; institutional continuity supports the interval, without a complete article census or global priority claim.

temporal_scope.note: Reviewed historical role; 2000 is the atlas boundary. A title-phase endpoint is not the end of the field.

edges.relationship: A society forum for social histories of medicine.
edges.evidence_note: The anniversary review places successive pre-2001 articles within the journal’s continuing programme.
edges.selection_note: One important social-history venue within a broader field; the 1988 journal launch does not found medical history.

temporal_scope.note: Reviewed historical role; 2000 is the atlas boundary. A title-phase endpoint is not the end of the field.

edges.relationship: A sustained forum organizing urban historical inquiry.

temporal_scope.note: Reviewed historical role; 2000 is the atlas boundary. A title-phase endpoint is not the end of the field.

edges.relationship: A continuing forum for urban historical research and debate.

sources.note: Reused the atlas’s existing gg_founders_preface check and bielefeld/journal_programme reading. Programme and intended discussion/thematic-issue mechanisms are documented, not an audit of their practical success or entire editorial history. Later reader introduction is not backdated.

These are contemporaneous reception notices reproduced by the journal, not a signed founding editorial. No original-page collation.

sources.title: Feminist Studies, institutional history
sources.note: History page read: organizing discussions from 1969, first publication in 1972, scholarly and political purposes, and early connections with the Berkshire Conference on the History of Women. Retrospective institutional account.

sources.title: Signs, A History of the Journal
sources.note: Institutional history read, including the reproduced 1975 editorial statement on new scholarship about women and its interdisciplinary aims. Not a separate full reading of the original first issue.

sources.title: Anne E. C. McCants, Editor’s Introduction to Volume 40, Issue 1, Social Science History (2016)
sources.note: Publisher text read: 1976 first volume and the founding SSHA constitution printed there, stating a programme of improving historical explanation through selective use of social-science theories and methods.

sources.title: Richard Trainor with Aris Grivokostopoulos, Whatever happened to social history?, Economic History Society centenary project (2026)
sources.note: Society’s historical research post read: first-issue economic-and-social subtitle and Ashley’s 1927 programme. The society’s 1926 establishment is separate from the journal’s 1927 publication start.

sources.title: Oral History Association Newsletter 7(2), June 1973, announcement of the new Oral History Review
sources.note: Read the launch notice: new annual Review combining papers from the 1972 Austin colloquium with contributed articles, distributed to members. This establishes a publication mechanism for the association’s field, not a claim about all later methodological positions.

sources.title: David Henige, On Method: An Apologia and a Plea, History in Africa 1 (1974), 1–7
sources.note: Publisher’s substantial opening extract read, not the entire seven-page article. The first-volume editor explicitly gives the new journal a methodological purpose: critical evaluation of sources and their use. DOI 10.1017/S0361541300005751.

sources.title: Antoinette Burton, Some origins of gender history as a field, Gender History: A Very Short Introduction (2024), chapter 1
sources.note: Publisher abstract read, not the chapter or the 1989 founding editorial. It explicitly identifies the 1989 launch and the journal’s purpose of examining gender’s historical experience, meaning and significance.

sources.title: Robert Rotberg interview with Ed Freedman, Fifty years of the Journal of Interdisciplinary History, MIT Press (2019)
sources.note: Publisher interview with the founding editor read: social-science and innovative historical methods, with a special place for quantification but a programme also encompassing art, climate and other approaches.

sources.title: Gerald Holton, George Sarton, His Isis, and the Aftermath, Isis 100(1) (2009), 79–88
sources.note: Read discussion of Sarton’s founding programme, dated November 1912 and published in volume 1 in 1913, together with the distinction between the initial synthesizing project and later pluralism. DOI 10.1086/597571.

sources.title: Sylvia L. Thrupp, Editorial, Comparative Studies in Society and History 1(1) (1958), 1–4
sources.note: Opening pages 1–3 read: comparative research across history, humanities and social sciences, communication between specialists, and attention to differences as well as recurring problems. DOI 10.1017/S0010417500000037.

sources.title: John Hutchinson, Nations and Nationalism: the first 25 years, Nations and Nationalism 25(1) (2019), 5–15
sources.note: Founding section of the accepted manuscript read, including the reproduced 1995 editorial aims: a research forum consolidating an interdisciplinary scholarly community. Separates ASEN’s earlier formation from the 1995 journal launch. DOI 10.1111/nana.12489.

sources.title: American Society for Environmental History, History of ASEH
sources.note: Institutional history read: joint journal/association organizing effort in 1976, journal launch in 1976 and society formation in 1977. Evidence of field-building, not merely a publisher remit. Earlier intellectual roots and traditions outside the US are not erased.

sources.title: JSTOR, Environmental History: title history
sources.note: User-supplied page and complete-title-history export checked. Family contains overlapping environmental and forest-history branches, not one succession chain. Listed modern-title coverage ends in 2020; page links current issues elsewhere. Coverage endpoints are not cessation dates.

sources.title: Oxford Academic, Environmental History Review: About the Journal
sources.note: Publisher record read: Environmental Review 1976–1989 continues as Environmental History Review 1990–1995, which merges with Forest & Conservation History in 1996 to form Environmental History. The archive’s 2006 endpoint is not cessation.

sources.title: Kathryn Norberg, History in Signs, in Signs at 40: Editorial Commentaries (2015)
sources.note: Norberg’s historical-corpus commentary and Hawkesworth’s early-article discussion read. Topic-model weights are not article counts or importance scores. Norberg’s incidental 1990 date for Journal of Women’s History is not adopted; its own retrospective gives 1989.

sources.title: Feminist Studies: institutional history
sources.note: History page read, including Berkshire Conference links and later editorial organization; paired with Norberg’s retrospective assessment of historical publishing.

sources.title: Teresa A. Meade and Leila J. Rupp, Journal of Women’s History at 25 (2014)
sources.note: Participant retrospective read: first volume in 1989, early international and theoretical work, and subsequent relationship between women’s and gender history. First-volume examples are not misdated to 1990.

sources.title: Comparative Studies in Society and History, Editorial Foreword: CSSH at Fifty (2008), 1–8
sources.note: Read pp. 1–2 on successive editors and the continuing comparative forum. The 2008 article summaries are not evidence of pre-2000 content; dated atlas articles supply earlier anchors.

sources.title: Immanuel Wallerstein, “The Rise and Future Demise of the World Capitalist System: Concepts for Comparative Analysis,” Comparative Studies in Society and History 16.4 (1974), 387–415.
sources.note: Reused atlas source wallerstein_rise_primary. Original check: Read printed 387–400 and 411–415 using OCR; 401–410 unread. Named Braudel, Polanyi, Luxemburg, Frank/Santos and Sweezy resources; direct Rostow and Dobb criticism. The division-of-labor unit permits external arenas. Coerced-labor, agricultural-capitalism and future-system claims are arguments, not consensus. Final page endorses archival and quantitative work. Quoted originals and detailed semiperiphery mechanisms in unread pages not independently checked.

sources.title: Joan W. Scott and Louise A. Tilly, “Women’s Work and the Family in Nineteenth-Century Europe,” Comparative Studies in Society and History 17, no. 1 (1975): 36–64.
sources.note: Reused atlas source scott_tilly_work. Original check: Publisher-hosted primary opening extract and original issue metadata read. Questions assumptions that domestic women were unproductive or that paid work and emancipation formed one linear sequence. Remainder of article and data unread; online 2009 date is not original publication.

sources.title: Sherry B. Ortner, “Theory in Anthropology since the Sixties,” Comparative Studies in Society and History 26.1 (1984), 126–166.
sources.note: Reused atlas source ortner_practice_primary. Original check: Scan transcription of primary 126–128 and beginning 129 read; remaining essay unread. Page 127 calls practice an orientation embracing several theories/methods and explicitly locates the author’s perspective. Publisher metadata at Cambridge confirms January 1984, not 2009 online date. Platform-generated summary ignored; cited genealogies are Ortner’s assessments.

sources.title: Hans Medick, “Missionaries in the Row Boat”? Ethnological Ways of Knowing as a Challenge to Social History, Comparative Studies in Society and History 29(1) (1987): 76–98.
sources.note: Reused atlas source medick_missionaries. Original check: Cambridge primary opening and notes checked at https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/comparative-studies-in-society-and-history/article/abs/missionaries-in-the-row-boat-ethnological-ways-of-knowing-as-a-challenge-to-social-history/3FC3FA5BAC8CA59E26CB341A4A24075D . Introductory note engages Bernard Cohn’s critique of ahistorical anthropology; note 10 documents the working group since 1978 and Medick/Sabean, Interest and Emotion (1984). This substantiates a particular exchange; full article and earlier German version unread.

sources.title: Anne E. C. McCants, Editor’s Introduction to Volume 40, Issue 1 (2016)
sources.note: Read retrospective account of forty years of SSHA’s journal, continuity of analytical commitments and expanding international scope. Includes both qualitative and quantitative methods.

sources.title: Richard Trainor with Aris Grivokostopoulos, Whatever Happened to Social History? (EHS, 2026)
sources.note: Read the society’s century review, based on sampled journal contents and institutional records. Samples cover founding decades, 1960s–1970s and 1987–2005. Current quantitative proportions are not projected backwards.

sources.title: Kathryn Nasstrom, Troy Reeves and Andrew Shaffer, OHA fiftieth-anniversary virtual issue: Editors’ Introduction (2016)
sources.note: Complete five-page retrospective introduction read. Fifteen selected articles span the journal; pre-2000 examples are distinguished from later selections. Editors explicitly acknowledge a US emphasis.

sources.title: Robert Rotberg and Ed Freedman, Fifty Years of the Journal of Interdisciplinary History (MIT Press, 2019)
sources.note: Full interview text read: retrospective examples of inventories, population reconstruction, slave-trade records, climate, arts and other methods. Editors’ assessment is attributed, not an independent ranking.

sources.title: Gerald Holton, George Sarton, His Isis, and the Aftermath (2009), 79–88
sources.note: Read longitudinal discussion of issues from 1913, 1924, 1934, 1944, 1954, 1984 and 1994, and the late-century assessment. The existing 1912 foundation / 1913 first-volume distinction is preserved.

sources.title: John Hutchinson, Nations and Nationalism: the first twenty-five years (2019), 5–15
sources.note: Accepted-manuscript founding and development sections read, including early contributions, the 1996 Miller symposium, ongoing lectures and institutional editorial continuity. Later statistics are not used to rank its 1990s importance.

sources.title: Brian Fay interview on History and Theory (Wesleyan, 2008)
sources.note: Interview read on the journal’s 1960 origin, editorial continuity from 1965, and recurring theory/philosophy theme issues. Self-description as the leading journal is not adopted as a measured ranking.

sources.title: New Left Review, A Brief History, 1960–2010
sources.note: Institutional retrospective sections on changing editorial phases read, including British-history theses, Marxist theory and later historical contributions. Predecessors and the 2000 new series are distinguished.

sources.title: Jack R. Censer, On a Mission: Peter Stearns and the Journal of Social History (2018), 444–456
sources.note: Publisher abstract read, not the full article. It explicitly describes sustained importance, changing methods and Stearns’s continuing defence of social history. Selection is limited to that longitudinal abstract claim.

sources.title: History Workshop, Our History
sources.note: Institutional history section read, distinguishing the movement, the 1976 journal and 2010 digital magazine; acknowledges increasing academic professionalization.

sources.title: Raphael Samuel, “Local History and Oral History,” History Workshop Journal 1(1) (1976): 191–208.
sources.note: Reused atlas source samuel_local_oral. Original check: OUP bibliographic record checked. Full article remains unread: the OUP page offers restricted PDF access and a university reprint download returned 404. Publication documents a specific early journal venue; the separate Davin/Taylor participant account supports the teaching mechanism. No detailed argument is attributed from the title alone.

sources.title: Doreen Massey, Places and Their Pasts, History Workshop Journal 39(1) (1995):182–192.
sources.note: Reused atlas source massey_places_pasts. Original check: Accessible primary OCR across the complete article and notes read at https://www.scribd.com/document/556785500/Massey-1995-Places-and-Their-Past ; numerous missing words marked [Link] and spacing errors prevent claiming complete textual collation. Publisher confirms date, pages and Spatial History section. Supports contested place histories, explicit Gilroy use and criticism of Harvey 303, independently checked here. Her political examples are attributed interpretations; original Gilroy/Wright/Bhabha passages not newly collated. Adjacent Ruskin course advertisement is separate.

sources.title: Past & Present, Celebrating Issue 250: selected articles and editorial commentaries (2021)
sources.note: Read commentaries on Hobsbawm 1952, Finley 1962, Lewin 1979, Davis 1981 and Stewart 1995. Contemporary evaluations are attributed to the retrospective editors; later selections are excluded.

sources.title: Michel R. Doortmont, Making History in Africa: David Henige and the Quest for Method in African History (2011), 7–20
sources.note: Read pp. 7–9 and 14–20: review of 36 volumes, source criticism and archival reports. Retains 1974 volume dating while noting the author’s April 1975 appearance date; no canonical chronology is changed.

sources.title: SHOT, Melvin Kranzberg: participant memorials
sources.note: Read recollections of journal editing, manuscripts, institutional development and the 1981 editorial handover; retrospective participant evidence, not a complete article census.

sources.title: World History Bulletin 28.2 (2012), Jerry Bentley remembrance
sources.note: Search-indexed retrospective passage read: the journal’s central role from its 1990 launch through Bentley’s editorship. Direct PDF now returns 404 and archive endpoint unavailable. No claim to have read the complete tribute.

sources.title: American Society for Environmental History, History: Publications
sources.note: Read institutional account of successive society journals and editors. This supports institutional continuity; title boundaries use the separately accepted publisher/JSTOR review.

sources.title: David Bloor, “Anti-Latour,” Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 30.1 (1999), 81–112.
sources.note: Reused atlas source bloor_anti_latour_primary. Original check: Downloaded original journal PDF. Read introduction 81–82, section-three opening 87–88, agency discussion 91–92, central symmetry paragraph on 102 and conclusion 110–111; additional adjoining passages read without claiming complete intervening pages or full article. Bloor distinguishes beliefs about nature from nature, includes material causes, and rejects equal credibility as the meaning of symmetry. His assessments of Latour and historical examples remain attributed claims. Final rejoinder at 131–136 unread. Additional reading in1.65: complete90 and opening91, including the response to Latour’s Pasteur example. Bloor proposes asking about interpretive resources and contrasts Koch’s response; historical case claims remain his.

sources.title: Bruno Latour, “For David Bloor… and Beyond,” Studies in History and Philosophy of Science 30.1 (1999), 113–129.
sources.note: Reused atlas source latour_bloor_reply_primary. Original check: Original journal PDF from author archive: complete 113–120 and opening 121 read, not remainder. DOI 10.1016/S0039-3681(98)00039-9 matches PubMed; 00038-7 belongs to Bloor. Page 114 and note 2 provide explicit debt and mediation testimony. Earlier CiteSeer, Melissa and legacy-page fetches failed; original located through author catalogue page 15. Claims about opponents and French epistemology remain Latour’s interpretations, not independent verdicts; translation credits are not separately collated.

sources.title: Anthony D. Smith and Ernest Gellner, Warwick debate, 24 October 1995; published in Nations and Nationalism (1996).
sources.note: Reused atlas source warwick_nationalism. Original check: Primary Smith opening read on the LSE resource page; Gellner’s reply at https://www.lse.ac.uk/researchAndExpertise/units/gellner/Warwick2.html consulted for cultural continuity and modern mobility/literate culture. The linked introduction dates the event to 1995, distinct from publication. Smith credits Gellner’s teaching but disputes sufficiency of modernist explanation; neither position is a consensus. Gellner’s provocative primordialist label does not define Smith’s own qualified ethno-symbolic position.

sources.title: Ernest Gellner, reply to Anthony D. Smith in the Warwick debate (published 1996)
sources.note: LSE primary reply consulted, previously read for atlas source warwick_nationalism. Event took place in October 1995; journal publication in 1996 is the venue date.

sources.title: Osvaldo Raggio, Microstoria e microstorie (Treccani, 2013)
sources.note: Read historical account through the microhistory laboratories section, especially the collective issues of 1976–1987. Participant scholarship; later book-series activity is distinguished from journal publication.

sources.title: Oladipupo Olugbodi and Olufunke Adeboye, Decolonization and Functionality of Knowledge in JHSN, 1956–1980 (2025), 19–48
sources.note: Downloaded published PDF; read historical development pp. 25–29 and conclusion pp. 41–43, plus abstract. The authors’ evaluation of practical relevance is attributed. Post-1980 continuity is not inferred; the conclusion records revival in 2005.

sources.title: JSTOR: Journal of the Historical Society of Nigeria
sources.note: Publisher-supplied title, society, 1956 start and ISSN checked. Archive endpoint 2021 is coverage, not cessation.

sources.title: Grace E. Riehm et al., What Is Ethnohistory? A Sixty-Year Retrospective (2019), 146–162
sources.note: University-hosted scholarly abstract read, not the full article. It reports sampled ten-year intervals from 1954 to 2013, North American predominance and expanding regional/methodological scope. No unreported quantitative results adopted.

sources.title: American Society for Ethnohistory: institutional history
sources.note: Read society history: Indian Claims Act research, changing institutional identity and journal publication since 1954. Present membership counts are not historical importance measures.

sources.title: Roberto Ceamanos Llorens, La historia obrera y social contemporánea en Francia a través del estudio de Le Mouvement Social (1960–2000), ACHSC 33 (2006), 311–336
sources.note: Published PDF read: abstract/introduction and conclusions pp. 334–335. Reconstructs the move from organized labour to broader social history. Its developmental judgment about overcoming Marxism is the author’s, not a claim adopted by the atlas.

sources.title: Pero Gaglo Dagbovie, Building upon a Century-Long Tradition of Excellence (2019)
sources.note: Read editorial retrospective, especially founding, segregation-era role and successive editors through 2001. Post-2002 topic percentages and current circulation are excluded from the pre-2000 selection.

sources.title: Annales / Cambridge University Press: Chronology of the journal
sources.note: Publisher’s explicit chronology read: 1929–1938, 1939–1941, 1942–1944, 1945, 1946–1993 and 1994 onward. These are title phases, not six unrelated journal foundations.

sources.title: Persée: Annales collection and title periods
sources.note: Checked post-1938 title identifiers and ESC/HSS boundaries. ESC and HSS share ISSN 0395-2649. The erroneous summary row naming 1929–1937 Mélanges is not adopted; publisher chronology governs. Holdings gaps are not missing publication years.

sources.title: Christoph Conrad, Une tradition d’innovation: Les Annales dans le paysage transnational des revues d’histoire, 1990–2020, Annales 75(3–4), 635–648 (2020 issue, online 2021)
sources.note: Published repository PDF read pp. 635–642, including scope/method, 1988–1994 transition and thematic examples. Exploratory comparison, not a representative global census. Later issue examples are not backdated.

sources.title: Peter Burke: Annales in its wider historical setting
sources.note: Reused scoped atlas check: Selected passages checked on generations, Berr, Pirenne, Simiand, and precedents. Comparative parallels are not automatically lines of transmission.

sources.title: Annales editors, “Histoire et sciences sociales. Un tournant critique?” (1988), “Tentons l’expérience” (1989); Bernard Lepetit, “L’histoire et les modèles” (1988), collected in the journal’s editorial archive.
sources.note: Reused scoped atlas check: Primary 1988 critical-turn text, Annales 43/2:291–293, read, including explicit microhistory/scale discussion; selected opening and closing 1989 passages, 44/6:1317–1323, and selected Lepetit model passages, 43/1:3–4, read. Experiments, evidence, comparison and generalization are discussed without declaring one replacement paradigm. Remaining archive, including the 1996 Lepetit obituary, not reviewed. The later collection date does not extend mapped coverage.

sources.title: Sergio Sismondo, 2012 Changes, part II, Social Studies of Science 42(5), 635–637
sources.note: Search-indexed opening retrospective read from the Citeseer-hosted published PDF: editorial succession and established STS role by the late 1970s. Direct Sage access unavailable and Citeseer download now 404. Complete editorial not read.

sources.title: JSTOR: Social Studies of Science title history
sources.note: Title history checked: Science Studies 1971–1974; Social Studies of Science from 1975. 2022 is archive coverage, not cessation.

sources.title: Trevor J. Pinch and Wiebe E. Bijker, “The Social Construction of Facts and Artefacts,” Social Studies of Science 14 (1984): 399–441.
sources.note: Reused scoped atlas check: Scanned journal pp. 399 and 402 visually inspected: authors explicitly combine SSK and technology research. Abstract names interpretative flexibility, closure and relevant groups; not a full-paper review.

sources.title: Robert Nye, Regard sur vingt ans de travaux: le Journal of the History of Sexuality, Clio 31 (2010), 239–266
sources.note: Read indexed opening of the article PDF and indexed journal abstract in issue abstracts (clio/pdf/9566), also matching author bibliography. Direct OpenEdition blocked by bot check; Cairn returned 403. Full article unread.

sources.title: Bob Weyeneth and John Dichtl, “Update on the Journal,” NCPH, 1 May 2012.
sources.note: Institutional account read: UCSB launch in 1978 and continuing editorial home, university/society/publisher partnership. A participant account of institutional continuity; it is not a quantified content survey or evidence for global representativeness.

sources.title: Robert Kelley, “Public History: Its Origins, Nature, and Prospects,” The Public Historian 1(1) (1978), 16–28.
sources.note: Downloaded scan; read pp. 16–20, including externally posed questions, museums, government, preservation, consultancy and Kelley/Johnson’s 1975 training discussion. Later pages unread. His claims for policy benefits are advocacy, not independent evaluation; this is a US professional formulation, not the origin of all public historical practice.

sources.title: Social History of Medicine editors, “Chairs’ Choices Anniversary Virtual Issue” (2020).
sources.note: Read introduction and dated pre-2001 selections: journal began in 1988 after the Society’s Bulletin; articles span public health, clinical records and medical knowledge through 2000. Editors attribute choices to teaching, reception and personal experience. Later examples are not backdated; a commemorative selection is not a representative content census.

sources.title: Cambridge University Press, Urban History: 50th Anniversary Collection, selected pre-2001 extracts and abstracts.
sources.note: Read extracts of 1974 editorial, Reeder’s 1979 Dyos appreciation and Rodger’s 1992 retrospect; abstract of Lees (1994) and Lilley (2000). Publisher dates distinguish issue years from 2009 digitization. Full articles unread. Supports institutional continuity and varied approaches, not a uniform school or global census.

sources.title: Cambridge: Urban History past titles
sources.note: Publisher lists Urban History Yearbook volumes 1 (1974)–18 (1991); Rodger’s volume 19 (1992) extract confirms the succeeding journal. Digitization dates are not publication origins.
